Furthermore, by evaluating the effect of temporal integration, we show that spatial and temporal aggregation robustly stabilizes these dynamic fluctuations into reliable, individual-specific traits. Finally, employing regularized predictive modeling, we demonstrate that these dynamic modulatory features can provide complementary predictive value beyond conventional static FC, particularly for capturing state-dependent affective traits such as internalizing behavior. Together, this framework unveils a structured, asymmetric, and behaviorally relevant higher-order modulatory architecture.

papers.title: Parietal Structural and Functional Differentiation Associated with Visual Tracking Across Motor Participation Profiles.
papers.authors: Zhang K, Qi M, Jiang L, Yan Q, Wang Y, Bai S, Cao C, Zhang D, Ma S.
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to examine whether structural and resting-state functional measures of parietal subregions differ across predefined motor participation groups with comparable physical activity levels, and whether these neural measures are associated with visual tracking performance. Methods We adopted an a priori motor-cognitive grouping framework and recruited athletes accordingly, using two representative sports as operational exemplars for each profile: (1) externally driven spatial updating and action planning (ESU; basketball and taekwondo), (2) body-environment calibration and rhythmic sensorimotor integration (SCP; skating and running), and 3) internally guided control and sustained attentional precision (IPS; tai chi and shooting). A sedentary control group (CON) with low habitual physical activity was also recruited. In total, 80 college students participated. Physical activity (PA) was assessed using a standardized questionnaire. All participants underwent structural MRI and resting-state fMRI to derive gray matter volume (GMV), fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), degree centrality (DC), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and functional connectivity (FC) within parietal subregions (S1, SPL, AG, and SMG). Supplementary SPL-based FC analyses further examined connectivity with regions of the broader visuospatial and sensorimotor network. Visual tracking was assessed using a multiple object tracking (MOT) task across three difficulty levels. Results PA levels were significantly higher in all athlete groups than in sedentary controls, with no differences among athlete groups. Across structural and resting-state functional measures, the most consistent group differences were selectively concentrated in S1 and SPL, whereas effects involving other parietal regions were less consistent across measures. Specifically, the ESU group exhibited the highest bilateral S1 GMV, the SCP group showed the highest bilateral SPL GMV, and the IPS group demonstrated the highest fALFF in both S1 and SPL. The IPS group also showed the highest ReHo in bilateral SPL. FC differed significantly across several parietal connections, with distinct connectivity patterns across the three athlete groups. MOT accuracy differed significantly across groups at all difficulty levels, with the ESU and IPS groups outperforming the SCP and CON groups overall. Across all participants, multiple S1 and SPL metrics showed modest associations with MOT performance (r = 0.20-0.40). Within athlete subgroups, stronger and task-specific associations were observed, particularly in the SCP and IPS groups (r = 0.50-0.80). Conclusions These findings identify distinct structural and functional patterns predominantly involving S1 and SPL across different motor participation profiles, despite comparable overall physical activity levels among the athlete groups. Such parietal differences are accompanied by difficulty-dependent differences in visual tracking performance and heterogeneous brain-behavior associations. Together, the results highlight S1 and SPL as the parietal regions showing the most consistent differentiation across structural and functional measures in association with distinct motor participation profiles and visual tracking performance, and provide a focused empirical basis for future investigations into the sources of this heterogeneity.

papers.title: Multivariate Prediction of White Matter BOLD Activity and Its Relationship to Marginal Connectivity.
papers.authors: Li M, Ding Z, Gore JC.
papers.abstract: Functional MRI studies have traditionally focused on gray matter, whereas white matter BOLD signals have often been treated as weak or artifactual. However, white matter BOLD fluctuations are robustly detectable and contain reproducible functional information, yet most gray-to-white matter analyses rely on only marginal functional connectivity, which cannot separate pairwise coupling from shared variance among distributed cortical systems. Here, we used a multivariate cortical prediction framework to test whether spontaneous white matter BOLD activity can be predicted from distributed cortical gray matter BOLD activity, and how this predictive structure relates to marginal connectivity. Resting-state fMRI data from 81 Human Connectome Project young adult participants were analyzed using a strict white matter mask with no overlap with cortical predictors. For each white matter voxel, time series from 400 cortical parcels were used to predict white matter BOLD signals with nested leave-one-run-out ridge regression. Cortical BOLD activity modestly but reliably predicted white matter BOLD dynamics, demonstrating consistent cross-validated prediction accuracy across a broad spatial extent of the white matter. Ridge β coefficients strongly recapitulated marginal functional connectivity fingerprints, indicating a shared functional backbone, but their first gradients differed reproducibly. The difference between these gradients defined a β-minus-FC G1 divergence axis that remained stable after broadly controlling for anatomical, signal-related, and spatial factors. At the low end of the axis, enriched in callosal and capsular structures, pairwise gray-to-white matter connectivity was relatively strong, but white matter BOLD fluctuations were predicted less well by distributed cortical BOLD activity than that connectivity would suggest. At the high end, enriched in posterior projection and association pathways, pairwise connectivity was relatively weak, but distributed cortical BOLD activity predicted white matter BOLD signals better than expected. These findings identify a reproducible, tract-organized contrast between marginal connectivity and its covariance-adjusted predictive representation.

papers.title: DA-S<sup>2</sup>RL: Disease-aware shared-specific representation learning for heterogeneous image-EHR Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
papers.authors: Wang W, Shi Y, Cheng J, Liu Y.
papers.journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
papers.abstract: Combining electronic health records (EHR) with medical images is important for improving the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, neuroimages and EHR differ greatly in semantic content and data distribution. Neuroimages mainly reflect brain structure and metabolic abnormalities, while EHR records clinical symptoms and behavioral changes. Directly fusing these heterogeneous modalities may mix shared disease information with modality-specific diagnostic cues, resulting in redundant and ambiguous representations. To address this problem, we propose DA-S2 RL, a disease-aware shared-specific multimodal representation learning framework for AD diagnosis. DA-S2 RL organizes heterogeneous image and EHR features into disease-related shared semantics and modality-specific diagnostic residuals. The core of DA-S2 RL is the shared-specific cross-modal coding (SCC) module. It strengthens cross-modal semantic consistency, suppresses redundant correlations, and enables mutual refinement between shared semantics and diagnostic residuals. Before SCC, image features are integrated into a compact image representation, and EHR features are encoded into the same feature space. Experiments on ADNI and NACC demonstrate that explicitly organizing heterogeneous image-EHR representations into shared disease semantics and modality-specific residuals improves multimodal diagnostic learning under different image-EHR settings.

papers.title: Role and mechanism of ATF6-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress in ITLN-1 against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Xu L, Zhang Z, Zhang C, Liu P, Li P, Wang S, Tian Y, Yang Y, Niu X.
papers.abstract: Aims Intelectin-1 (ITLN-1), a novel adipocytokine, exerts neuroprotective effects against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), yet its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study focused on activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), a key endoplasmic reticulum stress sensor, to explore its role in CIRI-induced neuronal injury and determine whether ITLN-1 mediates neuroprotection through ATF6 regulation. Materials and methods We established an N2a cell hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model and a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model. Using protein molecular docking, situ proximity ligation assay, Western blotting, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and TUNEL staining, we investigated ATF6 activation in neuronal apoptosis and its upstream regulatory mechanisms. Key findings H/R injury markedly induced ATF6 activation in N2a cells, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and promoting apoptosis. ATF6 overexpression further aggravated these effects, confirming its critical pathogenic role in CIRI. Mechanistic analyses revealed that ITLN-1 physically associates with ATF6. Both ITLN-1 overexpression and exogenous recombinant ITLN-1 administration significantly suppressed excessive ATF6 activation, modulated the JNK signaling pathway, improved cell viability, reduced intracellular calcium overload and reactive oxygen species accumulation, and attenuated neuronal apoptosis. In vivo, ITLN-1 ameliorated neurological deficits, reduced neuronal damage, and alleviated demyelination, whereas ITLN-1 knockdown produced opposite effects. Significance Excessive ATF6 activation underlies CIRI-induced neuronal injury. ITLN-1 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting ATF6 and modulating JNK signaling, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and reducing apoptosis. These findings highlight the ITLN-1/ATF6 axis as a promising therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

papers.title: Heterogeneity in Time-Outcome Associations After Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Binational Registry Study.
papers.authors: Lin CJ, Kim YS, Yang CH, Hsieh YC, Park JM, Chen CH, Kang K, Shan Sung P, Lee SJ, Chen YW, Cha JK, Lin KH, Park TH, Tang CW, Lee K, Chu HJ, Lee J, Fu CH, Hong KS, Chou CL, Yu KH, Lin CH, Kim DE, Yen SY, Kim JT, Chen PL, Choi JC, Kwon JH, Shin DI, Sohn SI, Chiou HY, Kim C, Park KY, Kim CK, Lien LM, Heo SH, Lee JT, Chan L, Tang SC, Kim BJ, Chung CP, Jeng JS, Bae HJ, TREAT-AIS and CRCS-K investigators.
papers.journal: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association
papers.abstract: Background Although "time is brain" remains a core principle in acute stroke care, the association between treatment timing and functional outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) varies across patients. Some individuals treated in extended time windows still achieve favorable outcomes, a phenomenon termed the "late window paradox." Differences in stroke pathophysiology across etiologies may contribute to heterogeneity in the time-outcome relationship after EVT. We investigated factors associated with heterogeneity in time-dependent EVT responsiveness, with particular attention to stroke etiology. Methods We analyzed data from two multicenter registries in Korea (CRCS-K) and Taiwan (TREAT-AIS) from January 2019 to April 2023. Patients with anterior circulation acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism (CE) or large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) were included. Multivariable regression and interaction analyses were performed to evaluate the association between onset-to-puncture (OTP) time and 90-day functional outcomes and to identify effect modifiers. Results Among 4,719 patients (mean age 72.0 years; 42.9% women; median NIHSS 15), longer OTP time was associated with lower odds of 90-day functional independence (adjusted OR per hour, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.98; p=0.001). The impact of OTP time varied by stroke characteristics. CE etiology, MCA occlusion, higher NIHSS, and male sex were associated with greater time sensitivity. In CE strokes, each hour of delay reduced the odds of functional independence by 4% (aOR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.94-0.97; p<0.001), whereas no significant association was observed in LAA strokes (P_interaction =0.028). Conclusion The association between EVT timing and functional outcome varies according to stroke etiology and clinical characteristics, highlighting heterogeneity in time-outcome relationships among EVT-treated patients and providing observational insight into outcome variability in extended treatment windows.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer for multimodal EEG-fMRI learning in ADHD diagnosis.
papers.authors: Guo J, Wang M, Guo X.
papers.abstract: Background Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with distributed alterations in large-scale brain systems, making reliable diagnosis from neuroimaging data challenging. EEG-derived and fMRI-derived static functional-connectivity profiles summarize patterns of electrophysiological coupling and hemodynamic covariation, respectively, but their heterogeneous signal mechanisms make direct multimodal alignment difficult. New method We propose a Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer (CM-MCT) for EEG-fMRI based ADHD diagnosis. Instead of imposing direct correspondence between individual connections, CM-MCT treats each Desikan-Killiany 68-region cortical atlas (DK-68) region of interest (ROI) as a connectivity-profile token and learns to recover masked ROI-level connectome information within and across modalities. The model contains modality-specific Transformer encoders, cross-modal masked connectome objectives, and a bidirectional cross-attention fusion module for diagnostic prediction. Cross-fitted mask perturbations are used to characterize ROI-level model dependence, with explicit assessment of associations with nodal strength and perturbation magnitude. Results Experiments using repeated five-by-five stratified evaluation of 210 paired HBN subjects demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 89.7% accuracy (95% confidence interval: 85.7%-93.3%) and 94.3% AUC (95% confidence interval: 91.5%-96.8%). Comparison with existing methods Compared with the evaluated methods under matched splits, preprocessing, validation, and model-selection rules, CM-MCT shows the highest mean performance, although the AUC difference from the strongest baseline does not reach statistical significance after multiplicity correction. Conclusions CM-MCT supports multimodal learning from the complementary network-level information provided by static EEG and fMRI connectivity profiles. Perturbation analysis yields modality-specific ROI sensitivity patterns that are modestly associated with the assessed factors. These heatmaps characterize model dependence without establishing causal involvement or identifying ADHD biomarkers.

papers.title: An adaptive fMRI paradigm of direction-specific, time-critical grip-force transitions.
papers.authors: Lubomierski R, Dzialas V, Zaalouki S, Eimeren TV.
papers.abstract: Rapid transitions between force states, including fast increases and rapid releases, are fundamental to voluntary movement and everyday object interaction. Converging evidence from movement disorders suggests that rapid force reduction can be disproportionately impaired relative to force production, motivating the hypothesis that these transition directions rely on partly distinct control mechanisms. Brain imaging studies suggest direction-sensitive neural contributions, but existing paradigms make it difficult to determine whether differences between force production and force reduction reflect transition direction itself or other task-related differences. Here, we present the YANK task, a new open-source grip-force paradigm that manipulates rapid force production and rapid force reduction within the same visuomotor task. As an initial clinical proof-of-concept, pilot data from a single participant with Parkinson's disease demonstrate within-participant, direction-specific modulation of yank. Trials designed to elicit positive yank produced higher peak scaled positive yank (p <.001), whereas trials designed to elicit negative yank produced more peak scaled negative yank (p <.001). The accompanying neuroimaging data demonstrate that the paradigm can be implemented during fMRI and provide qualitative within-subject proof-of-concept evidence of task-evoked BOLD responses in visuomotor and sensorimotor regions. Together, these findings position the YANK task as a novel, neuroimaging-compatible paradigm for investigating direction-specific rapid grip-force transitions.

papers.title: Reduced Somatomotor Cortical Thickness in Women With PTSD After Childhood Sexual Abuse: A Structural Correlate Distinct From Adult Sexual Dysfunction.
papers.authors: Nkrumah RO, Grießer L, Demirakca T, Brosch K, Zehirlioğlu L, Heim C, Sütterlin M, Ende G, Schmahl C.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is a major risk factor for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and adult sexual dysfunction in women. Although adverse childhood experiences have been linked to altered brain structure, cortical alterations specifically associated with CSA and PTSD in women remain poorly characterized, and their relationship to adult sexual functioning is unknown. Methods Women with CSA and current PTSD (n = 52), women with CSA without current PTSD (n = 32), and control women without CSA or PTSD (n = 48) underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Cortical thickness, surface area, and cortical volume were examined using whole brain vertex wise analyses. Sexual functioning was assessed in a subsample (n = 41). Results Women with CSA and current PTSD showed reduced cortical thickness within a left somatomotor cluster relative to controls (cluster wise p = .017). Anatomical characterization localized the cluster to motor and premotor regions involved in bodily self representation and sensorimotor integration. No group differences were observed in cortical surface area or volume. Women with CSA and PTSD also reported lower sexual functioning, particularly in arousal, lubrication, satisfaction and pain. Cortical thickness within the somatomotor cluster was unrelated to sexual functioning and did not mediate the association between CSA severity and sexual dysfunction. Conclusions These findings suggest that somatomotor cortical alterations represent neurobiological correlates of trauma related psychopathology following CSA in women. The absence of associations with adult sexual functioning suggests that structural alterations within the somatomotor cortex may be distinct from mechanisms contributing to sexual dysfunction.

papers.title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
papers.authors: Zhou D, Mei T, Oldehinkel M, Mennes M, Forde NJ, Dell'Acqua F, Banaschewski T, Ecker C, Holt RJ, Bourgeron T, Charman T, Loth E, Murphy DGM, Zhang Y, Li H, Cong F, Buitelaar JK, Beckmann CF, EU-AIMS LEAP group.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols. To separate biological from site-related variability and test the robustness of these subgroups, we assessed how well their findings replicate in a deeply phenotyped, prospectively collected autism dataset (EU-AIMS LEAP). Methods We included 270 autistic (7.5-30.3 years; 73% male) and 216 non-autistic participants (6.9-31 years; 63.4% male) from LEAP. Regularized canonical correlation analysis (RCCA) was conducted between functional connectivity and three clinical measures (verbal IQ [VIQ], and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 [ADOS-2] social affect [SA] and restricted/repetitive behavior [RRB]). Next, subgroups identified by hierarchical clustering based on canonical variates were characterized by behavior, functional connectivity patterns and gene enrichment analyses. Results Three of four autistic subgroups showed behavioral profiles consistent with the original study. Three subgroups shared stronger thalamocortical connectivity, while all four displayed distinct connectivity involving default mode network (DMN), salience (SN), visual and somatomotor networks. These subgroup-specific connectivity patterns were further linked to autism-associated and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related gene sets. Across preprocessing pipelines, subgroup assignments were partially preserved. Subgroup2 (globally affected behaviors) and Subgroup4 (less social difficulty, but more restricted behavior) retained more consistent behavioral profiles and connectivity alterations, whereas Subgroup1 and Subgroup3 were more sensitive to the precise preprocessing steps. Conclusions These four subgroups showed partly consistent behavioral profiles, connectivity alterations and genetic patterns, extending our understanding of the multi-level heterogeneity of autism.

papers.title: Inactivation of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) in osteoblasts increases post-natal trabecular bone mass and mechanical bone strength.
papers.authors: Dudakovic A, Jerez S, Paradise CR, Galvan ML, Kubrova E, Pichurin O, Deosthale PJ, Stein GS, Thaler R, Plotkin LI, van Wijnen AJ.
papers.abstract: The epigenetic methyltransferases Ezh1 or Ezh2 each interact with two structural proteins (Eed and Suz12) to form Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2). Inhibition of Ezh2 stimulates osteoblast differentiation and bone formation, but Ezh2 conditional knockout (cKO) mice have variable skeletal phenotypes. Ezh1 null mice are phenotypically normal. Here, we show that combined homozygous ablation of both Ezh1 and Ezh2 alleles results in a pronounced bone phenotype, suggesting genetic redundancy between Ezh1 and Ezh2. Transient loss of Eed, Suz12 or Ezh2 by siRNA depletion or treatment with distinct PRC2 inhibitors (A395, EED226 and GSK126) enhances differentiation of MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts (i.e., increased Bglap, Ibsp and mineralization). We compared Ezh2 cKO mice with Ezh1 null (KO) mice, and mice with both Ezh2 cKO and Ezh1 KO alleles (dKO mice) in the presence of the Osterix/Sp7-Cre recombination driver. During active bone development (post-natal 8 weeks), both male and female dKO mice exhibit significantly increased L5 trabecular bone mass, femoral cortical thickness and the relative midshaft bone volume (μCT), as well as bone strength (3-point bending) compared to Ezh1 KO or Ezh2 cKO mice. Suppression of Cre recombination using doxycycline (DOX) for 8 weeks prevents the dKO phenotype, but subsequent DOX removal increases trabecular bone mass in dKO mice by 14 weeks. Conditional Eed ablation (which inactivates PRC2/Ezh1 and PRC2/Ezh2) results in a similar high- bone and increased mechanical strength phenotype in male and female Eed cKO. Our findings identify PRC2 as a suppressor of post-natal bone accrual in Osx/Sp7 lineage cells, and a potential target for strategies to improve bone mass accrual.

papers.title: Neural Response to Monetary and Social Feedback in Childhood: Processing Reward and Loss in Relation to Peer Outcomes and Anxiety Symptoms.
papers.authors: Gu SJ, Redic MM, Kelly D, Tillman R, Gilbert KE.
papers.abstract: Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric conditions in childhood and are associated with social functioning impairment. How youth process rewards may contribute to the development of social impairment in childhood anxiety. Although aberrant reward processing is a well-established mechanism of psychopathology, associations with anxiety remain inconsistent and limited, especially in childhood. This study investigated neural response to monetary and social reward feedback in relation to anxiety and peer functioning in children. Children (N=106; Age=8.12±.68 years) completed the Doors Task and the Island Getaway Task while electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings assessed event-related potentials (ERPs) to wins and losses. Parents completed questionnaires assessing child anxiety, depression, and peer relations. Contrary to pre-registered hypotheses, we found a significant Valence (reward versus loss) by Condition (monetary versus social) interaction. Specifically, children exhibited greater neural response to monetary loss than reward, but showed the opposite pattern in the social condition, with greater neural response to social reward than loss. Higher child- and parent-reported total and generalized anxiety predicted significantly greater neural response to monetary reward, but not monetary loss or social feedback. As hypothesized, anxiety symptoms significantly moderated the association between neural response and peer relations, demonstrating that for highly anxious children, a greater neural response to social loss predicted worse peer relations. Findings demonstrate differences in neural response to monetary and social feedback processing. Moreover, the distinct vulnerability to social rejection might impair peer functioning in anxious children, suggesting that clinical interventions targeting social rejection processing may effectively improve peer outcomes in childhood anxiety.

papers.title: Green-synthesized Nanoparticles as Emerging Antidepressant and Anxiolytic Candidates: A Critical Review of Preclinical Evidence and Translational Prospects.
papers.authors: Murthy MK, Samal D.
papers.journal: Journal of neuroimmune pharmacology : the official journal of the Society on NeuroImmune Pharmacology
papers.abstract: The high incidence of depression and anxiety disorders worldwide, with figures of depression > 300 million and anxiety > 264 million, poses a serious challenge to health and wellness. Treatment is still limited by existing pharmacotherapies with delayed onset, adverse side effects, poor entry into the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and resistance in approximately 30% of patients. Green-synthesized nanoparticles (NPs) obtained via phytochemicals, microorganisms, and biomolecules are a promising sustainable route for neurotherapeutic applications. This critical review explores preclinical studies on the antidepressant and anxiolytic effects of green NPs, discussing their underlying mechanisms, translatability, and safety concerns in the context of the period 2015-2025. A comprehensive literature search on green synthesis, nanoparticles, Depression, Anxiety and Neurobehavioral outcomes was conducted using the Boolean operator in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Evidence suggests that green NPs can facilitate both serotonergic and dopaminergic signal modulation, minimize neuroinflammation, recruit NFκB, activate antioxidant activity via the Nrf2/ HO-1 axis and induce neuroplasticity (Akt/CREB/BDNF axis). Their biogenic characteristics on the surface may enhance BBB transport and biocompatibility and reduce cytotoxicity and environmental persistence. However, there is still inadequate evidence regarding chronic toxicity, biodistribution, synthesis reproducibility, mechanistic validation and clinical evidence. Nano optimization by AI (as well as characterizing nanomaterials in a standardized manner), nanoinformatics and personalized nano-neuropharmacology in the future are required. Green NPs have promising therapeutic potential; however, this has mainly been demonstrated in preclinical studies.

papers.title: Functional connectivity and treatment response in obesity and eating disorders: Current evidence and empirical data.
papers.authors: Miranda-Olivos R, Soriano-Mas C, De la Peña-Arteaga V, Baenas I, Lucas I, Camacho-Barcia L, Sánchez I, Granero R, Gaspar-Perez A, Sánchez-González J, Fernández-Formoso JA, Guerrero-Pérez F, López-Urdiales R, Vilarrasa N, Jiménez-Murcia S, Fernández-Aranda F.
papers.abstract: Alterations in large-scale brain networks have been reported in obesity (OB) and eating disorders (ED), but their relevance to treatment outcomes remains unclear. We reviewed evidence on neurobiological predictors of treatment outcome in ED and OB and present preliminary empirical analyses exploring baseline rsFC differences between individuals with anorexia nervosa (AN), obesity with comorbid ED (OB + ED), and obesity without ED (OB - ED) and healthy controls (HC), and examining whether these connectivity differences are associated with treatment outcome in the clinical groups. A total of 98 women (AN = 27, OB + ED = 25, OB - ED = 21, HC = 25) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). rsFC networks were subsequently identified using probabilistic independent component analysis (ICA), and their associations with treatment outcomes were examined within each clinical group. Both OB groups showed reduced rsFC relative to HC within a thalamic-basal ganglia network, specifically in a cluster located in the left inferior occipital cortex encompassing extrastriate visual regions. Baseline connectivity in this occipital cluster showed a positive, although non-significant, association with treatment outcome in the OB - ED group, whereas no significant associations were observed in AN or OB + ED. Given the non-significant nature of this exploratory association, the observed relationship should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in adequately powered samples. Further work is needed to clarify the role of sensory-integrative networks in treatment response across extreme weight conditions.

papers.title: Serum miR-329-3p as a potential biomarker for ischemic stroke: clinical association and in vitro neuroprotection via PTPN1.
papers.authors: Fang H, Zhou Q, Wang H, Wang L, Li H.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke, a prevalent disorder of the cerebral vasculature, is associated with substantial risks of long-term disability and death. Explore the expression profile, diagnostic and prognostic relevance, and underlying molecular mechanisms of miR-329-3p in ischemic stroke. 126 acute ischemic stroke patients and 92 healthy controls were enrolled. Serum miR-329-3p and PTPN1 mRNA were measured by qRT-PCR. Neurological function was evaluated via NIHSS and 3-month mRS scores. In vitro, OGD/R-induced SH-SY5Y cells were used. Cell proliferation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and PI3K/Akt pathway activity were assessed. The miR-329-3p-PTPN1 interaction was validated, and rescue experiments were performed. miR-329-3p was downregulated in stroke patients, showing good diagnostic efficacy, and negatively correlated with NIHSS and mRS scores. miR-329-3p is significantly associated with the prognosis of patients. In OGD/R cells, miR-329-3p overexpression improved proliferation, reduced apoptosis, alleviated oxidative stress and inflammation, and activated PI3K/Akt. PTPN1 was confirmed as a direct target; its overexpression abolished the neuroprotective effects of miR-329-3p. Serum miR-329-3p is a potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for ischemic stroke and exerts in vitro neuroprotection by targeting PTPN1.

papers.title: Chaihu-Jia-Longgu-Muli Tang ameliorates chronic restraint stress-induced depressive-like behaviors in association with modulation of the gut microbiota-NLRP3 inflammasome-microglia axis.
papers.authors: Wang B, Yang X, Xie Z, Li Z, Yan X, Li Y, Bai M, Xu E.
papers.abstract: Chronic stress-induced neuroinflammation and gut microbiota dysbiosis have been implicated in the pathogenesis of depression. The classic herbal formula Chaihu-Jia-Longgu-Muli Tang (CLM) has been reported to exert antidepressant effects, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate whether CLM ameliorates depressive-like behavior in chronic restraint stress (CRS)-induced mice and to explore its association with the gut microbiota remodeling, NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, and microglia activation. A mouse model of depression was established through exposure to CRS. Depressive-like behaviors were assessed using the sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), and open field test (OFT). Hippocampal neuronal damage was evaluated by HE and Nissl staining. Intestinal barrier integrity was examined by HE staining and immunofluorescence staining for ZO-1 and occludin. Colonic and hippocampal levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines were measured by ELISA. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed by 16 S rRNA gene sequencing. Hippocampal M1 microglial polarization and microglial NLRP3 localization were assessed by Iba-1/CD86 and Iba-1/NLRP3 double immunofluorescence staining, and NLRP3 inflammasome-related protein expression was further evaluated by Western blotting. CLM attenuated CRS-induced depressive-like behaviors and hippocampal neuronal damage, restored gut barrier integrity as indicated by increased ZO-1 and occludin expression and reduced colonic IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β levels, and reshaped the gut microbiota by increasing SCFA-producing Muribaculaceae, Alloprevotella, and Bacteroides and decreasing Dubosiella and Lactobacillus spp. Exploratory Spearman analyses identified several nominal associations between microbial taxa and behavioral or inflammatory variables; however, these associations did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction and should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. CLM-H also reduced hippocampal CD86⁺/Iba-1⁺ cells, decreased NLRP3+ /Iba-1+ co-localization, and reduced NLRP3, caspase-1 p20, and pro-IL-1β expression. CLM-H ameliorates CRS-induced depressive-like behavior and neuronal damage in association with modulation of the gut microbiota composition, NLRP3 inflammasome-related signaling, and microglial activation. These findings support the potential of CLM as a multi-target intervention for depression-related phenotypes, while further causal validation is still required.

papers.title: Gastrodin alleviates acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours rather than cognitive dysfunction by modulating gut microbiota and suppressing inflammation.
papers.authors: Song JL, Wu RC, Sun R, Gao YX, He BQ, Xie YJ, Xie JS, Li XR, Tong FX, Liu Y, Li H, Wang ZQ.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients frequently suffer from emotional disturbances, predominantly anxiety- and depression-like symptoms, and may also have cognitive dysfunction, but the mechanisms remain unclear, and no therapies targeting the gut or nervous system exist. Gastrodin (GAS), the primary active component of Gastrodia elata, has anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Whether GAS can alleviate acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours or cognitive dysfunction via the gut-brain axis is unknown. Using a 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, we administered GAS (240 mg/kg) by gavage for 7 days. The open field, elevated plus maze, tail suspension, and forced swimming tests showed that GAS improved behavioural abnormalities (including anxiety- and depression-like behaviours); it also restored colon length and reduced colonic histopathological injury. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that GAS reshaped the gut microbiota, increasing Sporosarcina and Nitrospirae while decreasing Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae. Untargeted metabolomics indicated that GAS shifted the metabolic profile away from DSS and normalized taurine levels, and KEGG pathway analysis suggested that GAS may partially ameliorate DSS-induced metabolic disturbances by downregulating virulence-related pathways and upregulating energy metabolic pathways such as the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation relative to DSS. Western blot confirmed that GAS restored the tight junction protein Occludin and decreased TNF-α. Quantitative proteomics demonstrated that GAS reversed the aberrant expression of 191 colonic proteins. These results demonstrate correlative associations between GAS treatment and the alleviation of acute colitis and behavioural abnormalities, alongside concurrent changes in gut microbiota composition, metabolite profiles, and intestinal barrier proteins. Whether these associations reflect a causal gut-brain axis mechanism requires direct experimental validation. GAS modulates the microbiota, partially restores metabolism, repairs the gut barrier, and suppresses local inflammation, suggesting a potential gut-brain axis mechanism. These findings position GAS as a promising candidate for further mechanistic and translational investigation in IBD-associated behavioural comorbidities.

papers.title: Cortical Cholinergic Pathway Degeneration Reflects Cognitive Impairment and Dementia in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.authors: Slater NM, Myall DJ, Shoorangiz R, Meissner WG, Kirk IJ, Keenan RJ, Lee RM, Horne KL, MacAskill MR, Le Heron CJ, Pitcher TL, Anderson TJ, Melzer TR, Dalrymple-Alford JC.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Background Cognitive impairment is a prevalent and debilitating feature of Parkinson's disease (PD). Increasing evidence from postmortem and in vivo positron emission tomography imaging studies supports cholinergic dysfunction in PD. There is, however, little evidence regarding the influence of the structural integrity of cortical cholinergic pathways that emanate from the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM). Objectives To investigate the association between cognition and the structural integrity of medial and lateral cortical cholinergic projection pathways in PD. Methods Neuropsychological assessment, T1 imaging, and high angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) were acquired from 108 participants with PD (41 female, mean age 71.3 years) and 41 control participants (22 female, mean age 70.6 years). Streamlines representing three cortical cholinergic pathways (one medial and two lateral) from the NBM were extracted from anatomically constrained tractography. Structural integrity was compared across controls and cognitive subgroups (PD with normal cognition [PD-N], with mild cognitive impairment [PD-MCI], and with dementia [PDD]) and using a continuous global measure of cognition. Results In PD, we found evidence that lower cognitive performance was associated with increased mean diffusivity across all pathways, especially the perisylvian component of the lateral pathway. In those individuals with dementia, increased free water fraction and decreased fractional anisotropy and fiber density and cross-section was detected across all pathways. Conclusions Degeneration of the cortical cholinergic system is associated with cognitive decline in PD. Future work should determine whether pathway degeneration predicts future cognitive decline and dementia. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
papers.authors: Peng S, Wang L, Ouyang J, Liu R.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Progressive Hippocampal Volume Reduction Beyond Normal Aging in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Longitudinal MRI Study.
papers.authors: Sone D, Shigemoto Y, Kagaya R, Kimura Y, Matsuda H, Sato N.
papers.abstract: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that epilepsy may show progressive brain structural changes over time. However, longitudinal hippocampal volume changes in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) have not been adequately compared with those observed in normal aging. In this study, we enrolled 46 patients with unilateral TLE and 25 healthy controls with longitudinal structural MRI scans using the same scanner. Hippocampal volumes were quantified using the Hipposeg software, and the annual percentage volume reduction relative to baseline (%Reduction/year) was calculated for each hippocampus. Compared to healthy hippocampi (median -0.37% per year, IQR = 3.97), both ipsilateral (median -1.04% per year, IQR = 3.65) and contralateral (median -1.08% per year, IQR = 3.17) hippocampi in TLE showed significantly greater volume reduction over time (both p < 0.05). Furthermore, annual ipsilateral hippocampal volume reduction was significantly correlated with disease duration (Spearman's rs = 0.366, FDR-corrected p = 0.036), suggesting that hippocampal atrophy progresses more rapidly during the early stage after epilepsy onset. These findings indicate that hippocampal volume loss in TLE exceeds that expected from normal aging and provide further evidence supporting progressive structural alterations during the course of the disease. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Temporal lobe epilepsy may cause progressive changes in the brain beyond those expected from normal aging. Using repeated MRI scans, we found that the hippocampus showed greater volume loss over time in people with temporal lobe epilepsy than in healthy individuals. This volume loss occurred bilaterally and appeared to be greater during the earlier stages of the disease. These results provide further evidence supporting progressive structural brain changes in TLE and contribute to a better understanding of disease progression and abnormal brain aging in epilepsy.

papers.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Xu Q, Li K, Zhang Q, Li Y, Li J, Liao W, Li J, Chen Y, Yao X, Yang F, Ji X, Lu G, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Objective This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM). Methods We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps. Results Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches. Significance In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

papers.title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
papers.authors: Philippe V, Tombroff L, Akbarian F, De Witte S, Trotta N, Van Schependom J, Engelborghs S, Bier J, Strauss M, De Tiège X, Wens V.
papers.abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease.

papers.title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
papers.authors: Gutiérrez-Jiménez E, Wied B, Lindhardt TB, Mikkelsen SH, Knopper RW, Skoven CS, Christensen OB, Dashkovskyi V, Mrotek F, Rasmussen PM, Andresen MH, Krmpot A, Khatib ME, Vinogradov S, Sakadžić S, Jensen MF, Pedroza-Pacheco I, Postnov D, Lin L, Just J, Hansen B, Østergaard L.
papers.abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

papers.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
papers.authors: Carreño-Muñoz MI, Chehrazi P, Ciancone Chama A, Knoth I, Fernandes do Nascimento AS, Campbell BF, Csicsvari J, Chattopadhyaya B, Lippé S, Di Cristo G.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

papers.title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
papers.authors: Lan Z, Onoe H, Tsukiyama T, Iwatani C, Chen C, Okita K, Ishizuka K, Endo R, Nakai R, Imamura K, Hikishima K, Tsuchiya H, Nakaya M, Fang Y, Kobayashi A, Shinto Y, Yamaguchi R, Matsunaga M, Oe K, Omori K, Ozeki Y, Tomoda T, Miura K, Urayama S, Oishi N, Okada T, Tanaka M, Inoue H, Takahashi J, Sawa A, Isa T.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

papers.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Yenikapati MS, Deshpande S, Desai SP, Santine DD, Roghani AK.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human.

papers.title: 5-Aminolevulinic Acid-Guided Glioma Resection During Awake Craniotomy: Systematic Review of Functional Safety and Oncologic Benefit
papers.authors: Mofatteh M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Maximal safe resection remains the cornerstone of glioma surgery, particularly in eloquent regions where oncologic gain must be balanced against functional preservation. While 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) fluorescence-guided surgery improves extent of resection in high-grade gliomas under general anesthesia, its role during awake craniotomy (AC) remains underdeveloped. We aimed to evaluate the oncologic and functional outcomes of 5-ALA-guided tumor resection during AC. Methods PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting original data on AC using 5‑ALA following PRISMA guidelines. Study quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Results Across 10 studies comprising 108 patients, fluorescence positivity was 76.5% in high‑grade gliomas and 17.5% in low‑grade gliomas. Gross‑total resection was achieved in 57.4% overall, reaching 66.7% in the largest cohort. Transient aphasia occurred in 25.9% of patients, while permanent aphasia and persistent hemiparesis were observed in 8.3% and 14.8%, respectively. In multiple studies, resection was intentionally halted despite persistent fluorescence when functional mapping identified an eloquent cortex, underscoring that mapping remained the decisive determinant of surgical boundaries. No study reported conversion to general anesthesia. Conclusions 5‑ALA-guided resection during AC appears feasible, functionally safe, and clinically useful, particularly for high-grade gliomas in eloquent regions. Across the available literature, 5-ALA consistently enhances intraoperative tumor visualization, supports identification of residual fluorescent disease, and integrates well with cortical and subcortical mapping without clear evidence of increased permanent neurological morbidity. Although functional mapping remains the decisive determinant of the final resection boundary, the available evidence supports 5-ALA as a valuable complementary adjunct in onco-functional glioma surgery. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized volumetric and survival endpoints are now needed to refine patient selection and quantify its added benefit.

papers.title: Depressive status modulates hippocampal-cortical dynamics during acute nicotine use
papers.authors: Ryu J, Torres L, Ward M, Topalovic U, Martelo MV, Zubair H, Bari A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Nicotine use disorder shows heterogeneity in treatment response, potentially reflecting differences in underlying neural circuitry, particularly in the presence of depression. We examined real-time neural dynamics during nicotine inhalation in two chronic users - one with depression and one without - using simultaneous hippocampal recordings from responsive neurostimulation (RNS) electrodes and scalp EEG. Oscillatory activity and hippocampal-cortical connectivity were analyzed in relation to mood and craving. Oscillatory activity tracked mood in the non-depressed individual but was attenuated or reversed in the depressed individual, suggesting reduced reward-related neural responsiveness. In contrast, both participants showed reduced alpha hippocampal-cortical connectivity following nicotine use, suggesting a shift from reward-seeking to reward and relief processing. These findings support a network-based framework of nicotine-driven neural dynamics and provide preliminary evidence that depressive status may modulate these processes. Although limited to two cases, this work highlights the potential for identifying neurophysiological subtypes of nicotine users and informs future efforts toward personalized treatment approaches.

papers.title: Behavioral and neural modulation effects of transcranial pulse stimulation of the dorsal cingulate cortex and anterior insula cortex in healthy adults: A prospective, randomized, sham-controlled trial
papers.authors: Qin PP, Chak IK, Lin TTZ, Jin M, Kan RL, Zhang BB, Xia AW, Wang SX, Lam V, Lin J, Yuan T, Chau BK, Bergmann TO, Padberg F, Kranz GS.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS) is a novel non-invasive brain stimulation technique with promising neuromodulation effects. No studies have examined target-specific deep brain TPS. This study assessed whether TPS of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and anterior insular cortex (AIC) modulates risk-taking behavior and brain circuits in healthy participants. Methods Seventy-five healthy adults were randomized in this subjects/raters-blind study to 10 sessions of active dACC-TPS, active AIC-TPS, or sham-TPS over 2 weeks. Balloon Analog Risk Task (BART), a psychological measure of risk-taking behavior with high ecological validity, was assessed at baseline, midpoint (Week 1), and endpoint (Week 2). Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) was measured at baseline and endpoint. Results Most participants experienced mild-to-moderate adverse events, primarily tingling and pain at the stimulation site. The overall dropout rate was 4%. Significant interactions emerged in the BART: dACC-TPS significantly decreased average pumps (average pumps on all trials), AIC-TPS significantly increased adjusted average pumps (average pumps on trials where the balloon did not burst), and sham showed no change. Target-specific rsFC changes were observed following active stimulation versus sham: dACC-TPS predominantly enhanced rsFC of dACC and AIC with precuneus, parietal, and occipital cortices, whereas AIC-TPS decreased rsFC of AIC with striatum. Conclusions Ten sessions of dACC-TPS and AIC-TPS are feasible and safe. dACC-TPS decreased risk-taking behavior, whereas AIC-TPS increased it. Bidirectional, target-specific rsFC changes were observed. Future large-scale studies with online neuroimaging or neurophysiological investigations are needed to confirm short- and long-term efficacy and clarify underlying mechanisms. Trial Registration ClinicalTrial.gov Identifier NCT06635161.

papers.title: Directional coordination along the cortical hierarchy is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia
papers.authors: Wiafe S, Soleimani N, Fu Z, Miller R, Calhoun V.
papers.abstract: Abstract Schizophrenia has long been framed as a disorder of the cortical hierarchy. Yet, the hierarchy has been studied almost entirely as fixed anatomy, leaving its moment-to-moment expression in ongoing brain activity unmeasured. By retaining the signed lead-lag geometry that conventional connectivity measures discard, complex-valued phase synchrony resolved a dynamic directional axis of coordination in which regions reversed their lead-lag relationship over time as the brain transitioned among feedback, feedforward, and integrative regimes. The three regimes replicated across seven datasets from four independent cohorts and aligned region by region with an independently defined cortical hierarchy. Neighboring organizing principles, including propagating waves, arousal, and the principal gradient, were insufficient to explain regime identity. Within the same subjects, GABAergic sedation shifted coordination toward feedback and motor imagery toward feedforward, demonstrating that the axis reflects a manipulable property of brain dynamics rather than a statistical partition. In schizophrenia (151 patients, 160 controls), the axis reorganized selectively: feedback coordination became less persistent, integrative coordination more persistent, feedforward comparatively spared, and trajectories less diverse. These effects replicated in an independent clinical cohort (68 patients, 89 controls). The reorganization tracked positive symptom severity, and its relationship to cognition reversed relative to controls: faster convergence to equilibrium was associated with better cognition in controls and worse cognition in patients. Directional coordination therefore identifies a reproducible and controllable dynamic expression of the cortical hierarchy that is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia and linked to both symptoms and cognitive function.

papers.title: Mapping post-translational modifications across amyloid-β deposits in Alzheimer’s disease: A neuropathologic survey with in vitro functional analysis of nitration
papers.authors: Basile S, Schipper F, Zimbone S, Vermorgen SM, Bellia F, Parisi C, Sortino S, Walter J, Giuffrida ML, Rozemuller AJ, Hoozemans JJ, Copani A, Boon BD.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) includes distinct types of plaques and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Post-translational modifications (PTMs) may define Aβ deposit-specific signatures. Among them, nitration of tyrosine-10 (3′-nitrotyrosine, 3-NT) links oxidative stress to Aβ modification and microglial activation, but its spatial distribution across deposit types and impact on aggregation dynamics remain unclear. Methods Parietal cortex tissue from AD and CAA cases (n = 19) and controls (n = 9) was analyzed by multiplex immunofluorescence for Aβ species (Aβaa1-8, AβN3pE, pSer8-Aβ), 3-NT, thioflavin-S, and CD68. Distinct deposits, including diffuse plaques (n = 70) classic cored plaques (n = 70), coarse-grained plaques (n = 40), capillary CAA (capCAA; n = 80), larger vessel CAA (n = 80), and leptomeningeal CAA (n = 25) were annotated, together with gray matter regions from control tissue lacking Aβ pathology (n = 90). In vitro assays evaluated how 3-NT affects Aβ aggregation kinetics, microglial morphology, and neuronal viability. Results We observed Aβ deposit-specific PTM signatures. Classic cored and coarse-grained plaques contained increased pyroglutamylated (Aβ N3pE ) and phosphorylated (pSer8-Aβ) species compared to diffuse plaques. In contrast, 3-NT showed a distinct vascular predilection, with the highest relative burden in larger vessel and leptomeningeal CAA. 3-NT colocalized with β-sheet–rich thioflavin-S-positive fibrils and areas of CD68-positive microglia. In vitro, nitration slowed oligomer-to-fibril conversion but accelerated the growth of pre-formed fibrils and sustained microglial activation without increasing neuronal toxicity. Conclusions Distinct PTMs delineate the compartment-specific architectural signatures of Aβ deposits. Whereas AβN3pE and pSer8-Aβ broadly label parenchymal plaques, 3-NT shows a vascular predilection, particularly in leptomeningeal CAA. This compartmentalized pattern identifies nitration as a candidate marker of vascular Aβ pathology and a possible risk indicator for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) during anti-Aβ immunotherapy.

papers.title: Unintentional Weight Loss Preceding Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Report and Review of Possible Mechanisms
papers.authors: Mohammadi HR, Mohammadifard MJ, Abotorabi-Zarchi M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Unintentional weight loss is not a recognized presenting feature of multiple sclerosis (MS) and is more commonly associated with malignancy, chronic infection, endocrine disorders, gastrointestinal disease, or systemic inflammatory conditions. We report an unusual case in which marked involuntary weight loss preceded the diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS). Case Presentation: A 37-year-old man presented with acute gait impairment and right lower-extremity weakness. Retrospective history revealed gradual unintentional weight loss from approximately 97 kg to 68 kg over nearly two years despite preserved appetite and the absence of gastrointestinal, infectious, endocrine, or constitutional symptoms. Extensive investigations, including laboratory testing, infectious screening, tumor markers, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, abdominal ultrasonography, and chest imaging, failed to identify an alternative cause. Neurological examination demonstrated right lower-extremity weakness, generalized hyperreflexia, bilateral pyramidal signs, and an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of 4.0. Brain and cervical spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple typical demyelinating lesions fulfilling the 2017 McDonald criteria for MS. The patient received intravenous methylprednisolone followed by rituximab (1000 mg every 6 months). During four years of follow-up, the EDSS score improved from 4.0 to 1.0, MRI studies remained stable, and body weight gradually returned to two years before the start of the disease. Conclusion This case describes marked, unexplained weight loss preceding the diagnosis of RRMS, which resolved after treatment initiation and disease stabilization. Although causality cannot be established, the temporal association suggests that clinically significant weight loss may represent an uncommon and underrecognized manifestation of active MS. Further studies are needed to clarify the frequency and mechanisms of weight changes in MS.

papers.title: Remote Ischemic Conditioning and Cerebral Oxygen Saturation: The Cerebral Oxygenation-Conditioning Response (Co-CoRe) Framework.
papers.authors: Couse T, Bruno A, Marin T.
papers.abstract: Remote ischemic conditioning (RIC) is a promising noninvasive intervention that may enhance endogenous cerebroprotective mechanisms following ischemic stroke. Although clinical studies suggest potential benefits, the physiological mechanisms underlying RIC remain incompletely understood, particularly whether RIC-associated hemodynamic changes are accompanied by changes in cerebral tissue oxygenation. No conceptual framework currently integrates these relationships to guide future research. The purpose of this paper is to present the Cerebral Oxygenation-Conditioning Response (CO-CoRe) Framework, a mechanistic conceptual framework describing the hypothesized relationships among RIC, compensatory cerebral blood flow, cerebroprotection, and cerebral regional oxygen saturation (CrSO₂) following ischemic stroke. The CO-CoRe Framework integrates evidence-supported relationships among RIC, compensatory cerebral blood flow, and cerebroprotection with a hypothesized relationship between RIC and CrSO2 , providing a mechanistic foundation for examining cerebral tissue oxygenation following ischemic stroke. By synthesizing current evidence on ischemic conditioning, cerebrovascular physiology, and cerebral tissue oxygenation, the CO-CoRe Framework generates testable hypotheses and provides a foundation for future research evaluating CrSO₂, measured using near-infrared spectroscopy, as a physiological response to RIC. Ultimately, the framework may advance understanding of RIC-associated cerebroprotection and inform physiologic monitoring strategies in ischemic stroke.

papers.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges.
papers.authors: Deng J, Shao Y, Jiang L, Wu B, Roberts N, Wang Q, Jia Z.
papers.abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefore not be viewed as uniformly additive or synergistic, but as a state-dependent process shaped by medication class, stimulation protocol and timing, cortical excitability, metaplasticity, and individual neurobiological context. This review integrates mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence and discusses how biomarker-, state-, and symptom-informed targeting, optimized treatment sequencing, and pragmatic implementation strategies could improve the precision and accessibility of combined treatment for depression.

papers.title: Altered intrinsic neural timescales in cocaine use disorder.
papers.authors: Tang X, Di T, Sheng J, Sun Y, Zhang M, Luo W.
papers.abstract: Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is a major public health challenge, but its neurodynamic and molecular mechanisms remain unclear despite evidence of structural and functional abnormalities. This study mapped whole-brain intrinsic neural timescales (INTs), reflecting temporal integration of neural activity, using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging in 44 CUD patients and 44 healthy controls. In the primary analysis with global signal regression (GSR), CUD showed increased network-level INTs in the visual, somatomotor, dorsal attention, frontoparietal control, and default mode networks compared with HC. In the sensitivity analysis without GSR, the visual and somatomotor network differences remained significant. Within the CUD group, regional and network-level INT variation was associated with individual differences in flanker-task performance, despite the absence of significant between-group differences in behavioral performance. Notably, the spatial distribution of INT differences was associated with normative maps of gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptors and the noradrenaline transporter. Atlas-based models showed modest discrimination and limited validation, while outcome-informed cluster-based models yielded higher but exploratory estimates. Importantly, classification performance in a mixed-source evaluation sample was close to chance, indicating limited generalizability. Together, these findings reveal widespread alterations in intrinsic neural timescales in CUD and highlight the relevance of spatiotemporal brain organization to addiction.

papers.title: Zona incerta circuits in cognition and the regulation of sleep and wakefulness: potential relevance to Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Kang J, Li Y, Yan W.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline and prominent disturbances in sleep and wakefulness, reflecting dysfunction across distributed neural networks. The zona incerta (ZI) is a highly heterogeneous subthalamic structure whose organization is defined by spatial location, molecular identity, neurochemical phenotype, and circuit connectivity. Recent studies demonstrate that distinct ZI cell populations and projections contribute to memory processing, novelty seeking, cortical plasticity, sleep promotion, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, transitions to wakefulness, and sleep homeostasis. Together, these findings suggest that the ZI is better viewed as a state-dependent subcortical regulatory platform than as a unitary cognitive or sleep center. Emerging pathological evidence further raises the possibility that the ZI may be relevant to neurodegeneration. Amyloid-β deposition has been reported in the ZI of 5xFAD transgenic mice, while experimental tau propagation, human tauopathies other than AD, and studies of other neurodegenerative disorders indicate potential cellular and circuit vulnerability. However, direct evidence from human AD remains lacking, and no study has established a causal pathway from AD pathology to selective ZI dysfunction and subsequent cognitive or sleep impairment. We therefore propose two testable models in which the ZI contributes to AD phenotypes either as a shared circuit node or through parallel, selectively vulnerable functional modules.

papers.title: Adaptive local region super-resolution for high-field MRI: A diffusion-based approach with structural and frequency-domain constraints.
papers.authors: Zuo J, Yang H, Tang Y, Wang X, Zhong K, Peng X, Luo J.
papers.abstract: High-field MRI offers superior SNR but is constrained by the trade-off between spatial resolution and acquisition time. Existing global deep learning super-resolution (SR) methods often incur computational overhead by ignoring regional image content. This motivates an adaptive local SR strategy to optimize efficiency and detail preservation. To address this, we developed a local SR method that adaptively allocates computational resources to information-rich regions. The proposed framework regularized an entropy-based local region processing strategy with a diffusion model fortified by frequency-domain and structural constraints. We retrospectively evaluated our method on two diverse datasets: a proprietary 7.0 T dental MRI dataset (25 T2-weighted DESS sequences from 10 beagle dogs) and a public 5.0 T brain MRI dataset (Diff5T, 50 diffusion-weighted sequences). Image quality was quantified using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FID. On the 7.0 T dental test dataset (2 subjects), our method achieved a PSNR of 27.31 [26.83, 27.79] dB and the lowest LPIPS of 0.19 [0.18, 0.20]. On the 5.0 T brain test dataset (10 subjects), the method achieved a PSNR of 27.15 ± 0.10 dB, an LPIPS of 0.14 ± 0.00 and an FID of 54.01, with lower perceptual metrics than the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies indicated that the proposed frequency-domain and structural constraints reduced LPIPS and FID, with trade-offs in PSNR and SSIM. In conclusion, the evaluated framework showed improvements in perceptual metrics by integrating targeted local processing with frequency-domain and structural regularization, accompanied by a trade-off in pixel-wise fidelity metrics, supporting the technical feasibility of addressing the resolution-time trade-off in high-field MRI. Future work will focus on expanding the dataset and evaluating the framework in human dental cohorts to address anatomical differences between the current canine model and human dental anatomy.

papers.title: Ginsenoside compound K inhibits complement C1qA/C3-CR3-mediated microglial synaptic pruning and neuronal pyroptosis.
papers.authors: Zhao X, Liu J, Wang S, Chen N, Zhao J, Zhang Y, Li J, Li H, Li N, Yang Q.
papers.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevance Ginseng (Panax ginseng C.A. Meyer), a classic traditional Chinese medicine, has long been used for "calming the mind and enhancing intelligence" to combat cognitive decline. Its major metabolite, ginsenoside compound K (CK), exerts neuroprotection, but the molecular mechanisms against Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. Aim of the study This study investigated the molecular mechanism by which CK attenuates microglial aberrant synaptic phagocytosis and neuronal pyroptosis via inhibiting the complement C1qA cascade. Materials and methods APP/PS1 mice were used as AD models and treated with CK (20 or 40 mg/kg/d) or memantine (MH, 3 mg/kg/d) by gavage once daily for 14 weeks. Morris water maze and open field tests were used to assess cognitive function and anxiety-like behavior, respectively. HE, Nissl and Golgi staining detected neuronal damage and synaptic integrity. Immunofluorescence and ELISA measured microglial polarization, activation and synaptic phagocytosis. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations analyzed the CK-C1qA interaction. Western blot, immunofluorescence and ELISA detected complement components (C1qA, C3, CR3) and pyroptosis-related proteins (NF-κB, NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, GSDMD-N, IL-18). In vitro cellular experiments, including BV2 cell monoculture and BV2-HT22 transwell co-culture systems, were further performed to validate the causal role of C1qA. Results CK improved cognitive and anxiety behaviors in APP/PS1 mice, attenuated hippocampal neuronal damage, increased Nissl-positive neurons, restored dendritic complexity and spine density, and upregulated PSD95 and SYP. CK induced microglial M1-like-to-M2-like polarization and reduced Iba1+ /CD68+ microglia colocalization with PSD95+ synapses, indicating suppressed synaptic engulfment. CK was predicted to bind to the C1qA globular head domain, reduced C1qA deposition at synapses, inhibited C3, and CR3 expression, suppressed NF-κB phosphorylation, downregulated NLRP3, ASC, cleaved-caspase-1, and GSDMD-N, decreased IL-18 release, and alleviated neuronal pyroptosis.
