Results PGRN expression was increased in mPFC neurons after CUMS exposure. Neuronal Grn knockdown in the mPFC partially reversed CUMS-induced despair-like behaviors and impaired dendritic plasticity. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that Grn knockdown restored CUMS-induced neuroplasticity-related transcriptional alterations, including genes involved in Ephrin signaling, planar cell polarity, and MYC-related transcriptional programs. Conclusion These findings suggest that neuronal PGRN in the mPFC contributes to the despair-like phenotype, likely through modulation of neuroplasticity. Targeting neuronal PGRN may represent a potential strategy for developing novel antidepressant interventions.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease: From glial cell states and molecular networks to biomarkers and precision therapeutics.
papers.authors: Samantaray P, Verma P.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now recognized as a biologically heterogeneous syndrome in which amyloid-β pathology, Tau-related alterations, and neuroinflammation are key interconnected processes. Microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, complement, inflammasomes, neurovascular cells, and peripheral immunity are implicated as both adaptive and disease-promoting contributors to the pathophysiology of AD. Here, we highlight mechanisms by which innate immunity and peripheral immune cells influence amyloid β-peptide metabolism, Tau pathophysiology, excitatory synaptic function, oxidative stress response, blood-brain barrier integrity, and systemic inflammation in the context of Alzheimer's disease. A particular focus is made on the role of TREM2-related microglial function and the NLRP3 inflammasome, complement-mediated synaptic pruning, astrocyte crosstalk, and the limitations of the M1/M2 and A1/A2 concepts. A distinction is made between biomarkers of core AD pathophysiology and those specific to neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. An emphasis is placed on the clinical utility of plasma p-tau217 in combination with Aβ42/Aβ40, GFAP, NfL, sTREM2, YKL-40, and neuroinflammation imaging. With respect to therapeutics, an effort is made to focus on the need to harness desirable inflammatory pathways while specifically targeting deleterious processes rather than adopting an overarching anti-inflammatory approach. Single-cell, spatial, multi-omics, and biomarker-driven approaches may enable patient stratification based on underlying pathophysiology, allowing for stage-specific combination therapeutic strategies. Overall, studies presented in this review highlight a precision-neuroimmunology concept in which neuroinflammatory processes are both triggers and effectors of disease pathology and can be selectively modulated for clinical benefit.

papers.title: Withdrawal of Life-Sustaining Treatment and the Severity-Matched Mortality Difference Between Abusive and Unintentional Pediatric Traumatic Brain Injury: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study of the ACS TQIP.
papers.authors: Mina AS, Wolf K, Chen JW, Buda AM, Vogel AM, Pryor HI.
papers.abstract: Purpose Abusive head trauma carries higher mortality than unintentional traumatic brain injury (TBI), but whether this persists at comparable presenting severity, and how much reflects withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WLST), is unclear. We compared severity-matched in-hospital mortality between abusive and unintentional severe pediatric TBI and quantified the contribution of WLST. Methods Retrospective cohort study of the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program registry (2019-2024) including children with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale ≤8) from abusive or unintentional blunt mechanisms. Abusive cases were matched 1:1 to unintentional controls on 43 indicators of demographics, presenting severity, and hospital factors. Mortality was analyzed with conditional logistic regression; WLST's contribution was assessed by restriction to patients without WLST, counterfactual decomposition, and multiple imputation retaining all abusive cases. Results Crude mortality was 40.5% (abusive) vs 17.2% (unintentional). In 395 matched pairs, abusive injury was associated with higher mortality (odds ratio [OR] 1.39, 95% CI 1.01-1.90) and more frequent WLST (19.0% vs 14.2%). The association was attenuated among patients without WLST (OR 1.11, 0.71-1.71), but this underpowered finding was not reproduced after multiple imputation (1,009 pairs: mortality OR 1.58, 1.21-2.07; without WLST 1.55, 1.03-2.34). WLST mediated one-third of the excess mortality (33%, 7-60%) and preceded half of the excess deaths; the excess was confined to deaths after hospital day 1 (OR 1.65, 1.22-2.23). Conclusion At comparable presenting severity, abusive TBI carries a modest excess mortality emerging after the first hospital day; roughly one-third runs through more frequent WLST and the remainder persists among children who continue treatment. Level of evidence III - retrospective comparative study (propensity-matched cohort).

papers.title: White matter-guided transtemporal corridors: An anatomical blueprint for safe access through the temporal lobe.
papers.authors: Bilgin B, Yuncu ME, Karadag A, Bozkurt B, Tanriover N.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
papers.abstract: Background Transtemporal approaches provide access to deep temporal and intraventricular lesions but may traverse critical white matter pathways, making tract-aware planning important for minimizing postoperative deficits. Therefore, the microsurgical anatomy of commonly used transtemporal corridors, the fibers encountered along each approach, and their tract-specific risk profiles should be defined to guide corridor selection. Methods Three formalin-fixed cadaveric brain specimens (six hemispheres) were dissected, proceeding stepwise from the cortical surface to the ventricular system. Results Posterior superior temporal gyrus approaches lay close to the arcuate fasciculus (AF) and superior longitudinal fasciculus, with the middle longitudinal fasciculus encountered at a deeper plane; trajectories toward the roof of the temporal horn or atrium approached the optic radiation (OR) and Meyer's loop. Middle temporal gyrus and inferior temporal sulcus corridors lay adjacent to the OR-particularly Meyer's loop-and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) within the sagittal stratum. Inferior temporal gyrus approaches remained distant from the AF and uncinate fasciculus (UF), with the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) most closely related to the trajectory, while the OR and IFOF remained superior and medial. The transsylvian corridor traversed the temporal stem near the UF and central IFOF, with superior extension toward the ventricular roof placing Meyer's loop and the OR at risk. Conclusion Safer transtemporal surgery depends on the relationship between the surgical corridor and associated fibers, rather than the cortical entry point alone. These findings provide an anatomical framework for white matter-guided planning and tract-sparing corridor selection.

papers.title: An efficient convolutional neural network model for classifying positive affective states from EEG data considering sleep condition.
papers.authors: Gazan MK, Moghaddamnia S, Habiboglu MG.
papers.abstract: Background The recognition of affective states from EEG recordings considering the sleep condition can be an important supporting tool in therapy and in the treatment of psychological or psychiatric disorders. New method Since sleep deprivation changes EEG characteristics, a two-stage framework is developed for affective state classification. First, a classification between "Normal Sleep" (NS) and "Sleep-Deprived" (SD) is conducted using resting-state EEG data. The data are then fed into one of two newly proposed, lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to recognize four affective states. Results In the first stage, CNN-BiLSTM achieves 95.96% accuracy under window-level splitting and 70.46% under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation, while in the second stage the proposed models achieve 93.40% (NS) and 90.95% (SD) under window-level splitting, and 38.98% (NS) and 38.97% (SD) under cross-validation. The lower subject-independent accuracies reflect the class imbalance and the clustering of scores near the class boundaries, which make cross-subject four-class generalization challenging. Comparison with existing methods As existing studies mostly classify momentary emotions without addressing sleep conditions, direct comparison with prior work is difficult; we therefore benchmarked our framework against several established baseline models, including SqueezeNet, EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest. Conclusions This study suggests that considering physiological states can improve multi-class classification of affective states from time-varying neurophysiological signals such as EEG. The framework performs strongly under window-level evaluation, whereas its performance under the stricter subject-independent setting is more limited and should be interpreted accordingly. It can nonetheless contribute to more comprehensive research in affective neuroscience.

papers.title: Aberrant amygdala subregion volumes in youth at high risk for bipolar disorder predict antidepressant-induced adverse events.
papers.authors: Tang B, Patino LR, Blom TJ, Welge JA, Strawn JR, Bruns KM, Zhang W, Lui S, DelBello MP, Singh MK.
papers.abstract: Youth with familial risk for bipolar disorder (BD) and current depression/anxiety are vulnerable to antidepressant-induced adverse events (AE), including mania. The amygdala, implicated in the pathophysiology of mood disorders, may play a key role in these AE. 105 youth with at least one first-degree relative with BD-I and a current depressive/anxiety disorder (high-risk) and 51 healthy controls (HC) underwent baseline MRI to investigate neurostructural risk factors for antidepressant-induced AE. High-risk youth were randomized to either psychotherapy plus escitalopram or psychotherapy plus placebo (2:1) for up to 16 weeks. Clinical efficacy was assessed using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised and Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale, and AE were assessed using the Pediatric Adverse Events Rating Scale and Treatment-Emergent Activation and Suicidality Assessment Profile. Baseline amygdala subregion volumes and their associations with the rates of change in clinical symptoms and AE over time were evaluated using linear regression models. Compared to HC, high-risk youth had reduced volumes in left lateral and medial nuclei, bilateral central and cortical nuclei, and bilateral corticoamygdaloid transition area and increased volumes in bilateral basal and accessory basal nuclei. In escitalopram-treated youth, but not those receiving placebo, smaller baseline volumes in bilateral cortical nuclei and left medial nucleus were associated with fewer arousal-related AE. Additionally, larger bilateral basal nuclei volumes at baseline were associated with more arousal-related AE. Widespread amygdala volume abnormalities provide insights into neurobiological mechanisms underlying the development of BD in high-risk youth, and specific subregion volumes may serve as neurostructural markers for predicting antidepressant-induced AE.

papers.title: Regional atrophy and hypoperfusion mediate the association between affective symptoms and cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Wang J, Zhao G, Lu Q, Zhang X, Piao Z, Lin A, Wang S, Feng Q, Wen X, Qin W, Zhang N.
papers.abstract: Objective Affective symptoms are common and associated with poor cognitive outcomes in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, their underlying neural correlations remain poorly understood. Methods This study included 105 patients with AD. Patients were classified into an AD with affective symptoms (AD-A) group and an AD without affective symptoms (AD-NA) group according to scores obtained on the depression and anxiety items of the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. All of the participants underwent neuropsychological assessments and multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. Results Compared with the AD-NA group, the AD-A group was younger and exhibited more severe, widespread cognitive impairments. Neuroimaging revealed that the AD-A group exhibited reduced grey matter volume (GMV) in the bilateral posterior cerebellum and right fusiform gyrus, along with reduced global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and lower CBF in the left parieto-temporo-occipital region. Mediation analyses revealed significant indirect associations between affective symptoms and cognitive function via cerebellar GMV and left parieto-temporo-occipital CBF. Conclusion Cerebellar structural atrophy and left parieto-temporo-occipital hypoperfusion are associated with both affective symptoms and cognitive impairment and may represent neural correlates of the affective-cognitive association in AD patients.

papers.title: Melatonin ameliorates behavioral deficits in 5xFAD mice through modulation of neurogenesis, neuroimmune responses, neurotransmission, and metabolic pathways.
papers.authors: Roy J, Tsui KC, Poon CH, Zhang J, Lai Y, Wong KY, Mihardja M, Tse V, Li PC, Au C, Ng J, Kocabicak E, Aquili L, Wong KH, Lu Z, Temel Y, Fung ML, Lim LW.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder with limited disease-modifying treatment options. Melatonin, an endogenous hormone, has been shown to have therapeutic effects on amyloid deposition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation in AD. However, the mechanisms of its neuroprotective effects in the hippocampus remain largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the multi-mechanistic neuroprotective effects of melatonin in AD. Eight-month-old female 5xFAD transgenic mice were treated with melatonin (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks. Temozolomide and bromodeoxyuridine were used to block neurogenesis and to label proliferating neurons, respectively. Our results showed that 5xFAD mice treated with melatonin exhibited improved exploratory behavior, enhanced memory performance, reduced depressive-like symptoms, and decreased levels of stress hormones. At the molecular level, melatonin reduced amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaque accumulation, elevated hippocampal neurogenesis markers (DCX and BrdU), increased Trem2 expression and anti-inflammatory microglial activation, restored serotonergic, dopaminergic, catecholaminergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission, and partially normalized broader hippocampal metabolic pathways. Notably, temozolomide treatment abrogated the beneficial effects of melatonin on memory performance and depressive-like behavior in 5xFAD mice, indicating a neurogenesis-dependent mechanism. Collectively, these findings suggest that melatonin ameliorates behavioral deficits in 5xFAD mice through both neurogenesis-independent (reduced Aβ plaque accumulation, Trem2-microglial activation, neurotransmission restoration, and metabolic remodeling) and hippocampal neurogenesis-dependent mechanisms. Overall, melatonin holds therapeutic potential for attenuating the neuropathology and behavioral deficits in AD.

papers.title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.
papers.authors: Erbil G, Aykora D, Uzun M.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

papers.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
papers.authors: Sung WH, Chen H, Hsu CW, Tsai MH.
papers.abstract: Objective Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. Methods We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. Results A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. Significance This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. Plain language summary We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

papers.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
papers.authors: Zhu F, Shi XR, Weng SW, Delazer L, Fearns N, Arafat T, Lv RJ, Hu WH, Zhang C, Koepp M, Wang Q.
papers.abstract: Objective Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level. Results Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation. Significance These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

papers.title: Empagliflozin in Lafora disease: A first-in-human 6-month pilot study with electroclinical and FDG-PET findings.
papers.authors: d'Orsi G, Liantonio A, Imbrici P, Lolli G, Dinoi G, Conte E, Altomare CD, Ciccone F, Calò E, Perrone E, Cazzanelli G, DEFEAT‐LD Study Group, Carella M.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Objective Lafora disease (LD) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative epilepsy with no approved treatments. Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has shown neuroprotective actions in preclinical models through modulation of glycogen metabolism, induction of a pseudo-ketogenic state, improved mitochondrial efficiency, and reduction of excitatory neurotransmission. Based on this rationale, we conducted a first-in-human pilot study of empagliflozin in two genetically confirmed LD patients. Methods Two patients with genetically confirmed LD received empagliflozin 10 mg/day for 6 months. Serial assessments included safety and tolerability, seizure frequency, myoclonus severity, electroencephalographic findings, neuropsychological and motor evaluations, brain MRI, and quantitative FDG-PET with regional Z-score analysis. Results Empagliflozin was safe and well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Seizure frequency, myoclonus, and overall clinical status remained largely stable over 6 months, although some neuropsychological and motor measures showed variable changes between patients. EEG background activity and spike index were largely unchanged. Brain MRI showed stable mild cortical atrophy in both patients. In contrast, FDG-PET revealed progressive and spatially expanding cerebral hypometabolism in both patients, with worsening regional Z-scores, particularly in the parietal and precuneus regions. Significance In this first-in-human, 6-month pilot study, empagliflozin showed acceptable short-term safety and feasibility in LD, but no definitive conclusions on efficacy can be drawn. The dissociation between relative electroclinical stability and progressive metabolic impairment suggests that quantitative FDG-PET may represent a sensitive biomarker for monitoring disease trajectory in this ultra-rare epilepsy.

papers.title: Expanded characterization of the valproic acid zebrafish larval model of autism spectrum disorder: Insights into dysregulation in the gut.
papers.authors: Pretorius L, Coetzee JA, Dos Santos AP, Smith C.
papers.abstract: Background Relative lack of data on mechanisms underpinning poor gastrointestinal (GI) health in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) limits patient management strategies. Although the valproic acid (VPA) model of ASD is widely used, a comprehensive profile of the model in zebrafish is still lacking, and almost no data are available on ASD-like GI symptomology or underlying mechanisms. Methods ASD-like craniofacial morphology, anxiety-like behavior, GI anatomical and functional dysregulation, and dysregulation of the monoaminergic system in both the brain and the gut were simultaneously assessed in zebrafish larvae at 7 days postfertilization. Results VPA exposure was associated with increased intraocular distance, neuroligin 3 (NLGN3) dysregulation, decreased muscle tone, and an anxious phenotype (increased thigmotaxis and dark zone preference [light-dark preference test]). In the brain, protein expression levels of tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (TPH2) and serotonin (5-HT), but not serotonin transporter (SERT), were downregulated, as well as tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine transporter (DAT), whereas dopamine (DA) was upregulated. In the gut, upregulated serotonergic (increased TPH1 and 5-HT) and downregulated dopaminergic (decreased TH, increased DAT) protein expression was linked to thinner-walled, longer intestinal tracts, and decreased spontaneous peristaltic activity. Conclusions Dopaminergic dysregulation aligns with the ASD literature. Novel findings include an association of hyposerotonergic tone with anxiety-like outcomes as core symptomology in ASD. Furthermore, we demonstrate compartment-specific dopaminergic and serotonergic dysregulation in the gut, which provides support for relatively decreased gut motility in ASD.

papers.title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder
papers.authors: Mishra R, Wamalwa AM, Guasoni G, Dupont MB.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia ( VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4 ), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNFα/NF-κB ( IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2 ) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways ( STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR ), complement activation ( CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3 ), extracellular matrix remodeling ( COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2 ), and unfolded protein response ( BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2 ). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

papers.title: Three-hinge gyri link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion organization
papers.authors: Chen M, Dong X, Cheng J, Hu D, Liu T, Zhu D, Li G.
papers.abstract: Individual differences in cortical folding are a hallmark of human brain anatomy, but what this variability reflects in the underlying tissue remains unclear. Three-hinge gyri (3HGs), where three gyral crests converge, provide an individualized higher-order folding landmark for probing this relationship. Using 7T diffusion MRI in six postmortem hemispheres, we found lower mean, axial, and radial diffusivity and higher fractional anisotropy at 3HGs than at matched gyral crowns, with the principal tensor pattern replicated in 414 age-matched in vivo adults. Diffusivity differences extended across the cortical ribbon, whereas anisotropy- and fiber-related differences strengthened toward and beneath the white surface. Ex vivo , diffusion measures also varied with gyral-skeleton degree, and streamlines sampled beneath 3HGs preferentially reached other 3HGs. These findings link individualized folding topology to cortical and superficial white-matter diffusion-inferred tissue properties, providing tissue-level context for understanding the microstructural correlates of individual folding variation.

papers.title: Synaptic microRNA dysregulation orchestrates aberrant glutamatergic transmission in a human neuronal model of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
papers.authors: Niu W, Guo J, Ran X, Parker D, Li X, Yu S, Imes S, Purcell R, Michalski C, Guo E, Jiang SY, Xu E, Bassell GJ, Mulle JG, Ousley OY, Pearce B, Feng Y, Bearden CE, Walker EF, Cubells JF, Qin Z, Duncan E, Wen Z.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (22q11DS), the most prevalent chromosomal microdeletion disorder in humans (incidence ∼1 in 4,000 live births), arises from hemizygous deletions of a 1.5-3.0 Mb region on chromosome 22. Notably, 20-30% of individuals with 22q11DS develop schizophrenia (SCZ) by early adulthood, making 22q11DS one of the strongest genetic risk factors for SCZ. However, the mechanisms by which the 22q11.2 deletion perturbs neuronal function and drive psychotic manifestations in 22q11DS remain poorly defined. In this study, we generated human 2D cortical neurons and 3D cortical organoids from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from clinically well-characterized individuals with 22q11DS. Cellular and electrophysiological analyses revealed that 22q11DS neurons exhibit hyperexcitability, reduced glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, which are pathophysiological hallmarks that may be relevant to the clinical, cognitive, and psychophysiological profiles of patients. Transcriptomic profiling of neurons and synaptosomes from 22q11DS cortical organoids uncovered dysregulated immune pathways and synaptic gene networks. Integrative mRNA-microRNA network analysis identified synergistic downregulation of hsa-miR-185-5p and hsa-miR-128-3p at synapses, driving aberrant regulation of immune and synaptic transcripts. Experimental knockdown of these microRNAs in control neurons recapitulated the molecular and functional phenotypes of 22q11DS neurons, thereby establishing a mechanistic link to synaptic dysfunction and impaired plasticity. Collectively, these findings delineate a multimodal mechanistic framework that bridges genetic vulnerability, synaptic pathology, and psychosis penetrance in 22q11DS, positioning dysregulated synaptic microRNAs as nodal regulators of neurodevelopmental networks and potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Brain FACTs: A same-section workflow for Fiber Architecture, Cytoarchitecture and cell Types in large-scale brain sections
papers.authors: Kooijmans RN, Axer M, Graessel D, Amunts K.
papers.abstract: Understanding the human brain's multiscale organization requires linking cells, connections and architecture, yet conventional methods are incompatible within a single specimen, and inter-individual variability confounds cross-brain comparisons. Multiple-label immunohistochemistry for different cell types has been applied in interleaved sections but remains challenging within a single large human brain section and, has never been combined on the same tissue with 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) for three-dimensional fiber architecture. Here we introduce a sequential multimodal workflow integrating 3D-PLI, multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry and Nissl staining on the same large human brain section, preserving each technique's quality and specificity. The method was validated on vervet monkey and Wistar rat sections. The resulting paired high-resolution images eliminate inter-subject variability and enable direct micron-scale mapping of fiber tracts relative to molecularly defined cell types, yielding previously inaccessible insights such as molecular identification of white-matter components, refined cortical layering and cytoarchitectural disambiguation.

papers.title: Beyond Usual Pace: Quick Walking Speed and Brain Health Outcomes in the Framingham Heart Study
papers.authors: Thomson A, Lu S, Young VM, Katragadda HV, Kolo F, Hromas G, Gireud-Goss M, Jacob ME, Murabito JM, Seshadri S, Beiser A.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT INTRODUCTION Stroke, dementia, and late-life depression share overlapping vascular pathophysiology, yet simple markers of shared neurological vulnerability across these conditions remain limited. Most gait research has relied on usual walking speed (UWS) alone, leaving it unclear whether quick walking speed (QWS) and gait adaptability (QWS minus UWS), relate to these conditions in the same way. METHODS We examined associations of UWS, QWS, and gait adaptability with executive function, verbal memory, depressive symptoms, and incident stroke and dementia in the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort. A larger sample (n=2,308; mean age 61.5±9.2 years; 54% women) was used for cross-sectional and stroke analyses, and a dementia-free sample of 1,148 participants aged ≥60 years (mean age 68.5±5.8 years; 53% women) was used for analyses of incident dementia. We estimated associations per SD slower walking or smaller adaptability using linear, logistic, and Cox regression (10-year follow-up), overall and in women and men. RESULTS Slower QWS and UWS were each associated with worse executive function, higher odds of high depressive symptoms (QWS OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07-1.45; UWS OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46), and greater hazard of incident stroke (QWS HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03-1.64; UWS HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.11-1.65). Executive function and stroke associations were observed primarily in men (stroke QWS HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.11-2.17). For incident dementia, slower QWS reached significance (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.10-1.63), while UWS did not (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.98-1.46). Lower gait adaptability was associated with worse executive function overall and in women and men, and with incident dementia in women (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.04-1.76), but not with depressive symptoms or stroke. No gait measure was associated with delayed recall. CONCLUSION Slower QWS was associated with incident dementia; UWS was not. Adding a brief quick walking trial to routine gait assessment may identify risk that habitual-pace screening overlooks. Key Points Quick-pace walking, which adds one instruction to the usual-pace test, was associated with higher 10-year dementia risk, whereas the usual-pace estimate was smaller and not statistically significant. The margin between quick and usual pace, which reflects the capacity to accelerate on demand, was associated with executive function and, in women, with incident dementia, but not with stroke or depressive symptoms, unlike either pace on its own. • Why does this paper matter? Gait speed is among the most widely collected measures in geriatric practice and aging research, yet it is almost always recorded at usual pace alone. This study shows that the margin between quick and usual pace carries a different pattern of brain health associations than either pace on its own, so adding one timed trial to an assessment clinicians already perform makes available information that habitual-pace testing cannot provide.

papers.title: Attenuated GlycoRNA-microglial transcriptional coupling in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of patients with major depressive disorder: an exploratory interaction-based in-silico analysis
papers.authors: Xu R, Zhang Y, Maes M.
papers.abstract: Background Glycosylated RNAs (GlycoRNAs) participate in immune recognition and intercellular communication 1 , but their relationship with brain cell-type transcriptional signatures in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. We examined GlycoRNA-related transcriptional coupling with microglial and other cellular signatures in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Method Postmortem DLPFC transcriptomic data from 22 controls and 26 MDD patients (GSE102556) 2 were analyzed. GlycoRNA-related pathway enrichment was quantified using gene set variation analysis (GSVA) 3 , whereas microglial, neuronal, astrocytic, and oligodendrocytic signatures were derived using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) 4–6 . Pearson correlations, linear regression, and generalized estimating equations (GEE) evaluated cell-type-specific associations and diagnostic interactions. Exploratory GEE results underwent false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results No differentially expressed genes survived FDR correction, and GlycoRNA-related and cell-type signatures did not differ significantly between groups. In controls, GlycoRNA enrichment was positively associated with the microglial signature (β = 0.447, FDR-P = 0.006), with significantly weaker associations for neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes (all FDR-P < 0.05). The two-way GlycoRNA × is_microglia interaction was nominally significant (β = 0.210, P = 0.048), confirming that GlycoRNA transcriptional coupling is substantially stronger for microglia than for the other three cell types combined. The microglial association was numerically attenuated in MDD (β difference = −0.273, P = 0.167), but diagnostic interactions were nonsignificant. Conclusions GlycoRNA pathway transcriptional enrichment exhibits preferential microglial association in control DLPFC. It’s possible attenuation in MDD remains.

papers.title: Motor Evoked Potentials in Preclinical Models of Spinal Cord Injury and Stroke in Rodents: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Shahid R, Cooke DF, Balbinot G.
papers.abstract: Motor Evoked Potentials (MEPs) serve as an invaluable tool for assessing corticospinal tract (CST) integrity and motor pathway function in preclinical models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. Despite their diagnostic and prognostic utility, substantial methodological variability persists across studies, complicating interpretation and cross-study comparisons. This systematic review synthesizes MEP acquisition and interpretation protocols from 83 rodent SCI and stroke studies published since 2015, aiming to outline common practices, identify sources of variability, and highlight methodological gaps. Our analysis reveals a predominance of SCI models and a focus on hindlimb MEPs, employing diverse stimulation protocols including transcranial electrical stimulation (TES), direct cortical stimulation (DCoS), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Anesthetic approaches are notably heterogeneous, representing a potentially large source of variability in MEP acquisition. Amplitude and latency, often measured jointly, emerged as the most frequently reported MEP parameters. Critically, MEPs bridge cellular and molecular changes to observable behaviour by reflecting the integrated functionality of neural cell populations and their circuits. However, a lack of standardization in reporting, particularly for secondary electrophysiological features and stimulation intensity, hinders reproducibility. We emphasize the necessity for standardized protocols for stimulation, electrode positioning, and data analysis, particularly the use of comprehensive recruitment curves. Adopting these best practices will enhance the transparency, comparability, and translational potential of MEP methodology in advancing our understanding and treatment strategies for neurological disorders. Graphical abstract Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in rodent models of spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke. This review focuses on various brain stimulation techniques (orange) and electromyographic approaches employed to quantify MEPs (green) and factors affecting MEP recording and analysis (blue). Future directions include greater standardization of stimulation, recording-electrode placement, and data-analysis practices; such as the potential use of recruitment curve features and high-density EMG recordings such as Myomatrix. Recruitment curves provide a more comprehensive characterization of evoked responses than single-pulse stimulation. While a single pulse only offers a snapshot of a subject’s motor threshold, recruitment curves yield a dynamic, S-shaped (sigmoidal) function that reflects the net excitability of upper and lower motor pathways across a range of stimulation intensities. This enables better control over sources of variability, such as stimulation and recording electrode placement, anesthetics dose, that can alter amplitude-based features. Because recruitment curves quantify the relationship between stimulus intensity and response rather than relying solely on absolute amplitude, the derived features are less susceptible to these artifacts (e.g., slopes, S50—stimulation intensity to reach half of the maximum amplitude). In addition, high-density recordings make it possible to better characterize the evoked activity of multiple motor units within the same target muscle and to identify the innervation zones of the motor units under study. TMS (Transcranial magnetic stimulation); DCoS (Direct cortical stimulation); TES (Transcranial electrical stimulation); MEP (motor evoked potential); Ch. (EMG channel) .

papers.title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
papers.authors: Lazarus MF, Nelson CA.
papers.abstract: Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent’s education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate ( p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus ( p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources. Lay Summary Paid family leave may give parents more time at home, steadier daily routines, and less financial worry in the months after a birth, all of which could change the care an infant receives. But these benefits may not be equal across families. In a national study of infants, we examined whether paid leave taken by mothers, fathers or partners was related to early language skills and to the organization of brain pathways involved in language. Paid leave was not directly related to language scores or brain development overall. However, maternal paid leave was associated with more mature organization in two language-related brain pathways only among infants whose mothers had higher levels of education. No similar pattern was found for father or partner leave. These findings suggest that paid leave alone may not reduce early developmental disparities, and that policies offering paid leave may need to be paired with additional support for families with fewer resources.

papers.title: Neurobiological alterations and autism-like phenotype in mice following regulatory-limit exposure to fungicides in drinking water
papers.authors: Salvador-Prince L, Vignon A, Alenda UG, Lafon P, Thobois D, Schneider B, Lehmann S, Crozet C, Torrent i Mas J, Chaloin L, Vignes M, Laboute T, Becker JA, Le Merrer J, Loulier K, Perrier V.
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental conditions, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorders (ASD), have increased markedly over recent decades. This rise parallels the widespread use of agrochemicals, suggesting a contribution of environme ntal exposures. We hypothesize that pesticide residues may disrupt brain development and promote neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we test whether concentrations permitted in drinking water affect brain development using a maternal exposure model in wild-type mice. Exposure to a fungicide mixture at 0.3 µg/L, below the current European regulatory limit of 0.5 µg/L, impairs corticogenesis and is associated with alterations in synaptic function and glutamate rgic signaling. Offspring exhibit delays in sensory development, reduced social interactions, and increased stereotyped behaviors. We identify the adenosine A2A receptor as a molecular target of anilinopyrimidine fungicides. Together, these findings indicate that low-dose exposure to this fungicide mixture can induce an autism spectrum-like phenotype in the offspring.

papers.title: The anxiolytic-like effect of the aqueous extract of Punica granatum depends on the stress level of fish and mice: Evidence of a homeostatic re-establishing effect
papers.authors: Pantoja ARB, Chan-Monroy JM, Leite M, Cervantes-Anaya N, Vega-Rivera NM, Rodrigues TRR, Meneses AOS, Costa BPD, de Siqueira-Silva DH, Lima-Maximino M, Estrada-Camarena E, Maximino C.
papers.abstract: Pomegranate ( Punica granatum ) has shown potential anxiolytic and antidepressant effects in preclinical research, but its mechanisms remain unclear. Importantly, some evidence suggests that the effects of P. granatum depend on previous stress, suggesting an adaptogenic effect. This study aimed to evaluate the anxiolytic-like effects of an aqueous extract of P. granatum (AE-PG) on lambaris and zebrafish exposed to acute restraint stress (ARS) and female BALB/c mice exposed to unpredictable chronic mild stress (CUMS). In addition, we evaluated antidepressant-like effects in female BALB/c mice. Acute administration of AE-PG (1 mg/kg, i.p.) was tested in the novel tank test (NTT) in lambaris and zebrafish and in the light/dark test (LDT) in zebrafish, while chronic (7 days) administration of AE-PG (1 mg/kg, i.p.) was tested in the elevated plus-maze (EPM), open-field test (OFT), splash test (ST), and forced swim test (FST) in mice. ARS increased geotaxis and erratic swimming in the NTT, as well as scototaxis, risk assessment, and erratic swimming in the LDT. Acute pre-treatment with AE-PG blocked the effects of ARS on these anxiety-like endpoints in both lambaris and zebrafish. CUMS increased open arm avoidance in the EPM, thigmotaxis and horizontal and vertical exploration in the OFT, and immobility in the FST, and decreased grooming in the ST. Chronic treatment with AE-PG blocked the effects of CUMS on anxiety-like endpoints, and depression-like endpoints, in mice. An in silico analysis of the main compounds in AE-PG suggested a possible mechanism of action on a wide network of targets that converge on PI3K/Akt and show differential expression in brain regions associated with fear- and anxiety-like behavior. Molecular docking suggests that a compound from AE-PG, ellagic acid, is likely to act through estrogen receptors, which could help reestablish homeostatic balance in response to stress.

papers.title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
papers.authors: Tang Z, Dowsett J, Taylor P, Ferreiro DN, Pecka M.
papers.abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration, active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects’ confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present. Significance Statement How well we judge the reliability of our perception, called metacognitive sensitivity, matters more than ever, as we increasingly are presented with information passively through screens rather than gathering it actively via self-initiated exploration. Does actively seeking information sharpen self-monitoring, and does the medium (body vs. screen) matter? We show that active search enhances metacognitive sensitivity and brain responses alike, whether embodied or screen-based. Only embodied search, however, anchors self-evaluation to the present: Behaviorally, embodiment facilitates coupling of confidence tracking directly to current evidence rather than the previous trial’s outcome, while neuronally, it enhances responses in frontal brain regions during periods of heightened subjective confidence. This embodied grounding of self-monitoring may prove pivotal for building reliably agentic AI systems.

papers.title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
papers.authors: Shams B, Fekonja LS, Vajkoczy P, Picht T, Aydogan DB.
papers.abstract: Introduction Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies Methods We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances ( R ² = 0.82–0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

papers.title: Dishevelled2 Condensates control Axon Initial Segment (AIS) assembly and function through MTCL1-Dependent microtubule recruitment
papers.authors: Belmonte S, Poirault-Chassac S, Villagomez J, Isch C, Dorrego-Rivas A, Donier M, Chagny E, Renou E, Vacher L, Aubailly N, Moreau MM, David M, Mondin M, Montcouquiol M, Sainlos M, Battefeld A, Sans N, Ezan J.
papers.abstract: SUMMARY In the epithelium, Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling coordinates cellular organization along the plane of the tissue, perpendicular to the apicobasal axis. In neurons, polarity is instead expressed through the structural and molecular asymmetry that separates the axon from the somatodendritic compartment. Core PCP proteins are essential for neuronal development and function, and have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy. However, their precise roles in the establishment of neuronal polarity remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Dishevelled2 (Dvl2), a central PCP signaling scaffold, as a novel component of the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal axonal domain that maintains neuronal polarity and initiates action potentials. We show that Dvl2 defines, both in vivo and in cultured hippocampal neurons, a proximal subdomain positioned upstream of the major AIS marker Ankyrin-G (Ank-G) and is closely associated with microtubule bundles. Dvl2 is already detected during early axon specification, suggesting that it participates in the initial organization of the proximal axon. Functional depletion of Dvl proteins disrupts AIS architecture, reduces the accumulation of Ankyrin-G and other core AIS components, and impairs the organization of AIS microtubule bundles. These structural defects translate into altered neuronal excitability, with a reduced AIS-dependent component of the action potential. Mechanistically, we identify MTCL1 as a microtubule-associated partner that recruits Dvl2 from biomolecular condensate assemblies onto microtubules. This recruitment requires the DIX and PDZ domains of Dvl2. Notably, selective intracellular binders targeting the Dvl2 PDZ domain perturb Dvl2 condensate organization and compromise AIS formation. Together, our data identify Dvl2 as an organizer of the proximal AIS and reveal a Dvl2-MTCL1-dependent mechanism coupling condensate scaffolding, microtubule organization, and neuronal excitability. HIGHLIGHTS Dvl2 is an early component of the proximal axon initial segment (AIS) Dvl2 associates with AIS microtubule bundles and depends on MTCL1 for microtubule recruitment Dvl depletion disrupts AIS cytoskeletal organization, AnkG accumulation, sodium channel clustering and action potential initiation Perturbing Dvl2 condensate organization impairs AIS integrity

papers.title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
papers.authors: Godfrey KJ, Grimsrud GJ, Ramirez JS, Corlett A, Houlihan K, Byington N, Gell M, Kretsch S, Dosenbach NU, Barch DM, Gordon EM, Greene DJ, Mueller BA, Betzel RF, Fair DA, Conelea CA, Tervo-Clemmens B, Nelson SM.
papers.abstract: SUMMARY Precision functional mapping (PFM) reveals stable individual differences in brain functional network organization and holds promise for advancing neuropsychiatric clinical care. PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. However, crosshair fixation acquisitions can be challenging especially for pediatric or patient populations, where alternatives like movie watching might be used to improve data quality and reduce participant burden. Here, we compare the use of resting state crosshair fixation and movie watching fMRI data to derive individual-specific functional brain network topography using PFM data (28–38 minutes of low-motion fMRI data per-participant per-condition) in nineteen adolescents (12-18 years) with a range of transdiagnostic psychiatric diagnoses. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Acknowledging individual differences and level of analysis, we conclude that movies are a viable alternative to resting state crosshair fixation for individual network definitions.

papers.title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory
papers.authors: Fricker F, Buzi G, Morantin M, Doidy F, Clochon P, Bordas R, Leroy N, D’Argembeau A, van Wassenhove V, Hinault T.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24±3) and 36 older (aged 69±6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (α: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults’ prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state α-burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with α-power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state α-burst activity predicted α-burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual α-power and α-burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

papers.title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
papers.authors: Guo C, Xie M, Qiu G, Lu J, Liu Y, Qu L, Huang Y, Guo Z, Tian J, Lin J, Zhang B, Zhang X, Zhao J, Liu X, Long H, Ma J, Zhou B, Ye X, Zhao P, Cao J, Lin Z, Zhang Z, Deng W, Wang J, Wu W, Wang J, Peng X, Zhao S, Na S, Li H, Liu W, Fu Q, Guo ZV, Zhao W, Chen L.
papers.abstract: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (C ortex-wide O bservational M iniature E pifluorescence T echnique ) , a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware–software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

papers.title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease
papers.authors: Zhao B, Li M, Yi L, Li J.
papers.abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2–PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT – gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K⁺ current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na⁺ current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K⁺ conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na⁺ current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target. Graphical Abstract

papers.title: Novel Neuroimaging Biomarker of Cortical Gray/White Border Integrity in Blast-Related Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.authors: Andreu Arasa VC, Fortenbaugh FC, Knoff AA, Fortier CB, Milberg WP, Salat DH.
papers.abstract: Background and purpose Recent studies suggest that blast or mid-impact neurotrauma are characterized by scar-border forming astrogliosis at the gray-white matter junction. Individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and blast trauma have increased neuroinflammation and impairment of axonal remyelination on postmortem histopathology. However, there are currently only limited methodologies to use in the assessment of the cortical gray/white interface using in vivo neuroimaging. The purpose was to investigate the gray-white matter contrast (GWC) at the gray-white matter junction that may be linked to neuroinflammation/astrogliosis in the setting of blast exposure and/or mTBI, through 3D T1-weighted MPRAGE images. Materials and methods Post-9/11 veterans (n =723) from the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders completed MRI. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: participants with a history of blast-related mTBI (blast-mTBI), participants with a history of mTBI due to other mechanical forces (blunt-mTBI), participants with a history of close blast exposure but no mTBI, and those without a history of lifetime mTBI or close blast exposure. MRI data processing for morphometry and cortical surface mapping was done using FreeSurfer image analysis. Signal intensities in gray and white matter along the cortical and white matter interface were used to calculate mean GWC value. Results Veterans in the blast-mTBI group showed diffuse patterns of increased GWC relative to the other groups, particularly in the frontotemporal lobes. This effect was driven primarily by a greater number of high GWC regions in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma and blunt-mTBI groups. Conclusions There was diffuse increased GWC on MR in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma, close blast exposure, and blunt-mTBI groups. These findings may be linked to astrogliosis and neuroinflammation in patients with blast-mTBI. Histopathologic correlation with imaging findings will be necessary to better understand these effects.

papers.title: Breaking the Cycle: Rewiring Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Through Physical Exercise
papers.authors: Thonon B, Brevers D.
papers.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia commonly exhibit debilitating negative symptoms, including avolition and anhedonia, which represent a significant barrier to engagement in goal-directed behaviours, including physical exercise. They are less physically active than the general population, yet physical exercise is known to improve their symptoms. This narrative review investigates the bidirectional relationship between negative symptoms and physical activity. We propose that negative symptoms hinder engagement in physical activity by altering the cost-benefit analysis of exercise. This is exacerbated by deficits in anticipatory pleasure and reward learning, underpinned by dysfunctions within dopaminergic and glutamatergic circuitry which are critical for motivated behavior. We hypothesise that physical exercise can rewire these deficits through enhanced dopamine transmission, modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic systems, and reduced inflammation. Furthermore, grounded in learning theories and adopting a cognitive-behavioural perspective, this review establishes a theoretical foundation for developing targeted interventions designed to enhance physical activity engagement in this population. We highlight that it is critical to ensure that physical activity is experienced as less effortful and more pleasurable than expected. By generating positive prediction errors (when the experience of exercise is less effortful or more pleasurable than anticipated) exercise helps individuals re-associate it with positive outcomes. Cognitive changes coupled with the biological effects of physical exercise on reward neural pathways are likely to have a synergistic effect, promoting a virtuous cycle of sustained engagement and symptom improvement.

papers.title: The Effects of Cognitive Load on Intergroup Empathy Biases [Registered Report Stage 1, Version 2]
papers.authors: Franks JE, Gutsell JN.
papers.abstract: Accurate and quick judgments of others’ mental and emotional states are crucial for social interaction. However, these judgments can be compromised by social biases, especially while cognitive demands are high and cognitive resources are low. Empathy is not always allocated to everyone equally, especially when the target is considered an outgroup member. One factor that may exacerbate such empathy biases is cognitive load, as cognitive load has been shown to increase ingroup biases and impair empathizing. This study investigates whether high cognitive load and racial outgroup membership interact, potentially worsening behavioral and self-reported indicators of empathy bias. To our knowledge, the present work is the first to directly manipulate cognitive load during intergroup empathizing, examining its effects on two distinct, yet interacting, routes of empathy—experience sharing and mentalizing. Mentalizing (cognitive empathy) and affective experience sharing (emotional empathy) activate different brain networks but interact during social situations, necessitating separate examination within the same paradigm. Using an empathy task designed to test racial empathy biases, we integrate behavioral and self-report measures to capture empathy dynamics in response to naturalistic stimuli. This approach allows us to test how group biases and cognitive load independently and jointly affect mentalizing and experience sharing.

papers.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Epilepsy: A Shared Language for Integrated Care
papers.authors: Elbanna I, Makke YA.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is among the most burdensome neurological disorders worldwide, with an impact that extends far beyond seizure frequency alone. Depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, and internalized stigma affect a substantial proportion of individuals with epilepsy, yet these comorbidities remain systematically undertreated in routine neurological care. Conventional psychoeducation, largely centered on passive information delivery, has shown limited effectiveness in addressing the psychological and social complexities of living with epilepsy. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Epilepsy (NIPE) offers a fundamentally different approach: one that translates the neuroscience of seizure generation, network dysfunction, and neuroplasticity into accessible frameworks, shifting patients from passive recipients of information to active, metacognitively engaged participants in their own care.This chapter presents NIPE as both a clinical framework and an integrative layer across the continuum of epilepsy management. Beginning with the neurobiological mechanisms underlying seizures and epileptogenesis, it highlights how the same neural networks implicated in ictal activity also contribute to the psychiatric and cognitive comorbidities that shape patients’ daily experiences. It further examines how NIPE interfaces with evidence-based psychological interventions, pharmacologic education, neuromodulation, epilepsy surgery, and the management of refractory epilepsy, as well as the unique needs of women and other populations with distinct clinical considerations.In addition, the chapter explores the digital expansion of NIPE, including adaptive telehealth platforms, wearable biosensors, digital phenotyping, and the emerging role of artificial intelligence in tailoring psychoeducational delivery. Importantly, it addresses current limitations and ethical considerations with transparency, including the absence of standardized NIPE protocols and the relative scarcity of randomized controlled trials specifically within epilepsy populations.The chapter concludes with a forward-looking perspective on the infrastructure, research agenda, and cross-disciplinary collaboration required to embed NIPE into routine epileptology practice. NIPE is positioned not as an adjunct to epilepsy care, but as a unifying framework, a shared language that enables truly integrated, patient-centered care.

papers.title: Baroreflex control of heart rate at rest and during exercise in microgravity conditions.
papers.authors: Perrone MA, Caminiti G, Aracri M, Volterrani M, Iellamo F.
papers.journal: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
papers.abstract: One of the most important features of prolonged weightlessness is a progressive impairment of muscular function. Physiological modifications related to exposure to microgravity, e.g. altered blood volume distribution, impaired myocardial function, and a decrease in stroke volume, in addition to the alterations in muscular function, contribute to the reduced physical exercise capacity commonly reported after space flight. The interplay between muscular, hemodynamic and body fluid modifications occurring in microgravity could alter also the neural mechanisms of cardiovascular regulation both in resting conditions and during exercise in comparison to those that are normally operating on the ground. Indeed, an impairment in arterial baroreflex control of heart rate has been reported in the resting state during spaceflight. Moreover, cardiovascular and autonomic responses to exercise have been reported to be either impaired or preserved after simulated or actual microgravity conditions. Differences in results might depend on different experimental settings: the majority of studies on exercise in microgravity have been conducted using handgrips as a convenient model of muscular exercise. However, microgravity-induced muscular impairment involves mainly the antigravity muscles, i.e. leg muscles, which are those primarily involved in the reduced exercise capacity and hence are more representative of the marked changes in the musculoskeletal system induced by microgravity. This brief review aims to summarize current knowledge on baroreflex control of heart rate in resting and exercise conditions in microgravity.

papers.title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial.
papers.authors: Sim J, Choi KS, Lee DH.
papers.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by restricted and repetitive behaviors and disturbances in social communication and interaction. Currently, there is no fundamental treatment for ASD, with only a few medications available for use on a limited basis to manage concomitant neuropsychiatric symptoms. The primary therapeutic goal of such treatments is to alleviate symptoms while maximizing the functional independence and quality of life of affected individuals. Many complementary and alternative medicine therapies have been reported to have effects on ASD symptoms; however, evidence is insufficient to confirm their clinical effectiveness. Acupuncture has traditionally been used as a complementary intervention to manage various neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases, including ASD, in East Asia. However, how acupuncture stimulation modulates neural activity at the macroscale level in individuals with ASD remains largely unknown. Objective This study aims to elucidate disease-related brain alterations and explore the acute neural mechanisms underlying acupuncture stimulation in patients with ASD and in typically developing (TD) individuals, using a multimodal neuroimaging approach. Methods This study was designed as a randomized, sham-controlled trial. In this stratified 2×2 design, 70 participants, including individuals with ASD (n=35) and TD controls (n=35), will each be randomly assigned to either the verum or sham acupuncture group, resulting in 4 groups. The verum acupuncture group will receive stimulation at specific acupoints clinically indicated for ASD, eliciting a deqi sensation. The sham acupuncture group will receive superficial needling at nonacupoints unrelated to ASD symptoms. Each group will undergo clinical assessments and multimodal neuroimaging measurements, including functional near-infrared spectroscopy and electroencephalography, before and after acupuncture stimulation. The primary outcome will be differences in resting state network metrics and relative band power in frontal areas by disease status. Secondary outcomes will include differences in these neural markers following acupuncture stimulation between the verum and sham groups, reflecting the group × intervention interaction. Exploratory outcomes will focus on identifying neural markers that correlate with clinical indicators of ASD. Results Recruitment began in April 2025. To date, 23 individuals with ASD and 21 TD individuals have participated in this study. The recruitment process is expected to continue until December 2026. Conclusions ASD presents a significant socioeconomic burden, with no definitive treatment established to date. Although acupuncture is a widely applied intervention for various neurological conditions, including ASD, its large-scale neural mechanisms remain poorly understood.
