papers.title: A brainstem module for backward locomotion reveals direction-selective premotor circuits.
papers.authors: Liu Z, Lu L, Di R, Cui Y, Liu Y, Ren Q, Dai R, Wu W, Wang R, Luo M.
papers.abstract: Smooth locomotion requires precise directional control, yet the neural circuits governing navigational transitions remain elusive. Here, we identify the pontine backward locomotion center (PBLC) as a key brainstem node for backward locomotion in mice. PBLC glutamatergic neurons are preferentially recruited during backward locomotion; their activation elicits robust backward walking with naturalistic gait features, whereas their inhibition suppresses backward movement across multiple behavioral contexts. PBLC neurons send ascending projections to the peri-fasciculus retroflexus and descending projections to the paramedian reticular nucleus (PMn). Activating spinal-projecting PMn glutamatergic neurons evokes backward locomotion, whereas PMn ablation suppresses PBLC-evoked backward movement. The PBLC lies within an anteroposteriorly organized set of brainstem regions that includes the cuneiform nucleus, ventral laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, and lateral parabrachial nucleus, associated with forward locomotion, ipsilateral turning, and locomotor arrest, respectively. Together, these findings define a supraspinal circuit for backward locomotion and reveal neighboring brainstem modules associated with distinct locomotor actions.

papers.title: Sexual dimorphism in high-fat diet-induced depression-like phenotypes in mice: astrocyte-centered molecular, circuit, and microbiota associations.
papers.authors: Hsu PL, Liu SC, Yeh MC, Huang WF, Wang TF, Liu TY, Tsai SF, Chou HW, Kuo YM.
papers.abstract: Metabolic disorders (MetD) are linked to depression, both of which exhibit sex differences in prevalence and clinical presentation; however, the mechanisms underlying sex-specific vulnerability to MetD-related depression remain unclear. Male and female C57BL/6 N mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks (8 to 20 weeks of age) to induce MetD. Depression-like behaviors were assessed using the sucrose preference and forced swim tests. Ventral hippocampus (vHPC) astrocyte-centered molecular, structural, and circuit alterations were evaluated using Fluoro-Gold retrograde labeling, immunohistochemistry, and immunoblotting. Gut microbiota composition was characterized by full-length 16S rRNA sequencing and correlated with behavioral, metabolic, and neurobiological measures. Despite equivalent HFD exposure, male mice, but not females, developed pronounced metabolic dysfunction and depression-like behaviors. HFD-associated behavioral alterations in males were accompanied by sex-dependent impairments in vHPC astrocytic glutamate regulation and morphology, along with increased vHPC- nucleus accumbens (NAc) circuit activity. Peripheral insulin resistance and selective lipid abnormalities, rather than obesity or elevated glucocorticoids, showed the strongest associations with behavioral outcomes. HFD induced broadly similar gut microbiota remodeling across sexes, superimposed on distinct baseline microbial profiles, with sex-stratified analyses identifying specific taxa associated with FST performance in males but not females. These findings provide evidence for sex-dependent alterations in vHPC astrocytic morphology and vHPC-NAc circuit activity following HFD exposure, underscoring the importance of biological sex in the neurobiological responses associated with MetD-related depression.

papers.title: MR-409 promotes neurogenesis and improves neurological function after cerebral ischemia through attenuation of microglial activation.
papers.authors: Wang T, Li Y, Zhang Y, Fu X, Fu R, Ding D, Liu W, Cao X, Zhou MS, Che X, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Neurological recovery during the chronic phase of ischemic stroke (IS) remains a major clinical challenge. Our previous studies showed that the growth hormone-releasing hormone analogue (GHRH-A) MR-409 promotes neurogenesis and improves neurological outcomes. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, a transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) mouse model was used to investigate whether early modulation of microglial activation mediates these effects. MR-409 (2.5, 5, or 10 μg, s.c.) was administered immediately after tMCAO and daily for 3, 7, 14, or 28 days depending on the experimental design. The GHRH receptor antagonist MIA-602 and the microglial inhibitor minocycline (MINO) were used to assess mechanism involvement. We found that MR-409 (10 μg, s.c.) significantly reduced infarct volume and brain edema and improved function and cerebral blood flow at 3 days. It suppressed hippocampal microglial activation and promoted M2 polarization at 3-7 days, decreasing TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 while increasing CD206, Arg-1, and YM1/2, which were reversed by MIA-602. MR-409 enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis, increasing Nestin+ , Tbr2+ , and DCX+ cells at 7-14 days and newborn neuron survival at 28 days. These effects were enhanced by MINO but abolished by MIA-602. Functionally, MR-409 or MINO improved motor performance at 7 days, whereas only MR-409 improved both motor and cognitive function at 28 days. These findings indicate that MR-409 promotes long-term neurological recovery by attenuating acute microglial activation, improving the post-ischemic microenvironment, and enhancing hippocampal neurogenesis, highlighting its therapeutic potential for IS.

papers.title: Hemolytic brain edema: a new pathophysiologic approach for diagnosis and management of neurotrauma patients.
papers.authors: Rubiano AM, González WD, Loaiza-Cardona LM, Huang Q, Godoy DA, Liu J, Paiva W, Gao G.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Among the mechanisms of secondary brain injury, hemorrhagic transformation and intraparenchymal bleeding are recognized as critical determinants of neurological outcomes. Current classifications of cerebral edema (vasogenic, cytotoxic, CSF-shift edema, interstitial, osmotic, and ionic) fail to fully account for the pathophysiological complexity observed in hemorrhagic neurotrauma. We propose the concept of hemolytic brain edema as a discrete pathophysiological entity, representing a novel form of posttraumatic brain edema driven by the biochemical consequences of erythrocyte lysis following traumatic hemorrhagic events in the central nervous system (CNS). Hemolytic brain edema encompasses erythrocyte membrane disruption and hemoglobin release; heme catabolism generating free iron and reactive oxygen species (ROS); thrombin activation with direct neurotoxicity; complement cascade activation; microglial polarization and cytokine-mediated blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption; and extracellular fluid accumulation with perivascular edema formation. Recognition of hemolytic brain edema may fundamentally alter monitoring strategies in neurocritical care, refine neuroimaging interpretation, and identify new surgical indications. Early iron chelation, thrombin inhibition, modulation of the complement pathway, and targeted antioxidant strategies may mitigate hemolytic edema formation and improve neurological outcomes.

papers.title: Cross-cohort transfer of clinical Alzheimer's EEG signatures to cognitively healthy APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 risk carriers using differentiable logic gate networks.
papers.authors: Dharia SY, Valderrama CE, Smith SD.
papers.abstract: Neural alterations associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) may emerge years before clinical diagnosis, and genetic risk factors such as APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 may identify individuals vulnerable to these shifts. We tested whether electroencephalography (EEG) signatures learned from clinically diagnosed AD patients transfer to cognitively healthy middle-aged adults carrying these variants. Differentiable logic gate networks (Diff-Logic) and neural baselines were trained on log-relative power spectral density features from a clinical cohort of AD patients and cognitively normal (CN) controls. These models were then applied without retraining to an independent genetic-risk cohort of neutral-risk non-carriers (N), APOE-ε4-only carriers (A+P-), and dual APOE-ε4/PICALM G-allele carriers (A+P+), yielding a continuous AD-like EEG signature score per participant. Diff-Logic matched neural baselines in clinical classification (balanced accuracy 0.809±0.028; AUROC 0.845±0.023) while enabling edge inference with a 7.4× model-size reduction and 0.22 ms model-only latency on a 7 W single-core CPU. In the genetic-risk cohort, scores were highest in A+P+ participants (0.393±0.167) relative to N (0.296±0.154) and A+P- (0.285±0.143; subject-level mean ± SD). This elevation was nominally significant before correction (A+P+ vs. A+P-, punc =0.036) but did not survive Holm correction (pHolm =0.109), and the cohort carried no AD pathology or conversion ground truth; the association was therefore exploratory. Integrated gradients attribution of the trained model showed genetic-risk relevance in delta, theta, and alpha, partially overlapping clinical AD topography. These findings support the feasibility of zero-shot EEG transfer in genetically at-risk individuals and highlight the need for replication in larger cohorts. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Shyamal-Dharia/ad-difflogic-transfer.

papers.title: Needle-knife attenuates excessive autophagy and ferroptosis in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia: Association with SDC1/NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Zhou Q, Yang S, Liu M.
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this study is to explore the molecular mechanism of needle-knife in inhibiting ferroptosis and excessive activation of autophagy, reducing nerve injury and improving motor function in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia (PSSH) rats. Methods A rat model of PSSH was established using middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Neurological function and motor performance were evaluated using modified Ashworth Scale (mASS), Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) and balance beam test. TTC staining, Nissl staining and transmission electron microscopy were used to detect the cerebral infarction area and neuronal injury. Levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), glutathione (GSH) and ferrous ion (Fe²⁺) were measured by ELISA. Protein expressions of SDC1, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), GPX4 and autophagy-related proteins (LC3, p62, Beclin1) were determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC) or Western blotting (WB). Results Compared with the sham group, the cerebral infarction area of rats in MCAO and Erastin groups increased, the neuronal damage was obvious and the mitochondrial structure was disordered. The levels of ROS, MDA and Fe²⁺ in the infarct area were significantly increased (P < 0.05), and the levels of GSH and GPX4 were decreased (P < 0.05). At the same time, the expressions of SDC1, NRF2, SLC7A11 and GPX4 in the infarction area were decreased (P < 0.05), the autophagy-related proteins LC3II/I and Beclin1 were increased (P < 0.05), and P62 was decreased (P < 0.05). Compared with the MCAO group, the needle knife treatment could improve the nerve damage in PSSH rats, restore their motor functions, and rescue the aforementioned molecular levels (P < 0.05). Compared with the needle knife group, the ferroptosis activator (Erastin), NRF2 inhibitor (ML385), and autophagy activator (rapamycin) significantly reversed the therapeutic effect of the needle knife (P < 0.05). Conclusions Needle-knife alleviates ferroptosis and inhibits excessive autophagy in PSSH rats, and the underlying mechanism may be potentially related to the upregulation of SDC1 and the NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway.

papers.title: Caffeine Consumption and Adolescent Mental Health: The Role of Sleep and Brain Structure.
papers.authors: Zheng J, Rakesh D.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Caffeine is a widely consumed psychoactive substance, with use beginning during adolescence, a sensitive period of neurodevelopment. Despite its widespread, unregulated use, links between caffeine consumption and adolescent brain structure and mental health remain poorly understood. Methods We examined the association between caffeine intake and brain structure in 9632 adolescents aged 9-11 years. Caffeine consumption (intake of coffee, tea and soft drinks) and mental health were assessed via self-report. Cortical thickness and surface area were derived from structural MRI scans. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between caffeine intake and brain measures. Structural equation modeling was used to test whether sleep duration and brain structure mediated the association between caffeine intake and mental health outcomes assessed at the 6-month and 18-month follow-up. Results Higher total caffeine intake was associated with lower total cortical surface area (B=-0.03,SE=0.01,p=.001) and lower surface area in 22 regions across four lobes, driven largely by soft drink consumption, with some additional associations emerging for coffee and espresso intake with cortical thickness. All associations were evident at consumption levels as low as one cup per week. Shorter sleep duration and lower surface area sequentially mediated the association between higher caffeine intake and greater mental health problems in the future. Conclusion Findings highlight the need for evidence-based guidelines on adolescent caffeine consumption to support neurodevelopment and mental health.

papers.title: Altered tissue-to-fibril strain transfer in cortical bone from juvenile female Klotho-deficient mice.
papers.authors: Xue K, Wang F, Xi L, Gupta H, Terrill N, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Juvenile female Klotho-deficient mice have severe cortical abnormalities, but how the remaining bone matrix partitions deformation across length scales is unclear. We combined in situ tensile testing with synchrotron small-angle X-ray diffraction to quantify tissue and mineralized-collagen-fibril deformation in femoral cortical bone from 5-week-old female wild-type, heterozygous, and homozygous Klotho-deficient mice (n = 5 per group). Quantitative backscattered electron imaging (qBEI) assessed tibial cortical thickness, mineralization and the dark-area fraction of the same sections; phase-contrast microtomography of femur provided qualitative structural context. Effective fibril modulus was higher in heterozygous (14.6 ± 3.5 GPa, p = 0.012) and homozygous mice (13.4 ± 5.5 GPa, p = 0.010) than in wild-type mice (4.3 ± 0.8 GPa). The fibril-to-tissue strain ratio was lower in both Klotho-deficient groups (p = 0.018 and p = 0.028), whereas fibril-orientation dispersion did not differ (p = 0.823). Tissue modulus, failure strain, and failure stress showed no statistically significant genotype differences. Tibial cortices were thinner in both Klotho-deficient groups; the dark-area fraction was higher in homozygous mice (p < 0.001), and mean calcium content was lower in homozygous than wild-type mice (p = 0.011). Mineralization heterogeneity did not differ (p = 0.811). These exploratory findings are consistent with altered tissue-to-fibril strain partitioning associated with Klotho deficiency, together with marked cortical structural deficits, but do not establish the molecular origin of the response. The local X-ray dose was estimated at approximately 0.6 kGy per measurement location, well below the absorbed dose at which X-ray irradiation alters the deformation behaviour of cortical bone. Only female mice at a single juvenile age were studied, so the findings cannot be extrapolated to males or to older animals.

papers.title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Malakar V, Raman R, Justin A, Sp D, Roy D, Malakar CC, Purohit D, Mali PC.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed for 128 active targets by STRING database and Cytoscape software. Further, active target-associated pathways analysed using ClueGO plugin Cytoscape software and the Reactome online public domain server. The non-competitive allosteric PTP1B inhibition through the design of Simufilam derivatives, with particular emphasis on A20, which is predicted to bind at the non-competitive allosteric site of the PTP1B protein (PDB ID: 1T49), involves α3, α6, and α7 helices that influence the WPD loop orientation. The proposed non-competitive allosteric binding mode is based on computational evidence and for that further experimental validation would be required to conclusively confirm binding of the designed compounds within this regulatory region. Using in-silico approaches, including molecular docking, identified A20 with the most favourable predicted binding energy score (-10.8 kcal/mol) compared to other derivatives. Molecular dynamics simulations further indicated structural stability of the PTP1B-A20, 26, and co-crystal complex, with consistent RMSD, RMSF, H-bond, Rg, and SASA. Principal component analysis suggested that A20 restricts conformational flexibility; hence MM-PBSA analysis displayed its stable binding free energies. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation characterized the polarity, stability, and reactivity of A20 studies supported its favourable electronic configuration. Overall, A20 displayed superior calculated binding energies, trajectory stability, and predicted drug-likeness, positioning it as a promising lead candidate for future empirical validation in AD research. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05086-2.

papers.title: Air-jet Pneumodissection in Neuroanatomy: a new method for the study of White Matter anatomy in the Human Brain.
papers.authors: Marrone S, Scalia G, De Notaris M, Corrivetti F, Umana GE.
papers.abstract: Traditional white matter (WM) dissection techniques, such as the Klingler method, employ wooden or metal instruments that may cause myelin wear and limit fine anatomical separation. Inspired by clinical water-jet applications, we investigated the feasibility of an air-jet dissector (pneumodissection) for WM dissection, leveraging the Coandă effect to gently separate contiguous fiber tracts while preserving their integrity. A portable air compressor was modified with an extended tube and an 18G blunt needle tip. A left cerebral hemisphere, prepared according to a modified Klingler freeze-thaw protocol, was dissected under exoscope magnification. Airflow was delivered at pressures between 0.8 and 3 bar. Dissection followed Klingler's stepwise protocol, adapted to the ergonomics and dynamics of the air-jet device. The air-jet dissector enabled progressive detachment of pia-arachnoid membranes, cortex and U-fibers, with clear exposure of commissural, projection, and association bundles. Low-pressure flow (0.8-1.2 bar) was used for delicate superficial planes and U-shaped fibers, whereas transient increases up to 3 bar were used for more resistant cortical or deep tissue planes. During this feasibility experiment, the air jet reduced broad direct instrument-tissue contact and helped clear loose debris and surface fluid from the operative field. Vessel-fiber interfaces and anatomical cleavage planes were sharply delineated. The device's portability and pressure modulation allowed both blunt and sharp dissection functions through a single tool. Air-jet dissection is a novel and complementary technique for white matter study. The present study does not establish superiority or reduced tissue damage compared with conventional manual tools because no matched quantitative comparison or histological assessment was performed. Further replicated and standardized studies are required to define reproducibility, tissue effects, and any objective advantage over established dissection methods.

papers.title: Restoring Neural Homeostasis via Class II HDAC Modulation: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.authors: Gupta R, Kumar R, K S BS, Modi DK, Kumari S, Kumar N, Singh P, Ravi K, Abomughaid MM.
papers.abstract: Class II histone deacetylases (HDACs) comprise class IIa enzymes HDAC4, HDAC5, HDAC7, and HDAC9 and class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10, which differ substantially in structure, catalytic activity, subcellular localization, and neural function. Class IIa HDACs exhibit weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and function predominantly as signal-responsive scaffolds that couple calcium and kinase signaling to transcription through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, recruitment of HDAC3-containing NCoR/SMRT corepressor complexes, and interactions with MEF2, CREB, and FOXO. Conversely, HDAC6 is a predominantly cytoplasmic deacetylase that regulates α-tubulin acetylation, cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, autophagy, and proteostasis. Dysregulated class II HDAC signaling contributes to neurodegenerative diseases through convergent mechanisms involving synaptic dysfunction, maladaptive transcriptional repression, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and defective clearance of pathological proteins. Disease-associated substrates include amyloid-β and tau in Alzheimer's disease, α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease, and TDP-43/SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Emerging evidence additionally links aberrant HDAC4/5 signaling to neurodevelopmental disorders through altered synaptic maturation, excitation-inhibition balance, and circuit development. This review integrates the structural and mechanistic biology of class II HDACs with their disease-specific roles and evaluates therapeutic approaches to restore neural homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on selective HDAC6 inhibitors, modulation of class IIa protein-protein interactions and subcellular trafficking, natural compounds, and RNA-based strategies. Finally, we discuss major translational challenges, including isoform specificity, brain penetration, context-dependent functions, and the need to distinguish catalytic from non-enzymic mechanisms when developing disease-modifying interventions for neurological disorders while preserving normal essential HDAC functions and minimizing off-target toxicity.

papers.title: C/EBPβ Drives Ischemia-Induced Microglial Inflammatory Reprogramming Through Transcriptional Activation of ATF3 and Exacerbates Brain Injury.
papers.authors: Zhang Z, Zhuo F, Ouyang H, Chi C, Zhang F, Chi Y, Lin Z.
papers.abstract: Microglial activation contributes substantially to secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke, but the transcriptional mechanisms governing this response remain poorly defined. Here, we identified CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein β (C/EBPβ) as a key regulator of ischemia-induced microglial inflammation. RNA sequencing of microglia isolated from mice subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming, characterized by activation of inflammatory pathways, including chemokine, TNF, IL-17, and efferocytosis signaling, as well as cell-cycle programs, together with suppression of homeostatic processes involved in synaptic regulation and neuronal support. Network analysis identified Cebpb as a highly connected hub across multiple inflammatory pathways. C/EBPβ expression was markedly increased in peri-infarct microglia after tMCAO and in primary microglia exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation. Microglia-selective Cebpb knockdown reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, CCL2, and CD16 expression, increased IL-4, IL-13, and ARG1 expression, and attenuated ischemia-induced morphological remodeling. Consistent effects were observed in primary microglia and BV2 cells, supporting a central role for C/EBPβ in microglial pro-inflammatory activation under ischemic conditions. Mechanistically, C/EBPβ directly bound the Atf3 promoter and activated its transcription, while ATF3 partially mediated C/EBPβ-dependent Il1b induction. In vivo, microglial Cebpb knockdown reduced acute ischemic lesion volume, neuronal apoptosis in the striatum and cortex, and long-term cerebral atrophy. These histopathological improvements were accompanied by sustained recovery of neurological function, somatosensory performance, motor coordination, recognition memory, and spatial learning and memory. Collectively, these findings establish the C/EBPβ-ATF3 axis as a transcriptional pathway that promotes microglial inflammation and secondary neuronal injury after cerebral ischemia. Targeting microglial C/EBPβ may therefore limit ischemic brain damage and improve long-term neurological recovery after stroke.

papers.title: Gut Microbiota Modulation in CNS Disorders: Therapeutic Strategies and Implications for Drug Efficacy.
papers.authors: Ahmed LA, Al-Massri KF.
papers.abstract: Various central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, depression, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and anxiety, present significant obstacles to public health because of their intricate causes and the scarcity of effective treatments. Recent studies have shown that gut microbiota (GM) and CNS communicate bidirectionally. Modulation of immune system, neurotransmitters, and neuroactive metabolites are only a few examples of how GM can significantly influence CNS. Dysbiosis or changes in composition and function of gut microbes play a contributing role in various CNS disorders. In these disorders, probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, antibiotics use, and interventions based on microbial metabolites have demonstrated beneficial effects in animal models and some clinical studies. By restoring microbial equilibrium, increasing microbial diversity, and promoting the generation of beneficial metabolites, these approaches can improve the efficacy of traditional medications while minimizing their side effects and the disease itself, based on preclinical evidence and emerging clinical studies. Nevertheless, several obstacles should be overcome before the clinical translation of these approaches, such as using of standardized methods for modulating GM, identifying specific microbial signatures linked to various CNS illnesses, and understanding the exact mechanisms of gut-brain communication. This review provides a novel integrated perspective by comprehensively clarifying the bidirectional interactions between CNS pharmacological agents and microbiota-based therapeutic strategies in different neurological and psychiatric disorders, offering a unified framework to improve traditional pharmacological therapies. Importantly, future studies should concentrate on exploring the mechanisms and the exact interconnections between GM and CNS problems to elaborate targeted therapies for these disorders.

papers.title: A pattern to rule them all: tracing a human brain map of molecular aspects shared by Alzheimer's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies.
papers.authors: Ferrari RR, Garofalo M, Di Gerlando R, Pellegrini E, Dragoni F, Rizzo B, Rossi M, Calatozzolo C, Guaita A, Davin A, Gagliardi S, Poloni TE.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (LBD) are the most widespread forms of degenerative dementia. However, little is known about the molecular aspects that link these conditions with each other and with aging itself. Whole transcriptome analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) have been carried out on brain samples from hippocampus (HI), temporal and parietal cortex (TC, PC), cingulate cortex (CG), and substantia nigra (SN) of subjects with a neuropathological diagnosis of AD or LBD. According to the Abbiategrasso Brain Bank (ABB) protocol, the neuropathological diagnosis was based on a complete histological characterization, including all the main proteinopathies and vascular scoring. Transcriptomic results show major differences in the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the two pathologies. In AD, gene expression is more affected compared to LBD. DEGs have peculiar spatial distribution: HI and TC show transcriptomic changes related to synapses, while in CG, SN, and PC, changes are related to proteostasis; in LBD, DEGs are predominant in SN and PC affecting proteostasis, oxidative stress, and inflammation. In AD, GSEA shows that different regions cluster by shared biological processes. AD appears much more complex, and different forms of AD do exist. Nonetheless, the molecular signature of same regions across the two pathologies can be interestingly overlapped. Exploring the molecular processes that occur before the deposition of pathological lesions may reveal individual neurodegeneration trajectory to achieve personalized therapies, which could be much more effective than the mere immunological removal of protein deposits.

papers.title: Targeting the P2X7 receptor in Alzheimer's disease: mechanistic insights and emerging therapeutic strategies.
papers.authors: Se ME, Ramalingam A.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide and is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, amyloid-β deposition, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Current therapies provide only limited symptomatic benefit, and although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have demonstrated disease-modifying potential in selected patients, additional disease-modifying targets are still needed. The purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R), an ATP-gated ion channel predominantly expressed on microglia and astrocytes, has emerged as a key regulator of neuroinflammatory signalling and AD progression. This narrative review summarizes and critically discusses recent preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence published through 2026. Evidence from cellular and animal models, post-mortem human brain analyses, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging studies, and pharmacological investigations was evaluated to assess the role of P2X7R in AD pathogenesis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that extracellular ATP-mediated activation of P2X7R promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β and interleukin-18, thereby sustaining chronic neuroinflammation. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of P2X7R reduced amyloid plaque burden, attenuated tau hyperphosphorylation, improved synaptic function, and ameliorated cognitive deficits in experimental AD models. Human studies further revealed elevated P2X7R expression and increased neuroinflammatory activity associated with AD pathology. Emerging therapeutic approaches include selective P2X7R antagonists, natural-product modulators, RNA-based interventions, nanotechnology-assisted drug delivery systems, and combination therapies targeting multiple pathogenic pathways. P2X7R represents a promising candidate target for disease-modifying therapeutic strategies in AD, based on convergent in vitro, animal-model, human post-mortem, and imaging/biomarker evidence linking ATP-mediated danger signalling to neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau pathology, and neurodegeneration. However, its clinical efficacy in AD remains to be established, as no clinical trial data for P2X7R-targeted therapies in this disease are yet available. Future clinical translation will require improved CNS-penetrant antagonists, enhanced receptor selectivity, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and precision medicine approaches.

papers.title: Intracranial metastasis as a mimic of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities.
papers.authors: Hwang J, Delman BN, Naasan G.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: This report describes a 79-year-old woman with biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's disease who developed progressive vasogenic edema initially interpreted as amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) with edema during lecanemab therapy, but was ultimately found to have multifocal intracranial metastases from recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma. The serial neuroimaging highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing ARIA from alternative causes of vasogenic edema in the era of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody treatment. In addition, this case raises an important and underexplored question regarding whether anti-amyloid therapies may alter blood-brain barrier integrity in a manner that could influence metastatic spread in susceptible patients.

papers.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in Alzheimer's disease and MCI: a meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Siqueira RGP, Ranalli C, Yılmaz D, da Silva M, Maltez BRP, Berton GG, Cummings JL.
papers.abstract: Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in older individuals and remains a major clinical and socioeconomic burden. Despite the success of anti-amyloid therapies in reducing biomarker burden, more effective and safer treatments are still needed. Given the emerging evidence of a role for metabolic dysfunction and brain insulin resistance in AD pathophysiology, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have been proposed as potential disease-modifying therapies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to April 22, 2026 to evaluate the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 RAs in AD and mild cognitive impairment. Randomized controlled trials comparing GLP-1 RAs with placebo, standard care, or non-intervention across the Alzheimer's continuum were eligible; abstracts and studies with unavailable results were excluded. Random-effects models were used. Risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for binary outcomes, and mean or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Results Seven studies comprising 4132 participants met the inclusion criteria. The mean age of the pooled studies was 72.1 years, while the mean baseline Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) varied from 2.71 to 3.8. GLP-1 RAs were not associated with significant improvement in cognition (Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale: standard mean difference -0.05; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.12 to 0.02; p = 0.1928) or disease progression (CDR-SB: mean difference: 0.09; 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.28; p = 0.362). They were associated with a higher frequency of adverse events (RR 1.07; 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.10; p < 0.0001) and weight loss (RR 5.01; 95% CI: 3.99 to 6.27; p < 0.0001). Biomarker and neuroimaging findings were inconsistent and failed to translate to clinical benefit. Discussion GLP-1 RAs did not improve cognitive or functional outcomes in AD and were associated with adverse events. Their role may be better explored in biomarker-enriched, metabolically selected populations or assessment of GLP-1 RAs with greater brain penetrance.

papers.title: Neuroprotective Effects of Food-Derived Cyanidin Glycosides in an Alzheimer's Disease-Like Zebrafish Model Through Modulation of PI3K/Akt/GSK3β Signaling.
papers.authors: Wu Y, Tie F, Gao Y, Li J, Wang R, Hu N, Dong Q, Wang H.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder lacking effective and safe interventions. Food-derived anthocyanins have gained increasing attention due to their neuroprotective potential; however, the specific mechanisms of individual cyanidin glycosides remain insufficiently understood. Notably, the comparative efficacy and mechanistic differences among structurally distinct cyanidin glycosides have not been systematically evaluated in vivo. In the present study, three cyanidin glycosides, cyanidin-3-O -rutinoside (C3R), cyanidin-3-O -sophoroside (C3S), and cyanidin-3-O -xyloside (C3X), were evaluated using an aluminum chloride (AlCl3 )-induced zebrafish model of AD-like pathology. The results showed that these compounds improved cognitive performance and anxiety-like behavior, while attenuating oxidative stress and neuroinflammation and restoring cholinergic function, as evidenced by biochemical and immunofluorescence analyses. In addition, neuronal damage and Tau phosphorylation at Ser396 were markedly alleviated. Among the tested compounds, C3R consistently exhibited the most pronounced effects across multiple indicators. Mechanistically, the three cyanidin glycosides modulated PI3K/Akt/GSK3β signaling, as reflected by overall increases in p-PI3K (Tyr458)/PI3K and p-Akt (Ser473)/Akt and decreases in p-GSK3β (Tyr216)/GSK3β and p-Tau (Ser396)/Tau. LY294002 attenuated the pathway-associated protective effects, supporting the involvement of PI3K/Akt signaling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate neuroprotective effects associated with modulation of PI3K/Akt/GSK3β signaling, with C3R showing the strongest overall efficacy.

papers.title: Extensive Parenchymal Brain Calcification in a Patient With Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease and Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease.
papers.authors: Khan N, Streicher N.
papers.abstract: Extensive parenchymal brain calcification is uncommon in chronic kidney disease (CKD): intracranial vascular calcification affects up to 10% of uremic patients, but widespread Fahr-type parenchymal deposits are rare and, where reported, have occurred in patients with a coexisting hypoparathyroid or parathyroid-hormone (PTH)-resistant state. We describe a man in his 50s with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and Stage 5 CKD who presented with word-finding difficulty, gait imbalance, and myoclonus and was found to have extensive symmetric calcification of the basal ganglia, thalami, dentate nuclei, and subcortical white matter. He carried an unverified childhood diagnosis of pseudohypoparathyroidism made at age 13. At presentation, total calcium was 6.1-6.3 mg/dL, phosphate 5.8 mg/dL, intact PTH 194 pg/mL, creatinine 6.21 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase normal. Over the following 10 months, intact PTH fell rather than rose, reaching 56 pg/mL during treatment with calcium, calcitriol, sevelamer, and hemodialysis, all of which lower PTH whatever the underlying cause. The calcium-phosphate product was low at presentation (36.5 mg2 /dL2 ) but rose to 58-62 mg2 /dL2 later, and single values cannot exclude earlier CKD-related mineral abnormality. No pathogenic variant was identified on an 866-gene panel. Neither the product nor the PTH trajectory separated renal from non-renal contributions. We present this as a diagnostic-reasoning case that raises, but cannot resolve, the question of causation and suggest that such calcification should not be attributed to CKD-mineral and bone disorder by default.

papers.title: Cross-state stability and maturational similarity of the social brain connectome in children and adolescents
papers.authors: Lee J, Eilbott J, Kelly C, Todd R, Vanderwal T.
papers.abstract: The intra-individual stability of functional connectivity (FC) across two or more scans and the inter-individual similarity of FC patterns relative to peers capture developmental variability in functional brain organization. Despite their different referents, these measures are strongly coupled at the whole brain level; however, it remains unclear whether this relationship emerges in development, whether it extends to the social brain, and whether it differs by sex. Based on the importance of social development in this age range, we hypothesized that known developmental relationships and sex-specific effects would be more pronounced in the social brain relative to the whole brain. Using a large psychiatrically enriched sample of 769 youth ages 6-21 (female N = 327, mean age = 12.27 years), we computed FC during rest and movie-watching scans and quantified stability across scans as well as similarity to mature subjects (n=36) within each condition. We then tested whether sex-dependent age relationships were captured by these measures or by the strength of their coupling. Our results showed that cross-state stability and maturational similarity are strongly coupled in development, and that this coupling is enhanced in the social brain relative to the whole brain. Furthermore, the strength of stability-similarity coupling increased as a function of age in females, while males showed the opposite effect. When assessing relationships between age and each FC measure independently, no individual effects were significant after FDR correction. However, our multivariate age-prediction models fared much better, demonstrating that edgewise stability and maturational similarity measures can capture spatially heterogeneous developmental effects that are lost when collapsing across edges. Together, these results support the emerging idea that the degree of FC stability across scans is related to how closely an individual’s functional architecture aligns to a shared template. Here, we newly show that this stability-similarity coupling is stronger in the social brain and varies with age in sex-specific ways. Future longitudinal work is needed to establish whether these cross-sectional relationships also characterize within-person developmental change.

papers.title: Virtual Brain Modelling Reveals Altered Network Dynamics and Predicts Symptom Severity in Schizophrenia: Relevance to Antipsychotic Treatment Response and Resistance
papers.authors: Vitacca M, Pischedda D, Ciccarelli M, Pontillo G, De Simone G, Cocozza S, Ćipranić F, Monteverdi A, Fusar-Poli P, Gandini Wheeler-Kingshott CAM, Palesi F, de Bartolomeis A, D’Angelo E.
papers.abstract: Background Schizophrenia (SZ) is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by positive, negative, cognitive and disorganisation symptoms, with pleomorphic phenotype and poorly understood aetiology. Dopamine dysregulation represents the most replicated in vivo pathophysiology finding. However, accumulating evidence suggests altered large-scale brain connectivity and excitation/inhibition balance disruption. While quantifying these alterations would help clarify SZ neurophysiology and guide therapy, single-patient identification remains impractical. This is particularly relevant for treatment-resistant SZ (TRS) whose pathophysiology remains unclear. Methods Using virtual brain modelling, we simulated large-scale brain dynamics from functional and structural MRI data in 43 healthy controls and 33 SZ patients, stratified into TRS and non-TRS. We used the Wong-Wang model to derive four network parameters reflecting GABAergic and NMDA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission: global coupling (G), local inhibitory (J i ) and excitatory (J NMDA ) coupling, and recurrent excitation (w + ). We performed simulations in the whole brain and in resting-state networks, compared model parameters between groups and tested their association with Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores. Results Compared to non-TRS, TRS patients showed increased J NMDA and decreased w + at the whole-brain level, increased J NMDA and G in the dorsal attention network, lower G in the limbic network and increased w + in the visual network. Moreover, J i in the default mode network predicted negative symptom severity while J NMDA in the limbic and ventral attention networks predicted total PANSS scores and disorganisation. Conclusions These findings suggest that TRS is characterized by network-specific alterations in excitation/inhibition profiles and support the use of personalised multiscale modelling to identify symptom biomarkers.

papers.title: Biologically inspired alignment reveals distributed and directionally asymmetric correspondence between rat and human cortices
papers.authors: Dong X, Luo Q, Cai A, Jin Z, Mu C, Wang F, Shan H.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Rodent models enable causal interrogation of brain circuits, but translating their systems-level organization to humans requires correspondence beyond one-to-one anatomical homology. Guided by the view that cortical areas are characterized by their relationships within distributed functional networks, we developed BrainMapping, a biologically inspired framework for aligning rat and human cortex using resting-state functional MRI. The framework combined a shared representation with optimal transport to derive probabilistic, bidirectional maps. These alignments revealed distributed, many-to-many correspondences that generalized to held-out subjects and preserved functional connectivity architecture, cortical gradients, and graph topology. Organizational preservation was directionally asymmetric. Human-to-rat mapping preserved organization more uniformly across rat cortical systems, whereas rat-to-human mapping showed stronger preservation in human association-related networks than in primary sensory and motor networks. The maps recovered literature-consistent default-mode and salience-system correspondences and generated testable non-canonical predictions. These findings provide a framework for expressing rat functional organization in human functional-network coordinates.

papers.title: Differential subcortical-cortical circuit reorganization in autism and ADHD
papers.authors: Zhou G, Xie K, Ngo A, Ding R, Cabalo DG, Wang Y, Smith M, Nakamura M, Royer J, Serediuc N, Toussaint PJ, Mottron L, Martino AD, Milham MP, Hong S, Evans AC, Bernhardt BC.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often co-occur and share symptoms as well as genetic risk factors. While subcortical-cortical networks have been implicated in both conditions, particularly involving thalamic and striatal circuits, patterns of shared and diverging disruptions remain unclear. Here we integrated resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and regression dynamic causal modeling (rDCM) across a transdiagnostic multi-site cohort. We used statistical group comparisons and individualized normative deviation mapping to map network deviations in ASD and ADHD relative to neurotypical controls and against one another. Multivariate associative techniques examined associations to clinical and cognitive phenotypes. Our transdiagnostic analyses revealed significant differentiation of ASD and ADHD across subcortical-cortical circuits. While ASD was characterized by widespread thalamocortical hyperconnectivity and bidirectional elevated coupling across thalamic subdivisions, ADHD exhibited a focal pattern of striatocortical disruption, anchored predominantly within the caudate. Multivariate analyses identified shared and disorder-specific brain-behavior associations. Across both conditions, aberrant striatocortical signaling was associated with reduced overall intelligence measures. Clinically, ASD-related thalamocortical connectivity disruptions mapped onto generalized cognitive impairment, whereas ADHD-related subcortical alterations tracked hyperactive and inattentive symptom dimensions. Our findings differentiate ASD and ADHD through distinct patterns of functional and directional subcortical-cortical dysregulations.

papers.title: Childhood Stress and Amygdala-Hippocampal Volume: A Multiverse Analysis in Adolescents
papers.authors: Sivakumar P, Hanson J.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Childhood adversity is robustly linked to differences in amygdala and hippocampal volume. However, findings across studies have been inconsistent and contradictory. This inconsistency stems partly from the many reasonable but arbitrary choices that researchers make when operationalizing brain regions, stress exposure, and covariates. To deal with this variability, we applied a multiverse analysis approach using adolescent data from the Boston Adolescent Neuroimaging of Depression and Anxiety (BANDA) study to evaluate how multiple analytic choices influence the relationships between stress and hippocampal/amygdala volume. Our primary analysis crossed three region-of-interest operationalizations (left, right, total), four intracranial volume scaling methods, and multiple sociodemographic covariates. Greater lifetime stress severity was associated with smaller amygdala volume across 72% of specifications, and with smaller hippocampal volume across 52% of specification models. Statistical significance was strongly influenced by the region of interest. Our secondary multiverse analysis tested six operationalizations of stress exposure (total/acute/chronic x count/severity). This analysis found that the laterality pattern in the primary analysis was not strongly influenced by stress operationalization. These findings demonstrate the robustness of the stress-medial temporal lobe association and identify specific analytic choices (i.e. hemisphere operationalization) that most strongly drive the variability observed in previous literature. Our study is one of the first that utilized multiverse analysis for adversity-neuroimaging research, and provides a strong framework for evaluating and interpreting inconsistent findings.

papers.title: An Imaging Risk Score for Bipolar Disorder: Multimodal Comparison and Integration with Polygenic Risk
papers.authors: Parker N, O’Connell KS, Shadrin AA, Parekh P, Kang MJ, Kopal J, Hagen E, Kennedy KG, Im Y, Alnæs D, Hughes D, Alda M, Alexander N, Altegoer L, Aquino-Servín A, Bauer J, Bedir D, Benedetti F, Berger K, Berk M, Blumberg HP, Borgers T, Bozaoglu K, Bravi B, Busatto GF, Canales EJ, Cannon DM, Caseras X, Chi I, Claramonte PF, Clementz B, Colic L, Corley E, Dandash O, Dannlowski U, Demro C, Díaz-Zuluaga AM, Einenkel-Brand K, Elvsåshagen T, Eyler LT, Favre P, Flinkenflügel K, Forte MF, Fullerton JM, Furno S, Fries GR, Gershon E, Glahn DC, Gotlib IH, Goya-Maldonado R, Green M, Grotegerd D, Gruber O, Haarman B, Hahn T, Hajek T, Hermesdorf M, Houenou J, Howells FM, Ivleva EI, Jamalabadi H, Janiri D, Jansen A, Javaheripour N, Keedy S, Kempton M, Keshavan M, Kircher T, Klahn L, Kraemer B, Laighneach A, Landén M, Lee Y, Lopez-Jaramillo C, Makhoul W, Malt UF, McDonald C, McWhinney S, Meinert SL, Mitchell PB, Mwangi B, Nenadic I, Olie E, Olivo D, Papenbrock S, Parker D, Pearlson G, Piras F, Piras F, Poletti S, Pomarol-Clotet E, Prisciandaro J, Quidé Y, Radua J, Rauer L, Ringels W, Ringin E, Roberts G, Rodrigue AL, Rosa PG, Rossell S, Sacchet MD, Salvador R, Sambataro F, Sani G, Sarró S, Satterthwaite T, Savitz J, Scheffler F, Serra-Navarro M, Sheline YI, Sim K, Soares JC, Soeiro-de-Souza MG, Sponheim S, Stein DJ, Stein F, Straube B, Tamminga C, Temmingh HS, Teutenberg L, Thomas-Odenthal F, Topolski N, Urosevic S, Usemann P, Vai B, Valencia-Echeverry J, Van Rheenen TE, Vecchio D, Vieta E, Vilajosana E, Wolf D, Wu M, Yang A, Yatham L, Zanetti MV, Zunta-Soares GB, Bearden CE, Goldstein BI, Kaufmann T, Westlye LT, Thompson PM, Dale AM, Ching CRK, Andreassen OA.
papers.abstract: Summary Background Biological risk scores provide objective markers of bipolar disorder (BD) liability. Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have led to polygenic risk scores (PRSs) that capture genetic liability to BD at the individual level. We lack a comparable large-scale effort to leverage a brain-wide association study (BWAS) to create an imaging risk score (IRS) that captures brain structural liability to BD at the individual-level. Here, we conduct the largest multivariate BWAS of BD and develop a BD IRS. We compare the BD IRS to the PRS and assess their combined predictive performance in multimodal risk score (MRS) models. Methods Our multivariate BD BWAS used 153 structural neuroimaging features from 3902 cases and 6855 controls (mean age (sd)=35.47 years (13.42), 56.70% female) in a cross-validated machine learning approach. Using the resulting model coefficients, we constructed an IRS. We then evaluated the out-of-sample performance of the IRS, PRS derived from the largest GWAS to date, and combined MRS model using logistic regression in a subset of individuals with imaging and genetic data (n BD =486, n controls =1701, age (sd)=33.10 (12.02), 56.47% female). We also performed stratified analyses for demographic and BD clinical groups. Prediction performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Subsequent analyses examined associations between each risk score and BD relevant symptoms in developing youth. Outcomes In predicting case status, the BD BWAS model achieved a mean AUC BD of 0.62 (sd BD =0.08) and in stratified analyses, had higher prediction than subgroup-specific BWAS models. The BD type II BWAS was the only exception (AUC BDII =0.60, sd BDII =0.07 vs AUC BD =0.58, sd BD =0.09). The BD PRS had an AUC BD of 0.65 (CI 95% =0.63-0.68) and a higher AUC than subtype-specific PRS in stratified analyses. The PRS typically attained a higher AUC than the IRS. Notably, the IRS and PRS were uncorrelated (r=0.03, p=0.11). MRS models outperformed the prediction of individual PRS and IRS with the strongest prediction for BD type I (AUC BD =0.74, CI 95% =0.70-0.78). The IRS had the strongest associations with BD-related symptoms in developing youth including increased energy (OR=1.21, p fdr =0.03) and distress from psychotic-like experiences (OR=1.23, p fdr =0.04). Interpretation Our BD IRS is a novel biological indicator of BD risk. The lack of correlation between the IRS and PRS along with improved MRS prediction suggests the two risk scores capture some orthogonal liability to BD. We show that integrating imaging and genetics is useful for biological characterization of BD and should be considered for the development of clinically relevant prediction models.

papers.title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
papers.authors: Huang Z, Goumas P, Bisby JA, Rodionov R, Diehl B, McEvoy AW, Walker MC, Vivekananda U, Burgess N, Bush D.
papers.abstract: In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that ‘theta sweeps’ of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.

papers.title: Beyond High-Amplitude Events: Amplitude-Resolved Spatial and Temporal ICA Representations in fMRI
papers.authors: Vu D, Calhoun V.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Functional MRI analyses commonly reduce high-dimensional brain activity using predefined spatial summaries, such as region-of-interest (ROI) averages, or temporally selective representations, such as co-activation patterns (CAPs) and high-amplitude events. These approaches provide useful summaries but do not explicitly characterize information distribution across the continuous magnitude of spatial and temporal network expression. We introduce an amplitude-resolved framework for systematically interrogating this continuum using independent component analysis (ICA). Resting-state fMRI data in the FBIRN dataset were decomposed using spatially-constrained ICA with NeuroMark. For the temporal representation, time points were stratified according to global ICA amplitude and frequency bands, with functional network connectivity (FNC) estimated for each amplitude range. For the spatial representation, we introduce an approach that stratifies voxels according to ICA loading magnitude and generates amplitude-specific spatial similarity matrices. Linear support vector machine (SVM) classification of schizophrenia (SZ) and healthy control (HC) participants was used to probe the information retained by each representation. Discriminative information varied non-monotonically across amplitude: intermediate ranges frequently matched or exceeded the highest amplitudes, while combinations of amplitude ranges further improved classification. These findings demonstrate that informative fMRI structure is distributed across the ICA expression continuum and motivate representations that complement fixed ROI summaries and high-amplitude approaches.

papers.title: Language-associated brain representations covary with disruption of selfhood under psilocybin
papers.authors: Cooper G, Stoliker D, Astl Delgado VS, Blackburne G, Novelli L, Green DW, Das R, Razi A, Skipper JI.
papers.abstract: Language helps organise experience into an idiosyncratic, temporally extended sense of self. We therefore used fMRI to investigate whether greater similarity between subjects in the activity of language-associated brain regions accompanied psilocybin-induced loss of selfhood using fMRI. Participants heard music and viewed moving clouds at baseline and after 19 mg psilocybin. At each brain location and time point, we tested whether similarity increased with each pair’s summed rank on the Ego Dissolution Inventory (EDI; N=43). We grouped independent components of these associations by time course and decoded each group’s map with Neurosynth. Elementary visual imagery (SI; N=49) and baseline activity served as comparators. Under psilocybin, one group formed a distributed, left-lateralised frontotemporal network matching the Neurosynth language map (r=.382, spatial-null p<.001, q=.003), nearly twice the largest comparator estimate (SI: r=.208, p=.004, q=.028; baseline: r≤.12). In exploratory analyses, resting-state connectivity of this network decreased with posterior visual cortex and increased with thalamic and frontal regions. Participants with higher EDI scores showed larger changes (ρ=.455, Bonferroni-adjusted p=.048; SI: ρ=.008), most strongly for items describing loss of ego or identity (ρ=.43–.51; other items, ρ=.22–.33). We propose that language-associated systems incorporate each person’s semantic and autobiographical context into experience, and that disrupting them contributes to loss of ego and identity.

papers.title: Examining the Link Between Inflammation and Post-Operative Delirium in a Hip Fracture Repair Cohort of Older Adults.
papers.authors: Umoh ME, Wang N, Irwin KE, Sharma A, Leoutsakos J, Hamilton R, Lyketsos CG, Inouye SK, Marcantonio ER, Rosenberg PB, Neufeld KJ, Abadir P, Sieber F, Oh ES.
papers.abstract: Background Advancing age and neurodegenerative disease are risk factors for postoperative delirium; both are linked to dysregulation of the immune system and imbalances in inflammatory mediators in the brain. One such mediator, Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha Receptor 1 (TNFR1), is a marker of chronic inflammation. Delirium frequently affects older surgical patients and is associated with cognitive decline. While the pathophysiology of delirium is poorly understood, inflammation likely contributes to its development. Objective We hypothesized that older adults undergoing hip fracture repair with higher chronic inflammatory profiles (measured by Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha Receptor 1 (TNFR1) levels in CSF and plasma) would be at increased risk of delirium after surgery and cognitive decline. Methods We completed a secondary analysis of data from the Randomized clinical trial STRIDE (A-Strategy-to Reduce-the-Incidence-of-Postoperative-Delirium-in-Elderly-Patients) and analyzed preoperative TNFR1 levels. Delirium and delirium severity (preoperatively and days 1-5 postoperatively) were assessed, and cognition (Mini-Mental-State-Examination [MMSE] and Clinical-Dementia-Rating-sum-of-boxes [CDR-SB]) preoperatively and at 12 months to measure cognitive changes. We used logistic regression to model delirium and linear regression to model delirium severity as functions of TNFR1 levels, and random-intercept linear spline models to examine relationships between TNFR1 and cognitive changes. Results Delirium developed in 37% of patients. In unadjusted models, a 1-SD difference in plasma TNFR1 levels was positively associated with incident delirium (OR 1.40, 95%CI [1.02, 1.93]), while a 1-SD difference in preoperative CSF TNFR1 levels was not statistically associated with delirium (OR 1.22, 95% CI [0.90, 1.66]). In adjusted analyses, preoperative plasma TNFR1 was not significantly associated with delirium or delirium severity (β =0.001, p=0.411). No consistent relationship was observed between preoperative CSF or plasma TNFR1 levels and cognitive changes. Conclusion We observed an association between preoperative inflammation, as measured by plasma TNFR1 levels, and postoperative delirium; this was attenuated in adjusted analyses. Future studies exploring mechanisms associated with delirium are needed as this may uncover targets for management.

papers.title: White matter differences in adults with developmental language disorder
papers.authors: Abbott N, Banel S, Cler GJ.
papers.abstract: Developmental language disorder is a highly common yet underdiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder which impacts receptive and/or expressive language abilities and cannot be attributed to another etiology such as hearing loss or a lack of early exposure to language. There is very little research into the brain differences that characterize developmental language disorder, especially in adult populations In this study, we used diffusion MRI to determine whether adults with DLD show differences in white matter microstructure of the brain when compared to adults with typical language. Participants included 23 adults identified as meeting criteria for developmental language disorder, as well as a group of 26 adults with typical language. White matter microstructure was examined with fractional anisotropy via diffusion tensor imaging and precise biophysical models of intra-axonal signal fraction and orientation coherence via the Standard Model of diffusion imaging, using tractometry to evaluate microstructure differences along white matter tracts. Analysis showed reduced myelin integrity in DLD in the corpus callosum, but increased myelin integrity in the left superior longitudinal fasciculus. It is yet unclear whether differences exist in childhood and are retained into adulthood, are a result of different language environments during childhood, or are a result of behavioral and neural compensation.

papers.title: EEG in Parkinson’s Disease: Mechanisms, Biomarkers and Translational Opportunities
papers.authors: Özdemir S, Allouch S, Auffret M, Hassan M, Vérin M.
papers.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration and basal ganglia dysfunction, yet these pathophysiological abnormalities alone do not fully explain its heterogeneous motor and non-motor manifestations. Over recent decades, electroencephalography (EEG) has evolved from a primarily descriptive technique into a quantitative approach for investigating cortical electrophysiological dynamics associated with PD. Accumulating electrophysiological evidence implicates altered oscillatory synchronization and interactions across cortical and subcortical circuits in PD-related dysfunction, suggesting disturbances in the temporal coordination of neural activity. Emerging approaches, including large-scale datasets, multimodal integration, individualized modeling and wearable EEG technologies, offer opportunities for physiological phenotyping and real-world monitoring. However, methodological heterogeneity, limited reproducibility, insufficient external validation and uncertainty regarding clinical utility continue to constrain translation. This Review critically synthesizes EEG-derived measures spanning spectral activity, oscillatory coupling, functional connectivity and dynamic brain states, examining their relationships with motor, cognitive and neuropsychiatric manifestations of PD. By distinguishing mechanistic interpretations, clinical associations and current levels of biomarker validation, it identifies opportunities and requirements for translating EEG-derived measures into reliable tools for individualized assessment and clinical decision-making.

papers.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
papers.authors: Peterzell DH.
papers.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

papers.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Schizophrenia: From Circuit Dysfunction to Insight and Functional Recovery
papers.authors: Elsabbahy M, Mohammadi Y, Khojasteh Zonoozi A, Anwar d, Khan MNS, Wannasewok K, Wancata J.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia remains a major challenge in psychiatric practice, characterized by a heterogenous constellation of symptoms, including positive symptoms (e.g., hallucinations and delusions), negative symptoms (e.g., social withdrawal and diminished motivation), cognitive impairments, and frequently, lack of insight. Standard psychoeducation has served as a vital partner to psychological medicine for decades, trying to reduce the relapse rates by emphasizing medication adherence. However, many conventional models often rely on descriptive clinical phenomenology that fails to resonate with the patient’s subjective experience and rarely explain the neurological causes behind the hallucinations or illogical thinking. This disconnection can inadvertently reinforce stigma and fail to support the patient's remaining cognitive capacities to reinforce recovery. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) emerges as a transformative paradigm, integrating cutting-edge insights from brain science into the educational dialogue. By establishing the explanation of symptoms in neurobiology and shifting the narrative from "mental illness" to "circuit dysfunction", NIPE aims to bypass psychological defenses, objectify the disorder, and foster a collaborative therapeutic alliance. This chapter presents the neurocognitive aspects of the psychoeducational content, the neurocognitive considerations that must be addressed when providing psychoeducation, and examples of NIPE for Schizophrenia, aiming to advance brain health literacy for practitioners who will support patients as active partners in recovery alongside daily functional restoration. Keywords: Schizophrenia; Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation; Psychoeducation; Neurocognition; Brain Health Literacy; Therapeutic Alliance; Patient Education

papers.title: MRI-Guided High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound in Movement Disorders: Targeting Pathologic Brain Circuits With Precision Imaging, From the AJR Special Series on Critical Anatomy.
papers.authors: Asturias A, Saez-Calveras N, Yu J, Feltrin F, Jha M, Sharma V, Maldjian JA, O'Suillebhain P, Shah BR.
papers.abstract: MRI-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (MRgHIFU) has emerged as an alternative to other neuromodulatory interventions for patients with medically refractory movement disorders, including open surgery, radiosurgery, and deep brain stimulation. Microelectrode recordings permit refinement of indirect targets during open procedures for movement disorders. However, their use is not possible during incisionless procedures, including MRgHIFU. Traditional MRgHIFU using indirect targets yields limited efficacy or adverse effects from anatomic or functional variability. Furthermore, the clinical efficacy associated with indirect targeting of subcortical gray matter structures is increasingly recognized as resulting from circuitwide neuromodulation distributed along white matter pathways. Additionally, diffusion tensor imaging tractography and white matter-nulled sequences (e.g., fast gray matter acquisition T1 inversion recovery) now enable patient-specific targeting of pathologic brain circuits. These developments are prompting growing interest in MRgHIFU for direct targeting of disease-specific white matter tracts. In essential tremor, dentatorubrothalamic tract targeting by MRgHIFU has shown high tremor suppression with few adverse effects; in Parkinson disease, pallidothalamic tract targeting has likewise emerged as a promising intervention. These tract-based approaches can leverage patient-specific targeting to improve precision, efficacy, and safety. Future developments, including artificial intelligence-driven approaches, are expected to enhance MRgHIFU targeting and broaden its role in personalized movement disorder therapy.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evaluation of Psilocybin in Neurodegenerative Disorders: Relevance of 5-HT2A Receptors and Downstream Pathways.
papers.authors: Chaudhary S, Dhankhar S, Saini M, Singh TG, Chauhan S, Kumar V.
papers.abstract: More than fifty million individuals worldwide are experiencing neurodegenerative disorders, which include Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, multiple sclerosis, and frontotemporal dementia. These disorders have a significant role in the gradual degradation of cognition and motor skills. Most current treatment approaches have little effect on changing the course of the disease and are largely symptomatic. Psilocybin, a naturally occurring tryptamine alkaloid from psilocybin mushrooms, has become a promising medicinal agent because of its hallucinogenic, neuroprotective, and neuroplastic properties. After being metabolically transformed into its active form, psilocin, it primarily activates serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and neurotrophic signaling pathways such as BDNF/TrkB and mTOR, which regulate synaptic remodeling, dendritic complexity, neurogenesis, neuroinflammatory response, and default mode network connectivity, all of which are linked to depression and dementia. Preclinical research studies demonstrate that psilocybin increases hippocampal plasticity, restores dendritic complexity, lowers proinflammatory cytokine levels, and promotes fear extinction in experimental models of stress, ischemic stroke, and neurodegeneration. Emerging clinical studies also indicate that individuals with moderate cognitive impairment, early-onset Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease may see long-term decreases in anxiety and depression as well as improvements in cognitive function, frequently after a single dose administration. Additionally, psilocybin has demonstrated promise in treating mental comorbidities that often accompany neurodegenerative illness, such as treatment-resistant depression, drug use disorders, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, there are still significant obstacles to overcome, such as optimizing dosing schedules, assessing safety issues such as temporary perceptual abnormalities and cardiovascular consequences, and translating preclinical results into extensive phase -III clinical studies. This review incorporates the most recent data on psilocybin's chemistry, pharmacology, metabolism, and mechanistic actions; it highlights the drug's therapeutic potential across a variety of neurodegenerative diseases and emphasizes the necessity of carefully planned randomized controlled trials to determine clinical efficacy, long-term safety, and its place in multimodal treatment approaches.

papers.title: Severe Hypoxic-ischaemic Encephalopathy and Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Following Accidental Butane Exposure: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Tiburzi SP, Nistico' R, Stivala V, De Luca A, Justiz-Pérez I, Putignano A, Vescio V.
papers.abstract: Background Butane is a highly lipophilic aliphatic hydrocarbon widely used as a domestic fuel and aerosol propellant. Acute exposure in enclosed environments may cause severe neurological and cardiovascular toxicity through oxygen displacement, respiratory depression, myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines, and potentially direct toxic effects. Case presentation A 45-year-old woman was found unconscious in a small, closed studio apartment, while her husband was found deceased in the same environment. Subsequent inspection by the judicial authorities identified deterioration of the gas tubing associated with a gas leak. The patient presented in deep coma (Glasgow Coma Scale score 5) and required tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Initial carboxyhaemoglobin was 16.9% and progressively normalised during oxygen therapy. Brain imaging demonstrated extensive cortical, deep grey matter, brainstem, cerebellar, and white-matter abnormalities consistent with severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury. Cardiac evaluation showed mild ST-segment elevation, increased cardiac biomarkers, and severe transient Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction (LVEF 25%) with a pattern highly suggestive of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy; LVEF subsequently improved to 44%. Severe neurological impairment persisted, and the patient was transferred to neurological rehabilitation. She died approximately six months after the index event; reliable documentation of the precise cause of death was unavailable. Conclusion This case illustrates the severe neurological and cardiovascular consequences that may follow accidental butane exposure in an enclosed environment. The coexistence of extensive hypoxic- ischaemic brain injury and transient stress-related ventricular dysfunction highlights the importance of integrated neurological, cardiological, and toxicological assessment.

papers.title: Lactoferrin-Modified Ultra-Sustained Release Propofol Nanoparticles for Multi-Pathway Therapy of Depression via Intraperitoneal Injection.
papers.authors: Wu Z, Deng J, Li S, Yu L, Zhang H, Xun Y, Bian J, Liu J, Zhang J, Lei P, Ma Q, Fan Y, Yang Z, Zhu F, Ma X, Wu D, Zhang S.
papers.abstract: Background Depression imposes a significant burden on global public health, and traditional antidepressants are limited by slow onset, low efficacy, and high recurrence rates. Intraperitoneal injection of propofol can rapidly exert anti-anhedonic effects by regulating the VTA-NAc dopaminergic and GABAergic signaling pathways. However, its application in depression treatment is limited by rapid systemic clearance, poor brain permeability, and significant systemic toxicity. Moreover, the simple lipophilic structure of propofol and the limited drug-loading and long-term controlled-release performance of conventional physically encapsulated nanocarriers hinder the development of long-acting propofol formulations. Methods Lactoferrin-functionalized PVA-propofol nanoparticles (LF-PVA@Pro NPs) were prepared based on the strong intermolecular affinity between PVA and propofol, as validated by molecular dynamics simulations. Their physicochemical properties, in vitro release behavior, brain-targeting efficiency, biosafety, and in vivo antidepressant efficacy were systematically characterized using CRS-induced depressive mouse models through multiple behavioral and histological assessments. Results LF-PVA@Pro NPs achieved a drug loading of 19.3% and exhibited sustained in vitro release for 100 h. Following intraperitoneal injection, the formulation maintained therapeutic brain concentrations for 100 h (6-8-fold longer than free propofol) and increased cerebral drug accumulation by 2.5-fold. Its LD50 was 2802 mg/kg, 2.36-fold higher than that of free propofol, ensuring safety at the therapeutic dose of 40 mg/kg. In vivo studies demonstrated that LF-PVA@Pro NPs markedly alleviated depressive- and anxiety-like phenotypes, reduced VTA/NAc neuronal injury, and restored c-Fos, GABA, and DAT expression, thereby reactivating reward circuits. Conclusion LF-modified ultra-sustained brain-targeted nanoparticles enable multi-pathway long-term depression intervention, offering a translatable strategy to repurpose propofol as a rapid-onset antidepressant for chronic stress-related depression.

papers.title: Cellular senescence changes and their association with brain structure in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder
papers.authors: Okada N, Seitz-Holland J, Ikegame T, Omileke F, Kiyota M, Shoji E, Mori S, Morita S, Koshiyama D, Satomura Y, Koike S, JINDE S, Yagishita S, Kamiya K, Abe O, Shenton M, Kubicki M, Kasai K.
