papers.abstract: Abstract Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and major depressive disorder (MDD) may experience accelerated biological aging, potentially linked to cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP index has been reported to be elevated in MDD, its status in SZ and its relationship with brain structure remain unclear. This study investigated whether the SASP index, a composite biomarker-based measure, is elevated in SZ and MDD, and examined its associations with brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) and regional brain morphology across SZ, MDD, and healthy controls (HCs). A total of 119 subjects (29 individuals with SZ, 40 individuals with MDD, and 50 HCs) underwent both peripheral blood collection and MRI scanning. First, across all subjects, the effects of diagnostic groups on SASP indices were assessed. Second, associations between age-adjusted SASP indices and brain-PAD were examined within each diagnostic group. Third, exploratory analyses tested associations between SASP indices and subcortical volumes as well as cortical thickness and surface area in each diagnostic group. We found a significant main effect of diagnostic group on SASP indices and significantly elevated SASP indices in both SZ and MDD. Although no significant associations were observed between SASP indices and brain-PAD in any diagnostic group, negative associations were identified in SZ between SASP indices and the surface area of the left transverse temporal gyrus and the right inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis, regions that play pivotal roles in auditory and language processing alterations observed in SZ. These findings suggest that SASP-related processes may contribute to the neural underpinnings of SZ through localized, rather than global, alterations in brain structure.

papers.title: Economic and Financial Burden of Traumatic Brain Injury Care in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Hassan AA, dirie MA, heyle YM, Salah Ma, Jama MS, Abdullahi Ahmed Ali1, Kiswezi A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) places a heavy financial strain on health systems, patients, families, and caregivers, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains fragmented. This scoping review mapped the economic and financial burden of TBI across LMICs and identified the main gaps in the evidence. Methods We conducted a systematic scoping review reported according to PRISMA-ScR. The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework on 12 September 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/4DQC9). We searched MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar between July and September 2026, supplemented by citation searching. We included empirical studies from World Bank FY2027 low-, lower-middle-, and upper-middle-income economies reporting direct medical or non-medical costs, out-of-pocket expenditure, catastrophic health expenditure, distress financing, productivity losses, caregiver burden, rehabilitation costs, provider or health-system expenditure, societal costs, or affordability barriers. Monetary estimates were kept in original currencies, with author-reported US dollar equivalents where available. Results Twenty studies from 14 LMICs, published between 2008 and 2026, met the inclusion criteria. Hospital or direct costs were reported in 17 studies, indirect or caregiver burden in 7, household financial burden in 5, rehabilitation or post-acute costs in 3, health-system or societal burden in 2, and affordability or access in 1. Greater TBI severity, intensive care, surgery, neuroimaging, complications, and longer hospitalization were generally linked to higher costs. Household studies documented out-of-pocket spending, catastrophic expenditure, income loss, and distress financing. In Tanzania, 15 of 67 patients could not pay for care, and affordability shaped treatment intensity. Evidence on long-term rehabilitation, caregiver productivity loss, and societal costs was limited. Conclusions TBI in LMICs drives substantial provider and household costs, including catastrophic expenditure, income loss, and affordability-related barriers to care. More standardized economic studies are needed to inform trauma-system financing, financial protection, and resource allocation.

papers.title: Sex-dependent differences in matrix metalloproteinase-9 and inflammatory markers in postmortem brain of depressed subjects: Effect of pharmacological treatment and suicide
papers.authors: Pilar-Cuellar F, Senserrich J, Grosselle T, Florensa-Zanuy E, Díaz Á, Pazos A, Callado LF, Meana JJ, Castro E.
papers.abstract: Abstract Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder affected by genetic and environmental factors and associated with inflammation and impaired neuroplasticity. This study investigated the role of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), inflammatory markers (STAT3 and NF-κB), and the neuroplasticity marker BDNF in the prefrontal cortex of subjects with MDD and their matched controls. The results showed increased MMP-9 expression and activity in MDD, particularly in those without detectable antidepressant treatment and in subjects who died by suicide. The association with suicide was especially pronounced in women, suggesting sex-dependent differences. Regarding inflammation, untreated subjects showed higher STAT3 and NF-κB levels, while antidepressant-treated subjects showed reduced STAT3 levels, particularly men, suggesting a possible anti-inflammatory effect of antidepressants. In addition, treated men showed higher BDNF levels, which may reflect enhanced neuroplasticity. Overall, this study suggests that MMP-9 may be a potential marker of depression severity and suicidal behavior, especially in women, while neuroinflammation may play a more prominent role in men. These findings further highlight the importance of considering sex differences when investigating the role of MMP-9 in the pathophysiology of MDD.

papers.title: Longitudinal neurochemical profiling after experimental stroke using edited MR spectroscopy
papers.authors: Grigoras IF, Clarke WT, Tachrount M, Gill L, Ligneul C, Cherix A, Lavda M, Szulc-Lerch K, Lerch JP, Stagg CJ, Couch Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Alterations in excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission contribute to stroke pathology and recovery, yet longitudinal assessment of these changes in vivo remains limited. We investigated the feasibility of longitudinal edited proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy ( 1 H-MRS) to quantify γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glutamate following experimental focal cerebral ischaemia. Methods Male Wistar Han rats underwent endothelin-1-induced striatal ischaemia or sham surgery. Longitudinal edited 1 H-MRS was performed at baseline and 2-, 7- and 30-days post-stroke. A voxel was positioned within the ipsilesional motor cortex adjacent to the lesion. Behavioural outcomes (grip strength, adhesive removal and CatWalk gait analysis) were assessed alongside spectroscopy, and immunohistochemistry for Iba1, GFAP and ICAM-1 was performed at 30 days. Results Stroke induced a transient reduction in GABA+/tCr within the ipsilesional motor cortex, with significantly lower concentrations than sham animals at 7 days (p < 0.05), returning to baseline by 30 days. Glutamate/tCr and GABA/glutamate ratio were unchanged throughout the study. Behavioural deficits were mild, with significant effects on motor outcomes such as grip strength, gait swing speed and paw placement, while sensory areas of the brain seemed largely unaffected. Histological analysis revealed no persistent differences in cortical Iba1, GFAP or ICAM-1 immunoreactivity at 30 days. Conclusions Longitudinal 1 H-MRS is a feasible approach for monitoring dynamic changes in inhibitory neurochemistry following experimental stroke. The transient reduction in peri-lesional GABA, despite minimal behavioural impairment and an absence of persistent cortical inflammation, supports the use of edited spectroscopy as a translational tool to investigate neurochemical mechanisms underlying network dynamics in post-stroke recovery.

papers.title: Peripheral BDNF regulation and inflammation in bipolar disorder: a multimodal study
papers.authors: Feliciani B, Girone N, Cavallotto C, Saluzzi S, Martella F, Bartolomeo MD, Bondi E, Pettorruso M, Granzotto A, Gesi C, Cremaschi L, Macellaro M, Giorgio AD, Martinotti G, Dell’Osso BM, D’Addario C.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Bipolar disorder (BD) is a severe, recurrent psychiatric condition in which neuroplasticity, inflammatory and epigenetic mechanisms are implicated but incompletely characterised. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is among the most investigated candidate biomarkers, yet its relationship to clinical staging, DNA methylation, microRNA regulation and peripheral inflammation remains unclear. This study integrates peripheral BDNF gene expression, BDNF promoter I and IV methylation, rs6265-CpG methylation, four BDNF -targeting salivary extracellular vesicle (EV)-associated miRNAs and eight peripheral cytokines in a multicentre cohort of BD patients stratified by clinical stage. Methods One hundred and thirty-four individuals with BD and 131 healthy controls were recruited across three Italian psychiatric centres within the BOARDING-PASS study. BDNF mRNA and cytokines were quantified from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) by qRT-PCR; BDNF promoter methylation was assessed by pyrosequencing; salivary EV miRNAs were profiled by qRT-PCR. Associations with clinical stage, childhood adversity (CTQ), pharmacotherapy and global functioning were examined. Results Peripheral BDNF mRNA was markedly reduced in BD patients versus controls (median 0.31 versus 1.45; p = 5.1×10⁻⁷), present from the earliest clinical stage and not deepening with progression. No BDNF methylation difference was detected at any of thirteen CpG sites (all q > 0.23). Among four pre-specified BDNF -targeting miRNAs, miR-16-5p was nominally elevated (p = 0.038) but did not survive correction. IFN-γ was the only cytokine significantly elevated after FDR correction (q = 0.003); IL-1β showed a nominal increase (p = 0.028). Within patients, BDNF expression correlated positively with most cytokines (IL-2 ρ = +0.82), indicating shared transcriptional co-regulation. Higher childhood adversity was associated with lower methylation at the rs6265 CpG (ρ = −0.46, q = 0.001). BDNF expression correlated inversely with global functioning (GAF: ρ = −0.23, p = 0.012) and was selectively elevated in BD-II patients receiving antidepressants (p = 0.009), with no parallel effect in BD-I. Conclusions Peripheral BDNF dysregulation in BD is better described as a multilayer, largely trait-related alteration than as a linear marker of illness progression. The expression deficit, its positive coupling to peripheral inflammation, its association with functioning, and the adversity-related epigenetic mark at rs6265 constitute convergent signals that do not map onto clinical stage. A composite, rigorously replicated biomarker strategy — integrating neurotrophic, immune and epigenetic readouts — appears more informative than any single molecule for characterising BD biology.

papers.title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis Reveals a Coordinated Molecular Signature of Neuroresilience in human MAPT-knockout hiPSC-derived Neurons with relevance for Alzheimer’s and Neurodegenerative Disease
papers.authors: Jajin EA, Zempel H.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Transcriptome data provides a robust analytical viewpoint about cellular processes in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD). Integrative multiomics analysis including transcriptome and proteome data elucidates the underlying mechanisms of this progressive disease. The microtubule-associated protein Tau ( MAPT ) is central to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathogenesis. We demonstrated that Tau loss confers resistance to amyloid-beta (Aβ) toxicity in AD-relevant human glutamatergic neurons, but the active molecular reprogramming driving this neuroresilience remains poorly defined. Methods We employed an integrative multiomics approach, combining temporal transcriptomics (3h and 24h post-Aβ exposure) with newly processed proteomic layers from terminally differentiated and electrophysiologically active human iPSC-derived neurons (WT vs. MAPT -Knockout (KO)). Analysis included DESeq2, WGCNA, and GSEA, followed by cross-layer integration to identify convergent molecular signatures and master regulators. Results Our analysis revealed a striking transcriptomic stagnation in WT neurons, which failed to mount an adaptive response to Aβ stress. In contrast, MAPT -KO neurons exhibited a pre-established resilience signature characterized by profound baseline reprogramming. WGCNA identified a co-expression gene cluster (turquoise module, r = 0.74) strongly associated with the MAPT -KO phenotype and enriched in mitochondrial transport, autophagy, and synaptic homeostasis. Key hub genes including SIM1, INPP5F, and AKR1C2 established a mitochondrial metabolic defense mechanism. Multiomics integration identified 27 core consensus hits (e.g., COL17A1, PER3, ST3GAL6) consistently preserved across both layers. Furthermore, transcription factor enrichment identified KLF4 (Kruppel-like Factor 4), a key regulator of neuronal differentiation and metabolic adaptation, as the master regulator orchestrating this protective network. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that Tau deletion induces an active, multilevel gain-of-resilience rather than passive resistance. By identifying a KLF4-driven molecular signature, this study highlights novel therapeutic targets that could be leveraged to induce synthetic resilience in AD patients, protecting neurons from amyloid-induced bioenergetic and structural collapse.

papers.title: Beyond Gray Matter: White Matter Functional Network Signatures of Major Depressive Disorder Track Symptom Severity
papers.authors: Calhoun V, Sridhar M, Baker B.
papers.abstract: Abstract Resting-state neuroimaging studies in major depressive disorder (MDD) have consistently identified abnormalities across large-scale gray matter (GM) networks, including the default mode, salience, and sensorimotor systems. Although prior work has primarily focused on GM, evidence suggests that white matter (WM) hemodynamic signals are meaningful and reliable, supporting an active role for WM in brain function. A key gap remains in understanding WM functional network connectivity (FNC) and spectral characteristics in MDD. We used resting-state fMRI scans from the MDD-DIRECT phase II study, comprising 1,944 participants across 13 sites, to examine WM FNC and spectral characteristics in individuals with MDD and healthy controls using a spatially constrained independent component analysis (ICA) framework. This hybrid framework leverages ICA’s ability to identify spatially robust, functionally meaningful brain networks guided by replicable spatial priors to examine WM (1) FNC differences and (2) spectral power alterations between MDD and healthy participants. MDD was characterized by reduced long-range integrative connectivity alongside increased localized and limbic–sensorimotor coupling within WM networks, highlighting a systems-level imbalance in neural communication that may underlie core cognitive, affective, and somatic symptoms of depression. We also observed reduced low-frequency spectral power within frontal and subcortical WM systems involved in cognitive control, emotional regulation, and decision-making. Notably, both functional and spectral alterations were associated with clinical measures of depression and anxiety, with opposing associations observed for frontal connectivity patterns. Studying WM function alongside GM may provide a more comprehensive understanding of functional pathology in depression.

papers.title: Frequency-Specific Age Associations in EEG Microstate Dynamics Across the Adult Lifespan
papers.authors: Sanjar K, Tarailis P, Griskova-Bulanova I.
papers.abstract: Abstract EEG microstates are conventionally derived from broadband signals, although their temporal dynamics may differ across frequency ranges. Whether age associations in conventional voltage microstates are similarly frequency specific remains unclear. We examined resting-state EEG from 60 healthy adults aged 20–78 years and derived microstates separately from broadband (1–30 Hz), delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), and beta (15–30 Hz) activity. The number of microstates was selected independently for each band using the Krzanowski–Lai criterion, yielding four classes for broadband, delta, alpha, and beta, and five for theta. Age associations were tested for duration, occurrence, coverage, global explained variance, observed transition probabilities, and transitions adjusted for those expected from class prevalence, with false-discovery-rate correction. Age associations showed a marked spectral dependence. Of 84 state-level tests, 13 survived correction: one in broadband, six in delta, one in theta, none in alpha, and five in beta. In delta, increasing age was associated with greater expression of MS B and reduced expression of MS C across duration, occurrence, and coverage. In beta, age was associated with greater MS A expression and reduced MS C expression. All significant state-level associations remained after adjustment for sex, education, and band-specific spectral power. Eight observed transition associations survived correction, all in broadband and delta, but only three remained after accounting for transitions expected from state prevalence. These findings indicate that age-related variation in EEG microstate dynamics is strongly frequency-specific and is expressed primarily through redistribution of state expression rather than through widespread alteration of transition preference. Frequency-resolved microstate analysis, hence, reveals age associations that are not evident in conventional broadband analysis.

papers.title: Neural correlates of cognitive enhancement after probiotic supplementation
papers.authors: Kim S, Kang S, Choi YY, Choi K, Lee KH.
papers.abstract: Abstract A previous randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial demonstrated that multistrain probiotic supplementation improved visuospatial cognitive performance in older adults with early cognitive impairment. Participants from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 68; probiotic, n = 32; placebo, n = 36) underwent T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging at baseline and after 52 weeks. Cortical surface area and thickness were quantified using FreeSurfer-based surface morphometry. Between-group differences in longitudinal changes were assessed using t-tests and analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline values and demographic covariates. Compared with placebo, the probiotic group showed increased surface area in the left lingual gyrus (+ 21.53 vs. −54.39 mm², p = 3.12 × 10⁻⁴) and cuneus (+ 5.31 vs. −26.28 mm², p = 0.002). Cortical thickness decreased modestly in these regions in the probiotic group. Structural changes in the lingual gyrus and cuneus were associated with visuospatial cognitive performance. Multistrain probiotic supplementation was associated with region-specific longitudinal cortical changes in the left lingual gyrus and cuneus, particularly in cortical surface area. These morphometric changes were associated with visuospatial cognitive performance in older adults with early cognitive impairment.

papers.title: The effects of Arf4 gene knockdown on Alzheimer's amyloid β deposition: Possible role in cognitive resilience
papers.authors: Hemmati S, Wang E, Wang M, Xie B, Salton S, Haroutunian V, Bennett D, Xu P, Peng J, Gandy S, Zhang B, Ehrlich M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Studying the factors involved in cellular and cognitive resilience is a crucial step toward designing preventive and targeted therapeutic approaches for Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Methods Systematic analysis of the proteomic landscape in the advanced aging populations identified ADP ribosylation factor 4 (ARF4) as one of the key driver genes associated with resilience among the oldest-old (OO) non-demented individuals. To assess the effects of Arf4 gene knockdown in AD animal models, we generated APP KM670/671NL x PSEN1 Δexon9 (PSAPP)/ Arf4 +/− mice. Results Protein signatures and protein coexpression network modules of the oldest-old (OO) non-demented individuals were identified. Integrative protein network analysis further revealed ARF4 as a top protein driver of OO. Mouse experiments showed that Arf4 knockdown was associated with increased amyloid plaque burden and enhanced microglial activity. The consequence of Arf4 knockdown was an alteration in amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization, which led to variations in mature APP levels. Arf4 knockdown further led to transcriptomic alterations in the mouse brain; most pronounced in pathways associated with immune regulation and microglial homeostasis. Conclusion Based on the exacerbated AD pathological features and transcriptomic alterations observed in Arf4 knockdown animals, ARF4 appears to play a critical role in AD resilience and may represent a potential prognostic factor worthy of further investigation.

papers.title: NPC-EVs ameliorate ischemic brain injury by enhancing microglial phagocytosis and anti- inflammatory responses via TREM2-mediated lipid metabolic reprogramming
papers.authors: Zhang L, Wei W, Xin W, Hou G, Xu X, Yang X, Pan Y, Jia F, Zhang X.
papers.abstract: Abstract Inflammation is one of the hallmarks during the pathophysiology of ischemic stroke, among which microglia, as resident immune cells of the brain, play a pivotal role. Despite the latter, recent studies analyzing the precise mechanism by which microglia affect post-stroke neurological outcome remain somewhat limited. Elucidating these mechanisms, however, remains a prerequisite before translational stroke trials are in order. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), significant mediators of intercellular communication, have been demonstrated to possess multiple function of neural repair and neuroregeneration in the pathogenesis and progression of CNS diseases. However, the regulatory role of neural progenitor cell-derived EVs (NPC-EVs) on the phagocytic capacity of microglia post-stroke remains elusive. Using an in vitro stroke model, NPC-EVs effectively drive cultured microglia towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype. Such morphological changes correlate with distinct functional properties of these microglia, which show reduced secretion patterns of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. In line with this, secretion patterns of anti-inflammatory products are significantly increased, facilitating the efficiency of microglial phagocytosis dependent on TREM2-centric pathways in an in vitro stroke model. NPC-EVs mitigate neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis via modulating microglial lipid metabolism, yielding improved neurological recovery in ischemic stroke mice. This provides a novel paradigm for EV-mediated intercellular communication mechanisms and suggests a promising therapeutic potential for NPC-derived EVs in the treatment of ischemic stroke.

papers.title: Effects of Metformin on Resting-State EEG and Associations with Adaptive Behaviors in Fragile X Syndrome
papers.authors: Lippé S, Buckser R, Davoudi S, Arutiunian V, Knoth ISK, Thurman A, Bélanger A, Martin C, Proteau-Lemieux M, Santos E, Rubanarayana K, Pham T, Whitlock K, Bennett J, Tassone F, Kim K, Biag H, Hessl D, Schneider A, Abbeduto L, Jacquemont S, Bolduc F, Hagerman R.
papers.abstract: Abstract Metformin has emerged as a candidate drug for Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) after promising results in animal studies and small-scale trials. A three-site registered clinical trial (RCT) demonstrated effects of metformin on behavioral symptoms in FXS in participants aged 6–11. Resting state electroencephalography (RS-EEG) was also collected during the RCT. We present results from analyses of RS-EEG and associated adaptive behavior measures. We observed significant metformin treatment effects on EEG measures associated with cortical excitation/inhibition balance (periodic gamma), brain maturation (periodic alpha), and signal complexity. Significantly affected EEG measures moved toward values associated with typical development. We also observed associations between more typical EEG activity and improved adaptive behavior scores in the treatment group. Additional significant effects and associations were observed when considering only participants without molecular mosaic. Results confirm metformin’s potential as a treatment option and encourage further research into its effects on functional brain activity.

papers.title: DeepSUM-DWI: A Joint Image Registration and Super-Resolution Convolutional Neural Network for Diffusion-Weighted MRI
papers.authors: Daniells Zaldívar C, García-Gomar MG, Ocampo Luna P, Solís-Pérez JE, Concha L, Fair MJ.
papers.abstract: Background: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is an important MRI technique for studying tissue microstructure and structural connectivity, but is limited by relatively low spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and sensitivity to inter-acquisition motion. A deep-learning framework was developed that jointly performs image registration and super-resolution on repeated low-resolution DWI inputs to generate a single registered, higher apparent spatial-resolution output. Methods: DeepSUM-DWI adapts a DeepSUM multi-image super-resolution architecture for repeated DWI. It comprises a shared 2D super-resolution feature extractor (SISRNet), a registration network (RegNet), and a 3D fusion network (FusionNet). Evaluation used (1) simulated repetitions with synthetic motion, (2) retrospectively downsampled acquisitions from 12 subjects, and (3) a prospective dual-resolution example with matched 1.0 × 1.0 and 2.0 × 2.0 mm² acquisitions. Results: DeepSUM-DWI reconstructed a single high-resolution-appearing DWI image from multiple low-resolution repetitions while preserving structural characteristics of the high-resolution acquisitions. The model remained robust across synthetic motion magnitudes. In retrospectively downsampled data, it improved NRMSE by 71–79% and PSNR by 10.6–13.5 dB, for super-resolution factors of 2–3, relative to averaging interpolated low-resolution images, with a mean SSIM > 0.99. In prospectively acquired data, it recovered finer structures than visible in the acquired low-resolution images while maintaining contrast consistency. Exploratory diffusion analysis suggested that some gains in apparent detail propagated to FA maps. Conclusions: DeepSUM-DWI provides a framework for joint registration and super-resolution of repeated DWI acquisitions, with potential to improve apparent spatial resolution while retaining the SNR benefits of repeated acquisition.

papers.title: Context-Dependent Functional Diversity of Dorsomedial Posterior Parietal Neurons Revealed by Single-Unit FMRI Mapping during Naturalistic Viewing.
papers.authors: Zhou X, Wang L, Tam SKE, Ortiz-Rios M, Yin D, Kwok SC.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: The dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (dmPPC) plays an important role in episodic processing by integrating sensory, cognitive, and motor information across distributed brain systems. However, how individual dmPPC neurons participate in large-scale functional organization during naturalistic experience remains poorly understood. To address this question, we combined single-unit electrophysiology and awake fMRI in five rhesus macaques of both sexes viewing identical naturalistic video stimuli. Using single-unit fMRI mapping, we generated whole-brain neuron-BOLD functional maps by correlating individual neuronal activity with voxel-wise fMRI signals across the brain. We found that neuron-BOLD functional maps exhibited strong context-dependent organization, with neurons recorded during the same video context showing substantially greater similarity than neurons recorded during different video conditions. Compared with neuronal spiking activity or critical fMRI frames alone, neuron-BOLD functional maps more robustly captured contextual structure. Despite this shared large-scale organization, a substantial subset of neighboring neurons recorded simultaneously from the same electrode displayed markedly distinct whole-brain association patterns, revealing substantial local functional heterogeneity within the dmPPC. This local heterogeneity was not readily explained by waveform-based putative cell class or by opposing neuronal firing dynamics. In addition, distributed cortical and medial temporal regions exhibited highly context-dependent neuron-BOLD association patterns during naturalistic viewing. Together, these findings demonstrate that dmPPC neurons participate in dynamic and heterogeneous large-scale functional organization during naturalistic episodic processing. More broadly, this study establishes single-unit fMRI mapping as a framework for linking single-neuron activity to distributed whole-brain dynamics across contextual conditions.

papers.title: Individualized Network Topography in Pre-adolescent Children and Adults Using Naturalistic Precision fMRI.
papers.authors: Rai S, Godfrey KJ, Graff K, Tansey R, Merrikh D, Yin S, Feigelis M, Demeter DV, Vanderwal T, Greene DJ, Bray S.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Group-averaged network definitions, commonly used in developmental functional connectivity research, limit our understanding of how network topography may change with age and can lead to inaccurate estimates of age effects on intra- and inter-network functional connectivity. Here, we collected a precision fMRI dataset from 24 parent-child pairs (children 6-8 years, 13 females; adults 33-47 years, 12 females) during passive video viewing and derived individual template-matched functional network maps from 60 min of motion-censored data per participant. Overall, large-scale network architecture was broadly shared between children and adults, with no age effects observed for network-level surface area, few age differences in network boundaries, and generally lower assignment confidence in children. Considering interindividual similarity in network topography, association networks showed stronger within-family similarity and no overall effect of age on similarity of networks between pairs of individuals. We further asked how individualized network definitions might impact estimates of age effects on dense functional connectivity. While all approaches pointed to greater within-network functional connectivity in adults, we found that individualized approaches had larger age effects and lower sensitivity to head motion. Together, our results suggest that, relative to adults, preadolescent children show reduced network assignment confidence and weaker within-network connectivity but limited differences in network borders and size and underscore the value of individualized mapping for improving topographic reliability and increasing sensitivity to age effects.

papers.title: Machine Learning Framework for Integration of Video and EEG Reveals Distinct Seizure Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Epilepsy.
papers.authors: Liu CJ, Martin C, Lee AC, Sands TT, Frankel WN, Makinson CD.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Video-electrocorticogram (VEEG) recordings are the gold-standard diagnostic tool for detecting and characterizing seizures in rodent models of seizure and epilepsy. Manual/visual scoring remains the prevailing strategy despite significant limitations. Alternatively, automated and semi-automated analyses have been applied to either EEG or video features alone but integrating these disparate data forms presents a challenge that has not been sufficiently addressed. Here, we introduce an integrated machine learning pipeline that jointly leverages EEG and behavioral video data to enable scalable and objective event classification. Integrated video-EEG analysis was initially validated using a well-established pharmacologically induced seizure paradigm in male mice, where overt generalized motor seizures provide a clear benchmark. We then tested the pipeline on a genetic mouse model of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) that displays a complex spike-wave discharge (SWD) seizure phenotype that poses significant challenges for traditional scoring methods. Machine learning-powered integrated analysis of video-EEG recordings outperformed unimodal EEG- or video-based approaches and performed favorably to experienced rodent EEG electrophysiologists while also uncovering distinct phenotypic relationships, including classes of atypical behavioral and typical non-behavioral SWD events. This framework provides a flexible tool for high-throughput, precise analysis of VEEG data, with potential to accelerate discovery in epilepsy and seizure research. Furthermore, this approach represents a generalizable strategy for the integration of diverse neurobehavioral time series data types.Significance Statement Seizure detection in animal models of epilepsy has relied heavily on manual analysis of video-EEG recordings, a process that is slow and subjective. We present a machine learning pipeline that integrates EEG and video data from mice to classify seizures with high accuracy. This work was validated across two models, first a pharmacologically induced generalized seizure model, and second, a spontaneous spike-wave discharge (SWD) model in genetic epilepsy. Our approach detected events missed by human reviewers and revealed previously uncharacterized SWD subtypes distinguished by their behavior. By combining open-source tools in a flexible framework, this work lowers the barrier to high-throughput, unbiased seizure phenotyping, and also offers a broadly applicable strategy for linking neural activity to behavior in neuroscience research.

papers.title: Unveiling the mysteries: neuroprotective potential of Mucuna monosperma seeds in combating haloperidol induced Parkinsonism.
papers.authors: Bhong P, Ingale S, Jadhav P.
papers.abstract: Objectives Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction and loss of dopaminergic neurons. Oxidative stress, defined as detrimental imbalance between free radicals and body's defense mechanism, is a critical contributing factor. This study evaluated the neuroprotective and antioxidant properties of methanolic extract of Mucuna monosperma seeds (MMMS) in haloperidol induced rat model of PD. Methods PD was induced in rats by intraperitoneal administration of haloperidol (HPD, D2 blocker) at 1 mg/kg for 21 days. MMMS was administered orally at 100, 200, and 400 mg/kg. Motor abilities were assessed using the catalepsy bar test, actophotometer test, and rotarod test. Biochemical assessments measured markers of oxidative stress, and brain dopamine levels. Histopathological analysis was used to evaluate neuronal integrity. Results Motor abilities were tested weekly for 21 days, followed by biochemical and histological analysis. HPD caused motor deficits, raised oxidative stress, and lowered dopamine. MMMS (400 mg/kg) improved motor function by decreasing catalepsy, increasing locomotion, and prolonging rotarod time (p < 0.0001). It also reduced oxidative stress, nearly normalized dopamine. Also, the levels of endogenous antioxidants like glutathione (GSH), super oxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT) are also boosted and reduction of malonaldehyde (MDA), indicator of lipid peroxidation which may help in prevention of degradation of dopaminergic neurons. Histology showed better neuron preservation in MMMS rats. Conclusions This study found MMMS is neuroprotective in HPD-induced PD. Its effects likely stem from antioxidant properties, and dopamine restoration. MMMS may merit further research for PD management.

papers.title: Short-term subjective and EEG responses following cervical rotatory manipulation are not reproduced by simulated cracking sound: A randomized controlled study.
papers.authors: Lin Y, Zhong W, Yu M, Yu Y, Tang L, Xue F, Wei J, Li J, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Background Cervical rotatory manipulation (CRM) is commonly used for neck-related symptoms and is often accompanied by a cracking sound. Whether a simulated cracking sound can reproduce the short-term subjective and neurophysiological responses to the complete CRM remains unclear. Objective This study compared short-term subjective and electroencephalography (EEG) responses to CRM with those following sham manipulation with or without a simulated cracking sound. Methods In this randomized controlled trial with three parallel groups and a single intervention session, 54 healthy volunteers were allocated to CRM, sham manipulation, or sham + simulated sound. Positive affect, negative affect, comfort, satisfaction, and eyes closed resting state EEG were assessed before and after the intervention. Prespecified EEG derived outcomes included frontal alpha power, frontal alpha/beta ratio, occipital individual alpha frequency, and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. Results CRM produced greater improvements in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction than sham manipulation or sham + simulated cracking sound, whereas no clear difference among groups was observed for negative affect. Differences among groups were also observed in frontal alpha/beta ratio and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. Sham + simulated sound did not reproduce the overall pattern of subjective and EEG responses observed after CRM. Conclusions CRM produced greater improvements over the short-term in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction and was accompanied by differences in selected resting state EEG outcomes compared with sham manipulation with or without simulated cracking sound. Adding simulated cracking sound to sham manipulation did not reproduce this pattern. Because CRM differed from the control conditions in several procedural components, the specific component or combination of components responsible for these differences could not be determined. Trial registration The trial was registered with the International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry (URL: https://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn; ITMCTR2025001112).

papers.title: Stimulation-stability and preclinical bench testing of a new auditory nerve interface.
papers.authors: Stump T, Strahl S, Crew J, Leber M, Hübner K, Negi S, Vankirk J, Adams ME, Lenarz T, Solzbacher F, Lim HH, Rieth L.
papers.abstract: Objective Cochlear implants are the flagship sensory neural prosthetic, enabling improved hearing and speech perception in >1 million patients with hearing loss. Despite over three decades of active work and innovations in cochlear implants, hearing performance for complex tasks such as speech-in-noise and music appreciation are still quite limited, putatively due to the challenge of selectively stimulating the auditory nerve with intracochlear electrodes through the bony cochlear wall. Our approach is to more selectively evoke hearing percepts through the development of an Auditory Nerve Implant (ANI) device that uses penetrating microelectrodes placed directly in the nerve for stimulation, and which will be evaluated through psychophysical testing as part of a first-in-human study. Stability and integrity of ANI electrodes during passive soaking and stimulation are needed to support initiation of the clinical trial, which we evaluated through thermal accelerated saline soak testing and stimulation stability testing. Methods The ANI electrode stability in saline was assessed by accelerated aging at ≥ 67 [Formula: see text]C with a 1.5-year equivalent endpoint using electrode impedance and microscopy to characterize outcomes. Stimulation stability testing evaluated electrode integrity after 6.3 billion pulses at 100 μA, which is the maximum clinical stimulation intensity, for a one-year equivalent use, and 1200 μA, for a high-dose protocol. Electrode impedance, longitudinal stimulation voltage, and microscopy outcomes were used to the quantify results. Results All electrodes had stable impedances around 2 kΩ at the end of the accelerated soak test, except for three with higher impedances but still below the 70 kΩ failure criteria. All but one electrode survived stimulation stability testing. Optical and electron microscopy largely showed little to no change during testing, indicating no observable tip degradation, with the exception of one soak-test device. Conclusions The outcomes from the studies indicate that ANI electrodes exhibit a high degree of integrity and impedance stability. Microscopy characterization proved effective for evaluating electrodes, providing complementary information to standard Backscattered Scanning Electron Microscopy (BSEM). This study suggests the ANI device tolerate a 1.5 year in-dwelling period for a 1 year perceptual study of stimulation evoked percepts, paving the way for clinical translation.

papers.title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
papers.authors: Liu ZP, Lee D, Tan Z, Wu A, Mei L, Xiong WC.
papers.abstract: Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. Methods Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα ) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. Results Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. Conclusions These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

papers.title: Neuroimmune-oligovascular signaling shapes oligodendrocyte precursor cell fate and repair after ischemic stroke.
papers.authors: Li B, Ming R, Wu Z, Pan S.
papers.abstract: Background Ischemic stroke causes neuronal and oligodendroglial injury, axonal and myelin damage, and neurovascular unit dysfunction. Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) are lifelong progenitors that generate oligodendrocytes while receiving and transmitting signals within neural, immune, and vascular microenvironments. This review examines how neuroimmune-oligovascular communication and intracellular signaling shape OPC survival, recruitment, state transitions, differentiation, and remyelination after ischemic stroke. Main body We first define OPC lineage identity, functional heterogeneity, and signaling interfaces with neurons, microglia/macrophages, astrocytes, endothelial cells, and pericytes. We then examine how excitotoxic, metabolic, redox, inflammatory, vascular, extracellular-matrix, and regulated cell-death signals converge on OPCs across lesion compartments and disease phases. Severe core ischemia depletes the progenitor pool, whereas partially perfused peri-infarct tissue permits reactive proliferation and migration. During the subacute phase, intercellular signals within the post-ischemic niche influence whether recruited OPCs adopt inflammatory, angiogenic, differentiation-competent, or arrested states. Long-term repair ultimately depends on lineage completion and stable myelin formation rather than OPC accumulation alone. The strongest causal evidence supports signaling from the surrounding niche as a regulator of OPC differentiation and demonstrates that OPC-derived myelin repair contributes to neuronal preservation and functional recovery. By contrast, evidence that endogenous OPCs themselves substantially regulate post-stroke inflammation, angiogenesis, blood-brain barrier integrity, or synaptic reconstruction remains less complete and often derives from culture, conditioned-medium, pharmacological, or transplantation paradigms. Therapeutic strategies are therefore organized according to the signaling and lineage bottleneck they target, including acute OPC preservation, niche remodeling, lineage completion, oligovascular reconstruction, and cell-based interventions. Conclusions OPC fate after ischemic stroke is determined by the interaction of cell-intrinsic signaling competence with temporally and spatially changing neuroimmune-oligovascular cues. Translation will require lineage-resolved causal studies, human spatial and longitudinal validation, signaling-linked target-engagement measures, and treatment strategies matched to lesion phase, compartment, and repair bottleneck. A cell-communication framework may therefore provide a more mechanistically testable basis for OPC-centered white-matter repair after stroke.

papers.title: The role of matrix metalloproteinases in Alzheimer's disease and small vessel disease.
papers.authors: Nguyen N, Huynh S, Mroczko B, Glodzik L.
papers.abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are a family of enzymes participating in maintenance and remodeling of the extracellular matrix. Their many types are involved in diverse, sometimes contrasting physiological processes, and they are ubiquitously present throughout the CNS. In this mini-review we focused on MMP-2, MMP-3, MMP-9, and MMP-14, highlighting their importance in pathways linked to Alzheimer's disease and small vessel disease. Despite overlapping roles in modulating brain-blood barrier impairment, neuroinflammation, and the accumulation of disease-specific proteins like amyloid-β and tau, they show somewhat distinct expression patterns in different cells and differ in their primary influences on disease mechanisms. Although our knowledge is still very limited, there is evidence linking them to imaging manifestations of cerebral vessel disease and suggesting they could be a target for therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Longitudinal Quantitative MRI of Blood-Brain Barrier Leakage in Chronic Cerebral Hypoperfusion Rat model.
papers.authors: Sampedro-Viana A, Fernández-Rodicio S, Castillo J, Hervella P, Alonso-Alonso ML, Iglesias Rey R.
papers.journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
papers.abstract: Objective-Methods:Chronic cerebral-hypoperfusion is a key contributor to vascular cognitive impairment, with blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction proposed as an early driver of white matter injury. The temporal-evolution and regional-heterogeneity of BBB-leakage remain poorly characterized in vivo. We longitudinally assessed BBB permeability in Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to bilateral-common carotid artery occlusion (2VO) versus sham controls using contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI 9.4T over 12-weeks. Gadolinium-leakage maps were generated and analyzed in predefined regions (cortex, hippocampus, striatum, corpus callosum). Exploratory histological observations included GFAP immunostaining, and circulating biochemical biomarkers (sTWEAK, MMP-9, GOT, cytokines) were quantified.Results:Localized BBB disruption was observed at weeks 3, 6 post-2VO and progressed heterogeneously, with pronounced leakage strictly targeted toward corpus callosum, hippocampus and striatum. Despite descriptive trends showing increased astroglial activation, systemic biochemical biomarkers did not correlate with imaging-derived central BBB-leakage. Volumetric analysis revealed subtle but significant brain atrophy (18% whole-brain reduction) preceding overt T2-signal abnormalities. In the 2VO model studied, BBB dysfunction in chronic-hypoperfusion appears to be a dynamic, region-specific process.Conclusion:Longitudinal contrast-enhanced MRI detected changes that were not mirrored by the circulating biomarkers studied, suggesting its potential utility as a surrogate endpoint in preclinical studies, which should be confirmed in larger cohorts and complementary models.

papers.title: The Brain-Gut-Microbiome Axis: Exploring the Link Between Depression and Irritable Bowel Syndrome.
papers.authors: Chang L, Freimer NB, Hsiao EY.
papers.abstract: The brain-gut-microbiome system is an integrated communication network linking the central nervous system, enteric nervous system, immune pathways, and intestinal microbiota. Increasing evidence indicates that dysregulation of this bidirectional signaling system contributes to both gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a disorder of gut-brain interaction, and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently coexist and share multiple biological and environmental risk factors. Advances in microbiome science, neuroimaging, and multi-omics technologies have revealed that microbial metabolites, neuroimmune signaling, and stress-responsive neuroendocrine pathways influence neural circuits regulating mood, visceral perception, and gastrointestinal function. These interconnected mechanisms may explain the high comorbidity between IBS and MDD and suggest that both conditions arise from disturbances across overlapping biological systems. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of genetic, neurobiological, and potential microbial contributors to IBS and depression, discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting the brain-gut-microbiome system, and highlight future directions for developing mechanistically informed treatment strategies.

papers.title: Preclinical and first-in-human evaluation of VG-3927/SAR448851, an oral small-molecule TREM2 agonist for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Dejanovic B, Figley MD, Weisman E, Kiragasi B, Gergits FW, Larson K, Renoux A, Rajagovindan R, Pandya B, Houze J, Huang L, Gaudreault F, O'Mara R, Clarkson JH, Turnbull MT, Meier A, Colonna M, Stromme J, Gray D, Thackaberry EA, Kaufmann P, Mirescu C.
papers.abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV ), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.

papers.title: Vitamin D binding protein in ventral CA3 of the hippocampus drives stress-induced depression.
papers.authors: Kong Y, Huang Z, Zeng C, Xu Y, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: The ventral hippocampus plays a crucial role in regulating emotional and motivated behaviors. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD) remain poorly understood. Here, we identified elevated expression of vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) in the hippocampi of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-susceptible mice, which correlated with the severity of depression-like behaviors. Notably, VDBP up-regulation was specifically in ventral CA3 excitatory (vCA3CaMKIIα ) neurons. CA3CaMKIIα VDBP overexpression led to inhibited neuronal activity, synaptic and dendritic impairments, and, ultimately, depression-like behaviors. Conversely, vCA3CaMKIIα -specific VDBP knockdown enhanced resilience to chronic stress. Mechanistically, VDBP directly interacted with PIK3R3 to inhibit the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway in a cell-autonomous manner, leading to excessive autophagy and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. Chemogenetic activation, intervention using the Akt-specific activator SC79, and site-specific mutation disrupting the VDBP-PIK3R3 interaction ameliorated vCA3CaMKIIα VDBP-induced depression-like phenotypes. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical involvement of vCA3CaMKIIα neuron-derived VDBP in stress-induced depressive pathology and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for MDD.

papers.title: Thirty-Five Years of Change: Shifts in Demographic and Injury Profiles of Traumatic Brain Injury Cases Enrolled in the Traumatic Brain Injury Model Systems (1988-2024): A NIDILRR TBIMS National Database Study.
papers.authors: Ketchum JM, Tefertiller C, Beaulieu CL, Bodien YG, Callender L, Dams-O'Connor K, Giacino JT, Hammond FM, Hanks R, Ivanhoe CB, Pinto SM, Zhang JJ.
papers.journal: The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
papers.abstract: Objective To characterize long-term changes in demographic and injury profiles among individuals with traumatic brain injury (TBI) admitted to inpatient rehabilitation and enrolled in the TBI Model Systems (TBIMS) National Database (NDB). Setting Twenty-three inpatient rehabilitation hospitals participating in the TBIMS program. Participants 20 990 persons 16 years and older with TBI who received inpatient rehabilitation and enrolled in the TBIMS NDB between 1988 and 2024. Design Repeated cross-sectional analysis of a prospectively collected longitudinal database across 7 admission cohorts. Main measures Sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, employment, marital status, payor source) and injury characteristics (etiology, Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS], command following, post-traumatic amnesia [PTA], Functional Independence Measure [FIM], acute and rehabilitation length of stay [LOS]). Results Mean age at injury increased from 34.6 years in 1988-1994 to 48.4 in 2020-2024, accompanied by a rise in fall-related injuries, a decline in violence-related injuries, and a shift in vehicular injuries from earlier increases to more recent declines. The proportion of participants who were retired increased substantially, while the proportion who were unemployed declined. Racial/ethnic minority representation declined from 1988-1994 to 2000-2004 and then increased through 2020-2024, particularly among younger individuals. Medicare coverage increased while Medicaid coverage declined. The proportion of participants with complicated mild TBI increased while moderate and severe classifications declined, accompanied by shorter time to command following and PTA duration. Despite these indicators of decreasing injury severity, FIM motor scores at rehabilitation admission declined modestly. Acute LOS declined slightly while rehabilitation LOS declined substantially. Conclusions Over the past 35 years, the TBIMS population has shifted toward an older cohort, accompanied by changes in demographic patterns associated with aging, mechanisms of injury, functional profiles, payor source, and lengths of stay. These changes should be considered when interpreting TBIMS longitudinal outcomes, evaluating representativeness, translating prior research findings to contemporary populations, and planning rehabilitation services for individuals with TBI.

papers.title: Bridging the Translational Gap in Sex-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Using Human iPSC-Based Neural Cell Models.
papers.authors: Supakul S, Phisalaphong R, Changchai M, Okano H.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits marked sex differences in disease prevalence, progression, and therapeutic responsiveness, with women disproportionately affected by both cognitive decline and neuropathological burden. Although sex hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone have demonstrated neuroprotective effects in experimental systems, clinical outcomes of hormone-based interventions remain inconsistent. Emerging evidence further indicates that sex-specific molecular programs extend beyond endocrine signaling alone and include cell type-specific transcriptional architectures established across the lifespan. Recent single-cell transcriptomic studies have suggested that biological sex fundamentally shapes multicellular brain vulnerability. However, prevailing preclinical systems incompletely model human endocrine aging, sex chromosome biology, and patient-specific genetic heterogeneity, thereby limiting translational relevance. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neural systems provide a new platform for mechanistically interrogating sex-specific pathways within human genetic backgrounds. By preserving donor-specific genetic backgrounds and sex chromosome complement, iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and multicellular systems enable controlled investigation of hormone-responsive phenotypes, APOE-associated mechanisms, and cell type-specific transcriptional programs. However, their developmental immaturity and incomplete representation of systemic aging, vascular, immune, and endocrine physiology limit direct extrapolation to patients. Integration of these cellular systems with human omics datasets, neuropathological observations, and clinical studies may therefore help address specific components of the translational gap in AD.

papers.title: Multimodal Evidence for Large-scale Network Imbalance in Etomidate Use Disorder.
papers.authors: Le J, Wang X, Tang Y, Chen H, Chen X, Wang X, Tang Y, Zhao L, Zhao L, Shen H, Huang Q, Liao Z.
papers.abstract: Background Etomidate use disorder (EUD) is an escalating public health issue in East and Southeast Asia, yet its neuroimaging features remain poorly understood. This study used simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to examine multimodal functional connectivity alterations in individuals with EUD. Methods A total of 54 individuals with EUD and 46 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited and underwent simultaneous resting-state EEG and fNIRS recordings. Psychological dimensions including impulsivity, aggression, and craving were evaluated using standardized and validated scales. Source-level EEG functional connectivity and fNIRS hemodynamic connectivity were analyzed to identify group differences. Associations between altered connectivity features and clinical measures were examined within the EUD group. Machine learning analyses were conducted as exploratory assessments of the discriminative information contained in multimodal connectivity features. Results In unadjusted exploratory analyses of BIS-11 and BPAQ subscales, the EUD group showed higher cognitive impulsivity, non-planning impulsivity, physical aggression, anger and self-directed aggression (t=2.32 to 4.54, p<0.05), but lower motor impulsivity, compared with HCs. Source-level EEG analysis revealed significant group differences only in the delta band, with reduced large-scale connectivity in EUD involving default mode, dorsal attention, visual and sensorimotor systems. fNIRS analysis showed reduced hemodynamic connectivity across multiple frontal subregions and motor-related areas. Weaker connectivity between the primary motor cortex and the triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus was associated with stronger negative reinforcement craving (rho=-0.471, p_FDR<0.05). Exploratory machine learning analysis showed preliminary discriminative performance, with the random forest model producing the numerically highest test-set AUC (0.80) in this particular data split. Conclusions Convergent EEG-fNIRS findings suggest delta-band network decoupling and reduced frontal hemodynamic connectivity as multimodal neural features of EUD. These findings provide preliminary evidence for the neural mechanisms of EUD and may inform future objective assessment and treatment-monitoring studies.

papers.title: Metabolic connectivity and memory in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
papers.authors: Strýček O, Říha P, Kojan M, Brichtová E, Hummelová Z, Řehák Z, Brázdil M.
papers.abstract: Memory decline after anterior mesial temporal resection in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (MTLE-HS) remains incompletely explained by structural and clinical factors, suggesting that networks may contribute to cognitive vulnerability. We investigated whether presurgical metabolic connectivity (MC), derived from fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) and reflecting metabolic network organization, is associated with memory performance and postsurgical cognitive outcome in MTLE-HS. We studied 83 patients with MTLE-HS who underwent anterior mesial temporal resection. All had interictal FDG-PET and pre- and postsurgical neuropsychological testing. MC was computed using a normative connectivity framework and examined in relation to memory performance, analysed separately for left and right TLE. The effect of resection extent on cognitive outcome was also assessed. Presurgical analyses revealed distinct lateralized patterns. In right temporal lobe epilepsy (RTLE), immediate visual memory correlated positively with MC across widespread fronto-cingulate-temporal networks, frequently including the lesional hippocampus. In left temporal lobe epilepsy (LTLE), immediate verbal memory showed only negative correlations with extratemporal MC. In RTLE, presurgical MC also correlated with postsurgical change in immediate visual memory. Predominantly negative associations involved ipsilateral hippocampal-cingulate and fronto-temporal pathways, whereas positive correlations were confined to contralateral posterior cingulate connections with frontal and temporal regions. In LTLE, no significant correlations with postsurgical memory change were identified. Extent of resection did not correlate with cognitive outcome. MC was significantly associated with memory performance in MTLE-HS, showing clear lateralized differences. In RTLE, presurgical MC was associated with postsurgical outcome: ipsilateral hippocampal-cingulate connectivity was linked to decline, whereas contralateral posterior cingulate pathways supported preservation. No such associations were found in LTLE, consistent with more constrained network reorganization within left-lateralized verbal memory systems. These effects were independent of resection extent, indicating that memory prognosis after AMTR in RTLE may depend on network-level mechanisms and that FDG-PET-derived MC could serve as a biomarker for cognitive risk assessment.

papers.title: Explainable fMRI decoding reveals neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal complementary to traditional analyses.
papers.authors: Agostinho D, Borra D, Castelo-Branco M, Simões M.
papers.abstract: Objective. Understanding how emotional arousal is represented in the brain is fundamental for elucidating affective regulation and its alterations in autism spectrum disorder. Classical neuroimaging approaches, such as the general linear model (GLM), have provided important insights into emotional processing. However, the extent to which data-driven decoding and traditional model-based analyses provide complementary information about emotional arousal remains unclear.Approach. We introduce an explainable artificial intelligence framework that combines the lightweight functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) decoder (fMRINet) with Deep Learning Important FeaTures to derive data-driven neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal. The framework enables interpretation of spatiotemporal neural contributions during emotional processing. We applied the framework to fMRI data acquired while neurotypically and autistic participants viewed naturalistic emotional videos and compared the resulting signatures with categorical and parametric GLM analyses.Main results. The framework identified distinct spatiotemporal neurobiological signatures associated with emotional arousal. Neurotypical participants engaged a distributed perceptual-limbic-prefrontal network under high arousal and frontoparietal executive regions under low arousal. In contrast, autistic participants exhibited a more spatially restricted and posterior-biased pattern under high arousal, with reduced ventromedial prefrontal and limbic contributions, while low-arousal patterns resembled typically developing, suggesting preserved executive mechanisms during low-arousal processing. The GLM analyses revealed partly convergent and partly distinct findings: categorical GLM detected no significant group differences, whereas parametric GLM identified widespread cortical-subcortical modulation in neurotypical individuals and cerebellar-restricted effects in autistic, consistent with compensatory reliance on motor-timing circuits.Significance . The proposed framework provides an interpretable, data-driven perspective on emotional processing and reveals neurobiologically plausible patterns consistent with existing literature. Together, the explainable decoding and GLM results highlight complementary aspects of emotional arousal processing, suggesting that explainable decoding approaches may provide additional insights alongside traditional model-based neuroimaging analyses.

papers.title: Nine minutes is enough: An accelerated fMRI protocol for reliable connectivity mapping in healthy young adults.
papers.authors: Falkowski A, Szwed K.
papers.abstract: Introduction Resting‑state fMRI is widely used to map brain connectivity, yet the field lacks a clear, data‑driven standard for acquisition duration. We compared traditional Single‑Band (SB) imaging with an accelerated Multiband factor 4 (MB4) protocol to identify a time‑efficient approach for capturing stable network topology. Methods Twenty‑five healthy young adults completed two sessions one month apart, each including counterbalanced 13‑minute SB and MB4 scans. Test-retest reliability was evaluated across multiple durations using Portrait Divergence, a multiscale graph‑theoretic metric. Supplementary analyses compared Portrait Divergence with the field-standard Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, assessed robustness across preprocessing pipelines and parcellation schemes, and examined MB4's ability to capture both cortical and subcortical connectivity. Results MB4 consistently outperformed SB across all tested durations, with peak topological stability at 9 minutes. Stability declined beyond this point, likely due to cumulative motion artefacts. Supplementary analyses confirmed MB4's robustness across preprocessing strategies and atlas choices and demonstrated effective whole‑brain coverage. Conclusions In healthy young adults, MB4 captures network topology more effectively than SB and reaches peak stability at 9 minutes before declining, challenging the assumption that longer scans are always better. These findings require validation in clinical, paediatric, and geriatric cohorts.

papers.title: Targeting protein misfolding and aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases: challenges for the identification and validation of targets for small molecules.
papers.authors: Choudhury A, Prabha S, Saeed MU, Sulaimani MN, Hassan MI.
papers.abstract: Introduction Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and related proteinopathies are characterized by the misfolding, aggregation, and accumulation of specific proteins that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, leading to neuronal death. Despite major advances in structural biology and molecular neuroscience, identifying and validating druggable targets in neurodegenerative diseases remains challenging. Many involved proteins are intrinsically disordered, exhibit conformational heterogeneity, and form highly dynamic toxic species. Areas covered This review summarizes the mechanisms of protein folding, misfolding, aggregation, and prion-like propagation in major neurodegenerative proteinopathies, including amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD), alpha-synuclein (α-syn) in synucleinopathies, TDP-43 and FUS in ALS/FTLD, polyglutamine-expanded proteins, prion proteins, and rare hereditary amyloidosis. We also discuss major barriers to target identification and validation, including conformational flexibility, oligomer toxicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, and target engagement complexity. Finally, we highlight emerging strategies integrating structural biology, computational methods, and improved experimental models to discover small-molecule inhibitors for neurodegenerative diseases. Expert opinion Effective therapeutic discovery will require moving beyond single-target models toward ensemble-based validation strategies. Integrating structural biology, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and computational approaches may improve the identification of druggable targets and support precision-medicine-based interventions for neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Osteocalcin and impaired cerebral resting-state functional connectivity in postmenopausal osteoporosis: a pilot case-control study.
papers.authors: Pickering ME, Morel V, Pereira B, Pickering G, Chapurlat R, Tournadre A, Chassain C, Sontheimer A.
papers.abstract: Purpose Postmenopausal osteoporosis and circulating osteocalcin have been suggested to influence brain function. Objectives aim to explore associations between brain network resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) connectivity, bone status, and circulating osteocalcin with the hypothesis of an impairment of the bone-brain axis in osteoporosis. Methods This pilot fMRI case-control study included postmenopausal osteoporosis women and matched healthy volunteers, and took place in University Hospital, Clermont-Fd, France. Endpoints were the comparisons between cases and controls of intra- and internetworks connectivity and correlations with bone mineral density (BMD) and osteocalcin. Results Twenty women with osteoporosis and ten matched healthy volunteers were included. Salience, visual and language intranetwork connectivity were all decreased compared to controls (False Discovery Rate (FDR)-corrected p = 0.006, 0.0132 and 0.0199, respectively). Internetwork connectivity was also impaired. For visual network, with three regions of the default mode (p-FDR = 0.0265, 0.0296 and 0.0265) and one with dorsal attention network (p-FDR = 0.0296), and for salience, with dorsal attention networks (p-FDR = 0.0494). Circulating osteocalcin correlated with connectivity between right anterior insula (salience network) and bilateral intraparietal sulci (dorsal attention network) (p-FDR = 0.0145 right side, p-FDR = 0.0421 left side). BMD correlated with connectivity between left regions of the dorsal attention and language networks (p-FDR = 0.0164). Conclusion This pilot study suggests possible impairment of brain connectivity and compensatory protective mechanisms/maladaptive mechanisms in postmenopausal osteoporosis. It also unveils that lower osteocalcin concentrations and BMD may be associated with altered cerebral connectivity, confirming animal studies, and providing preliminary findings for further research.

papers.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation.
papers.authors: Parada GE, Bretschneider H, Li JD, Fine JL, Dupas SJ, Ellis JD, Braunschweig U, Bonnal S, Dalal T, Engchuan W, Zarrei M, Wei W, Zafar N, Hemberg M, Attisano L, Ellis J, Irimia M, Wainberg M, Trost B, Scherer SW, Morris QD, Blencowe BJ.
papers.abstract: Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

papers.title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice.
papers.authors: Yan LX, Pan ZH, Sun GY, Pan DH, Wang XY, Xu YP, Yan JJ, Wang LZ, Cui GY, Chen CY, Yang M.
papers.abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (KD = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

papers.title: Examinations of the heterogeneity in the structural brain connectome in schizophrenia.
papers.authors: Zhao S, Jin Q, Wang Z, Liu MY, Liu M, Zhao JN, Xu Y, Zhang YH, Wu WJ, Wu D, Liu Y, Wei Y, Cui LB.
papers.abstract: Background Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a heterogeneous disorder characterized by widespread brain dysconnectivity, yet it remains unclear whether variable structural dysconnectivity patterns reflect biologically and clinically meaningful subtypes. Methods We recruited 105 SCZ patients and 97 healthy controls, collecting magnetic resonance imaging, clinical assessment, and laboratory test data. Double generalized linear models were first applied to estimate group differences in the mean and inter-individual variability of structural connectivity between SCZ and controls. Subsequently, nonnegative matrix factorization was used to identify SCZ subtypes according to dysconnectivity profiles. Results We observed a significantly altered subnetwork that exhibited increased inter-individual variability in SCZ, with its connections and regions predominantly enriched in the ventral-attention, frontal-parietal, and default-mode networks that support higher-order cognition. Connectivity-derived subtype analysis grouped patients into two subtypes, with subtype-II tending to show more severe positive symptoms (t = 2.272, nominal P = 0.025), a lower neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio (t = -2.383, nominal P = 0.025), a better treatment response (t = 2.366, nominal P = 0.021), and greater short-term symptom improvement (t = 3.509, nominal P = 0.006) within the olanzapine monotherapy subgroup.
