This subtype also demonstrated distinct neuroanatomical features, including a subtype-specific cortical thickness change pattern unrelated to SCZ or bipolar disorder, as well as subtype-specific brain epicenters, such as left posterior cingulate and rostral middle frontal regions. Conclusions Our study demonstrates increased inter-individual variability in the structural connectome of SCZ and highlights the potential of connectome-based subtyping approaches for characterizing disease heterogeneity related to pathophysiological processes.

papers.title: Rhythmic nasal air-puff as a potential noninvasive brain stimulation approach for stabilizing integrated brain network states.
papers.authors: Mohammadi S, Hossein-Zadeh GA, Raoufy MR.
papers.abstract: Breathing modulates neural oscillations and large-scale brain network organization, partly through mechanical stimulation of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs). To investigate the mechanosensory contribution of olfactory input, we compared rhythmic, odorless nasal air-puff stimulation (~0.2 Hz) with oral breathing during resting-state fMRI in healthy adults (n = 21). Dynamic functional connectivity was analyzed using a hidden Markov model (HMM) applied to BOLD fluctuations centered on the stimulation frequency. Four recurrent brain states were identified, spanning a continuum from highly segregated to globally integrated configurations. Relative to oral breathing, nasal air-puff stimulation increased the fractional occupancy and lifetime of the integrated state characterized by higher global and local efficiency and lower modularity, reduced the overall switching rate, and selectively reshaped transition probabilities away from fragmented configurations. These effects partially reproduced key features observed during natural nasal breathing in our prior work, suggesting that rhythmic mechanosensory activation of OSNs contributes to the stabilization of integrated large-scale brain states. The findings support a respiration-entrained framework in which olfactory input contributes to the organization and temporal stability of large-scale brain networks.

papers.title: Low-dose radiotherapy ameliorates Alzheimer's-like pathology in 5xFAD mice and is associated with HIF-1α-related inflammatory signaling downregulation.
papers.authors: Jiao H, Huang H, Chen S, Wang P, Xiang J, Xiang G, Zhao L.
papers.abstract: Background Whether fractionated low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) alleviates Alzheimer's disease-like pathology and whether these effects are associated with microglial HIF-1α-related signaling remain unclear. Methods Male 5xFAD mice received whole-brain irradiation at 2 Gy per fraction for 5 fractions (total dose, 10 Gy). One month later, cognition was assessed by the Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests, and brain pathology was evaluated by immunofluorescence and Western blot. LPS-stimulated BV2 cells were used as an in vitro model to examine the effects of LDRT on nitric oxide, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Transcriptomic analysis was performed with 3 biological replicates per group, followed by pharmacological validation using the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1. Results LDRT improved spatial and recognition memory, reduced Aβ plaque burden in the hippocampus and cortex, and attenuated microglial activation in 5xFAD mice. In particular, LDRT decreased the hippocampal Aβ plaque area fraction (P = 0.0065) and reduced HIF-1α expression in Iba1-positive microglia in the hippocampus (P = 0.0077). In addition, LDRT reduced Iba1 expression and CD68-positive area while preserving Aβ phagocytosis by primary microglia. In BV2 cells, LDRT inhibited LPS-induced inflammatory responses and altered 123 differentially expressed genes enriched in the HIF-1, IL-17, TNF, MAPK, and p53 signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of HIF-1α by YC-1 recapitulated, but did not further enhance, the anti-inflammatory effects of LDRT. Conclusions Fractionated whole-brain LDRT ameliorates cognitive deficits and Aβ pathology in 5xFAD mice, with effects associated with downregulation of microglial HIF-1α-related signaling.

papers.title: Corrigendum to "Depression: higher temporal variability of the functional connectivity of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and hippocampal system" [NeuroImage: Clinical 52 (2026) 104073].
papers.authors: Chen Y, Rolls ET, Yu Y, Huang CC, Luo Q, Cheng W, Wang X, Zhang T, Feng J.

papers.title: The ferroptosis-neuroinflammation feedback loop in traumatic brain injury: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
papers.authors: Fang Y, Xu X.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability worldwide, with secondary injury processes such as ferroptosis and neuroinflammation adding to its detrimental effects. Recent studies reveal a profound bidirectional interaction. On one hand, inflammation drives ferroptosis by disrupting iron homeostasis through the IL-6/Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)-hepcidin axis, impairing the system Xc- /glutathione (GSH)/GPX4 antioxidant system and promoting immune cell infiltration. Conversely, ferroptotic cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and lipid peroxidation end-products like 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), which activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and fuel a neuroinflammatory vicious cycle. We further discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting this axis, including ferroptosis inhibitors (Fer-1, Lip-1), dual-regulatory agents (annexin A5, melatonin, and H2 S), and exosome-based delivery systems, while highlighting translational difficulties presented by the BBB and complex time windows. This review presents a framework to comprehend the interplay between ferroptosis and inflammation and to guide the development of dual-targeted treatments in TBI.

papers.title: Deficiency of synaptotagmin 9 in the hippocampal region induces synaptic damage and cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease mice via BDNF/TrkB signaling.
papers.authors: Xu N, Du C, Li Y, Yang W, Li W, Perez RG, Yu S, Lou H.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a prominent non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) that severely affects patients' quality of life, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of hippocampal Synaptotagmin 9 (Syt9) in PD-related cognitive deficits. We found that Syt9 expression was significantly downregulated in the hippocampus of both MPTP-induced subacute PD mice and A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice, concomitant with cognitive impairment and synaptic damage. To determine causality, we performed hippocampal Syt9 knockdown and overexpression using AAV-mediated gene delivery. Syt9 knockdown exacerbated, while Syt9 overexpression alleviated, cognitive deficits and synaptic structural abnormalities in PD mice. Proteomic sequencing and pharmacological manipulations revealed that Syt9 may regulate the BDNF/TrkB signaling pathway at the protein level, likely by influencing BDNF vesicular transport, release, or stability. Intra-hippocampal BDNF supplementation rescued synaptic damage and cognitive impairment, whereas the TrkB antagonist ANA-12 reversed the protective effects of Syt9 overexpression. Collectively, our findings identify the Syt9/BDNF/TrkB axis as a key mechanism in PD-related cognitive impairment and suggest that targeting this pathway may offer a novel therapeutic strategy for PD.

papers.title: Highly replicable multisite patterns of adolescent white matter maturation.
papers.authors: Meisler SL, Cieslak M, Bagautdinova J, Hendrickson TJ, Pandhi T, Chen AA, Hillman N, Radhakrishnan H, Salo T, Feczko E, Weldon KB, McCollum R, Fayzullobekova B, Moore LA, Sisk LM, Davatzikos C, Huang H, Avelar-Pereira B, Caffarra S, Chang K, Cook PA, Flook EA, Gomez T, Grotheer M, Hagen MP, Huque ZM, Karipidis II, Keller AS, Kruper J, Luo AC, Macedo B, Mehta K, Mitchell JL, Pines AR, Pritschet L, Rauland A, Roy E, Sevchik BL, Shafiei G, Singleton SP, Stone HL, Sun KY, Sydnor VJ, Tong TT, Yablonski M, Yeatman JD, Rokem A, Shinohara RT, Fair DA, Satterthwaite TD.
papers.abstract: Adolescent brain development is difficult to study at scale because diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures are sensitive to technical variability across scanning environments. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is the largest US-based longitudinal neuroimaging study of adolescent brain maturation. We present ABCD-Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) Community Collection (ABCC) release 3.1.0, a curated resource of more than 24,000 fully processed human ABCD dMRI datasets from participants aged 8-17 years. ABCC provides processed images, nuanced image quality metrics, advanced microstructural measures, and person-specific white matter bundle tractography. Across 62 bundles, measures of diffusion restriction and non-Gaussianity-including intracellular volume fraction from neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), mean kurtosis tensor from diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and return-to-origin probability from mean apparent propagator (MAP)-MRI-were more sensitive to development and more robust to variation in image quality than tensor-derived measures. Longitudinal harmonization of microstructural features with ComBat-GAMM markedly improved the cross-vendor generalizability of developmental effects. Together, ABCC accelerates reproducible, rigorous research on adolescent white matter development.

papers.title: Fucosylated Chondroitin Sulfate Modulates Microglia-Associated Responses and Reduces Aβ Burden with ERK1/2-Related Signaling Changes.
papers.authors: Xiao X, Gao F, Xie J, Lu Y, Lv K, Mo H, Chen J, Liu J, Meng Q, Guan Y, Chen Q.
papers.abstract: Introduction Fucosylated chondroitin sulfate (FCS) is a sulfated polysaccharide derived from the marine organism Apostichopus japonicus. This study aimed to investigate its neuroprotective potential, specifically focusing on microglial modulation and ERK1/2 signaling, in Alzheimer's disease (AD) models. Methods An integrated in vitro and in vivo approach was employed. In vitro, Aβ42-stimulated BV2 microglia were treated with FCS, and the broad protein kinase C activator TPA was used as a pharmacological perturbation to examine whether the FCS-associated ERK1/2 signaling changes were reversible. Cytokine levels, microglial phenotype markers (CD86, CD206, iNOS, Arg-1), Aβ handling, and MAPK pathway proteins (p-ERK1/2, p38, JNK) were analyzed. In vivo, 5xFAD transgenic mice received intraperitoneal FCS for 28 days. Aβ plaque burden, soluble/insoluble Aβ levels, cognitive performance (Morris water maze, Y-maze), cortical Iba1-positive cell counts, activation state (Iba1+ CD86+ , Iba1+ CD206+ ), and expression of p-ERK1/2, iNOS, and Arg-1 were assessed. Results In vitro, FCS attenuated Aβ42-induced pro-inflammatory responses (reduced IL-6, TNF-α; increased IL-10), modulated phenotype (decreased CD86/iNOS; increased CD206/Arg-1), and increased the cell-associated Aβ fraction while reducing supernatant Aβ. FCS reduced Aβ42-associated ERK1/2 phosphorylation and the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic p-ERK1/2 fluorescence signal ratio, and these changes were partially attenuated by TPA. In vivo, FCS treatment reduced cerebral Aβ burden, improved spatial and working memory, decreased the number and proportion of cortical Iba1+ CD86+ microglia, and increased the Iba1+ CD206+ subset. Cortical p-ERK1/2/total ERK1/2 and iNOS expression were downregulated, while Arg-1 was upregulated. Conclusion FCS reduced Aβ-related pathological burden, improved selected behavioral outcomes, and modulated microglia-associated inflammatory and phenotype-related readouts in AD models. These effects were accompanied by ERK1/2-related signaling changes, supporting a pathway-associated interpretation rather than definitive proof of ERK1/2 causality in vivo.

papers.title: Convergent Microglial and Astrocytic Responses across Diverse Stress Paradigms: Integrating Inflammation, Metabolism, and Behavior.
papers.authors: Suk K.
papers.abstract: The central nervous system responds to diverse challenges through convergent glial mechanisms, yet most reviews examine single stressor paradigms in isolation. This review uniquely integrates current knowledge across five major stress categories (psychosocial, immune/inflammatory, infectious, injury/damage, and metabolic), revealing both shared pathways and stimulus-specific glial responses that have not been systematically compared. Because microglia and astrocytes are the principal immune-metabolic sensors mediating these responses, this review is centered on these two cell types, while acknowledging that oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and ependymal cells also participate in stress-related glial pathology, particularly with respect to white matter and cerebrospinal fluid homeostasis. While all stressors activate common inflammatory cascades including NF-κB signaling, complement activation, and inflammasome assembly, they elicit distinguishable molecular signatures. For instance, psychosocial stress uniquely engages type I interferon responses driving microglial synapse elimination. Viral infections produce severe metabolic reprogramming, hijacking host metabolism to support viral replication while depleting cellular NAD+ and ATP. Autoimmune inflammation generates lipid-laden disease-associated microglia with upregulated cholesterol metabolism genes. Unlike previous reviews focusing solely on inflammation or metabolism, we emphasize their bidirectional integration as a unifying principle. Inflammatory signals trigger metabolic shifts toward aerobic glycolysis, generating lactate serving dual functions as neuronal fuel and inflammatory mediator. This metabolic reprogramming, orchestrated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, and mTOR, creates feedback loops linking glial dysfunction to neuronal alterations. Complement-mediated synaptic pruning, disrupted neuron-glia metabolic coupling, and impaired neurotrophic support converge to produce depression, cognitive impairment, and sickness behaviors. Individual variability reflects interactions among genetic factors, sex, age, and blood-brain barrier integrity. This cross-paradigm comparative approach identifies high-value therapeutic targets applicable across multiple conditions rather than single diseases. We propose integrated intervention strategies simultaneously targeting inflammatory and metabolic pathways, guided by single-cell profiling for personalized medicine tailored to individual patient molecular signatures. We further discuss the conceptual overlaps inherent to the five-category classification scheme adopted here and outline the limitations of extrapolating across heterogeneous stress paradigms, glial cell types, and species.

papers.title: A homozygous GABRA2 variant associated with infantile spasms evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome alters receptor gating.
papers.authors: De Waele J, Diaz-Bustamante M, Aourz N, Cottyn S, De Smet G, Raedt R, Schreiber JM, Gaillard WD, De Bundel D, Smolders I, Bosmans F.
papers.abstract: Variants in GABAA receptor subunits are increasingly implicated in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Although GABRA2 variants have been associated with early-onset epilepsy, the functional consequences of individual variants, particularly those located outside canonical ligand-binding and transmembrane pore-forming regions, remain incompletely understood. We identified a homozygous GABRA2p.A407K variant in a patient with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS) evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). Functional effects were assessed using two-electrode voltage clamp in Xenopus laevis oocytes and whole-cell patch clamp recordings in HEK293T cells expressing α2 β3 γ2 GABAA receptors. A Gabra2p.A407K/A407K knock-in mouse model was generated to examine neuronal membrane properties, provoked seizure responses, and behavioral phenotypes. The p.A407K variant did not impair receptor trafficking but slowed receptor desensitization. In hippocampal slices from adult knock-in mice, CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibited a more depolarized resting membrane potential and were positioned closer to action potential threshold, while action potential threshold itself was unchanged. In a limited adult EEG cohort of Gabra2p.A407K/A407K mice, no spontaneous seizures or overt epileptiform activity were detected. However, mutant mice showed prolonged seizure duration following 6 Hz corneal stimulation. Behavioral analyses revealed increased locomotor activity and altered exploratory behavior. These findings show that a rare homozygous GABRA2 intracellular loop variant alters α2-containing GABAA receptor gating and produces measurable neuronal, behavioral, and provoked seizure-response effects in a knock-in mouse model. The model does not reproduce the full human developmental epileptic encephalopathy phenotype but supports the conclusion that p.A407K is functionally consequential and provides a platform for studying variant-specific effects of GABRA2 dysfunction.

papers.title: Dorsolateral prefrontal TMS-evoked N100 as a neurophysiological correlate of symptom change in adolescent depression.
papers.authors: Klomfass S, Loy JK, Wunram HL, Biermann L, Pokorny L, Bender S.
papers.abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly prevalent in adolescence. Up to 30% of patients insufficiently benefit from first-line treatments, underscoring the need for improved treatment strategies and better understanding of pathophysiology. In depression, an imbalance between cortical excitation and inhibition in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), assessed by the TMS-evoked N100 potential, is suggested as one of several contributing neurobiological mechanisms. While elevated N100 amplitudes have been observed in depressed adults and adolescents, its association with symptom change remains insufficiently investigated. Methods In a randomized controlled trial, N = 54 adolescents (38 girls, 16 boys) with MDD received six weeks of whole body vibration training (exercising on a vibrating plate that triggers involuntary muscle contractions through a neurological reflex) or light stretching as add-on treatments to treatment as usual. TMS-EEG was applied before and after the intervention to assess N100 amplitudes over the left and right DLPFC. Depressive symptoms were measured using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised. Changes in N100 amplitudes were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA. Multiple regression analyses with intervention group as predictor examined associations between changes in N100 amplitudes and depressive symptoms, including sex as moderator and a subsequent girls-only analysis. Results Across both groups, N100 amplitudes significantly decreased from pre-to post-intervention. No differential effects between interventions were observed. Reductions in right-hemispheric N100 amplitudes were significantly associated with improvements in depressive symptoms. This association reached statistical significance in girls. Conclusions Our findings support the N100 as a candidate neurophysiological correlate of depressive symptom improvement.

papers.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study.
papers.authors: Liu KW, Pang RTE, Durongbhan P.
papers.abstract: Background The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient tests. New method We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks (global weight reshuffle or strength-conditioned null) with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study using data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling beyond nodal strength. Results An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared only under the pipeline combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs. Under the empirical resampling ensemble, that pipeline reported a group difference in 43% of pseudo-studies, always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. Comparison with existing methods Unlike global weight reshuffling, strength-conditioned nulls approximately preserve nodal strengths; fixing observed hubs also retains the identity of the core being tested. Conclusions The same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on these choices. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

papers.title: Microstructural changes in prefrontal-cingulate networks following bilateral dorsomedial prefrontal cortex-targeted intermittent theta-burst stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: A diffusion tensor imaging study.
papers.authors: Ersungur Çelik EB, Poyraz BÇ, Arslan S, Kargın OA.
papers.abstract: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) is a transcranial magnetic stimulation protocol used in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), yet its effects on brain structural connectivity remain incompletely understood. The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), a key node within emotion regulation networks, has emerged as a promising therapeutic target. This study investigated white matter microstructural changes associated with bilateral dmPFC-targeted iTBS and their relationship with treatment response. A total of 21 patients with TRD and 32 healthy controls were included. Diffusion tensor imaging was acquired in all participants and repeated in patients after a full course of dmPFC-targeted iTBS. Analyses focused on longitudinal changes in white matter microstructure within prefrontal-cingulate-limbic pathways, group differences, and their associations with changes in depressive symptom severity. Correction for multiple comparisons was applied throughout. iTBS treatment was associated with a significant reduction in depressive symptoms. At the microstructural level, a post-treatment increase in fractional anisotropy was observed in a left prefrontal-cingulate pathway. Notably, changes in several pathways showed associations with clinical improvement. The tract-level findings were significant under tract-wise FDR correction but did not survive correction across all tract-metric comparisons, and are therefore interpreted as exploratory. Baseline microstructural properties within orbitofrontal-subgenual cingulate connections were also related to treatment response. These findings indicate tract-specific changes in diffusion metrics within prefrontal-cingulate-limbic pathways over the course of dmPFC-targeted iTBS. Given the modest sample size and the absence of a sham-controlled comparison, the results should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and require confirmation in larger, sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: Differences in neurovascular coupling in patients with major depressive disorder: Evidence from simultaneous resting-state EEG-fNIRS.
papers.authors: Yan F, Wang X, Zhao Y, Yang S, Wang Z.
papers.abstract: Neurovascular coupling (NVC), the relationship between neural activity and cerebral hemodynamic responses, remains poorly understood in major depressive disorder (MDD). To investigate alterations in NVC associated with depressive symptom severity, we simultaneously recorded resting-state electroencephalography (rsEEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in 206 participants, including 134 patients with MDD and 72 healthy controls stratified by age to disentangle disease-related alterations from age-associated effects. NVC in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) was characterized by the consistency and temporal lag between spontaneous electrophysiological peaks and corresponding hemodynamic responses. We found that age significantly enhances the NVC consistency (p < 0.05), whereas this relationship was altered in patients with MDD during both the oxygen-consumption phase and the subsequent hemodynamic compensation phase. Furthermore, among patients with MDD, the strength of this consistency decreased more significantly with greater illness severity (partial r = -0.336, p = 0.0601). These findings suggest that changes in neurovascular coupling effects are strongly associated with the severity of depression. By leveraging wearable neuroimaging techniques, this study provides multimodal evidence for altered neurovascular coupling in depression and highlights its potential as a biomarker for disease monitoring and recovery trajectories.

papers.title: Selective CB2 receptor activation attenuates neuroinflammation and preserves immune responsiveness after photothrombotic stroke.
papers.authors: Bietar B, Tanner S, Abdolmohammadi P, Kasheke G, Zhou J, Lehmann C.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke triggers neuroinflammation that can drive CNS injury-induced immunodepression syndrome (CIDS), a peripheral immunosuppressive state associated with increased infection risk. The endocannabinoid system, particularly cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2), represents a promising immunomodulatory target because of its anti-inflammatory actions and limited psychoactive liability. In this study, we investigated whether CB2 receptor activation confers neuroprotection and preserves systemic immune responsiveness in a murine photothrombotic stroke (PTS) model. Male C57BL/6 mice underwent PTS or sham surgery and were treated before stroke induction with the non-selective CB1/CB2 agonist WIN-55212, receptor antagonists, the selective CB2 agonist HU-308, or vehicle. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, cerebral inflammatory gene expression, and intestinal leukocyte-endothelial interactions following lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge were assessed using Neuroscore, TTC staining, RT-qPCR, and intravital microscopy. SIM-A9 microglia were used to evaluate the effects of HU-308 on viability and cytokine release under inflammatory conditions. PTS induced a CIDS-like phenotype characterized by reduced baseline leukocyte rolling and a markedly blunted leukocyte adhesion response following LPS challenge. Non-selective cannabinoid receptor activation improved neurological scores and reduced infarct size, while CB2 blockade abolished this protection. Selective CB2 activation with HU-308 reduced infarct volume, improved neurological outcome, and suppressed stroke-associated TNF and IL-6 expression in the ischemic hemisphere. In vitro, HU-308 reduced TNF release from LPS-stimulated microglia, while IL-4 enhanced microglial viability and IL-10 production. Importantly, HU-308 preserved leukocyte adhesion after LPS challenge following stroke, suggesting maintained peripheral immune responsiveness. These findings identify CB2 receptor activation as a promising neuroimmune strategy that limits acute stroke injury while attenuating the development of CIDS.

papers.title: Advancing early detection of Alzheimer's disease: from established biomarkers to future innovations.
papers.authors: Qu L, Wang Y, Ren L, Zhang C, Guo Z, Zhang L, Pang X, Sha S.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a major form of dementia, imposes an escalating global burden on public health and social care. Pathological changes in AD occur years before clinical symptoms, defining a prolonged preclinical phase. Currently, there is no effective treatment exist for late-stage AD, making early diagnosis and intervention indispensable, in which biomarkers play a pivotal role. While cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) biomarkers improved AD diagnostic accuracy, their clinical application is limited by invasiveness, high costs. Advances in ultrasensitive immunoassay technologies has rendered peripheral blood biomarkers easily accessible, cost-effective, minimally invasive, and suitable for continuous monitoring, offering noval opportunities for AD screening, diagnosis and progression tracking. Additionally, non-invasive body fluids including saliva, urine and tears are being explored as potential biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven multimodal fusion, integrated with large-scale multimodal computing frameworks, significantly improve the accuracy of early AD diagnosis. Recent studies have identified a series of promising synaptic and neuronal biomarkers, such as neurofilament light chain (NFL), neurogranin (Ng), β-secretase 1 (BACE1) and synaptosomal-associated protein 25 (SNAP-25). Inflammatory mediators and genetic factors also contribute to AD pathological evaluation. This review systematically characterizes biomarker profiles of emerging non-invasive carriers (saliva, urine and tears). It further synthesizes cohort-derived quantitative diagnostic metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity) of multimodal AD biomarkers and conducts head-to-head comparison to clarify their respective strengths and translational limitations, aiming to provide evidence-based insights for optimizing early AD screening and diagnostic strategies.

papers.title: Incidence of severe mountain bike-related injuries and mortality: A 15-year statewide analysis.
papers.authors: Course G, Sharman JE, Otahal P, Tran V.
papers.abstract: Background Mountain biking has grown in popularity and has seen widespread trail development but carries risk for severe trauma. No studies have analysed severe injuries in the context of contemporary mountain biking to understand trends and modifiable risk factors. Aim To describe the incidence and longitudinal characteristics of severe injuries related to mountain biking in Tasmania, Australia. Methods Retrospective analysis of all patients admitted to Tasmanian public hospitals with severe mountain bike (MTB)-related injuries from 1st January 2010-31 st December 2024. Main outcome measures Incidence of severe MTB-related injuries (including mortality) as defined by hospital admission to an intensive care unit or neurosurgery high dependency unit; for emergency surgery (in <4 h); or transfer intra- or interstate for definitive treatment. Secondary outcomes were annual injury trends in mechanism of injury, body regions, injury profiles, and incident location. Results For the total period there were 85 severe injuries (including 4 mortalities) from 6643 MTB-related emergency department (ED) presentations. Annual severe MTB-related cases increased over the 15 years from 0.8 cases/year before 2015, to 8.1 cases/year in later years. Severe injury cases accounted for only 1.3% of all MTB-related ED presentations. Most severely injured riders were male (97%); the mean age was 36 years (SD 16.9) for the total period, but this increased from 18.5 years (SD 5.8) pre-2015-36.9 years (SD 16.8) post-2015. Executing a jump was the dominant mechanism of injury (44%), followed by fall over handlebars (14%), obstacle collision (11%) and adverse trail conditions (9%). The most injured body regions were abdomen (31%), neck (23%) and thorax/chest (20%). The most common types of injuries were fracture/dislocation (44%), abdominal organ injury (24%) and thoracic organ injury (15%). Spinal cord injury occurred in 6% of cases and traumatic brain injury in 7%. Over 50% of severe injury incidents occurred on purpose-built MTB trails. Conclusions Severe MTB-related injuries increased proportionally to all MTB-related injuries suggesting the increase was largely driven by rider exposure. Targeted injury prevention strategies, safe trail design, and understanding risk factors are needed to ensure safe progression of this popular sport.

papers.title: Does delayed removal of stereo-EEG electrodes following radiofrequency thermocoagulation increase haemorrhage?
papers.authors: Tjangdjaja N, Pardoe HR, Dalic LJ, Bulluss KJ, Archer JS.
papers.abstract: Background Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC) is used in the assessment and treatment of medically refractory epilepsy, typically with electrode removal immediately following ablation. Our SEEG-guided RF-TC protocol includes the option of three further days of recording following thermocoagulation, prior to electrode removal. It is not known whether delayed removal of electrodes following RF-TC may increase the risk of haemorrhage. Objective To compare the rate and volume of intracranial haemorrhage with immediate versus delayed electrode removal following RF-TC. Methods 217 SEEG electrodes from 16 consecutive patients were retrospectively reviewed for haemorrhage. 3D T1-weighted (T1w) and Susceptibility Weighted (SWI) imaging were reviewed for haemorrhage along the electrode tract and at the site of RF-TC. The primary outcome measure was the per-electrode volume of T1w detectable haemorrhage at the site of RF-TC in electrodes removed immediately after RF-TC, compared to electrodes removed 3-days after RF-TC. Secondary outcomes compared the incidence and volume of T1w haemorrhage along the electrode tract in thermocoagulated versus non-thermocoagulated electrodes, presumed due to reflect haemorrhage from electrode insertion/removal. We also describe the temporal evolution of the MRI appearance of haemorrhage following SEEG-guided RF-TC. Results No clinically significant haemorrhages occurred. At the site of RF-TC a small amount of blood product is universally present but there was no significant difference in per-electrode haemorrhage volume following delayed (93.8 ± 39.8 mm3 ; ~diameter 5.6 mm) and immediate (80.0 ± 37.5 mm3 ; ~ diameter 5.3 mm) removal of electrodes (Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.10). At the cortical surface there was no significant difference in the rate of T1w haemorrhage between thermocoagulated and non-thermocoagulated electrodes (63.1% vs 52.5%, p = 0.12, chi-squared). Conclusion Delayed removal of electrodes post-RF-TC allows assessment of response to RFA and the opportunity for further thermocoagulation if necessary. This exploratory study found no significant increase in haemorrhage volume with delayed electrode removal following RF-TC but a larger study would be required to definitively estimate haemorrhage risk.

papers.title: CNPY3 variants associated with a recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy affect inflammasome and TLR function.
papers.authors: Garloff V, Grimmel M, Maroofian R, Efthymiou S, Stengel S, Bello D, Tille C, Ghait M, Ohlenschläger O, Dieckmann A, de Vries H, Waginger M, Nadeef S, Barkhordari E, Kaiyrzhanov R, Bühler S, Pjeci I, Beck-Wödl S, Alvi JR, Sultan T, Chassevent A, Smith-Hicks C, Mishina I, Rodríguez-Palmero A, Wassmer E, Vogt J, Meudt CM, Jamra RA, Abbaszadegan MR, Ajami N, Azizimalamiri R, Galehdari H, Chamanrou N, Zamani M, Shariati G, Nourbakhsh P, Ali FB, Fatima A, Hashmi SN, Iqbal Z, Kaleem S, Toft M, Afzal E, Maqbool S, Rahman F, Salpietro V, Grisval M, Racine C, Januel L, Cheillan D, Acquaviva-Bourdain C, Al Alam C, Alfadhel M, Umair M, Oehl-Jaschkowitz B, Haider S, Jain V, Narang B, Amer F, Elkhateeb N, Alvarez C, Pérez-Palma E, Ríos-Pohl L, Møller RS, Baruah D, Lingappa L, Farooq A, Zaki MS, Svyatova G, Murtazalieva A, Burabayeva A, Salayev K, Guliyeva U, Kahrizi K, Najmabadi H, Revah-Politi A, Mulhern MS, Sands TT, Mustafa HM, Rao HA, Oprea G, Rad A, Miryounesi M, Mardi A, Gowda VK, Srinivasan VM, Alanazi RM, Abumansour IS, Alhaddad B, Bakur K, Bauer M, Alkuraya FS, Huppke P, Houlden H, Haack TB, Rubio I, Husain RA.
papers.abstract: Background Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. Methods 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. Findings Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. Interpretation CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. Funding Interdisciplinary Center of Clinical Research and Jena School of Molecular Medicine, Jena University Hospital; Friedrich Schiller University Jena; The Wellcome Trust; The Medical Research Council; The MSA Trust; The National Institute for Health Research University College London Hospitals Biomedical Research Centre; The Michael J Fox Foundation; Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council; The Fidelity Trust; Rosetrees Trust; Ataxia UK; Brain Research UK; Sparks GOSH Charity; Alzheimer's Research UK; CureDRPLA; UK Dementia Research Institute; Parkinson's UK; South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, Norway; France Genomic Medicine Plan 2025; Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft; European Commission; Federal Government of Germany; State of Thuringia; Pakistan Science Foundation; King Abdullah International Medical Research Center; Science and Technology Development Fund; King Salman Center for Disability Research.

papers.title: Integrating graph attention networks and deep learning with multi-stage computational screening: Bisdemethoxycurcumin as a potent A₂A receptor inhibitor for Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Otmanine K, Hammoudi M, Bendriss H, Feraoun B, Mekhane S, Gherioune N, Benmehache C, Kerrouzi I, Ayadi K, El Miloudi K, Benghalia MA, Otmanine MK, Hentabli M.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) remains a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with limited disease modifying therapies, as current treatments such as L-DOPA offer only symptomatic relief and are associated with severe adverse effects. This study presents an integrated multi-stage computational pipeline that combines quantitative structure activity relationship (QSAR) modelling enhanced by graph attention networks (GATs), molecular docking, density functional theory (DFT), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and ADMET profiling to identify natural inhibitors targeting four key PD related proteins: adenosine A₂A receptor (A₂AR), gamma aminobutyric acid type A receptor (GABA-A), nuclear factor erythroid 2- related factor 2 (Nrf2), and (α-synuclein). A comprehensive dataset of 1393 structurally diverse compounds derived from 6- hydroxybenzothiazole 2-carboxamide and related scaffolds was assembled and used to train and validate seven regression algorithms. GATs achieved superior predictive performance (R2 = 0.991, Q2 = 0.987, RMSE = 0.487), outperforming Extra Trees (R2 = 0.742), Random Forest (R2 = 0.761), and SVR-RBF (R2 = 0.65). The large dataset size enhanced model generalizability, reduced overfitting risk, and enabled robust feature selection from an expanded descriptor pool of 312 molecular descriptors. Y-randomization with 100 permutations confirmed that all models with meaningful predictive performance were free from chance correlation (ΔQ2 > 0.50), validating the robustness of the QSAR workflow. Molecular docking of six phytochemicals derived from Curcuma longa (ar-turmerone, α -turmerone, bisdemethoxycurcumin) and Salvia officinalis (camphor, 1,8-cineole, α, β-thujone) revealed that bisdemethoxycurcumin BDMC exhibited the strongest binding affinity to the A₂A receptor (-9.1 kcal/mol) among the evaluated phytochemicals. L-DOPA, the current clinical standard of care, displayed weak affinity to the A₂A receptor (-7.2 kcal/mol), consistent with its known mechanism as a dopamine precursor rather than an A₂A ligand. DFT calculations at the B3LYP/6311G(d,p) level showed that BDMC possessed the lowest HOMO- LUMO energy gap (0.1428 eV) and the highest electrophilicity index (ω = 0.1477), indicating superior chemical reactivity and electron accepting capacity. A 200 ns MD simulation confirmed stable BDMC A₂A receptor binding, with 3-8 (mean ≈ 5) persistent hydrogen bonds and no dissociation events throughout the trajectory, as evidenced by centre of mass distance analysis and principal component analysis. ADMET profiling using SwissADME and ProTox II classified BDMC as blood brain barrier (BBB) permeable, compliant with Lipinski's Rule of Five, and safe (LD₅₀ = 2560 mg/kg, toxicity Class 5), compared to L-DOPA (Class 4, LD₅₀ = 1460 mg/kg). Comparative analysis demonstrated that BDMC offers superior predicted binding affinity to the A₂A receptor and a more favourable predicted toxicity profile compared to L-DOPA, positioning it as a compelling A₂A receptor-targeting lead candidate for PD therapy. Collectively, these findings establish a robust computational framework for accelerating drug discovery in neurodegenerative diseases and highlight BDMC as a promising A₂A Receptor inhibitor warranting further in-vitro and in- vivo experimental validation.

papers.title: The Evolving Paradigm of Autism: Folate Receptor Autoimmunity deranging Epigenetic Programming in fetal and postnatal Brain Development.
papers.authors: Ramaekers VT, Quadros EV.
papers.abstract: This review on autism provides a summary of the multiple genetic, epigenetic and environmental changes setting the stage for disturbed brain development due to aberrant synaptogenesis and corticogenesis during the prenatal and post-natal periods. The emphasis is placed on nonmendelian transmission driven by epigenetics. Folate deficiency appears to play a critical role in influencing many of the structural changes contributing to developmental deficits. Impaired passage of folate across the placental and the blood-brain barriers to the fetal and postnatal brain because of folate receptor autoantibodies (FRAb) emerges as the major cause. Cerebral folate deficiency with or without autism has been associated with FOLR1 gene defects, a rare disorder. On the other hand, FRAb in association with low CSF folate is present in most children diagnosed with autism. These autoantibodies are present in more than 1/3 of asymptomatic parents of children with autism or are acquired by the child during the first two years of life. Early detection of FRAb amongst autistic children is necessary to enable high dose folinic acid treatment. The use of folinic acid before conception and during pregnancy among mothers or both parents with FRAb, represents a promising strategy to reduce the risk of autism in future offspring. Interventational treatments in parents prior to pregnancy and optimal therapeutic approaches in infants are needed to prevent disordered development of the pre- or post-natal brain.

papers.title: Sex-Specific Neurobehavioral Programming in Offspring by a Maternal High-Fat, Plant-Based Diet: A Central Role of the Hippocampus.
papers.authors: Djurić E, Šutulović N, Puškaš N, Jerotić D, Djukić T, Matić M, Hrnčić D, Škrijelj D, Stanojlović O, Macut D, Rašić-Marković A.
papers.abstract: Introduction Long-term maternal high-fat diets (mHFDs) and obesity have been associated with an increased risk of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders in offspring, likely due to altered neural circuit programming. This study aimed to investigate the effect of plant-based mHFD on activity, mood regulation, and cognition in offspring of both sexes. Methods Female rats were assigned to an HFD or a control diet (CD) (45 vs. 4% fat) for 4 weeks before mating, and throughout gestation and lactation. The offspring were weaned to CD and assigned to either mHFD groups (FH-female HFD, MH-male HFD) or CD groups (FC-female CD, MC-male CD). Behavioral assessment included the open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), novel object recognition test (NORT), sucrose preference test (SPT), and the forced swimming test (FST). Immunochistochemical staining was performed to evaluate Ki67+, DCX+, and PV+, while serum hormone levels were measured by ELISA. Results The mHFD induced hyperactivity in the OFT and impaired learning and memory in the NORT in both sexes. In females, it reduced anxiety-like behavior in the OFT, but increased depression-like behavior in both SPT and FST. These effects were accompanied by decreased neurogenesis in females, as observed in both Ki67+ and DCX+ cells. The mHFD also decreased estradiol and increased corticosterone in females, and decreased testosterone in mHFD males. Conclusion A long-term plant-based mHFD exerts sex-specific effects on offspring activity levels, mood regulation and cognition, which may be attributed to impaired hippocampal neurogenesis and hormonal regulation.

papers.title: Olfactory dysfunction and limbic volumetric changes in relapsing-remitting and secondary progressive multiple sclerosis.
papers.authors: Tekmen E, Kozan B, Mungan S, Hatipoğlu HG, Yıldırım İ, Baysan I, Aydoğan E, Akgül KK, Erdil İI, İncekaş C, Pelin C.
papers.abstract: Objective To compare olfactory performance and olfactory-related brain region volumes between patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (SPMS) and to examine the relationship between olfactory performance and regional brain volumes. Materials and methods This prospective cross-sectional study included 65 patients with MS (43 RRMS and 22 SPMS). Olfactory function was assessed using the Sniffin' Sticks-12 Odor Identification Test. Bilateral volumes of the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, and insular cortex were obtained from three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI using the vol2Brain automated analysis pipeline available through the volBrain platform. Both raw and total intracranial volume (TIV)-normalized regional volumes were analyzed. For volumetric outcomes, multivariable analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and TIV, whereas analyses of olfactory performance were adjusted for age and sex. Additional sensitivity analyses incorporated disease duration and EDSS. Results In unadjusted comparisons, patients with SPMS had significantly lower Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores than those with RRMS (p = 0.004), and raw hippocampal volume was significantly lower in the SPMS group (p = 0.028). However, after adjustment for age, sex, and TIV, clinical subtype was not independently associated with hippocampal, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, or insular cortex volume (all p > 0.05). These findings remained non-significant in sensitivity analyses additionally accounting for disease duration and EDSS. The between-group difference in Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores was also attenuated after adjustment for age and sex (B = - 1.06; 95% CI, - 2.15 to 0.04; p = 0.058) and remained non-significant in further sensitivity analyses. No significant correlations were observed between Sniffin' Sticks-12 scores and regional volumetric measures. Conclusion Although patients with SPMS showed poorer olfactory performance and lower raw hippocampal volume in unadjusted comparisons, clinical subtype was not independently associated with regional brain volumes after adjustment for age, sex, and TIV, and the olfactory difference did not reach statistical significance after adjustment for age and sex. Furthermore, olfactory performance was not directly associated with regional volumetric measures, suggesting that olfactory dysfunction in MS may reflect mechanisms beyond regional structural volume alone.

papers.title: NAD+ Attenuates Neuroinflammation in Ischemic Stroke by Suppressing the cGAS- STING Pathway via Mitochondrial Homeostasis Restoration.
papers.authors: Jiang S, Liao B, Wang G, Sheng R, Han C, Jiang Z, Pan S, Wu C, Liang G, Zhu Y, Cheng M, Zhao F, Jiang Z, Yao X, Qin Z, Huai Y, Lu Y, Yang W, Bao J, Zhang Q, Zhao G, Deng J, Lv ZG, Wu J, Luo L, Qin Y.
papers.abstract: Stroke remains one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide, with neuroinflammation playing a critical role in its pathogenesis. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a major driver of innate immune responses activated by endogenous DNA, including mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and contributes significantly to post-ischemic neuroinflammation. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+ ), a vital metabolic coenzyme, has demonstrated anti-inflammatory potential in various diseases, including stroke; however, its specific role in regulation of neuroinflammation following stroke remains unclear. In this study, we examined the protective effects of NAD+ against ischemic stroke and explored its role in modulating cGAS-STING-mediated neuroinflammatory responses. Utilizing a transient middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion mouse model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation BV2 microglia model, we observed that NAD+ treatment significantly reduced infarct volume and brain edema, and improved neurological outcomes. NAD+ reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and facilitated the polarization of microglia from pro-inflammatory M1 to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. This effect was associated with the inhibition of cGAS-STING-TBK1 signaling pathway activation. Pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockdown of STING largely abrogated the anti-inflammatory effects of NAD+ in BV2 microglia, indicating a STING-dependent mechanism. Furthermore, NAD+ restored mitochondrial respiratory function and reduced cytoplasmic mtDNA leakage, suggesting that the improvement of mitochondrial homeostasis may underlie the suppression of cGAS-STING-TBK1 signaling pathway by NAD+ . Our findings indicate that NAD+ alleviates neuroinflammation following brain ischemia/reperfusion injury by regulating mitochondrial homeostasis and attenuates the cGAS-STING-TBK1 signaling pathway activation in microglia, thereby providing new therapeutic insights for ischemic stroke.

papers.title: "Morphological, Functional, and Molecular Progression of Blood-Brain Barrier Dysfunction in Alzheimer's Disease".
papers.authors: León-Arcia K, Martínez-Orozco H, Guerra-Crespo M, Díaz-Miranda SY, Soto-Rojas LO.
papers.abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early pathological event in sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD), which represents over 95% of cases. Vascular risk factors and cerebral insulin resistance are considered potential contributors to its initiation. This review synthesizes evidence available through March 2026 on the temporal progression of morphological, functional, and molecular BBB alterations in AD patients and experimental models. This review emphasizes the proposed role of BBB disruption in perpetuating neurodegeneration through feedback loops involving pericyte damage, hypoxia, perivascular inflammation, and dysregulation of amyloid-β transport systems. By integrating data from neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers, and post-mortem studies, available evidence suggests that BBB alterations can be detected from preclinical stages, most consistently in the hippocampus, and may exhibit sex-specific differences. The review compares findings from familial transgenic models with the more limited characterization available in sporadic AD models (notably the intracerebroventricular streptozotocin model), and highlights key knowledge gaps regarding temporal dynamics. This synthesis supports further exploration of strategies to preserve BBB integrity. An integrated vascular approach may usefully complement current amyloid- and tau-centered therapies, particularly in sporadic AD.

papers.title: The role of neighborhood socioeconomic environment in the association between glycemic control and the developing brain.
papers.authors: Chandra A, Hsu E, Luo S.
papers.abstract: Metabolic health and socioeconomic environments may jointly shape neurodevelopment during adolescence, a sensitive period of brain maturation. This cross-sectional study investigated overall and neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation moderated associations between glycemic control and brain structure in youth. Data were analyzed from 705 healthy 10-13-year-olds participating in the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® across 21 sites in the United States. Glycemic control was assessed using hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), brain structure was evaluated via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and neighborhood deprivation was measured with the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). Mixed-effects models examined associations between HbA1c and brain structural measures while controlling for sociodemographic covariates, with additional analyses stratified by ADI tertiles. Higher HbA1c was associated with lower mean cortical thickness and smaller total cortical gray matter volume. Each one percent increase in HbA1c corresponded to a 0.024 mm reduction in mean cortical thickness and a 9,611 mm3 reduction in total cortical gray matter volume. Regionally, higher HbA1c was associated with thinner cortex and smaller gray matter volumes primarily within frontal, cingulate and occipital areas. Exploratory analysis found that higher HbA1c was associated with lower total cortical gray matter volume among youth living in medium and high ADI neighborhoods, but not low ADI neighborhoods, whereas higher HbA1c was associated with lower mean cortical thickness only among youth living in high ADI neighborhoods. These findings highlight the interplay between metabolic health and neighborhood deprivation, supporting a model in which socioeconomic disadvantage may magnify the neurodevelopmental impact of metabolic variation, even within the non-diabetic range.

papers.title: Early cerebral hypoperfusion promotes spatially biased tau pathology in tau-seeded PS19 mice.
papers.authors: Zhao S, Zhang X, Zhong S, Li K, Yan Y, Zhang B, Chen Y.
papers.abstract: Growing evidence has demonstrated a significant association between reduced cerebral blood flow and Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related cognitive impairment. Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (CCH) has been reported to exacerbate tau hyperphosphorylation and behavioral deficits in rodents, but whether CCH promotes tau pathology at the initial stage of tauopathy remains unclear. Here we show, using a tau-seeded PS19 mouse model with unilateral common carotid artery occlusion, that early CCH exacerbates spatially biased tau pathology, inducing ipsilateral enrichment of insoluble tau in the hippocampus and, in the cortex, an ipsilateral increase that was dependent on the presence of tau seeds. Early CCH also induces myelin loss in the cortex and dorsal fornix, although no synergistic interaction was detected between tau seeds and CCH. Additionally, early CCH promotes microglial activation and IL-1β elevation, and increases hippocampal neuronal loss. In the Morris water maze, early CCH-exposed mice display a marginal trend toward reduced spatial memory performance that did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that early CCH facilitates tau pathology and neuroinflammation at the early stage of tauopathy, with only a marginal trend toward early cognitive changes, providing experimental evidence that vascular hypoperfusion may act as a disease modifier in the initial phase of tau pathology, with potential implications for early detection and therapeutic targeting of vascular contributions to tauopathies.

papers.title: Rheum undulatum Linné Exerts Neuroprotective Effects Against Aβ Oligomer-Induced Neuronal Damage by Modulating p53-Mediated Signaling.
papers.authors: Lee M, Lee S, Kim JH, Oh MS.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline and synaptic dysfunction. Accumulating evidence indicates that β-amyloid oligomers (AβO), the most neurotoxic form of β-amyloid, play a critical role in the pathogenesis of AD by inducing synaptic loss, neuronal death, and neuroinflammation. Therefore, targeting AβO-driven pathological processes through multi-target therapeutic strategies represents a promising approach to treating AD. This study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective effects of Rheum undulatum Linné rhizome (RUL) and the underlying mechanisms of its action against AβO-induced neurotoxicity using integrated in vitro, in vivo, and in silico approaches. RUL treatment protected HT22 and N2a neuronal cells from AβO-induced neurotoxicity and reduced extracellular AβO levels. In AβO-injected mice, oral administration of RUL alleviated memory impairment, preserved synaptic integrity, as evidenced by increased PSD95 and SYP expression, and suppressed microglial and astrocytic activation, as indicated by reduced Iba-1 and GFAP immunoreactivity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, systems-level network analysis identified p53-related signaling as a central regulatory axis in the AD-associated pathway. These network-level insights were experimentally validated by demonstrating that RUL suppressed p53 phosphorylation, increased the BCL2/Bax ratio, inhibited caspase-3 activation, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-1β, in the hippocampus. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that RUL exerts neuroprotective effects by preserving synaptic integrity and concurrently suppressing apoptotic and neuroinflammatory pathways through the network-level modulation of AβO-driven pathology, supporting its potential as a multi-target therapeutic candidate for AD.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid amino acid alterations are associated with oxidative stress and neuronal injury markers in multiple sclerosis.
papers.authors: Bartová R, Slezáková D, Ďurfinová M.
papers.abstract: Altered glutamatergic neurotransmission and oxidative stress are implicated in the pathophysiology of multiple sclerosis (MS), yet their interplay remains incompletely understood. This study investigated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels of neuroactive amino acids (aspartate, glutamate, glycine, γ-aminobutyric acid) in relation to markers of lipid peroxidation, antioxidant capacity, and neuronal injury. Amino acids were quantified using a validated high-performance liquid chromatography method with fluorescence detection. Aspartate levels were significantly elevated in MS compared with other neurological diseases (ONDs), while glutamate showed a non-significant trend toward higher concentrations. Glycine concentrations were significantly higher in MS and RR-MS than in the non-neurological control group (CG), whereas GABA showed no significant group differences. Correlation analyses revealed a positive association between glutamate and 8-iso-PGF₂α in MS and RR-MS, whereas the correlation between aspartate and 8-iso-PGF₂α was observed only in ONDs and was based on a small number of observations (n = 6). Glycine showed a significant negative association with neuron-specific enolase in MS and RR-MS, while a positive association with total antioxidant status was observed in CG. These associations should be considered exploratory and do not establish causal or mechanistic relationships. The SP-MS subgroup showed the highest median concentrations of 8-iso-PGF₂α and MDA, while TAS was lower than in RR-MS; however, these findings were based on limited numbers of observations and should therefore be considered exploratory. These biochemical changes were observed in the absence of marked abnormalities in the measured CSF indicators of intrathecal IgG synthesis or blood-CSF barrier function. Together, these findings indicate associations between CSF amino acid homeostasis, oxidative stress and neuronal injury in MS. CSF amino acid profiling may provide complementary information on metabolic and neurotransmission-related alterations in MS and warrants further evaluation alongside established biomarkers in larger, independently characterized cohorts.

papers.title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
papers.authors: Gündoğdu AA, Özkan NG, Adapınar DÖ.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

papers.title: Gentiopicroside alleviates depression-like symptoms in animal models through regulating COX-2-mediated autophagy and inflammation.
papers.authors: Ke W, Liu G, Lin M, Yao T, He C.
papers.abstract: Depression is a serious mental illness affecting millions of people worldwide. This study investigates the effects of gentiopicroside, a compound found in traditional Chinese medicine, on depression-like animal models and its potential mechanism of action. The study utilized rat models with corticosterone-induced depression and treated them with various concentrations of gentiopicroside. The effects on hippocampal cells, serum 5-HT levels, inflammation, autophagy, and oxidative stress markers were observed. The role of Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression and mitophagy was also examined using in vitro neuron cell models. Gentiopicroside demonstrated dose-dependent effects on alleviating hippocampal cell damage, restoring serum 5-HT levels, and inhibiting inflammation and oxidative stress markers. It also promoted autophagy and modulated COX-2 expression in the rat models. The in vitro study revealed that gentiopicroside could regulate COX-2 expression, reduce mitochondrial membrane potential loss and cell apoptosis, and inhibit NLRP3 (NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain-containing 3) inflammatory complex-related proteins and cytokines. Overexpression of COX-2 significantly reversed the positive effects of gentiopicroside, while PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1) overexpression promoted mitophagy, inhibited NLRP3 inflammatory complex activation, and reduced oxidative stress. Gentiopicroside ameliorates depression-like symptoms in animal models by suppressing COX-2 expression. This suppression is necessary for the subsequent enhancement of PINK1-mediated mitophagy, which helps to re-establish mitochondrial homeostasis and attenuate neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. This novel mechanism may potentially lead to the development of new therapies for depression treatment.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Microstate Dynamics and their Associations with Acclimatization Index and Serum Albumin in Healthy Adults with Chronic High-Altitude Exposure.
papers.authors: Yong Y, Cheng J, Xu J, Li H, Ma H, Wang N.
papers.abstract: High-altitude hypoxia has been examined with conventional electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials, and neuroimaging, but its association with millisecond-scale resting-state EEG microstate dynamics and peripheral physiology remains unclear. We studied healthy adults including 124 low-altitude (LA) participants (50 men, 74 women) and 174 high-altitude (HA) participants (42 men, 132 women; age 28.05 ± 8.59 years; age unavailable for LA). Coverage, duration, global explained variance (GEV), occurrence, and transition probabilities were extracted for four canonical microstates. LA-HA differences were tested using unadjusted linear models; within-HA associations among the high-altitude acclimatization index (AAI), serum albumin, and Microstate A-related indicators were examined using covariate-adjusted regressions and exploratory bootstrapped mediation analyses. Compared with LA participants, HA participants showed increased Microstate A duration and GEV, decreased occurrence, and unchanged coverage, together with reduced Microstate B-related indicators, enhanced Microstate C-related indicators, and increased A→B and A→C transitions. Within HA participants, AAI was negatively associated with serum albumin, and exploratory mediation analyses indicated indirect associations between AAI and Coverage A, Occurrence A, GEV A, and Microstate A-originating transitions through serum albumin. These findings suggest that chronic high-altitude exposure is associated with resting-state EEG microstate reorganization in healthy adults and that acclimatization-related individual differences may be linked to Microstate A dynamics through serum albumin-related peripheral status.

papers.title: Performance Analysis of Laplacian Re-Decomposition-Based PET-MRI Fusion for Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease Classification.
papers.authors: Moslehi M, Sharma R, Khorasani A, Alzheimer’s Disease NeuroimagingInitiative.
papers.journal: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
papers.abstract: Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent critical stages along the continuum of cognitive decline. This study investigates the Laplacian Re-decomposition (LRD) method for fusing positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to develop a quantitative imaging biomarker for the classification of AD. Material and method Data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database were used in this study. T1 , T2 , T2 -FLAIR, and T2 *-weighted MRI sequences, together with [18 F]FDG-PET images, were preprocessed and fused using the LRD algorithm. Hippocampal and frontal lobe WM segmentation, performed via U-Net, enabled relative signal contrast (RSC) calculation as a quantitative biomarker for each modality and fused image. Fusion and segmentation performance were assessed using standard metrics. RSC statistically compared between diagnostic groups after adjustment for demographic confounds, and evaluated for classification performance using ROC/AUC analysis. Results The mean Dice coefficient achieved by the trained U-Net for hippocampus and frontal lobe WM segmentation were 0.93 and 0.95, respectively. ROC analysis revealed that the RSC extracted from T1 -weighted images fused with PET outperformed other modalities for AD vs. Cognitively normal (CN) classification (AUC = 0.88, accuracy = 0.90). Also, T2 -weighted images fused with PET, using RSC as a quantitative biomarker, achieved the best classification performance for AD vs. MCI (AUC = 0.81, accuracy = 0.81) and MCI vs. CN (AUC = 0.84, accuracy = 0.88) classification. Conclusion Our findings indicate that RSC extracted from LRD-fused images achieves competitive classification performance, supporting its potential as a quantitative biomarker for AD.

papers.title: Impaired visual-motor integration function in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: potential neural correlates from resting-state fNIRS.
papers.authors: Wang W, Qian H, Dong M, Pan M, Li H, Yue X, Si F, Liu L, Qian Q.
papers.abstract: Visual-motor integration (VMI) impairment is common in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), yet its underlying neurobiological basis remains unclear. This study aimed to explore the characteristics of VMI in children with ADHD and its statistical role in the association between functional connectivity (FC) and core symptoms. A total of 332 children with ADHD and 103 healthy controls (HC) completed the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (Beery VMI). Group comparisons and dimensional correlation analyses were performed to explore the VMI characteristics of children with ADHD. Subsequently, 127 children with ADHD and 91 HC children underwent resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Mediation analyses were performed to investigate the role of VMI in the relationship between atypical FC and core symptoms of ADHD. Children with ADHD exhibited deficits in VMI performance, with 28.92% showing abnormal VMI. VMI was negatively correlated with core ADHD symptoms. At the network level, VMI showed significant statistical indirect associations in the relationship between FC of DMN-DMN, DMN-DAN, and DMN-VAN networks and inattention symptoms, and between FC of the DMN-DAN networks and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. At the channel level, VMI was also indirectly associated with FC of the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG)-right middle occipital gyrus (MOG) and ADHD core symptoms. Children with ADHD have deficits in VMI, and poorer VMI performance is associated with greater severity of core ADHD symptoms. Altered intra- and inter- network FC of the DMN may represent a potential neural correlate of VMI impairment in ADHD.

papers.title: Management and outcomes of moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures: a 10-year experience from an Australian Level 1 Trauma Centre.
papers.authors: Tay TH, Rosley M, Patel B, Wullschleger M.
papers.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
papers.abstract: Purpose Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures are associated with high morbidity and mortality despite advances in resuscitation, development in trauma systems and multispecialty haemorrhage control. This study aimed to describe the management strategies and clinical outcomes of moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures over a 10-year period at an Australian Level I Trauma Centre. Methods A retrospective observational cohort study was performed of patients aged ≥ 16 years with moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures (Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) ≥ 3) treated between January 2015 and December 2024. Data were obtained from the institutional prospectively collected trauma registry. Results A total of 313 patients met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 47.0 years and 69.3% were male. Motor vehicle (35.1%) and motorcycle collisions (24.9%) accounted for 60.1% of injuries. Median ISS was 26 (IQR 19-34), with 70.6% sustaining pelvic AIS 4-5 injuries. 20.1% of patients underwent at least one haemorrhage-control intervention, including angioembolisation (14.4%), preperitoneal pelvic packing (5.8%) and external fixation (5.8%). Angioembolisation utilisation increased from 6.7% in 2015 to 40.0% in 2024. In-hospital mortality was 7.7%, with traumatic brain injury accounting for 62.5% of deaths and haemorrhagic shock for only one death. Conclusion Moderate-to-severe pelvic ring fractures remained characterised by high-energy mechanisms and severe multisystem injury over the study period, while management evolved with increasing utilisation of angioembolisation. In-hospital mortality was numerically lower compared with historical cohorts, with most deaths attributable to associated traumatic brain injury rather than pelvic haemorrhage.

papers.title: Limited sex-specific structural alterations across common epilepsies: A worldwide ENIGMA study.
papers.authors: Wen H, Wan B, Gholipour T, Xie K, Chen J, Serio B, Hettwer MD, Alvim MKM, Arienzo D, João RB, Bauer T, Bernasconi A, Bernasconi N, Bonanni P, Caligiuri ME, Cendes F, Christin R, Concha L, Dascal A, Boyd ED, Devinsky O, Focke NKN, Fortunato F, Galovic M, Gambardella A, Guerrini R, Hatton SN, Iliza M, Inati S, Ives-Deliperi V, Juster RP, Kleen JK, Koubeissi MZ, Labate A, Larivière S, Law M, Lenge M, Meletti S, Moloney PB, Naish M, Ngo A, O'Brien TJ, Pana R, Panzeri S, Pardoe H, Rauf EHU, Riva A, Rodríguez-Cruces R, Royer J, Rüber T, Sahlas E, Scárdua-Silva L, Schubert KM, Sepeta LN, Severino M, Sinclair B, Soltanian-Zadeh H, Stoub T, Striano P, Thomopoulos SI, Valientes NV, Vaudano AE, Vivash L, Yasuda CL, Thompson PM, Sisodiya SM, McDonald CR, Bernhardt BC, Valk SL.
papers.abstract: Objective Epilepsy is characterized by widespread cortical and subcortical structural alterations beyond the epileptic zone. Importantly, the clinical manifestation of epilepsy, including seizure types, psychiatric comorbidities, and treatment responses, has been shown to differ between sexes. However, sex differences in structural alterations in epilepsy are seldomly reported in neuroimaging studies, partly due to limited sample sizes and single-center designs. We therefore tested whether epilepsy-related structural alterations differ between males and females, and whether the associations between structural measures and clinical characteristics vary by sex. Methods We analyzed clinician-assigned biological sex differences in common epilepsies and their related clinical variables using structural neuroimaging biomarkers in an international multicenter cohort of 1253 epilepsy patients and 1077 healthy controls. We studied cortical thickness and subcortical volume in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE). Results Both male and female patients with TLE showed widespread cortical and subcortical alterations in sex-stratified analyses, whereas GGE showed more extensive alterations in female patients and only subtle alterations in male patients. However, no significant sex-by-diagnosis interactions were identified in either the TLE (t = -2.153 to 1.705, all pFDR >.05) or GGE (t = -1.797 to 2.774, all pFDR >.05) cohort. Likewise, no significant interactions were found between sex and age at onset (tTLE = -1.835 to 1.092, tGGE = -2.394 to 1.392, all pFDR >.05) or disease duration (tTLE = -2.643 to 2.048, tGGE = -1.234 to 2.017, all pFDR >.05) in either patient group. Significance Overall, although sex differences in behavioral and clinical outcomes of epilepsy have been consistently reported in previous studies, our results indicate that sex-related clinical differences in epilepsy are not strongly captured by macroscale structural magnetic resonance imaging measures, and may instead arise from hormonal, neurochemical, or functional-network mechanisms.

papers.title: Affective symptoms in focal epilepsy: A scoping review of localization and lateralizing findings.
papers.authors: Sanchez-Boluarte SS, Lagunas A, Acton E, Guevara-Lazo S, Carrazana E, Freund B, Nascimento FA, Beniczky S, Tatum WO.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Emotional experiences during focal seizures are often misinterpreted as psychiatric disorders. We aimed to evaluate symptoms involving affective symptoms at seizure onset. We aimed to identify the most prevalent affective symptoms at seizure onset and characterize their localizing and lateralizing value. We performed a scoping review based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses-extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A systematic search identified records from 4 databases: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL (via EBSCOhost), and Web of Science. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. This review focused on patients with focal seizures, as affective symptoms may occur in generalized epilepsies. The affective symptoms: fear, anxiety, panic, sadness, mystic, ecstatic, sexual, and mirth were identified, and semiology was evaluated in accordance with ILAE guidelines. Symptom onset, frequency, brain localization, and video-EEG monitoring technique were evaluated to assess localization and lateralization of regional networks. Scalp EEG, invasive EEG recordings, and electrical stimulation were analyzed. A total of 1276 documents were identified, with 98 studies included for review. Fear was the most frequently reported ictal emotion, identified in 274 patients (66%), predominantly in temporal lobe epilepsy. Sadness and sexual, ecstatic symptoms were also consistently associated with temporal networks. Mirth was more frequently reported with frontal onset seizures. Evidence, primarily from Class IV studies, reported right hemispheric predominance for ecstasy, mystic, and sexual symptoms at seizure onset. Ictal affective symptoms at seizure onset yield localizing information. The limbic system, especially the temporal lobe, followed by the frontal lobe, was the most common site of origin.
