Fear was the most common spontaneous and electrically elicited symptom, followed by anxiety. While bi-hemispheric lateralization occurred, right lateralization predominated. Recognizing paroxysmal affective symptoms as ictal phenomena may reduce misdiagnosis and aid presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.

papers.title: Hemispheric Asymmetry of Neuroimaging Biomarkers in Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease: Clinical and Cognitive Outcomes.
papers.authors: Ziontz J, Blazhenets G, Visani A, Chiotis K, Maiti P, Lin Z, Hills AR, Yballa C, Rocha S, Shankar R, Sturm VE, Vemuri P, Hammers DB, Eloyan A, Carrillo MC, Dickerson BC, Apostolova LG, Rabinovici GD, La Joie R, LEADS Consortium.
papers.abstract: Objective Individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD) often exhibit amyloid, tau, and atrophy predominantly in the left or right hemisphere, but group-level analyses typically ignore inter-individual variability and changing asymmetry patterns when averaging data across participants in phenotypically diverse cohorts. Methods We examined left/right hemispheric asymmetry in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET), tau PET, and cortical atrophy in sporadic early-onset AD from 585 deeply phenotyped individuals across 2 cohorts to investigate its clinical correlates. For each imaging biomarker, we computed a global asymmetry index reflecting left/right hemisphere signal difference, and an analogous asymmetry value for PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) voxels. We examined clinical and cognitive correlates of this asymmetry across phenotypes cross-sectionally and longitudinally in a subset of 218 participants. Results Both left and right asymmetry were common for all clinical phenotypes and was correlated between imaging biomarkers. Asymmetry patterns varied spatially within phenotypes, and asymmetry in tau PET and MRI volumes was related to hemisphere-dependent cognitive deficits and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Longitudinal analyses revealed stable amyloid PET asymmetry, decreasing tau PET asymmetry, and increasing MRI volume asymmetry. Interpretation Hemispheric asymmetry is common in early onset AD and correlates with clinical outcomes. Our longitudinal findings suggest a time-lagged asymmetry peak in amyloid, then tau, then atrophy. Taken together, our results position asymmetry as an important feature of AD heterogeneity, as it provides insight into disease mechanisms and trajectories. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: CausalCellInfer: Prioritizing Cell-Type-Specific Disease Associations From Genetically Predicted Transcriptomes in Biobank Cohorts.
papers.authors: Yin L, Shi Y, Zhang R, Xiang Y, Qiu J, Sham PC, So HC.
papers.abstract: Integrating single-cell RNA sequencing(scRNA-seq) with the phenotypic depth of population-scale biobanks is essential for elucidating the cellular basis of complex diseases. However, this is hindered by limited scRNA-seq sample size and the lack of cellular resolution in biobanks. We present CausalCellInfer, a scalable computational framework bringing cellular resolution to bulk and genotype-imputed transcriptomes. CausalCellInfer employs an invariant causal prediction-inspired method(scRNA-seq-based invariant generalized covariance measure, scI-GCM) to select environment-stable marker genes, a parsimonious deep neural network for cell-fraction deconvolution, and regularized matrix completion to reconstruct cell-type-specific (CTS) expression profiles. This design is optimized for biobank-scale data with technical heterogeneity and limited gene overlap. Validated across simulated data, pseudo-bulk and real peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) datasets, CausalCellInfer demonstrated superior accuracy and efficiency over existing methods. Applied to ∼500 000 UK Biobank (UKBB) participants across 29 traits, it captured known pathological shifts, such as reduced pancreatic β-cell proportions in type 2 diabetes, and identified novel biological signals, including disrupted excitatory neuron-oligodendrocyte interactions in depression. Inferred CTS differential expression patterns showed significant concordance with independent single-cell studies and were enriched for Open Targets disease genes. Overall, CausalCellInfer bridges single-cell insights and population-scale genomics, enabling systematic discovery of putative disease mechanisms at cellular resolution.

papers.title: Reduced dorsal CA1 activity limits retention of the temporal component of declarative memory in the Cntnap2 knockout mouse model of autism.
papers.authors: Rawlinson EC, McCullough MH, Sellami A, Marighetto A, Al-Abed AS, Dehorter N.
papers.abstract: Growing evidence implicates the hippocampus in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorder, particularly in the domains of social interactions and cognition. Yet, the mechanisms driving the hippocampal-dependent cognitive atypicalities in autism remain poorly defined. Here, we characterized how dysfunction of the CA1 subfield of the dorsal hippocampus drives abnormalities in critical components of declarative memory. Using trace fear conditioning in the Cntnap2 knockout mouse model of autism, we found that capabilities to retain the association of temporally distant stimuli (i.e. temporal binding) were reduced relative to wildtype mice. Fiber photometry and optogenetic experiments demonstrated that reduced CA1 activity during temporal gaps underlies this impairment, linking CA1 dysfunction to a deficit in long-term memory retention in autism. Using a relational/declarative memory task, we also revealed a deficit in flexible spatial memory, and a preferential use of egocentric learning strategy. This inflexible learning strategy resulted from an imbalance between memory system activity, promoting frontostriatal-dependent procedural learning instead of dorsal CA1/hippocampus-dependent relational/declarative memory. Overall, this study establishes dorsal CA1 dysfunction as a circuit-level mechanism underlying cognitive inflexibility in autism, providing a neurobiological framework for hippocampal-dependent memory deficits in the condition.

papers.title: Linking anterior cingulate sulcal variability to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder behavior
papers.authors: Hadveck RF, Paras A, Anctil M, Martinez E, Gallardo CM, Maboudian SA, Willbrand EH, Weiner KS.
papers.abstract: Background The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is consistently implicated in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ACC variability, including its most variable structure, the paracingulate sulcus (PCGS), has been known since the late 1800s, and since then, has been linked to cognitive control, impulsivity, and psychiatric conditions comorbid with ADHD, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Yet, the role of the PCGS in ADHD remains unexamined at the individual level. Methods We characterized PCGS incidence, asymmetry, and morphology in 247 children and adolescents (144 ADHD: 10.9 ± 2.73 years old, 75% male; 103 neurotypical: 12.2 ± 3.17 years old, 50% male) from the ADHD-200 dataset. The PCGS was manually identified in FreeSurfer cortical surface reconstructions. Morphometric measures, including sulcal length, depth, and cortical thickness, were extracted and normalized to hemisphere-wide variables. Between-group analyses tested whether PCGS presence, asymmetry, and quantitative morphology differed by diagnosis, while behavioral analyses examined associations with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and cognitive measures. Age and gender were included as covariates. Results Analyses revealed that, in both NT and ADHD individuals, there was significant leftward asymmetry in PCGS presence. Between groups, the PCGS was less likely to be present in individuals with ADHD in the left hemisphere. Leftward PCGS absence was also associated with significantly higher ADHD index and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. Conclusions These findings advance understanding of how early neurodevelopmental variation in cortical folding may serve as a structural intermediary between genetic liability and the behavioral expression of ADHD.

papers.title: Thoughts and cortical responses are shaped by the type of change at event boundaries
papers.authors: Ketcheson S, Wallace RS, Zhou SS, Hardikar S, Mulholland B, Chitiz L, Gallivan J, Leech R, Smallwood J, Jefferies E, Wammes JD.
papers.abstract: Continuous experience is divided into discrete and meaningful events, but different kinds of event transitions may shape thought and brain activity in different ways. We examined how perceived event boundaries relate to visual, auditory, and semantic features, ongoing thought, and large-scale cortical states during movie-watching. We combined three independent samples who viewed the same eight movie clips, aligning these measures to a shared stimulus timeline: One marked event boundaries, one reported ongoing thought, and one was scanned with fMRI. Whole-brain spatial correlations showed that event boundaries correlated positively with visual change and negatively with auditory change, but not with any thought pattern. Time-resolved analyses showed that boundaries were associated with a reduction in distracted thoughts and brain states positioned toward visual processing. Clustering boundaries by movie feature change profile identified visual, semantic, interruption, and narrative boundary types. All four types showed a shift toward visual processing in the brain, but their other associations differed. Visual boundaries were associated with less distraction, semantic boundaries with thoughts related to past experience and prior knowledge, and narrative boundaries with more detailed and deliberate thoughts. Visual and semantic boundaries also showed distinct shifts in brain state that were not apparent in the other two types. These findings suggest that event boundaries mark a set of state shifts in ongoing experience, with a shared reorientation toward visual processing and changes in thought and brain state that vary with the type of transition.

papers.title: A Multiverse Approach to Brain Age Prediction: Exploring the Impact of Modality, Bias Adjustment, and Atlas
papers.authors: Festor J, Smolders L, De Baene W.
papers.abstract: Brain age, an individual’s age predicted from neuroimaging data, is a promising biomarker of brain health. Yet brain age estimates may depend on methodological choices within the prediction pipeline. We used a multiverse approach to systematically investigate effects of data modality, bias-adjustment method, and brain parcellation on brain-age prediction using data from 560 healthy adults (18.6-89 years) from the CamCAN dataset. Across 84 pipeline conditions, chronological age was predicted from connectivity features with elastic net regression, and performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE). A multilevel model tested the effects of the pipeline factors and their interactions; moreover, cross-atlas consistency of the most predictive connections was assessed. MAEs varied substantially across conditions (5.26-18.30 years). Modality and bias adjustment had significant effects on MAE and interacted significantly. Concatenating structural and functional connectivity performed similarly to structural connectivity alone, and structure-function coupling produced the highest MAE in most conditions. Beheshti-based bias adjustment outperformed Cole-based adjustment, while combining adjustment procedures did not consistently improve performance. Atlas choice had no main effect on MAE, its interaction with modality was significant but negligible in size, and finer parcellations did not systematically improve performance. However, the network-level features driving predictions showed limited spatial overlap across atlases, and importance was distributed over many features. Brain-age prediction is thus sensitive to methodological choices, particularly modality and bias-adjustment strategy. Atlas choice appears less important for predictive accuracy but may affect which connections appear most predictive. These findings highlight the importance of systematically evaluating analytical choices in brain-age research.

papers.title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
papers.authors: Weaver KJ, Abdon B, Toth B, Jack A, Giblin W, Burgess CR, Pletcher SD, Truttmann MC.
papers.abstract: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle’s responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila , pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that d Fic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation. Significance Statement Loss of motivation is a disabling, poorly treated feature of depression, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, addiction, and aging, and it is often attributed to alterations in dopaminergic pathways. Our work points to a distinct and underexplored mechanism of dysfunction: the capacity of neurons to fold and deliver dopamine receptors to their functional sites. By connecting a conserved enzymatic ER switch to motivated behavior across species, this study links cellular protein quality control to neuromodulation. It suggests that behavioral drive depends on how well neurons tune folding capacity to receptor demand. Because G-protein–coupled receptors are the largest class of drug targets, enhancing receptor maturation may offer new therapeutic avenues for motivational disorders.

papers.title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
papers.authors: Agnorelli C, Peill J, Kurtin DL, Mallon O, Sawicka G, Shatalina E, Godfrey K, Murphy R, Ahmad K, Oestreich LKL, Sumner R, Alberti M, Wall M, Ertl N, Searle G, Clarke M, Zhou K, Osugo M, Sarem U, Weiss B, Greenway K, Jauhar S, Fagiolini A, Carhart-Harris R, Matthews PM, Rabiner E, Nutt D, Erritzoe D.
papers.abstract: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: Location-specific Longitudinal Patterns of Subcortical and Lobar Cerebral Microhemorrhages in Preclinical Alzheimer Disease
papers.authors: Hill C, Michopoulou S, Niranjan M, Kipps CM.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives Cerebral microhaemorrhages influence eligibility and monitoring for anti-amyloid therapies. Emerging evidence and expert opinion suggest that subcortical microhaemorrhages may be less closely related to cerebral amyloidosis than lobar lesions and may therefore warrant separate consideration in anti-amyloid treatment eligibility criteria. Using longitudinal MRI data from cognitively unimpaired individuals with preclinical Alzheimer disease in the A4 study, we hypothesised that lobar and subcortical microhaemorrhages would show distinct location-specific patterns of progression and associated risk profiles. Methods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal cohort analysis of centrally assessed MRI data from A4 study participants with at least two evaluable MRI examinations. Baseline and follow-up were defined as the first and last evaluable scans, respectively. Participants were classified according to the anatomical distribution of baseline microhaemorrhages as lobar or subcortical, and subsequent location-specific lesion accumulation was examined. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess whether baseline lobar and subcortical microhaemorrhage counts were independently associated with the development of additional lobar and subcortical microhaemorrhages. Results Among 1,146 participants followed for a mean of 4.55 years (SD = 1.78), 38 had subcortical-only and 157 had lobar-only microhaemorrhages at baseline. Subsequent lesions preferentially accumulated in the same anatomical compartment. Baseline subcortical microhaemorrhage count was associated with additional subcortical lesions (OR 3.60, 95% CI 2.00–6.47), but not with additional lobar lesions (OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.73–2.15). Conversely, baseline lobar microhaemorrhage count was associated with additional lobar lesions (OR 2.74, 95% CI 2.06–3.64), but not with additional subcortical lesions (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.77–1.53). White matter hyperintensity burden was associated with subcortical progression, while APOE ε4 homozygosity and greater cerebral amyloid burden were associated with lobar progression. Systolic blood pressure was directionally positive but not associated with lobar microhaemorrhage accumulation in either analysis. Discussion Our findings support the emerging view that subcortical and lobar microhaemorrhages exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns and associated risk profiles. Longitudinal studies in patients receiving contemporary plaque-clearing therapies are needed to determine whether microhaemorrhages should be considered differently according to anatomical location in treatment eligibility and monitoring guidelines.

papers.title: Turbulent dynamics and in silico perturbation-based measures are disrupted across biological stages of Alzheimers disease
papers.authors: Martinez-Molina N, Aquilue-Llorens D, Rass L, Montana-Valverde G, Patow G, Escrichs A, Sanz-Perl Y, Kringelbach ML, Palva S, de Maestu F, Deco G.
papers.abstract: According to the AT(N) framework, Alzheimers disease (AD) can be biologically characterised by amyloid deposition, tau pathology, and neurodegeneration, yet how these processes relate to whole-brain dynamics remains unclear. Here, we investigated these relationships and the link between whole-brain dynamics and cognitive dysfunction using multimodal neuroimaging from 145 ADNI3 participants. We combined multiscale measures of turbulent dynamics with responses to in silico perturbations obtained from whole-brain models. AD progression was characterised by a scale-dependent reorganisation of turbulent dynamics where information flow showed the strongest contribution to the dynamics-related variance in cognitive performance. Large-scale turbulence was associated with all three AT(N) components. Model-based information capability and susceptibility measures progressively decreased across AD stages and were associated with amyloid burden and regional tau deposition. Model-free features discriminated comparisons involving AD dementia, whereas adding model-based measures produced modest, metric-dependent changes in classification performance. Exploratory analyses showed spatial alignment between large-scale turbulence alterations and AD-risk gene-expression gradients, with APOE among the strongest associations in both disease-stage contrasts examined. Lastly, we found a progressive decoupling between turbulent dynamics and the E:I balance across AD stages. Together, these findings link model-based and model-free measures of whole-brain dynamics to proteinopathy, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, supporting their complementary value for characterising AD progression.

papers.title: Discrete cortico-hippocampal circuit states underlie mood state transitions in depression
papers.authors: Elbau IG, Lee AM, Chang M, Anderson E, Nilchian P, Victoria L, Manfredi N, Gallagher N, Iatckova V, Sabetfakhri N, Alvarez J, Slepneva N, Summerville I, Chou J, Johnson M, Ho C, Goldwaser E, Rossi J, Khambhati A, Allawalla A, Astudillo Maya D, Moia S, Caballero-Gaudes C, Aloysi A, Murrough J, Gunning FM, Zebley B, Power JD, Williams N, Grosenick L, Chang E, Sellers KK, Krystal A, Lynch CJ, Liston C.
papers.abstract: The hippocampus has long been implicated in depression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Leveraging precision functional mapping in densely sampled individuals and large cross-sectional cohorts, and validating key results in direct intracranial EEG recordings from the human brain, we show that hippocampal connectivity alternates between two discrete and opposing network states on the order of minutes: one dominated by default mode network (DMN) coupling and another by sensorimotor system (SM) coupling. This dynamic switching is a fundamental property of hippocampal function in both healthy brains and in major depressive disorder (MDD). In MDD, this equilibrium is disrupted, such that the DMN-dominant state is overrepresented. In densely sampled individuals, hippocampus-DMN coupling tracks symptom fluctuations over time and normalizes after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), which drives switches in hippocampal connectivity away from the DMN-dominant state and toward the SM-dominant state—an effect that was closely linked to a positive treatment response. Direct intracranial recordings in patients with MDD identified analogous fluctuations in hippocampal–DMN theta synchrony, which tracks symptom fluctuations over hours and days. Together, these findings identify a dynamic cortico-hippocampal mechanism underlying depression and indicate that successful neuromodulation treatments such as ECT act in part by restoring a dynamic equilibrium in hippocampal network connectivity.

papers.title: Muscle and Lipid Suppression: MUSLIS MRI, a novel approach to musculoskeletal MRI
papers.authors: Gambarota G, Beaumont J, Tanner M.
papers.abstract: Purpose to introduce a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique, MUSLIS MRI ( mus cle and li pid s uppression), that generates two co-registered 3D sets of images in a single acquisition: one set with lipid signal suppression (MUSLIS1) and a second set with muscle signal suppression (MUSLIS2). Materials and Methods Numerical simulations based on Bloch equations were performed to optimize the sequence parameters; the MP2RAGE sequence was employed for the implementation of MUSLIS imaging. MRI experiments were performed in vivo at 3 T. Quantitative measurements of signal contrast were carried out on MUSLIS1 and MUSLIS2. Various combination images and T1 parametric maps of the thighs were generated from the two co-registered 3D sets. Results and Discussion Optimal sequence parameters to achieve lipid suppression in one dataset (MUSLIS1) and muscle suppression in the other dataset (MUSLIS2) were determined by numerical simulations. MUSLIS imaging was validated in vivo at 3 T: MUSLIS1 images and MUSLIS2 images displayed excellent lipid and muscle suppression, respectively. The values of the signal contrast between subcutaneous lipids and muscle, as well as between bone marrow lipids and muscle reached values close to 0.8. Thus, MUSLIS would allow for tissue characterization of lesion/masses and direct visualization of the adipose tissue. Combination images, generated from these two intrinsically co-registered sets of images (MUSLIS1 and MUSLIS2), displayed different contrasts and improved signal characteristics, such as mitigation of signal inhomogeneities. The development of MUSLIS imaging for musculoskeletal imaging followed the concept introduced with the FLAWS, an MRI sequence designed for brain MR imaging to generate two 3D sets of images, one with white matter suppression and the other with cerebrospinal fluid suppression. Similarly to FLAWS, which provides T1 maps of the brain, MUSLIS imaging yields T1 parametric maps of the musculoskeletal system. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of the combination images make MUSLIS imaging a potentially attractive technique at field strengths higher than 3 T. Conclusion The proof-of-concept of a novel approach to musculoskeletal imaging, MUSLIS MRI, is proposed here and demonstrated by numerical simulations and MRI experiments performed in vivo at 3 T. Graphical Abstract

papers.title: BrainPT, a Cognitive Mini-Game App for Short-Form Video Use in Young Adults: Neural and Behavioral Pilot Study
papers.authors: Jeong Y, Kim C, Ha S, Choi S, Han S.
papers.abstract: Background Short-form video elicits a stimulus-driven, passive neural state, yet existing interventions target time of use alone and cannot show whether the mechanism of cognitive control has changed. Objective This pilot study developed BrainPT, a mini-game-based cognitive intervention, and evaluated whether a single insertion alters the neural state during short-form viewing (Study 1) and whether repeated use improves behavioral self-regulation (Study 2). Methods Study 1 used a within-subject design (n=9) in which electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) were recorded in the same session across short-form viewing, a single BrainPT set, and goal-directed tasks. Study 2 used a nonrandomized 2-week pretest-posttest design comparing an experimental group that used BrainPT daily (n=13) with a control group (n=8). Both visits followed the same in-laboratory protocol, and app logs and self-report indices were collected over the intervention period. Results In Study 1, short-form viewing was accompanied by prefrontal deactivation: EEG power fell below baseline in all four bands and most in alpha (−1.72 dB, P =.01; q =.054 after correction). Prefrontal activation was opposite in sign between the goal-directed tasks and viewing (+0.180 vs −0.093, P =.002), and the viewing block immediately after a BrainPT insertion exceeded the block before it (+0.110 vs −0.093, P =.02). The same condition ordering appeared in an independent preintervention sample (n=18). In Study 2, daily short-form use fell from 143.5 to 50.9 min in the experimental group and rose from 104.8 to 132.9 min in the control group, a between-group difference in change of 120.7 min ( P =.004). The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale did not differ between groups ( P =.39), and no neural index separated the groups after 2 weeks. Conclusions A single insertion produced a measurable neural change: prefrontal state during the viewing that followed moved toward the goal-directed task. After 2 weeks of use that neural difference was not detectable between groups although behavior differed, so repeated use may act through the momentary state during viewing rather than by reorganizing the resting state. Both samples were small and nonrandomized, the primary outcome was self-reported, and the analyses were exploratory and not preregistered, so these estimates require confirmation in a preregistered randomized trial with objectively logged use. Trial Registration Clinical Research Information Service (CRIS), Republic of Korea, KCT0012762; https://cris.nih.go.kr

papers.title: Population-based Ethnoracial Disparity in Life’s Essential 8 Vascular Health, Cerebral Small Vessel Disease & Cognition
papers.authors: Husein NK, Ho MP, Lin K, Chan DKE, Hayashi S, Sachdev SP, Hassanzadeh T, Jiang J, Sachdev PS, Wen W.
papers.abstract: Background Whether ethnoracial differences in cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) appear in multimarker burden, particular MRI manifestations, or both, and how they relate to Life’s Essential 8 (LE8) cardiovascular health and cognition, is unclear. Methods This cross-sectional study included 44,982 participants and an age- and sex-matched subsample of 1,426 with reviewed lacune and cerebral microbleed (CMB) ratings. White, South Asian, Black, Chinese and Mixed participants were compared on 0–2 (white matter hyperintensity [WMH]/enlarged perivascular space [ePVS]) and 0–4 (adding CMB and lacunes) composite scores and each marker. LE8 was related to WMH and composite burden, and cognitive means were compared by group. Models were age-, sex- and center-adjusted with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Both composite scores differed across groups (0–2: P=0.00010; 0–4: P=0.0011), with greater burden in Black than South Asian (0–4: OR 1.66; 95% CI, 1.21–2.28) and Chinese participants (OR 2.36; 1.51–3.70), whereas Black–White contrasts were not detected. Black participants had higher WMH volume than White participants (β=0.209; 0.110–0.308), robust to deprivation adjustment and segmentation method; South Asian participants had fewer ePVS (0.82; 0.72–0.93). No ethnoracial-group differences in lacune or CMB counts were detected after correction. Higher LE8 was associated with lower WMH volume (β=−0.13 per SD; −0.17 to −0.09) and lower two-marker burden (OR 0.89 per SD; 0.87–0.91) without detected ethnoracial moderation. Black participants, who had the least favorable LE8 scores, and South Asian participants had lower global cognition than White participants (z −0.76 and −0.57 versus 0.24) despite differing WMH profiles; the pooled WMH–cognition association was null. Conclusions Ethnoracial differences in multimarker cSVD burden were evident but marker-dependent: WMH showed the clearest Black–White difference; focal-lesion contrasts were inconclusive. Better cardiovascular health related to lower WMH and aggregate cSVD burden across groups, whereas cognitive differences did not track cSVD burden, supporting prospective prevention and cognition studies.

papers.title: Normative transcriptomic clues to thalamic developmental vulnerability in C9orf7 2-FTLD
papers.authors: So I, Bouzigues A, Ferry-Bolder E, Cullen E, Russell LL, Foster PH, Farley S, Convery R, van Swieten JC, Jiskoot LC, Seelaar H, Galimberti D, Vandenberghe R, Laforce R, Bruffaerts R, Bertoux M, Lebouvier T, Solje E, Levin J, di Fede G, Thompson A, Ber IL, Migliaccio RL, Körtvélyessy P, Schroeter ML, Logroscino G, Otto M, Uzelac Z, Illán-Gala I, Krüger J, Nacmias B, Gerhard A, Langheinrich T, Ducharme S, Santana I, Tartaglia MC, Masellis M, de Mendonça A, Rowe JB, Graff C, Moreno F, Synofzik M, Borroni B, Sanchez-Valle R, Rademakers R, Brushaber D, Forsberg LK, Heuer HW, Kantarci K, Kolander T, Mester C, Boeve BF, Boxer AL, Rosen HJ, Lee SE, Rohrer JD, Andrews TS, Finger EC.
papers.abstract: C9orf72 encodes a protein that is important for both typical neurodevelopment and homeostatic processes across the lifespan. Pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions constitute the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Collectively, preclinical models and clinical neuroimaging studies have observed smaller thalamic volumes in C9orf72 -associated FTLD, including in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 repeat expansion carriers across 18 to 30 years old, supportive of potential neurodevelopmental origins. However, it is unknown whether asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers demonstrate volume differences in specific thalamic nuclei, as reported in older asymptomatic carriers and symptomatic patients; if so, normative transcriptomic patterns could reveal relevant neurodevelopmental and/or FTLD-related neurodegenerative processes. This study investigated volumetric MRI differences of the thalamic nuclei in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers, and examined spatial associations with normative thalamic transcriptomics from 8 weeks post-conception through middle age. Young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers ( n =72) and non-carriers ( n =48) were enrolled in the Frontotemporal Dementia Prevention Initiative across Europe, Canada, and the USA (ages: 18-30 years; sex: 57% female). Spatial associations between young adult thalamic nuclei volumes and normative transcriptomics from the Allen Human Brain Atlas were examined using complementary data-driven and hypothesis-driven approaches. Spatial expression patterns of transcripts of interest were characterized across prenatal and postnatal neurodevelopment using BrainSpan data. Smaller volumes of the pulvinar, mediodorsal, and lateral nuclei were observed in young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers. These nuclei showed higher normative expression of transcripts involved concurrently in neurodevelopmental and C9orf72 -associated FTLD neurodegenerative processes (including lysosomal, autophagic, and small GTPase functions), and lower normative expression of CALB1 , a marker of prenatal human thalamic development. Normative expression of CALB2 (another human thalamic development marker) yielded positive correlations with C9orf72 across prenatal development to adulthood. These findings identify candidate transcripts that may provide insight into the molecular architecture leading to smaller thalamic nuclei volumes in C9orf72 -associated FTLD.

papers.title: Integration of Neuroimaging and Histopathology in a Squirrel Monkey Model of Spontaneous Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy and Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities
papers.authors: Wadghiri YZ, Khan S, Soliman MT, Szabo J, Murray A, Patel AG, Kingsley C, Swain J, Nehete PN, Veraart J, Mulholland MM, Hopkins WD, Wisniewski T, Scholtzova H.
papers.abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a prevalent cerebrovascular pathology in AD and contributes to amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a major complication of current anti-amyloid immunotherapy. Despite its growing clinical importance, critical gaps remain in the development of reliable biomarkers for antemortem diagnosis of CAA. Squirrel monkeys (SQMs) are a valuable non-human primate model with translational relevance due to their universal propensity to develop abundant CAA and spontaneous ARIA in geriatric animals. The present study employed R 2 *, the apparent transverse relaxation rate, which is sensitive to susceptibility-related tissue properties, including iron content and blood oxygenation levels, to monitor age-related brain pathology in SQMs with varying CAA severity. Young, early geriatric, and late geriatric SQMs underwent 7T MRI using a dual-purpose T 2 *-w 3D multi-gradient-echo sequence for high-resolution anatomy and quantitative R 2 * mapping, alongside T 2 -w/FLAIR imaging. Whole-brain and gray matter R 2 * increased with age. In contrast, white matter R 2 * showed an initial increase followed by a late-life reversal, likely reflecting age-related changes in myelin integrity, tissue microstructure, and tissue water content. MRI-histopathology correlation linked T 2 *-w MRI hypointensities to CAA-positive iron-laden vessels associated with perivascular inflammation and, in some cases, hemosiderin deposits. Here we confirmed the occurrence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E events in geriatric animals. SQMs provided a valuable opportunity to examine the underlying pathology of spontaneous ARIA-E, revealing distinctive tissue signatures associated with its manifestation. ARIA-E hyperintensities were characterized by reactive gliosis and BBB disruption, whereas more advanced lesions exhibited perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and evidence of myelin and axonal injury. The current study presents compelling evidence linking R 2 * alterations with CAA severity and ARIA-related tissue injury, providing a foundation for further advancing early detection of CAA, ARIA risk assessment, and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration
papers.authors: Bagade AV, Miller R, Dearborn JT, Basore K, Summers B, Readnour B, Koelling M, O’Shea J, Wright ER, Dhavale DD, Kotzbauer PT.
papers.abstract: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.

papers.title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During
papers.authors: Rezaei S, Tomoda T, Marcotte M, Prevot TD, Banasr M, Bansal Y, Ezzeddine A, Guan A, Vieira E, Sibille E.
papers.abstract: Background Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-γ receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst ( p= 0.0006), neuropeptide Y ( Npy ) ( p= 0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor ( Bdnf ) ( p <0.0001), and synapsin 1 ( Syn1 ) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 ( Aif1 , encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.

papers.title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
papers.authors: Emura R, Jeong H, Kawachi Y, Komuro R, Koizumi M.
papers.abstract: Introduction Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., “who did what to whom,” relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

papers.title: Bath-related sudden death in pregnancy associated with post-hemorrhagic epilepsy: An autopsy case report.
papers.authors: Watanabe A, Hata Y, Nishida N.
papers.abstract: Sudden unexpected death is a rare but clinically important event in pregnant women with epilepsy. This case report describes a fatal bathtub drowning in a pregnant woman with epilepsy secondary to pregnancy-related intracerebral hemorrhage. A 31-year-old woman at 6 months' gestation was found submerged in a bathtub filled with 41 °C water, and resuscitation attempts were unsuccessful. At age 29 years, she experienced intracerebral hemorrhage requiring hematoma evacuation during delivery of her first child and subsequently developed poststroke epilepsy. She had three nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizures before death. Autopsy revealed increased lung weight and frothy fluid in the airways, consistent with drowning. Neuropathological examination revealed a previous right frontal white matter hemorrhage involving the cortical surface, considered a potential epileptogenic focus. Microscopic examination revealed significant hemosiderin deposition and associated chronic inflammatory changes in the affected area, which may be linked to epileptogenesis. Despite treatment with the maximum dose of levetiracetam (3,000 mg/day), the postmortem blood concentration was near the lower limit of the therapeutic range. This case highlights the structural basis of epilepsy following pregnancy-related intracerebral hemorrhage, the difficulty in preventing fatal seizure-related events in pregnant women, and the potential role of hyperthermia during bathing as a seizure trigger.

papers.title: Therapeutic Significance of Natural vs. Synthetic Coumarins in Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.authors: Patel R, Sinha S, Shukla KS, Singh B, Ved A, Kumar A, Yadav N, Singh V.
papers.abstract: Introduction/objective Coumarin, a naturally occurring aromatic compound bearing a benzopyrone scaffold, represents a versatile motif in synthetic drug design. Recent therapeutic developments have highlighted its potential as a privileged pharmacophore for neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), with particular efficacy targeting Alzheimer's disease (AD). This study presents a critical, comparative review of natural versus synthetic coumarins, evaluating their neuroprotective mechanisms across various preclinical, non-transgenic models of sporadic Alzheimer's disease (sAD). Methods Natural coumarins (e.g., umbelliferone, esculetin, and scopoletin) exert potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and moderate enzyme-inhibitory activities, particularly against acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and β-amyloid (Aβ) aggregation. These phytochemicals attenuate neurodegeneration by modulating oxidative stress and neuroinflammatory pathways across various cellular and rodent models, including 5xFAD mice, as well as streptozotocin (STZ)-and scopolamine (SCOP)- induced Alzheimer's disease (AD) rat models. However, their clinical utility remains constrained by poor bioavailability and modest potency. To address these limitations, synthetic coumarin derivatives, including coumarin-pyrrolidine, coumarin-triazole, coumarin-chalcone, and coumarin-donepezil hybrids, as well as hydroxycoumarins, have been developed. These heterocyclic hybrid architectures exhibit superior therapeutic potency, enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability, and synergistic inhibition of core pathological targets, including AChE activity and Aβ aggregation. Result Both in vivo preclinical models and in silico docking simulations substantiate the neuroprotective capacity of coumarin-based frameworks, demonstrating substantial cognitive rescue, restored synaptic plasticity, and favorable safety margins. Moving beyond the baseline safety of naturally derived coumarins, structural optimization and hybrid design strategies serve as a compelling framework for developing potent, multi-target therapeutics for neurodegenerative diseases. Discussion According to the review, Alzheimer's disease treatment is shifting from natural coumarins to multi-target-directed ligands (MTDLs) because natural compounds, such as esculetin, scopoletin, and daphnetin, are often limited by narrow target specificity and lower potency than synthetic coumarin derivatives. Conclusion Herein, the authors review the biological activities of natural coumarins and their synthetic analogs as potential therapeutics for Alzheimer's disease (AD). This study systematically compared and evaluated the therapeutic efficacy and structural scaffold variations of both natural and synthetic derivatives. To support their translational potential, this study also summarizes current ADMET profiles and pharmacokinetic evaluations, which represent key prerequisites for clinical advancement.

papers.title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
papers.authors: Zhao B, Li M, Yi L, Li J.
papers.abstract: Abstract The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2–PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT–gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K⁺ current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na⁺ current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K⁺ conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na⁺ current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Geometry HCFIM features for data-limited EEG screening of Alzheimer’s disease and Frontotemporal Dementia
papers.authors: Rojas-Pescio H.
papers.abstract: Abstract Resting-state EEG is a scalable modality for neurophysiological screening, but conventional spectral descriptors capture only part of the signal organization altered in neurodegenerative disease. This study evaluates a reproducible information-theoretic geometry framework based on entropy (H), statistical complexity (C) and Fisher Information Measure (FIM) for data-limited EEG characterization of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Using the public OpenNeuro resting-state EEG dataset comprising 29 healthy controls, 36 AD patients and 23 FTD patients, preprocessed eyes-closed 19-channel recordings were segmented into epochs, transformed into finite probability distributions, projected into HC and HFIMplanes and HCFIMspace, and aggregated at subject level. Synthetic signal regimes were first used to verify the behavior of the probability-domain geometry. Regional and lateralized cortical schemas were then compared against PSD baselines using leakage-aware subject-level validation. Then, various machine learning classification models were applied to distinguish between healthy and neurologically affected individuals. In the regional schema, the most consistent AD-related geometric displacement was found in temporal alpha rhythms, using Permutation entropy with m = 4, τ = 1 (inter/intra ratio = 0.847; silhouette = 0.141), while in FTD it was found in temporal broadband (inter/intra ratio = 1.140; silhouette = 0.073); both silhouette values indicate modest, overlapping group geometry rather than well-separated clusters. For AD classification, PSD + HCFIM with Extra Randomized Trees achieved ROC AUC = 0.818 and balanced accuracy = 0.803; adding lateralized differences increased ROC AUC to 0.832 and sensitivity to 0.833, with lower specificity. For FTD, regional HCFIM-only features achieved the highest ROC AUC (0.810), while regional PSD + HCFIM achieved the best balanced accuracy (0.740). Lateralization highlighted left temporal broadband displacement in FTD but did not improve classification. These results support HCFIM as an interpretable, reproducible complement to spectral EEG features for preclinical methodological research, while emphasizing the need for independent validation before clinical or device-specific claims.

papers.title: Whole-Brain, Region-Specific Astrocyte Reactivity and Morphological Remodeling After Diffuse Traumatic Brain Injury in A Gyrencephalic Ferret Model
papers.authors: Bagherian A, Perez C, Kosub A, Gonzales RCY, Patterson A, Bieniek K, Seidi M, Memar M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers pathological cascades that evolve across acute, subacute, and chronic phases. Astrocytes play a central role across these phases, and astrocyte reactivity is commonly evaluated using glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunolabeling. However, in many TBI studies GFAP changes are characterized qualitatively or with manual or simple threshold-based measures on a small set of sections, limiting throughput and constraining analysis of region-specific heterogeneity in astrocyte responses. To overcome these limitations, we employed a ferret model of diffuse TBI (5 TBI, 5 sham), leveraging the ferret's gyrencephalic cortex, human-like regional fractional brain volumes, and astrocyte features that more closely resemble the human brain than rodent models. An AI-driven segmentation model validated for GFAP-stained ferret histology was integrated with atlas-based mapping to achieve whole-brain, region-resolved quantification of astrocyte reactivity over an average of 10 coronal slices per animal. Morphometric analysis using a custom SMorph-based pipeline characterized branching complexity and spatial domain features across defined regions. At seven days post-injury, TBI animals showed elevated astrocyte reactivity and hypertrophic remodeling, with significant expansion of convex hull area and elongation of secondary branches at the whole-brain level, most pronounced in the atlas-defined gray-matter region and cerebellum and brain-stem subregions, whereas white-matter showed a similar but less marked trend. Morphological changes were also detected in the hippocampus that did not show significant increases in astrocyte reactivity, indicating that structural remodeling represents a partially independent dimension of the astroglial response. These regional patterns are consistent with expected large tissue deformation and axonal strain in brainstem-cerebellar pathways and gray-matter at gray-white junctions in sagittal rotation, motivating future computational studies to quantify these links more directly. By combining region-resolved GFAP mapping with large-scale morphometry, this work provides a scalable framework for region-specific astrocyte mapping to support future multimodal, computational, and targeted neuroprotective studies.

papers.title: Clonidine Ameliorates Anxiety-Like Behavior via GRIN2B Demethylation and NR2B Activation in a Two-Vessel Occlusion Rat Model
papers.authors: Wang K, Zhang W, Wang Q, Li G, Chen Y, He Z.
papers.abstract: Abstract Post-stroke anxiety (PSA) is a prevalent neuropsychiatric complication that impairs neurological recovery and quality of life. Clonidine, an α2-adrenergic receptor (α2-AR) agonist, has demonstrated anxiolytic effects; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain elusive. In this study, we established a PSA paradigm using a two-vessel occlusion (2-VO) rat model to investigate whether clonidine exerts its anxiolytic effects through epigenetic modulation of the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B. Behavioral assessments, including the open field test and elevated plus maze, confirmed that 2-VO induced significant anxiety-like behaviors, which were attenuated by clonidine pretreatment (40 µg/kg/d, intraperitoneal). These protective effects were abolished by co-administration of yohimbine, a selective α2-AR antagonist, confirming a receptor-specific mechanism. Mechanistically, 2-VO rats exhibited reduced NR2B expression at both protein and mRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and hippocampus, accompanied by decreased membrane-bound NR2B and phosphorylated NR2B (p-NR2B). Clonidine reversed these deficits, enhancing functional membrane insertion of NR2B in neurons. Immunofluorescence revealed that clonidine restored NR2B immunoreactivity in PFC neurons and hippocampal subfields (CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus). Furthermore, clonidine differentially modulated KIF17-mediated dendritic trafficking of NR2B in the hippocampus and suppressed aberrant CaMKII/CREB signaling in a region-specific manner. Notably, 2-VO induced global DNA hypermethylation and upregulation of DNA methyltransferases (DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B), which were reversed by clonidine. Methylation-specific PCR demonstrated that clonidine specifically reversed GRIN2B promoter hypermethylation in both the PFC and hippocampus, effects that were blocked by yohimbine. These findings establish a novel epigenetic-synaptic axis whereby α2-AR activation suppresses DNMT-mediated GRIN2B promoter hypermethylation, thereby restoring NR2B transcription, membrane trafficking, and phosphorylation to alleviate anxiety-like behaviors. Our results position the α2-AR–DNMT–GRIN2B axis as a promising therapeutic target for precision treatment of PSA and related neuropsychiatric sequelae of cerebral ischemia.

papers.title: The Energy-Deficit Hypothesis of Autism: Prenatal Cytokine Convergence on Persistent Mitochondrial Dysfunction
papers.authors: Kang B.
papers.abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition with substantial genetic contributions but incompletely understood biological mechanisms. Family history of autoimmune disease is associated with elevated ASD likelihood (pooled odds ratio 1.28), while maternal immune-mediated conditions show additional associations, suggesting that inherited immune susceptibility and the gestational inflammatory environment may contribute to risk. A mechanism linking these observations to the characteristic developmental trajectory of ASD remains unresolved. Hypothesis: I propose an immune-metabolic framework in which multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines—including TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-γ—act through distinct molecular pathways yet converge on mitochondrial dysfunction and an ATP supply that cannot meet the developing brain’s energy needs. Within this framework, cumulative prenatal inflammatory burden, rather than any single cytokine, drives the energy deficit. Potential contributors include inherited immune susceptibility and fetal exposure to maternal inflammatory signaling arising from a clinically silent but biologically consequential chronic low-grade state. In this account, the resulting energy constraint disrupts synaptic refinement, real-time social processing, synaptic protein synthesis, and flexible predictive inference—the last offering a bioenergetic interpretation of restricted repetitive behaviors and insistence on sameness as compensation for chronic energy limitation. Crucially, the mitochondrial dysfunction is proposed to persist beyond birth, with the gap between cerebral energy demand and supply widening during the rapid brain growth of the first postnatal years. The model links this trajectory to the emergence of clinical symptoms between 12 and 24 months of age, the selective vulnerability of metabolically demanding brain regions, and regression in a substantial subset of children. The framework further proposes that the reported firstborn association may partly reflect incomplete maternal immune adaptation during first pregnancies. Implications: By uniting prenatal initiation with postnatal persistence into a single developmental trajectory, this framework offers an integrative account of otherwise disparate observations. The model predicts that preserving ATP availability relative to demand in relevant cells during appropriate developmental windows should prevent or attenuate abnormalities attributed to energy limitation. This effect should occur across distinct prenatal cytokine exposures even when cytokine signaling remains intact.

papers.title: Potential links between PCOS/PMOS and Alzheimer disease and related dementias.
papers.authors: Amiri M, Kakavand Hamidi A, Farkas DL, Buyalos RP, Azziz R.
papers.abstract: Background Polycystic ovary syndrome/polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PCOS/PMOS) is a common endocrine disorder with significant metabolic and reproductive implications. Increasing attention has focused on its potential long-term neurological consequences, including possible links to cognitive impairment and Alzheimer disease (AD), through overlapping biological pathways. Methods We conducted a comprehensive PubMed search, from inception through October 2025, identifying studies on cognitive performance, brain structure and function, neurodegenerative biomarkers, and dementia risk in PCOS/PMOS patients. Results Evidence supports multiple potential mechanistic pathways that could connect PCOS/PMOS to AD-relevant biology, such as insulin resistance (IR), chronic inflammation, hormonal dysregulation, and cardiovascular dysfunction. These pathways converge on neurodegeneration processes such as impaired Aβ clearance, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, and cerebral metabolic deficits. Clinically, PCOS/PMOS patients exhibit mild but reproducible impairments in executive function and memory, alongside structural and functional brain alterations, including hippocampal and white matter changes, and altered network connectivity. However, these findings are influenced by coexisting metabolic dysfunction, and direct epidemiological evidence linking PCOS/PMOS to increased dementia incidence remains limited and inconsistent. Conclusion Current evidence indicates that any association between PCOS/PMOS and AD risk is likely mediated by metabolic comorbidities, particularly IR and obesity, rather than an independent effect of PCOS/PMOS itself. However, clinical evidence for increased PCOS/PMOS risk for cognitive vulnerability and dementia remain inconsistent and cognitive benefits from PCOS/PMOS-specific interventions are lacking. Clinical focus should therefore remain on optimizing metabolic health, while longitudinal and interventional studies are required to clarify long-term neurological relationships and outcomes.

papers.title: Ischemic paralysis caused by internal iliac artery embolism after endovascular recanalization for lower extremity arteriosclerosis obliterans: a case report.
papers.authors: Wang J, Li J, Zhang X, Zhang X, Zhang T.
papers.abstract: Background Lower extremity paralysis is a devastating complication after endovascular therapy for lower extremity arteriosclerosis obliterans (LEAOD). Common mechanisms include ischemia-reperfusion injury, acute arterial embolism, and thrombosis. Paralysis caused by internal iliac artery embolism is exceptionally rare and may be overlooked when postoperative neurologic deficits are initially attributed to spinal or cerebral causes. Case presentation An 86-year-old man developed recurrent bilateral intermittent claudication 3 years after endovascular treatment for LEAOD, followed by right toe ulceration. Preoperative computed tomographic angiography showed severe multilevel stenosis and in-stent reocclusion in both lower limbs. He underwent bilateral thrombus aspiration, balloon angioplasty, and catheter-directed thrombolysis. One hour after the procedure, acute left lower limb weakness (muscle strength grade 0-1) and hypoesthesia below the mid-calf occurred. Emergency abdominal-pelvic non-contrast CT, lumbar spine MRI, brain imaging, and lower limb CTA excluded lumbar canal disease and stroke, while suggesting new internal iliac artery occlusion. Emergency thrombus aspiration and balloon angioplasty of the left internal iliac artery restored substantial patency and improved muscle strength to grade III-IV in the thigh and grade III in the leg. Because pain persisted and distal perfusion remained insufficient, femoral endarterectomy and infrapopliteal balloon angioplasty were subsequently performed. After 1 month of rehabilitation, muscle strength remained grade III, with persistent sensory impairment and assisted ambulation. Conclusions Internal iliac artery embolism is a rare but clinically important cause of ischemic paralysis after peripheral endovascular intervention. In patients with extensive multilevel occlusive disease, preoperative assessment of internal iliac collateral perfusion and cautious staged procedural planning may reduce risk. Sudden postoperative limb paralysis should prompt urgent spinal and vascular imaging, followed by timely revascularization when ischemia is suspected.

papers.title: Mechanical ventilation in acute brain injury.
papers.authors: Ratibondi L, Newcombe V, Samanta RJ.
papers.abstract: Acute brain injury (ABI) includes traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and global hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and patients often require admission to intensive care. Although pathologically heterogeneous, they share common mechanisms of primary injury followed by secondary brain injury. Systemic derangements such as hypoxaemia, dysregulated carbon dioxide tension and elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) may exacerbate secondary injury and should be avoided. Patients with ABI often require invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), and of these up to 19-22% may develop acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) strategies using low tidal volumes and moderate positive end-expiratory pressure to minimise ventilator-induced lung injury are established practices in patients requiring IMV. However, strict application of LPV principles may conflict with neuro-protective goals, particularly carbon dioxide control to optimise cerebral blood flow and avoid rises in ICP. This review examines the physiological tension between lung and brain protection, focusing on neuro-respiratory interactions and brain-lung crosstalk. We synthesise the evidence on ventilatory strategies in the context of patients with ABI, discuss the implications for neurological and pulmonary outcomes, and highlight the need for an integrated, individualised approach to ventilation in these patients.

papers.title: Gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation prevents scopolamine-induced damage to EEG activity and spatial memory.
papers.authors: Yuan Y, Xing S, Ren P, Chen Z, Fu Y.
papers.abstract: BackgroundDementia is a serious public health concern, primarily caused by Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) can improve cognitive function by modulating neural oscillations. While tACS shows therapeutic potential for dementia, its preventive effects remain unknown. Because tACS has long-lasting modulatory effects, we propose that these offline effects may help prevent dementia.ObjectiveThis study aims to determine whether pre-administered 40 Hz tACS prevents scopolamine-induced impairment of electroencephalogram (EEG) activity and spatial cognition. Scopolamine induces cholinergic dysfunction in animal models, mimicking AD-related behavioral and EEG abnormalities.MethodsScopolamine (3 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered to induce a mouse model of dementia. Prior to induction, tACS targeting the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and/or hippocampus (Hip) was performed for five days (40 Hz, 300 μA, 20 min/day). EEG activity was recorded from the PFC and Hip during spontaneous and task-related (Y-maze) states. In addition, spatial memory was evaluated using the Barnes maze test, and general activity including locomotion and anxiety was evaluated using the open field test.ResultsScopolamine reduced spontaneous EEG activity in gamma frequency band and task-related PFC EEG activity across multiple frequency bands. Prior Hip tACS prevented these EEG reductions. Behaviorally, scopolamine induced spatial memory deficits and increased locomotion and anxiety-like behaviors. Notably, dual-site tACS reversed memory impairment and PFC tACS reduced locomotion. In addition, tACS had little effect on anxiety.ConclusionsPrior gamma tACS exerts region-specific protection against scopolamine-induced EEG and behavioral impairments, providing first evidence for its potential as a preventive strategy for dementia-related deficits.

papers.title: The ferroptosis-lipid metabolism-neuroinflammation axis in Alzheimer's disease: A review of mechanistic interplay and therapeutic implications.
papers.authors: Zhu T, Deng X, Lu J, Zhou X, Wang Y, Xu D, Song J, Xie X, Chen C.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves multiple pathological pathways, with ferroptosis and lipid metabolic dysregulation forming a coupled mechanism across the disease course, and neuroinflammation acting as a key mediator. While existing reviews often focus on isolated processes, they frequently lack an integrative analysis of the "ferroptosis-lipid-neuroinflammation axis" as a systemic pathological core. This review specifically addresses this gap by proposing a unified mechanistic framework for neuronal injury, synaptic dysfunction, and immunometabolic remodeling in AD, centered on this tripartite axis. We comprehensively summarize how key pathways involving glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), the cystine/glutamate antiporter system Xc- , solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), and N6-methyladenosine (m6 A) regulation shape neuroinflammation within this context. Furthermore, we explore how advanced methodologies, including spatial omics, single-cell transcriptomics, organoid models, and engineered exosome methods, are instrumental in elucidating regional specificity, optimal intervention windows, and targeted delivery strategies for modulating this iron-lipid-inflammation interplay. This axis functions as a pathological amplifier, linking metabolic, oxidative, immune, and structural dysfunctions. Its systemic reprogramming offers a new paradigm for AD subtyping, biomarker discovery, and multitarget interventions, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional amyloid-β/tau-centric approaches. This review integrates literature published up to the submission date, ensuring the inclusion of the latest mechanistic insights and translational advances in the ferroptosis-lipid metabolism-neuroinflammation axis.

papers.title: Emerging Patterns of Mental Health Comorbidities Among Those With Blast or Blunt Mechanism TBI: Leveraging Total Brain Diagnostics Data.
papers.authors: Sullan MJ, Clauss K, O'Neil M, Vlajic S, Baker-Robinson W, Holliday R, Kinney AR, Fortier CB, Cifu DX, Milberg WP, Brenner LA.
papers.journal: The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
papers.abstract: Objective Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with postinjury mental health (MH) sequelae, yet associations between injury-related risk factors (eg, injury mechanism, multiple injuries) and outcomes remain poorly understood. We leveraged a newly harmonized national dataset to evaluate relationships between TBI characteristics and MH outcomes. Data sources We analyzed data from the Total Brain Diagnostics (TBD) dataset, a harmonized data source including 2 large, multisite, longitudinal prospective cohort studies: the Long-term Impact of Military-relevant Brain Injury Consortium's (LIMBIC) and the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders (TRACTS). Participants Veterans and Service Members (n = 3771). Design Pooled cross-sectional analyses of harmonized data. Main measures TBI Characteristics (Predictors): Number of TBIs, whether the participant had experienced a blast-related TBI, and whether the participant had experienced loss of consciousness secondary to a TBI. Mental Health Conditions/Symptoms (Outcomes): Probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), probable depression, probable anxiety, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and probable unhealthy alcohol use. Results Blast TBI was associated with greater odds of probable PTSD (OR 1.85, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.57-2.17), probable depression (OR 1.66, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.42-1.95), and probable anxiety (OR 1.73, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.45-2.05) compared with blunt TBI. Post-hoc analyses suggested differences in the frequency of co-occurring MH outcomes among those with blast versus blunt TBIs. Conclusions Findings suggest unique MH outcomes driven by blast injury mechanism, highlighting potential differences in underlying etiology.

papers.title: TRIM25 promotes neuronal ferroptosis in ischemic stroke by suppressing YBX1/H3K4me1/FTH1 axis.
papers.authors: Zeng K, Peng JJ, Lan Z, Gao D, Zhu P, Zhu Z, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Background Ferroptosis impairs neurological function in ischemic stroke (IS). This study elucidated the mechanism by which Tripartite motif 25 (TRIM25) promotes neuronal ferroptosis during IS. Methods CCK-8 detected cell viability. Flow cytometry and corresponding kits quantified ferroptosis-related parameters. TTC staining determined cerebral infarct volume. Neurological impairment was assessed using neurological deficit scoring and Nissl staining. RT-qPCR, Western blot, and immunohistochemistry assessed the mRNA and protein expression. Co-IP analyzed the ubiquitinated level of Y-box binding protein 1 (YBX1) and the interaction between TRIM25 and YBX1. ChIP assessed the binding of YBX1 and H3K4me1 at the Ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) promoter. Peptide pull-down assessed the interaction between YBX1 and H3K4me1. Results TRIM25 promoted neuronal ferroptosis in IS. TRIM25 promoted YBX1 ubiquitination and degradation. YBX1 knockdown counteracted the suppressive outcome of TRIM25 depletion on OGD/R-induced ferroptosis. YBX1 upregulated FTH1 by recognizing H3K4me1 enrichment at the FTH1 promoter, thus inhibiting OGD/R-induced neuronal ferroptosis. In vivo , TRIM25 knockdown attenuated MCAO/R-induced brain injury via YBX1 upregulation. Conclusion TRIM25 induces YBX1 ubiquitination and degradation, impairing YBX1-dependent H3K4me1 enrichment at the FTH1 promoter to downregulate FTH1, thereby promoting neuronal ferroptosis in IS.

papers.title: Openness to Experience Modulates the Neural Dynamics of Semantic Processing.
papers.authors: Li B, Huang CM, Lin Q, Huang HW.
papers.abstract: Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to Experience (openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes increasing as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

papers.title: Psychoneuroimmunology of glioblastoma: How emotional states shape tumor biology.
papers.authors: de Melo MVG, Bezerra TPW, de Souza PC, Sales VS, da Rosa MM.
papers.abstract: Psychological states profoundly influence physiological processes, with growing evidence linking emotional dysregulation to cancer progression. Within the framework of psychoneuroimmunology, recent findings have shown that chronic stress, depression and anxiety disrupt immune surveillance and promote a pro-inflammatory environment that favors tumor growth. Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), the most aggressive brain tumor, appears particularly sensitive to these neuroimmune influences. Some stress mediators and neurotransmitters-such as glucocorticoids and catecholamines- modulate the GBM microenvironment, fostering tumor-supportive pathways and epigenetic changes. This comprehensive review synthesizes evidence connecting emotional disturbances and glioma biology, highlighting shared neuroimmune mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
