We propose that integrating psychosocial and neuropharmacological strategies into GBM care could improve patients outcomes by targeting both tumor biology and emotional well-being.

papers.title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation.
papers.authors: Yu F, Wang R, Di R, Xu K, Gao J, Shang H, Yuan Z, Dai R, Wu W, Weng D, Gao X, Li H, Yu T, Zhang Y, Wang X, Luan G, Zhao F, Luo M.
papers.abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Effects of intensive sensorimotor rehabilitation in resting state functional connectivity in a rodent model of Cerebral Palsy.
papers.authors: Sanches E, Gabriel Schirmbeck G, Mairesse J, Ho D, Dennez C, Baud O, Sv SS.
papers.abstract: Background Sensorimotor stimulation has been shown to protect against brain damage and function impairments following experimental Cerebral Palsy (CP). Functional ultrasound (fUS) gives valuable information about brain connectivity at unprecedented spatial and time resolutions with high translational potential. We tested brain function and connectivity using fUS following experimental CP and the effects of early sensorimotor rehabilitation in the model. Methods Pregnant Wistar rats were exposed to maternal immune challenge at E18-19. Pups received perinatal anoxia at postnatal day 0 (P0) and restriction of the hindlimbs from P2 to P21. Rehabilitation (EETT) used environmental enrichment (EE) and Treadmill Training (TT) from P21 to P28. At P29, fUS was performed to access brain connectivity and graph theoretic analysis was used to distinguish patterns of brain connectivity. Results CP increased intrinsic brain functional connectivity compared to Controls and EETT animals. Connectivity was increased in CP animals in cortical areas related to sensorimotor function and subcortical myelinated structures. EETT animals showed levels of brain connectivity similar to Controls. Conclusions Sensorimotor stimulation changed brain hyperconnectivity profile induced by CP. Brain connectivity pattern alterations can be detected using fUS with high accuracy, suggesting great potential to be used as earlier biomarker for neurodevelopmentalal disorders such as CP.

papers.title: Default mode network mechanisms of trait rumination in treatment-resistant depression and rTMS: evidence from source-localized EEG.
papers.authors: Chu SA, Valles TE, Citrenbaum CC, Leuchter MK, Shamas M, Leuchter AF, Corlier J.
papers.abstract: Background Rumination is a transdiagnostic feature of multiple psychiatric disorders and is a critical risk factor for more severe episodes and poor treatment outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) ameliorates both depressive and ruminative symptoms in TRD. While prior literature has linked rumination to abnormal default mode network (DMN) connectivity, the electrophysiological correlates of rumination in the DMN are not well understood. Methods Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) data were examined in a cohort of 66 TRD subjects who underwent 30 sessions of rTMS treatment for TRD administered to left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We employed source-localization and calculated four metrics of functional connectivity (Amplitude Envelope Correlation [AEC], weighted Phase Lag Index [wPLI], magnitude-squared coherence, and Spectral Correlation Coefficient [SCC]) across five frequency bands within the DMN to identify the neural correlates of rumination in TRD. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using the Network Based Statistic (NBS). Results Baseline severity of rumination and depression were positively correlated, but AEC alpha band connectivity was positively associated only with baseline rumination severity and not depression. Rumination severity prior to treatment was not associated with any other connectivity metric. Severity of rumination and depression decreased following rTMS treatment, but alpha AEC connectivity did not charge after 30 sessions of rTMS treatment. Conclusion Higher DMN connectivity, as measured by alpha-band AEC, is a stable trait-like neurophysiological marker of rumination that is not significantly affected by rTMS administered to left DLPFC.

papers.title: Neurophysiological signatures underlying preserved lexical-semantic proficiency in healthy aging.
papers.authors: Nurmi P, Ala-Salomäki H, Renvall H, Liljeström M.
papers.abstract: Although semantic cognition remains behaviorally stable with age, neuroimaging studies report age-related alterations in response to semantic context. To address these inconsistent findings, we combined behavioral and magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures and examined the neural mechanisms underlying lexical-semantic processing in healthy aging. Forty-six Finnish-speaking adults across younger (22 - 32 years) and older (62 - 69 years) cohorts performed a semantic congruency judgment task on word pairs. Both age groups performed the task with high accuracy, with older adults responding faster than younger. While task performance was retained in older adults, MEG revealed a shift in the neural activation patterns with advancing age. Younger participants exhibited the canonical N400 effect in the left temporal cortex 300 - 400 ms post-stimulus, followed by a late semantic effect, whereas older adults showed less pronounced congruency effects, and the activation distribution was shifted toward frontal and bilateral regions. Despite the absence of the canonical N400 effect in older participants, multivariate time-resolved decoding demonstrated that the congruency effect was decodable from the MEG activation patterns in both groups from ~300 ms post-stimulus, indicating preserved sensitivity to congruency with age. Decoding performance further correlated with response times, suggesting that greater neural separation between semantic concepts, indicated by higher decodability, is associated with rapid decision-making. Critically, age groups were distinguishable based on their neural responses 300 - 800 ms post-stimulus, indicating a functional reorganization of semantic processing in older adults. Overall, our findings suggest that healthy aging involves a reconfiguration of neural systems associated with preserved semantic proficiency, despite broader age-related cognitive changes.

papers.title: D2 dopamine and CB2 cannabinoid receptor cooperation restores striatal LTP in an epilepsy model.
papers.authors: Sciaccaluga M, Bellingacci L, Imperatore V, Taddei AA, Tozzi A, Di Filippo M, Barzasi M, Gardoni F, Sánchez MP, Serratosa JM, Parnetti L, Mancini A, Costa C, DEFEAT-LD Study Group.
papers.abstract: Increasing evidence suggests that subcortical structures contribute to seizure susceptibility and cognitive impairment in several epileptic syndromes. However, research into mechanisms linking neuronal excitability and synaptic dysfunction in epilepsy has mainly focused on the cortex and hippocampus, leaving basal ganglia contributions largely unexplored. Using a genetic murine model of Lafora disease (LD), a drug-resistant form of neurodegenerative epilepsy, we performed ex vivo patch-clamp recordings to assess neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and plasticity of striatal medium spiny neurons. Our results reveal progressive alterations in corticostriatal transmission and long-term synaptic plasticity, including long-term potentiation (LTP). Electrophysiological and biochemical assessments showed a reduced NMDA/AMPA ratio and reduced expression of NMDA receptor subunits and dopamine receptors in striatal neurons of LD mice. Exposure to a dopamine D2 receptor agonist and to cannabidiol restored long-term plasticity in LD mice, suggesting a D2R- and CB2R-dependent synergic action on striatal LTP. Our findings highlight basal ganglia dysfunction in experimental epilepsy and suggest an unconventional dopaminergic-endocannabinoid interplay.

papers.title: Differential changes in frontolimbic functional connectivity following 12-week psychostimulant monotherapy in ADHD youth with and without familial risk for bipolar I disorder.
papers.authors: Li Q, Li F, Qin K, Lei D, Tallman MJ, Patino LR, Sweeney JA, Gong Q, DelBello MP, McNamara RK.
papers.abstract: Background Although attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), psychostimulant medications, and BD family history are risk factors for developing bipolar I disorder (BD), their contribution to the aberrant ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) and amygdala (AMY) functional connectivity (FC) implicated in the pathophysiology of BD remain unclear. Methods We investigated the effects of 12-week daily oral psychostimulant monotherapy on AMY-VLPFC FC during emotional and task-related attentional processing in ADHD youth with ('high-risk', HR) and without ('low-risk', LR) a first-degree relative with BD. LR received mixed amphetamine salts-extended release (MAS) and HR were randomized to MAS or placebo (PLA). Functional magnetic resonance scans were acquired at baseline and week 12 during a continuous performance task with emotional distracters. Generalized psychophysiological interaction analysis assessed AMY-VLPFC FC during emotional and task-related attentional processing. Results The study included 116 youth [healthy controls n = 38, LR-MAS n = 42, HR-MAS n = 24, HR-PLA n = 12]. Following treatment, neither LR-MAS nor HR-MAS exhibited changes in bilateral AMY-VLPFC FC during emotional processing. During task-related attentional processing, HR-MAS youth showed greater longitudinal increase in right AMY-VLPFC negative FC compared with LR-MAS (P = 0.034) and HR-PLA groups (P = 0.007). Compared with HR-MAS, LR-MAS exhibited greater reductions in ADHD total and inattention symptoms. Conclusions These findings suggest that familial BD risk may be associated with a differential longitudinal neurofunctional response to a regimen of psychostimulant monotherapy during attentional, but not emotional, processing.

papers.title: Targeting Nrf2 signaling in Parkinson's disease: Mechanisms, strategies, and therapeutic perspectives.
papers.authors: Cao Y, Zhang J, Peng S.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of α-synuclein. Disease progression is driven by a complex interplay of chronic oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. As a central regulator of the cellular antioxidant response, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) protects against these cellular insults by driving the expression of various cytoprotective genes. In this review, we summarize the regulatory mechanisms of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and evaluate how its activation counteracts core PD pathologies. We also highlight the extensive crosstalk between Nrf2 and other major signaling networks that collectively determine dopaminergic neuronal survival. Finally, we examine the therapeutic potential of current Nrf2 modulators, including natural phytochemicals, clinical-stage candidates, and repurposed drugs, and critically discuss the pharmacokinetic barriers, electrophilic off-target toxicities, and the Nrf2 paradox that must be overcome to successfully translate these compounds into disease-modifying therapies for PD, highlighting the transition toward non-covalent PPI inhibitors.

papers.title: Antidepressants and cognitive function in major depressive disorder: Mechanisms, clinical evidence, and implications for precision treatment.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Tan Y, Hashimoto K.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a core feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) and significantly impairs functional recovery. This review summarizes current evidence on the effects of antidepressants on cognitive function and discusses the underlying mechanisms. Antidepressants may exert their effects through multiple mechanisms, including modulation of monoaminergic neurotransmission, enhancement of neuroplasticity, and regulation of stress and inflammatory pathways. Available studies indicate that antidepressants differ in their cognitive benefits, with vortioxetine showing the most consistent procognitive evidence. Duloxetine, bupropion, and some augmentation strategies may also improve specific cognitive domains, though the evidence is limited. Importantly, cognitive improvement may result from direct drug effects on cognition or indirectly via alleviation of depressive symptoms, highlighting the need for mediation analyses in future research. In patients with late-life depression, vortioxetine and duloxetine have shown relatively clear benefits, and augmentation with cognitive enhancers has demonstrated some potential. The long-term cognitive protective effects of antidepressants remain unconfirmed. Immuno-metabolic depression subtypes, high-dose-related adverse effects, and comorbidity with anxiety and sleep disorders may constitute important sources of residual cognitive deficits. Emerging treatments such as ketamine, psychedelic compounds, and interventions targeting the gut-brain axis may offer new opportunities for addressing cognitive dysfunction in MDD. Current evidence is limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous cognitive assessments. Future research should prioritize large, randomized controlled trials with cognition as the primary endpoint, using standardized assessment tools. A better understanding of the cognitive profiles and mechanisms of antidepressants may support precision medicine strategies and promote functional recovery in patients with MDD.

papers.title: Harnessing cGAS-STING in neurodegeneration: From mitochondrial DNA leakage and microglial reactivity to species-specific translational barriers.
papers.authors: Wang M, Li J, Wang X, Chai X, Luo J, Zhang Y, Chang X, Sun Y, Wang H.
papers.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, a cornerstone of innate immunity, has emerged as a critical driver of sterile neuroinflammation in the aging brain. Age-related decline in mitochondrial quality control, coupled with nuclear and lysosomal erosion, fosters the aberrant accumulation of cytosolic self-DNA, establishing a permissive environment for chronic cGAS-STING activation. This review synthesizes recent breakthroughs elucidating how major neurodegenerative diseases-Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease-converge on this pathway through distinct, disease-specific triggers, ranging from PINK1/Parkin deficiency-driven mitochondrial DNA leakage to TDP-43 proteinopathy-associated retrotransposon de-repression. Critically, we evaluate the translational landscape, highlighting the profound challenge posed by species-specific pharmacology, as exemplified by the failure of the covalent inhibitor H-151 to engage human STING. We argue that the future of therapeutic intervention lies not in wholesale pathway ablation, but in nuanced, context-dependent fine-tuning that disentangles its detrimental chronic effects from its indispensable homeostatic functions. This review positions the cGAS-STING axis as a promising yet delicate frontier for combating age-related neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Hippocampal ALKBH5 contributes to depression-like behaviors in a mouse model of inflammatory pain.
papers.authors: Deng S, Zhu J, Zhou H, Tang X, Gong W.
papers.abstract: Background Chronic pain and depressive symptoms frequently coexist and mutually reinforce each other, severely compromising patients' quality of life, yet the underlying central molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. ALKBH5, an m6A demethylase, has been implicated in the regulation function of central nervous system. However, whether ALKBH5 contributes to depression-like behaviors induced by chronic inflammatory pain remains unknown. Methods The Complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA)-induced inflammatory pain model was employed in this study. ALKBH5 expression and behavioral performances were examined in CFA-treated mice. To further validate the role of hippocampal ALKBH5 in this model, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated shRNA was delivered to knock down ALKB5 in the hippocampus. Results ALKBH5 protein levels were significantly unregulated in the hippocampus of CFA mice. Adenovirus-mediated knockdown of hippocampal ALKBH5 markedly alleviated CFA-induced depressive-like behaviors, possibly due to the reduced expression of iNOS. Conclusion our findings identify hippocampal ALKBH5 as a key regulator of depression-like behaviors in chronic inflammatory pain and suggest that targeting ALKBH5 may provide a novel therapeutic strategy for alleviating affective disorders associated with chronic pain.

papers.title: State-specific dynamic functional connectivity disturbances in spinal cord injury-related neuropathic pain.
papers.authors: Sun C, Xin H, Wang L, Chen Q, Wang Y, Yang B, Chen X, Li F, Lu J, Chen N.
papers.abstract: This exploratory study aimed to characterize dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) alterations in spinal cord injury-induced neuropathic pain (SCI-NP) and dFNC-related metrics as biomarkers for treatment guidance. A total of 23 SCI individuals with NP (SCI-NP), 20 SCI individuals without NP (SCI-N), and 20 healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. SCI-NP individuals were predominantly chronic (≥12 months post-injury), whereas SCI-N individuals were predominantly acute/subacute (<12 months post-injury). Resting-state fMRI data were analyzed using independent component analysis (ICA) combined with a sliding-window approach to characterize dFNC. Recurring connectivity states were identified using clustering algorithms. Group differences were assessed using ANCOVA, adjusting for age and sex. P values were FDR-corrected for multiple comparisons. Spearman's correlation analyses examined associations between dFNC metrics and pain and clinical scores. Twenty-two whole-brain independent components were identified, and seven functionally meaningful components were selected for dFNC analysis, which revealed six distinct connectivity states. Compared with the SCI-N group, the SCI-NP individuals showed increased State 1 connectivity between the medial visual network (mVN) and sensorimotor network (SMN) and between the default mode network (DMN) and SMN (both p < 0.05, uncorrected), reflecting enhanced cross-modal sensory integration and maladaptive plasticity commonly observed in chronic neuropathic pain. In contrast, State 6 exhibited significantly reduced DMN-visual network (VN) connectivity in the SCI-NP group (p < 0.05, uncorrected), representing a low-interaction resting configuration that may reflect preserved functional segregation preferentially maintained in the SCI-N group. The SCI-NP individuals had shorter mean dwell time (p = 0.04, uncorrected) and fraction of time (p = 0.03, uncorrected) in State 6 relative to SCI-N individuals. None of these differences survived FDR correction.These findings indicate that SCI-NP individuals exhibit state-specific dynamic connectivity disturbances, including maladaptive hyperconnectivity involving sensorimotor, visual, and default mode networks. Metrics of dFNC-including state-specific connectivity and dwell time may serve as sensitive imaging features for guiding targeted rehabilitation strategies in SCI-NP.

papers.title: Metformin alleviates neuronal injury in MK-801-Induced Schizophrenia-Like mice by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis.
papers.authors: Lin Y, Wen G, Hu X, Hu R, Duan Y, Wu N, Xiong P, Jin X.
papers.abstract: Background and objective Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a severe mental disorder, and its pathological mechanism is closely associated with neuronal ferroptosis. Metformin (Met) has a well-defined anti-ferroptotic effect. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate whether Met improves neuronal injury and behavioral abnormalities in MK-801-induced SCZ-like mice by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis. Methods Mice received dizocilpine (MK-801) to induce a SCZ-like phenotype. The behavioral activities of mice were evaluated using the open field test, Morris water maze test, and forced swim test. Neuronal injury in the hippocampus was evaluated by Nissl staining. The mitochondrial structure in the hippocampal tissue was observed using transmission electron microscopy. Ferroptosis was assessed by measuring the levels of glutathione (GSH), malondialdehyde (MDA), and Fe2 ⁺; lipid peroxidation; mitochondrial membrane potential; and p53, SLC7A11, and GPX4 expression in the hippocampus. Results Hippocampal neurons in MK-801-induced SCZ-like mice exhibited typical ferroptotic characteristics, including obvious neuronal injury; reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, GSH, SLC7A11, and GPX4 levels; and elevated lipid peroxidation, MDA, Fe2 ⁺, and p53 levels. Met intervention significantly reversed these ferroptosis-related indicators and inhibited hippocampal neuronal ferroptosis. Furthermore, Met alleviated MK-801-induced ferroptosis in HT22 cells. Behavioral results revealed that Met ameliorated behavioral abnormalities in the MK-801-treated mice. The ferroptosis inducer RSL3 partially reversed the behavioral improvements induced by Met. Further studies demonstrated that risperidone (RIS) or Met alone alleviated behavioral abnormalities in MK-801-induced SCZ-like mice, whereas their combined treatment produced greater improvement than either monotherapy. Conclusion Met can alleviate neuronal damage and cognitive dysfunction in MK-801-induced SCZ-like mice, at least in part, by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis. Moreover, combined treatment with Met and RIS is more effective.

papers.title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention.
papers.authors: O'Reilly Sparks KC, Pedapati EV.
papers.abstract: Introduction Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities. Methods This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies. We organize the findings into four overlapping functional-computational domains and relate these domains to the Research Domain Criteria Social Processes framework. Results The four domains are: (1) Social Reward and Social Interest, encompassing the incentive and hedonic value of social contact and motivation to engage; (2) Social Memory and Social-Affective Value, encompassing recognition of familiar individuals and learned affective or motivational associations; (3) Social Cue Perception, Action Representation, and Social Prediction/Timing, encompassing the processing and forecasting of dynamic social information; and (4) Higher-Order Social Cognition and Model Updating, encompassing mental-state inference and the updating of person-specific social models. Because these domains are not independent, interactions among reward, memory, cue processing, prediction, and higher-order inference create multiple possible developmental entry points, such that early differences in one process may alter experience-dependent learning in others. Evidence for specific causal cascades remains preliminary and requires longitudinal testing. Conclusions A circuit-and-development framework may improve hypothesis generation, domain-specific phenotyping, target-engagement assessment, and mechanism-aligned outcomes. Clinical translation, however, requires caution. Biomarkers should be validated as predictors of treatment response, cascade models should be tested longitudinally, and interventions should combine mechanism-informed targets with behavioral support that promotes generalization to daily life.

papers.title: A tunable brain-targeted PEGylated ginsenoside Rg1 derivative disrupts the ROS-mediated inflammasome-pyroptosis cascade to ameliorate Alzheimer's cognitive deficits.
papers.authors: Zhu X, Liang H, Fan L, Bo J, Diao F, Qian Y, Zhang G, Li W.
papers.abstract: The pathogenic cascade of oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and pyroptosis serves as a core driving factor in the pathogenesis and progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although ginsenoside Rg1 exhibits pleiotropic neuroprotective activities, its poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability severely hinders its clinical translation. To overcome this limitation, a brain-targeted delivery system was constructed using a covalent conjugation strategy, linking purified Rg1 with rhodamine B-modified polyethylene glycol (PEG) of varying chain lengths (Rg1s-PEG). After screening, the derivative Rg1s-PEG-600 was identified as achieving an optimal balance between hydrophilic stealth properties and steric hindrance, demonstrating enhanced brain accumulation and favorable biosafety profiles. In both in vitro and in vivo models of lipopolysaccharide-induced acute neuroinflammation, Rg1s-PEG-600 attenuated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, inhibited canonical neuronal pyroptosis mediated by the NLRP1/3 inflammasomes, and significantly ameliorated behavioral deficits and synaptic loss. Furthermore, in chronic 5xFAD transgenic mice, systemic administration of Rg1s-PEG-600 for 12 weeks markedly reversed spatial memory decline, anxiety-like behavior, and synaptic protein depletion. Mechanistic studies further revealed that this targeted nanotherapeutic not only suppressed the ROS-NLRP1 signaling axis and subsequent neuronal pyroptosis in the AD brain but also comprehensively inhibited amyloidogenesis and Tau hyperphosphorylation. This work provides a promising, multitarget nanotherapeutic strategy to overcome BBB limitations and disrupt the complex pathological networks underlying neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Conformational allocation of mitofusin 2 in neuronal mitochondrial dynamics: Mechanisms and therapeutic targeting.
papers.authors: Zhang ZY, Qin BQ, Wu SZ, Zhang H.
papers.abstract: Neurons must sustain functional mitochondria far from the cell body. Mitofusin 2 (MFN2), a dynamin-like large guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase), coordinates outer mitochondrial membrane remodeling with axonal transport, bioenergetic support, inter-organelle communication, and stress-responsive quality control. Studying these activities separately obscures how disruption of one protein produces diverse neuronal phenotypes. We propose a testable conformational-allocation framework in which molecular state distributions and transition kinetics bias MFN2 participation across cellular outputs. Integrating structural and functional evidence, we distinguish experimentally resolved mechanisms from working models. Variants associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) are compared by the molecular step or functional output affected. Fusion loss alone does not capture this mechanistic diversity. Structure-guided docking supports local compatibility at a shallow, conformationally conditional C-terminal surface, without establishing native accessibility, affinity, or therapeutic response. CMT2A provides the strongest context for intervention, combining causal genetics, direct mitofusin engagement studies, and multiscale rescue. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) provides secondary preclinical evidence, whereas Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases remain exploratory. The mitofusin pathway is chemically tractable, but paralog selectivity and state-dependent target engagement remain unresolved. A state- and variant-informed strategy may better match intervention to the affected output than indiscriminate enhancement of fusion.

papers.title: Parsing the relationships among gut microbiome, neurotransmitter metabolome, glymphatic function, and cognition across healthy elderly, mild cognitive impairment, and probable Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Tao C, Wan K, Song Y, Xu X, She M, Sun Z, Zhu J, Yu Y.
papers.abstract: Background Evidence has suggested brain glymphatic dysfunction and gut microbial metabolic disturbance in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the relationships among gut microbiota, neurotransmitter metabolites, glymphatic function, and cognition across clinically defined groups of healthy elderly, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and probable AD remain unclear. Methods Using metagenomic sequencing, targeted metabolomics, and multi-modal magnetic resonance imaging, we measured the gut microbiome, neurotransmitter metabolome, and a variety of glymphatic markers in 30 patients with clinically diagnosed probable AD, 75 individuals with MCI, and 59 healthy controls (HC). Results Although global microbial diversity showed no group difference, MCI and AD showed shared and unique species-level microbial alterations relative to HC. Despite the absence of overall metabolomic divergence, AD exhibited reduced levels of multiple neurotransmitter metabolites compared with MCI and HC. Prominent alterations in multiple glymphatic markers were present in AD rather than in MCI. Further integrated analyses revealed a wide range of associations among these multi-omics changes and established potential serial mediation pathways, manifesting as a pattern of gut microbiota → neurotransmitter metabolites → glymphatic function → cognition. Conclusions These findings could enrich our understanding of the biological mechanisms involved in cognitive impairment and clinically diagnosed probable AD, but also may inform future preventive and therapeutic interventions by targeting the established pathways.

papers.title: Altered frontal and dorsal hemodynamic engagement during mandarin aspiration processing in post-stroke aphasia: an fNIRS study.
papers.authors: Cheng J, Ren T, Liu Y, Ma Y, Luo M, Zhou F, Wang Y, Chen A, Lu C.
papers.abstract: Auditory and speech-perception difficulties are common in post-stroke aphasia (PSA), but cortical responses during passive listening to Mandarin speech remain underexplored. Seventeen Mandarin-speaking individuals with PSA and 18 matched healthy controls listened to auditory oddball blocks containing /ba/ standards and /pa/ deviants during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Although these syllables instantiate an aspiration contrast strongly cued by voice onset time (VOT), standard and deviant trials were combined within a single block-level condition. The resulting measures therefore indexed activation during speech-containing blocks relative to silent inter-block intervals rather than phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT-specific processing. Seven theory-driven channels covering bilateral auditory, sensorimotor, inferior frontal, and dorsolateral prefrontal regions were analyzed using three HbO indices: β coefficient, peak amplitude, and temporal centroid. The PSA group showed an overall reduction in task-related HbO activation, reflected by a significant Group effect for the β coefficient. Peak amplitude also showed significant Group and Group × Channel effects, although no individual channel remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Temporal centroid showed no significant group or interaction effects. These findings provide preliminary evidence for reduced block-evoked cortical recruitment during passive auditory exposure to Mandarin speech sounds in PSA. Because the analysis did not include a direct standard-deviant or active auditory control comparison, the findings do not establish a selective impairment of phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT processing. Because patients were assessed 6-7 months after stroke onset, the activation differences may reflect both persistent impairment and recovery-related reorganization during the early chronic stage.

papers.title: Preoperative white matter lesions and functional recovery after revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia.
papers.authors: Doita T, Kikuchi S, Hikasa E, Jinno H, Kuriyama N, Takahashi K, Ohira S, Kamada K, Shikota M, Hosoya N, Miyake K, Miyagawa S, Ota T, Azuma N.
papers.abstract: Objective Restoring ambulation is an important goal of revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), but predictors of functional recovery remain limited. We investigated whether preoperative white matter lesion (WML) burden was associated with ambulatory recovery after revascularization. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort included 196 patients with CLTI, tissue loss, Wound, Ischemia, and foot Infection (WIfI) ischemia grade 2 or 3, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 3 months before revascularization. Preoperative brain MRI was routinely obtained in patients considered for open surgical revascularization for cerebrovascular risk assessment. Periventricular and deep subcortical white matter hyperintensities were graded using the Fazekas scale; a total score of 3 or greater defined high-grade WML burden. The primary outcome was achievement of a Functional Ambulation Category score of 3 or greater within 180 days. Associations were evaluated using multivariable Cox models. Results High-grade WML burden was present in 120 patients. Six-month ambulatory recovery was lower in the high-grade group than in the low-grade group (63.1% vs 82.4%; P = .019). High-grade WML burden was independently associated with slower ambulatory recovery (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.65; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.43-0.96; P = .032) and delayed final discharge (adjusted HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.43-0.92; P = .017), but not with wound healing or wound-free functional limb achievement. Conclusions High-grade WML burden was associated with impaired ambulatory recovery and delayed discharge after CLTI revascularization. When preoperative brain MRI is available, WML assessment may complement limb staging and help anticipate rehabilitation and discharge needs.

papers.title: The mechanism of dietary intervention in delaying brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.authors: Luo B, Liu S, Zheng L, Zhang B, Chen B, Shang T, Zheng J, Kuang B, Zhou Y, Sun Y, Zou W.
papers.abstract: With the global aging population, age-related neurodegenerative diseases and cerebrovascular diseases have become major public health challenges. As a modifiable lifestyle strategy, dietary intervention shows significant potential in delaying brain aging and reducing the risk of neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases. Caloric restriction (CR) and dietary restriction (DR), two important nutritional intervention approaches, exhibit substantial neuroprotective potential through multiple mechanisms. This review systematically summarizes the mechanisms of CR and DR in brain aging and related diseases, focusing on: (1) modulating gene expression and epigenetic modifications; (2) regulating proteostasis and autophagy; (3) inhibiting neuroinflammation to delay inflammaging; (4) improving mitochondrial function and oxidative homeostasis; and (5) optimizing nutrient-sensing pathways and metabolism. Additionally, this review discusses the mechanistic evidence of CR and DR in disease models such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Parkinson's Disease (PD), stroke, and Vascular Dementia (VaD). Despite promising preclinical findings, their clinical translation faces challenges including individual variability, safety concerns, and uncertainty regarding mechanism prioritization. Future research should focus on conducting more high-quality clinical trials, integrating multi-omics technologies with precision nutrition strategies to promote the practical application of CR and DR in advancing healthy brain aging.

papers.title: De novo MAP2K4 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome and impaired JNK signaling in iPSC-derived neurons.
papers.authors: Nomakuchi TT, Rippert AL, Santos De León SA, Gonzalez EM, Li D, Angireddy R, Finoti LS, Faletra F, Musante L, Tuula R, Amor DJ, von Wintzingerode L, Jamra RA, Stover SR, Buchan JG, Hayek J, Leon E, Attie-Bitach T, Rio M, Baujat G, Wallach E, Smail A, Dias KR, Pfeifer U, Peterson A, Ahrens-Nicklas RC, Bhoj EJK.
papers.abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

papers.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
papers.authors: Ko JS, Jung W, Suh PS, Heo H, Shim WH, Kim DH, Lee SH, Kim M, Lee N, Kim S, Kim SJ, Suh CH.
papers.abstract: Rationale and objectives To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions. Materials and methods A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors. Results Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors. Conclusion Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

papers.title: Evidence that intrinsic brain connectivity moderates the association between gait and neurocognitive function in people living with HIV.
papers.authors: Ipser JC, Smuts S, Gouse H, Freeman C, Stein DJ, Joska J.
papers.abstract: Globally, a substantial proportion of the approximately 40 million people living with HIV (PLWH) experience some degree of HIV-associated brain injury (HABI), which is often linked to accentuated or accelerated aging in this clinical population. We set out to test the hypothesis that gait speed is associated with cognitive deficits in middle-aged PLWH in a low-middle income (LMIC) setting, and that this is comparable to what is seen in much older healthy adults. In addition, we sought to identify, as a potential marker of HABI, intrinsic functional brain connectivity abnormalities that moderate the association between gait and cognitive function in PLWH. Thirty-nine participants (17 HIV + and 22 HIV-, mean age = 39 +-8.99 years) were recruited from a community health centre in Cape Town. Bivariate and multiple linear regression models compared PLWH and controls with respect to associations between gait speed and neurocognitive domain scores, with relations between these factors and functional connectivity of seven resting state networks assessed within a multivariate regression modelling framework. We found that slower gait speed in PLWH was associated with lower global neurocognitive scores (t = -3.12; p < 0.008), and that this association was replicated in a large public domain cohort of healthy older adults. Moreover, intrinsic connectivity of the frontoparietal network in PLWH was a significant predictor of both gait speed and executive function, a finding that may implicate impaired compensatory mechanisms in this patient population. Our findings underscore the potential utility of gait tests in screening for HABI in PLWH in low resourced settings.

papers.title: Inhibition of soluble epoxide hydrolase rescues cognitive deficits by preserving neurovascular integrity and attenuating glial and neuropathology in diabetic-related dementia.
papers.authors: Fang X, Border JJ, Zhang H, Morgan GC, Gregory A, Hanscom-Trofy Y, Dong R, Yang J, Hwang SH, Morisseau C, Hammock BD, Fan F, Roman RJ.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major risk factor contributing to the development of Alzheimer's disease-related dementias (ADRD). While one of the early symptoms of both Alzheimer's disease (AD) and DM-related ADRD is a reduction in cerebral blood flow, the underlying biological mechanisms driving this decline remain to be fully elucidated. Genome-wide association studies have linked AD/ADRD to single-nucleotide polymorphisms in the gene encoding soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), an enzyme we previously reported to be upregulated in the brains of an AD rat model. Our previous studies also demonstrated that chronic sEH inhibition with 1-trifluoromethoxyphenyl-3-(1-propionylpiperidin-4-yl) urea (TPPU) preserves hippocampal-dependent spatial learning and memory and improves cerebral hemodynamics in both AD and DM-ADRD models. In the present study, we found that chronic TPPU treatment (1 mg/kg/day) reduced sEH expression in the brain, improved cortical-based non-spatial recognition memory involving both cortical and hippocampal networks, and reduced anxiety in DM-ADRD rats. TPPU improved brain perfusion and normalized impaired whisker-evoked functional hyperemia, an effect associated with increased Kir2.1 expression and neurovascular coupling in cerebral capillaries. Furthermore, TPPU increased tight junction protein expression (ZO-1 and OCLN), mitigated capillary rarefaction, and suppressed astrocyte and microglial activation in DM-ADRD rats. At the cellular level, TPPU attenuated hippocampal neurodegeneration, restored the expression of synaptic proteins (PSD95 and SY38), and reduced levels of proinflammatory chemokines, including MCP-1, RANTES, and MIP-1α, in the hippocampus of DM-ADRD rats. In conclusion, TPPU preserves cognitive function in DM-ADRD by mitigating cerebrovascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation and gliosis, thereby preserving synaptic integrity and neuronal survival, and represents a promising therapeutic strategy for DM-ADRD.

papers.title: Regional oxygen extraction fraction is higher in older adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity: associations with cognition and metabolic markers.
papers.authors: Elsharydah MN, Al-Khoury Y, Ragunatha Rao S, Schaffert J, Saha A, Kaufman J, Rezaei A, Leary J, Jin A, Almandoz JP, Gauthier CJ, Thomas BP.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity are highly prevalent among older adults and associated with increased Alzheimer's disease and related dementia (ADRD) risk, but underlying mechanisms linking T2D and obesity to cognitive impairment remain partially understood. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM)-derived oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) provides a noninvasive MRI-based marker of cerebral metabolism and may capture early alterations in brain physiology. In this single-center, cross-sectional pilot study, we examined QSM-derived OEF in older adults with T2D + obesity (N = 14) and age- and sex-matched controls (N = 18) and evaluated associations with blood markers and cognitive performance. Whole-brain OEF was higher in participants with T2D + obesity (29.5% vs 27.3%; p = 0.019), with higher OEF observed across all examined lobar regions (p < 0.05). The T2D + obesity group demonstrated lower Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) Attention (p = 0.035) and Global Cognition (p = 0.022) indices and lower Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS) Color-Word Switching (p = 0.001) scores. Whole-brain OEF was positively associated with leptin (p = 0.018) and negatively associated with HDL (p = 0.030). Higher regional OEF significantly correlated with lower cognitive performance, particularly D-KEFS (r = -0.40 to -0.62) and RBANS Attention (r = -0.36 to -0.41). This is the first study to support a potential link between altered cerebral oxygen extraction, metabolic dysfunction, and cognitive performance in older adults with T2D and obesity. Larger, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm these associations and determine their relevance to cognitive decline and ADRD risk.

papers.title: Computational Modeling of Neurotransmitter Cycling Predicts Human Brain Glutamate and GABA Dynamics in Response to Acute Administration of Exogenous Ketones.
papers.authors: Antal BB, Mujica-Parodi LR, Strey HH, Ratai EM, Mangia S, Rothman DL.
papers.abstract: Administration of ketones is used as a therapeutic option in multiple conditions, including epilepsy, mental health disorders, and brain aging. A proposed mechanism of action involves the modulation of glutamate and GABA, the brain's primary excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, which jointly regulate the excitatory-inhibitory balance. However, the precise mechanism by which ketones influence these neurotransmitters remains unclear. In this study, we hypothesize that ketones modulate glutamate and GABA through the pseudo-malate-aspartate shuttle (PMAS). To test this, we developed a computational model of neurotransmitter cycling centered on the PMAS, simulating the temporal dynamics and steady-state concentrations of glutamate and GABA as functions of ketone metabolism. We then compared the model outputs with MRS data from ketone administration experiments and found agreement with the model predictions, providing quantitative support for the model. Building on this agreement, we performed metabolic control analysis, which identified partial displacement of glucose metabolism through the PMAS as the dominant mechanism underlying the observed reductions in glutamate and GABA and revealed key enzymes that selectively modulate each neurotransmitter. Overall, the model provides researchers and clinicians with a framework for hypothesis testing and treatment optimization, while also serving as a foundation for future model expansions.

papers.title: Pericyte loss and endothelial activation define distinct vascular states in cerebral small vessel disease.
papers.authors: Chagnot A, Jaime Garcia D, McQuaid C, Cholewa-Waclaw J, McDade K, Dando O, Wardlaw JM, Smith C, Montagne A.
papers.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) is a leading cause of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying microvascular dysfunction in human disease remain incompletely understood. In particular, the relationship between pericyte alterations and endothelial activation, two key features of blood-brain barrier dysfunction, remains unresolved. Here, we performed a quantitative single-vessel analysis of the human cortical microvasculature across increasing cSVD severity and ageing. Using multiplex immunohistochemistry combined with spectral unmixing and automated image analysis, we analysed 11,409 microvascular fragments from post-mortem brain tissue derived from 20 cases. Endothelial cells, pericytes, and endothelial activation were assessed using PECAM-1, PDGFRβ, and VCAM-1, respectively. Microvascular density and diameter differed between cortical grey matter and the underlying white matter, with white matter vessels being less dense and wider in controls. While vessel diameter remained stable across cSVD severity groups, microvascular density increased with cSVD severity and age in the white matter. At the molecular level, PDGFRβ signal decreased markedly with increasing cSVD severity, consistent with reduced pericyte coverage. This reduction was observed in both grey and white matter and correlated with disease severity and age. Notably, intermediate severity groups displayed marked heterogeneity, with vessels exhibiting either preserved or markedly reduced PDGFRβ signal. In parallel, endothelial markers PECAM-1 and VCAM-1 increased significantly with disease severity, reflecting endothelial activation. Unsupervised Gaussian mixture clustering of marker expression identified three vascular states characterised by (i) preserved PDGFRβ signal with low endothelial activation, (ii) reduced PDGFRβ signal without endothelial activation, and (iii) reduced PDGFRβ signal combined with endothelial activation. These clusters broadly aligned with neuropathological severity but revealed heterogeneity not captured by post-mortem diagnosis alone. Together, these findings suggest that pericyte alterations and endothelial activation are partially dissociated processes in human cSVD and identify distinct microvascular phenotypes across disease severity. These cross-sectional observations provide a framework for future longitudinal and experimental studies to determine their temporal and mechanistic relationships.

papers.title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
papers.authors: Kee TR, Masters BM, Tran KD, Jeon H, Long M, Xu G, Khan SA, Vázquez-Rosa E, Sridharan PS, Koh Y, Fujioka H, Chaput D, Wang X, Zhao X, Pieper AA, Kang DE, Woo JA.
papers.abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

papers.title: Risk Factors for Poor Outcomes of Mild and Moderate Traumatic Brain Injury Patients in Tanzania: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using Latent Class Analysis.
papers.authors: Barcenas L, Elahi C, Nkenguye W, Krishnamoorthy V, Joseph S, Sakita FM, Vissoci JRN, Staton C.
papers.abstract: Background and aims Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major global health concern, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). LMICs have higher injury rates and limited quality of care. TBI patients can be stratified as mild, moderate, and severe risk based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Although most poor outcomes are from severe TBIs, mild and moderate TBI patients significantly contribute to the overall morbidity and mortality, and may benefit from early monitoring to identify deterioration of status. Our goal was to identify unique subgroups within the mild and moderate TBI population at a high risk for poor outcomes. Methods We selected mild (GCS 14-15) and moderate (GCS 9-13) TBI patients from a TBI registry collected at a small city, regional referral hospital in Moshi, Tanzania, from May 2014 to April 2017. With these subsets (mild: n = 1738, moderate: n = 346), we performed a latent class analysis (LCA) to define unique patient classes based on clinical course, vital signs, and demographics. We then performed a survival analysis using a Cox proportional hazard model to examine the association of the defined latent classes with clinical outcome. The predictor variables were demographic variables, hospital interventions, and vital signs. The outcome of interest was a dichotomized discharge Glasgow outcome scale extended score (good outcome 7-8 and poor outcome 1-6). Results The LCA identified five classes among mild TBI patients: Adolescent (18.8%), Assault (31.5%), Young Adult Polytrauma (32.7%), Adult Polytrauma (9.2%), and RTI with ICU (7.8%). Three classes were identified among moderate TBI patients: Assault (20.2%), RTI with ICU (26.3%), and RTI without ICU (53.5%). Road traffic injury was the predominant mechanism in both severity groups (67% and 68%, respectively), and poor outcomes occurred in 4% of mild and 16% of moderate TBI patients. Relative to the lowest-risk reference class, all other mild TBI classes had higher hazards of poor outcomes. Among moderate TBI classes, RTI with ICU had a higher hazard of poor outcome than RTI without ICU (HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.26-5.24). Conclusion We identified clinically distinct latent classes within GCS-defined mild and moderate TBI groups, with differences in discharge outcomes across classes. These findings suggest that combining GCS category with demographic, physiological, injury, and care-process information may provide additional prognostic stratification. The results do not establish that GCS is inadequate; rather, they support further evaluation of complementary, context-appropriate risk-stratification approaches.

papers.title: Exploring medical food supplementation as an adjunct strategy for microbiota restoration and seizure reduction in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.
papers.authors: Borghi E, Marsiglia MD, Triva F, Ottaviano E, Viganò I, Savini MN, Costabile V, Vignoli A.
papers.abstract: Objectives CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by early-onset, treatment-resistant seizures and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. Increasing evidence suggests that alterations in the gut-brain axis may contribute to disease pathophysiology, raising interest in microbiota-targeted interventions. In this study, we evaluated the effects of a prebiotic-based nutritional intervention on clinical outcomes, gut microbiota composition, and fatty acid profiles in individuals with CDD. Methods Thirteen participants with drug-resistant epilepsy were enrolled (one male; median age, 12 years [IQR, 8.8-17.5]), and ten completed the longitudinal intervention protocol. The protocol comprised two medical-food interventions separated by washout periods: MF1 contained alpha-lactalbumin, inulin, and fructo-oligosaccharides, whereas MF2 contained the MF1 formulation supplemented with sodium butyrate. Clinical assessments, gut microbiota profiling, and fecal and systemic fatty acid measurements were performed at predefined study time points. Results Seizure response varied substantially between participants. Two subjects showed a 52% and 57% reduction in monthly seizure frequency during MF1, whereas two different participants experienced reductions greater than 90% during MF2 (94% and 100%, respectively). At the cohort level, the lowest median seizure frequency was observed at the final study time point. A progressive decrease in CDD severity scale scores was also observed over the course of the study. Intervention phases coincided with transient enrichment of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera, including Faecalibacterium, Blautia, and Dorea. Microbiota composition differed between responders and non-responders: higher seizure burden was linked to increased Veillonella, whereas lower seizure frequency corresponded to enrichment of Dialister and Gemmiger. Fecal and systemic SCFA concentrations generally decreased during intervention phases, regardless of clinical response. Significance Overall, these findings support a possible interaction between nutritional supplementation, microbial dynamics, and clinical manifestations in CDD. Larger studies will be necessary to clarify the therapeutic relevance of personalized microbiota-targeted approaches in CDD-related epilepsy. Plain language summary CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a rare condition that causes severe developmental difficulties and seizures that are difficult to control. We studied whether two medical food interventions targeting the gut microbiota, one of which also contained sodium butyrate, could influence seizures, disease severity, gut microbiota composition, and metabolite production in people with CDD. Some participants experienced substantial reductions in seizure frequency alongside changes in gut bacteria, although responses varied considerably between individuals. These preliminary findings suggest that microbiota-targeted, non-pharmacological approaches may have potential as supportive strategies in CDD, but larger studies are needed to confirm these observations.

papers.title: UBA5-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder
papers.authors: Bonkowski E, Almanza Fuerte E, Wang JY, Mefford HC.
papers.abstract: Clinical characteristics UBA5-related neurodevelopmental disorder (UBA5-NDD) is characterized by typically severe-to-profound global developmental delay, axial hypotonia, intellectual disability, ophthalmologic involvement (absence of visual fixation, poor visual pursuit, nystagmus, strabismus, and cerebral visual impairment), spasticity, appendicular hypertonia, epilepsy, movement disorders (dystonia, chorea, ataxia, and non-epileptic myoclonus), feeding difficulties, faltering weight, growth deficiency, and postnatal microcephaly. UBA5-NDD can be life-limiting, with age at death ranging from 16 days to 21 years. Causes of death include intractable seizures and neurologic decline with multiorgan failure (cardiac, respiratory, gastrointestinal). Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of UBA5-NDD is established in a proband with suggestive findings and biallelic pathogenic variants in UBA5 identified by molecular genetic testing. Management Treatment of manifestations: Developmental and educational support; treatment of refractive errors and strabismus per ophthalmologist; low vision services as needed; standard treatments for spasticity and epilepsy; pharmacologic therapies for movement disorders; feeding therapy; gastrostomy tube placement as needed; physical therapy, occupational therapy, and management per orthopedics of large joint displacements or scoliosis; medical management for constipation; palliative care and transitional care when needed; social work and family support. Surveillance: Assess developmental, educational, and therapy needs at each visit; ophthalmology exam per ophthalmologist; assess for new neurologic manifestations at each annual visit; monitor seizures with EEG as indicated; assess growth, nutritional status, safety of oral intake, and constipation at each visit; assess respiratory function, mobility, self-help skills, contractures, and hip dysplasia at each visit; spine examination annually; assess family needs at each visit; assess and develop transitional care plan by age ten years. Genetic counseling UBA5-NDD is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a UBA5 pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. Once the UBA5 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

papers.title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG.
papers.authors: Quinn AJ, Pitt J, Kohl O, Gohil C, van Es MWJ, Nobre AC, Woolrich MW.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

papers.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
papers.authors: Dutta S, Pradhan LK, Chen J, Wang N, Gao X, Das A.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI. Graphical Abstract

papers.title: Attenuated alpha state transitions and disrupted repetition-dependent temporal adaptation in mild cognitive impairment
papers.authors: Wang X, Zhu Y, Zhang J, Zheng Z, Yu M.
papers.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may involve impaired dynamic regulation of brain states that is not captured by conventional resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We quantified occipital alpha (8–12 Hz) transitions during three repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles in 60 healthy controls (HC) and 77 participants with MCI. Eye-state events were refined from frontal ocular artifacts. Transition magnitude was measured by the log-transformed post-/pre-event energy ratio, and transition success by the expected direction of alpha change. For canonical transitions meeting prespecified fit-quality criteria, mono-exponential fitting yielded transition onset (t onset ) and the post-onset time constant (τ). MCI showed weaker alpha suppression during eye opening, weaker alpha enhancement during eye closure, and lower odds of transition success. No significant group difference in τ was detected within the canonical quality-controlled subset. In contrast, t onset showed significant Group × Trial interactions in both conditions: HC developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across repetitions, whereas MCI showed no comparable change. These findings suggest reduced alpha state-transition capacity and altered repetition-dependent temporal organization in MCI.

papers.title: Intranasal L-MYC Neural Stem Cells Restore Neurovascular and Neuroimmune Homeostasis After TBI via CX3CL1 Upregulation and ICAM-1 Downregulation
papers.authors: Enright B, Cheng JP, Adhikarla V, Vasquez I, Yuan Y, Bondi CO, Rockne R, Kline AE, Gutova M.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers persistent neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction that contributes to secondary brain injury and limits recovery. Here, we investigated whether a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 could reprogram post-traumatic neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses and whether these effects were conserved across biological sex. Immunocompetent male and female rats underwent a controlled cortical impact (CCI) or Sham surgery and 7 days later received a single bolus dose of LMNSC01 (6 × 10 6 cells/dose) or vehicle. Integrated histological and transcriptomic analyses and multiplex tissue ELISA were used to characterize injury- and treatment-associated responses. CCI induced persistent but sex-dependent transcriptional changes. Male rats exhibited prominent innate immune, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and tissue remodeling responses, whereas females demonstrated broader activation of microglial, interferon, complement, MHC/antigen presentation, and humoral/adaptive immune pathways. LMNSC01 treatment reprogrammed these distinct injury states through partially sex-specific mechanisms. In males, LMNSC01 increased endogenous immune-regulatory mediators, including Il1rn , and reduced pathways associated with adhesion and immune-cell trafficking. In females, treatment decreased expression of genes related to microglial, leukocyte, MHC/antigen-presentation, cytokine, and adhesion pathways, and reduced macrophage- and CD45-positive cell signatures. Despite these sex-dependent transcriptional changes, LMNSC01 produced conserved protein changes in both sexes, reducing injury-associated ICAM-1 and restoring CX3CL1 proteins, proposing a novel molecular mechanism of LMNSCs modulating endothelial activation and neuron– microglia communication post injury. Our study provides further insight into sex differences in responses to injury and treatment after TBI and highlights candidate repair mechanisms, supporting further development of LMNSC01 as a minimally invasive therapy for TBI. Significance Statement This study provides evidence that a single intranasal dose of LMNSC01 can reprogram chronic neuroimmune and neurovascular dysfunction after TBI in both sexes. Despite distinct male and female injury and treatment responses, LMNSC01 produced a conserved reduction in ICAM-1 and increase in CX3CL1, suggesting reduced endothelial activation and restoration of homeostatic neuron–microglia signaling. Identification of shared changes in neurovascular and neuroimmune signaling provides a candidate mechanism for neural stem cell-mediated repair and supports the translational development of non-invasive intranasal LMNSC01 therapy for TBI.

papers.title: A rapid, genetically-tractable human iPSC-derived model for studying tissue-resident macrophage biology in Alzheimer’s and other diseases
papers.authors: Lee H, Peppler GB, Sewell M, Münch A, Podleśny-Drabiniok A, Kim JJ, Orrick J, Marcora E, Goate AM.
papers.abstract: Large-scale genetic and preclinical studies strongly implicate myeloid cells, particularly brain-resident macrophages, in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Efferocytic clearance of apoptotic cells and other cholesterol-rich cellular debris is a core macrophage function and represents an active area of AD research. However, human tissue-resident macrophages remain difficult to model in vitro as they acquire their transcriptional and functional identities in response to signals from their host tissue microenvironment. Many existing differentiation protocols mimic human brain macrophage developmental trajectories, but these protocols rely either on multi-step cytokine cocktails and lengthy differentiation or transduction of multiple transcription factors, both of which introduce variability and complicate genetic manipulation. To address these limitations, we developed a simplified protocol that generates high-purity (>90% CD45+CD11b+) human iPSC-derived macrophage-like cells (iMacs) from cryopreservable erythro-myeloid progenitor (EMP)-like intermediates in 19 days, including a final 7-day maturation step driven by macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) alone. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that iMacs show enrichment for phagocytic and lysosomal programs, processes integral to efferocytosis. At both the transcriptional and protein level, iMacs have higher expression of scavenger receptors such as CD36 , CD163 and MRC1 , and of AD risk genes such as TREM2 and APOE . Functionally, iMacs show enhanced phagocytic uptake of diverse substrates relative to iPSC-derived microglia, including carboxylated latex beads, zymosan, amyloid-β 1-42, and amyloid-β 1-40, and exhibit expanded lysosomal mass. Robust TREM2 expression and signaling make iMacs a sensitive platform for interrogating TREM2 biology, with markedly higher phosphorylation of SYK and PLCγ2 in response to TREM2 engagement compared to iPSC-derived microglia. iMacs also tolerate lipid-mediated siRNA transfection with high survival and knockdown efficiency, enabling rapid genetic perturbation of AD risk genes. Together, these features make iMacs a practical, scalable, and genetically tractable human macrophage model for studying the regulation and cell biology of core macrophage functions that are known to play critical roles in AD, aging, and other disorders.

papers.title: Astrocyte-Specific dsRNA–ADAR1 Signalling Links Innate Immunity to Complement Activation in Parkinson’s Disease
papers.authors: Liu Y, Halliday GM, Fu Y.
papers.abstract: Background Dysregulated innate immune activation is a key feature of Parkinson’s disease (PD), but the upstream triggers and cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unclear. Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) has emerged as a potential driver of innate immune responses. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1), particularly its interferon-inducible p150 isoform, edits dsRNA to limit aberrant immune activation. Whether this dsRNA–ADAR1 axis contributes to neuroinflammation in PD in a cell-type-specific manner is unknown. Methods We performed immunofluorescence on post-mortem cingulate cortex tissue from PD cases and controls to localise dsRNA, ADAR1 p150 and pathological α-synuclein protein. We integrated these findings with single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from three independent human brain datasets. An eight-module gene scoring framework was applied to assess dsRNA processing, sensing, and downstream innate immune pathways in neurons and astrocytes. Results In PD cortex, the proportion of dsRNA-positive astrocytes was higher than in controls, whereas neuronal dsRNA positivity did not differ between groups. ADAR1 p150 positivity increased in both astrocytes and neurons, and the proportion of ADAR1 p150 positive astrocytes correlated with astrocytic α-synuclein burden. Transcriptomic analyses showed that neurons were enriched for dsRNA editing and processing machinery, whereas astrocytes exhibited higher expression of dsRNA sensing pathways, innate immune responses, and transposable element control. While overall pathway activity did not differ between PD and controls after covariate adjustment, network analyses revealed cell-type-specific coupling patterns. Notably, complement gene expression showed a strong and selective association with dsRNA-related pathways in astrocytes, whereas interferon and NF-κB signalling were shared across cell types. In both cell types, ADAR1-associated gene programmes were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation and PD-related pathways. Conclusions These findings identify astrocytes as a central site of relative dsRNA accumulation and ADAR1 p150 induction in the PD cortex. The selective coupling of dsRNA sensing to complement activation in astrocytes highlights a cell-type-specific innate immune pathway that is constitutively present rather than induced by disease. Together, our protein-level and network-level findings converge on a coherent and testable model in which a constitutive astrocytic circuit is engaged by disease-associated dsRNA accumulation, with potential relevance for disease progression and therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
papers.authors: Pouya TL, Sotero RC.
papers.abstract: Resting-state BOLD fluctuations show reproducible spatiotemporal propagation that is not accounted for by conventional zero-lag functional connectivity. Travelling wave analyses based on phase gradients or statistical decomposition have problems when multiple wave generators overlap or when wave origins have to be localized. This work introduces a wave-informed physics-informed neural network that represents the parcellated BOLD signal as a superposition of seven spatially extended damped travelling wave generators, each periodically re-excited at its own characteristic frequency and fixed at initialization to one of the seven canonical Schaefer resting-state networks. A soft anatomical prior derived from each subject’s diffusion-tensor structural connectivity is included to encode the hypothesis that white-matter pathways constrain wave direction. The pipeline is validated on synthetic data by three simulation studies, creating the operating envelope, and then applied to 41 cognitively normal participants of the ADNI 3 cohort. A within-subject ablation showed that mean alignment between recovered wave directions and underlying white-matter geometry increased by a small but statistically detectable amount when using the structural prior (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.026), with exploratory network-level effects most evident in the visual, dorsal-attention, and salience/ventral-attention networks. The contribution is a network-anchored parametric inverse method returning subject-specific propagation descriptors from short resting-state scans.

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.authors: Vlček P.
papers.abstract: Introduction Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation. State of the art Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks.
