Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies. Clinical implications Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies. Future directions Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: Cerebral Oxygenation-Guided Indexed-Flow Normothermic Cardiopulmonary Bypass with Vasopressor-Sparing Pressure Management: A Retrospective Descriptive Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Chibisov N, Kornienko A, Malyshev A, Rodionov E, Glushenko I, Shtrymov M.
papers.abstract: Context Mean arterial pressure targets during cardiopulmonary bypass remain debated; vasopressor-driven pressure augmentation may not improve oxygen delivery. Aims The aim of the paper is to describe clinical outcomes and physiologic markers during normothermic cardiopulmonary bypass managed with indexed flow, cerebral oximetry, calculated indexed oxygen delivery (DO2i), and vasopressor-sparing pressure management. Settings and design Single-center retrospective descriptive cohort study at a cardiac surgery center. Material and methods Consecutive adults undergoing elective or urgent cardiac surgery with normothermic cardiopulmonary bypass from June 2023 to December 2025 were included if complete anesthesia-perfusion, regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2), circuit-derived venous oxygen saturation (SvO2), DO2i, and early outcome data were available. Circulatory arrest was excluded. Indexed pump flow was 2.2-2.4 L/min/m². Mean arterial pressure was interpreted with indexed flow, rSO2, SvO2, DO2i, hemoglobin, acid-base status, venous return, and surgical context. Baseline rSO2 was recorded before ventilation on room air; maximal relative decrease during bypass was recorded. Statistical analysis used Descriptive statistics and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were used. No comparative testing or causal modeling was performed. Results Two hundred patients were analyzed. Operating-room extubation was achieved in 172 patients (86.0%). Stroke occurred in six (3.0%), acute kidney injury in two (1.0%), and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was required in six (3.0%). Baseline right and left rSO2 were 57.5 ± 11.2% and 58.5 ± 11.3%; maximal relative rSO2 decrease was 28.5 ± 3.4%; circuit-derived SvO2 was 67.4 ± 5.9%; and calculated DO2i was 611 ± 74 mL/min/m². Conclusions This flow-oriented, cerebral oximetry-guided, oxygen-delivery-aware strategy was accompanied by favorable early recovery. Because the study was retrospective and noncomparative, the findings are hypothesis-generating.

papers.title: Associations Between Resting-State EEG Delta-band Activity at Selected Parietal Electrodes and Cognitive Changes Following Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Exploratory Analysis.
papers.authors: Wang L, Ouyang H, Zhang J, Lu X, Zhang S, Zhao Y, Liang Y, Hao L, Wang Y, Rong P.
papers.abstract: Introduction Transcutaneous auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation (taVNS) may improve cognition in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), but its electrophysiological correlates remain unclear. We explored whether parietal delta-band changes were associated with cognitive changes following taVNS. Methods This exploratory secondary analysis included 26 participants with MCI from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (taVNS, n = 14; sham, n = 12) who had valid resting-state EEG data at baseline and Week 24. Absolute and relative 1-3 Hz delta power at Pz, P1, P2, and P5 were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA and EEG-cognitive correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Results Absolute delta power showed significant time effects at all four electrodes after FDR correction (all q = 0.008). Relative delta power at Pz showed an uncorrected group effect (F = 5.007, p = 0.035; q = 0.218). In the taVNS group, MoCA-B improvement was positively associated with relative delta-power changes at P1, P2, and P5 (r = 0.629-0.652, p = 0.012-0.016), whereas AVLTN7 improvement was negatively associated with absolute delta-power changes across Pz, P1, P2, and P5 (coefficients = -0.418 to -0.613, p = 0.020-0.048). Although these correlations did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons, they showed a relatively consistent direction across multiple electrodes. Discussion Relative and absolute delta power may reflect complementary aspects of spectral modulation. The convergent cross-electrode associations provide preliminary EEG evidence linked to cognitive response to taVNS. Conclusion Parietal delta-band power may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of cognitive change following taVNS in MCI. These exploratory findings support further validation of predefined EEG biomarkers in larger, prospectively powered studies. Clinical trial registration http://www.chictr.org.cn (ID: ChiCTR2000038868).

papers.title: Disease-Specific Perturbational Convergence Between Genetic-Risk and Disease-State Transcriptomic Signatures in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.authors: Williams G.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) genetic susceptibility and disease-associated transcriptional changes are typically studied separately. Whether genetically inferred molecular mechanisms converge with transcriptional changes observed in post-mortem brain tissue remains unclear. Methods Cell-type-specific AD differential expression signatures were generated from five independent single-cell transcriptomic studies comprising over two million brain cells. In parallel, polygenic risk score (PGS)-associated expression signatures were inferred across 3,202 individuals using GTEx eQTL effect estimates. Both representations were compared at the individual gene, pathway, and drug-perturbational levels using large-scale perturbational profiles from Connectivity Map (CMap) and LINCS resources. Results AD single-cell signatures exhibited substantial reproducibility across cell types and correlated positively with bulk-brain pathology signatures. Genetically inferred signatures showed minimal concordance with disease-derived profiles at the level of individual genes and biological pathways. In contrast, there was a positive association when projecting both signatures onto drug-response space. Vasodilators, antihypertensives, and metabolic agents were enriched among compounds showing consistent reversal signatures across both disease representation. Conclusions In the present analysis, genetic risk and end-stage AD pathology are largely decoupled at the level of individual genes and pathways but converge on a shared, pharmacologically modifiable response landscape. This convergence is consistent with biological mechanisms linked to established vascular and metabolic dementia risk factors, suggesting perturbational profiling as a potential framework for future therapeutic investigation rather than a basis for immediate drug prioritisation.

papers.title: An astrocyte-neuron HSPB1 axis preserves lysosomal integrity and protects from tau pathology
papers.authors: Jimenez-Sanchez M, Lobo PB, Yang F, Power C, Böken D, Verlin L, Guzman-Hernandez R, Cantallops-Jimenez S, Pollack S, Chakka A, Crichton J, Witton J, Croft C, Klenerman D, Noble W.
papers.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by a decline in neuronal proteostasis that favours the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Molecular chaperones are essential to prevent protein aggregation and, although typically studied as intracellular proteins, chaperones can also be secreted with functions that remain to be elucidated. Here, we identify a mechanism by which astrocyte-secreted HSPB1 is internalized by neurons to increase neuronal proteostasis and prevent the aggregation of pathological tau. We characterized HSPB1 as an astrocytic protein that can also be acquired post-transcriptionally by neurons in AD brain and in culture. Upon internalization into the endolysosomal system through macropinocytosis, HSPB1 prevents lysosomal damage and promotes tau clearance, thereby positioning HSPB1 as a key protein in maintaining organelle and protein homeostasis across astrocyte-neuronal networks. This work identifies a mechanism by which astrocytes boost neuronal capacity to protect from protein aggregation in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Engineered probiotic co‑expressing IL‑10 and Amuc_1100 modulates the gut‑brain axis to improve ASD‑like behaviors in BTBR mice
papers.authors: Li H, Li Y, Liang Z, Ji Y, Lin Y, Wang X, Liu S, Xie X, Zhang Y, Tong X, Zhong L.
papers.abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disease characterized by social deficits and repetitive behaviors, yet no pharmacotherapy targeting its core symptoms currently exists. Immune dysregulation and neuroinflammation are increasingly recognized as key contributors to ASD pathogenesis, with deficient anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10) representing a potential therapeutic target. However, systemic IL-10 delivery is limited by short half-life, poor bioavailability, and off-target toxicity. Here, we developed an engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 strain that constitutively co-expresses murine IL-10 and the Akkermansia muciniphila outer membrane protein Amuc_1100 for oral delivery, and evaluated its therapeutic efficacy in the BTBR mouse model of ASD. Daily oral administration of IL-10/Amuc_1100-engineered bacteria to BTBR mice for four weeks significantly rescued sociability deficits in the three-chamber test and attenuated repetitive grooming behaviors. Mechanistically, the treatment alleviated intestinal inflammation, as evidenced by improved villus architecture and reduced lipocalin-2 levels, and remodeled the gut microbiota by increasing beneficial genera such as Muribaculum and Prevotella while suppressing pro-inflammatory taxa. In the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), treatment downregulated the IL-17 signaling pathway and reduced expression of pro-inflammatory genes including Tnf and Il17e . Single-cell RNA sequencing of mPFC microglia revealed a shift from a disease-associated inflammatory state toward a homeostatic, neuroprotective phenotype, accompanied by reduced pathological synaptic pruning. Collectively, these findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that oral delivery of IL-10/Amuc_1100 via an engineered probiotic is sufficient to induce concurrent changes in peripheral inflammation, central IL-17 signaling, and microglial state, together with behavioral improvements in BTBR mice. While further studies are required to establish causal relationships and long-term safety, this approach warrants consideration as a potential oral therapeutic strategy for ASD.

papers.title: Clinical Efficacy and Electrophysiological Mechanisms of Closed-Loop Neuromodulation for the Treatment of Drug-Resistant Epilepsy
papers.authors: Wang Z, Hu T, Xie H, Zhang D, Sun Y, Zhang J, Cui X, Zheng J, Yu J, Zhang S, Song X, Wang M, Gao X, Li B, Zhao X, Zhang Z, Zhang Y, Liu W, Li W.
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the clinical efficacy of closed-loop neuromodulation for drug-resistant epilepsy and to characterize its electrophysiological mechanisms by combining intracranial and scalp EEG, thereby providing experimental evidence for optimizing treatment protocols and identifying multidimensional efficacy biomarkers. Methods Eight patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who underwent closed-loop neuromodulation implantation were enrolled and followed for 12–24 months. Clinical efficacy was evaluated using the seizure reduction rate and the responder rate. Linear mixed-effects models and within-subject Spearman rank correlation analyses were used to systematically characterize the population-level associations and inter-individual heterogeneity between stimulation parameters and clinical efficacy. Interictal intracranial EEG (recorded before stimulation onset and at 12 months postoperatively) and scalp EEG (international 10–20 system) were collected, and power spectral density and the phase lag index were used to quantify frequency-band-specific EEG activity and brain functional connectivity, with correction for multiple comparisons. Results At 12 months postoperatively, the overall seizure reduction rate was 56.3% (P < 0.05), with a responder rate of 75.0%. At 24 months, the reduction rate increased to 75.0% (P < 0.05) and the responder rate reached 85.7%, indicating a progressive, cumulative improvement in efficacy with treatment duration. At the population level, no significant independent associations were found between stimulation amplitude, frequency, pulse width, or target changes and the seizure reduction rate, and the parameter–efficacy relationship exhibited marked inter-individual heterogeneity. Intracranial EEG revealed significantly increased gamma and high-gamma band power after treatment (Cohen's d > 0.8, large effect sizes), with no significant changes in the low-frequency bands. The high-gamma band exhibited a heterogeneous network reorganization pattern characterized by significantly enhanced functional connectivity within the epileptogenic zone and suppressed long-range propagation pathways. Scalp EEG showed diffuse changes, with significantly increased whole-brain delta power and significantly decreased beta power, whereas inter-electrode phase synchrony showed no statistically significant differences across frequency bands. Gamma-band power changed in opposite directions between intracranial and scalp EEG. Conclusion Closed-loop neuromodulation is a safe and effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. Its efficacy accumulates over time and is patient-specific, with no universally optimal programming parameters. The electrophysiological mechanism is closely related to the plastic reorganization of epileptic networks induced by chronic targeted stimulation: the increased intracranial gamma/high-gamma power suggests functional restoration of local parvalbumin (PV)-positive inhibitory interneuron microcircuits in the epileptogenic zone, with the excitation–inhibition balance re-established toward a physiological steady state; the heterogeneous changes in high-gamma connectivity may limit the transregional propagation of epileptiform discharges. The scalp EEG pattern of enhanced slow-wave and attenuated fast-wave activity reflects an overall downregulation of whole-brain cortical excitability. The opposite changes in intracranial and scalp gamma-band power may provide key experimental evidence for a deeper understanding of the mechanisms of closed-loop neuromodulation and for establishing a multidimensional electrophysiological biomarker system for efficacy evaluation.

papers.title: TMS-EEG Investigation of Cortical Activity Induced by Individualized rTMS in Patients with Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness
papers.authors: Zhang Y, Yan X, Zhu Z, Du J, Cao L, Song W, Wang Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To establish an individualized repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) target selection protocol based on resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) directed functional connectivity for patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC), and to explore the underlying electrophysiological mechanisms using transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with EEG (TMS-EEG). Methods We enrolled 42 pDoC patients and randomly assigned to an individualized rTMS group, a conventional rTMS group, and a sham stimulation group. The individualized rTMS group selected the target with stronger directed functional connectivity between F3 and Pz as the stimulation site based on Granger causality analysis. The conventional rTMS group received random stimulation at either F3 or Pz. Both active groups received 10 sessions of high-frequency rTMS over 10 consecutive days, while the sham group underwent sham stimulation. Behavioral improvement and cortical connectivity were assessed before and after treatment using the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) and TMS-EEG, respectively. Results CRS-R scores significantly increased in both the individualized and conventional rTMS groups ( p < 0.05), whereas no significant improvement was observed in the sham group ( p > 0.05). TMS-EEG analysis demonstrated that the amplitudes of N100 and P180 components significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05), with no statistically significant changes in the sham group ( p > 0.05). Global mean field amplitude (GMFA) significantly increased post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Specifically, significant increases were found in the 1-100 ms and 101–200 ms time windows post-treatment in both active groups ( p < 0.05). Additionally, the individualized rTMS group showed a significant increase in the 201–300 ms window ( p < 0.05), which was not observed in the conventional group ( p > 0.05). No significant differences were found in the sham group across any time windows (1-100 ms, 101–200 ms, 201–300 ms, 301–400 ms, 401–500 ms; p > 0.05). Correlation analyses indicated that the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in N100 amplitude in both the individualized ( r = 0.82, p < 0.001) and conventional ( r = 0.79, p = 0.001) treatment groups. Similarly, the change in CRS-R score positively correlated with the change in P180 amplitude in the individualized ( r = 0.77, p = 0.0002) and conventional ( r = 0.62, p = 0.025) groups. Conclusion Individualized rTMS based on resting-state EEG directed functional connectivity is more effective in promoting consciousness recovery in pDoC patients. Compared to conventional rTMS, this approach may better facilitate the sustained propagation of post-stimulation cortical activity along residual consciousness networks and promote integration during middle-to-late stages. This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the transition of neuromodulation therapy for pDoC from fixed-target interventions to individualized precision regulation. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05682248. Ethics approval : Ethics Committee of Xuanwu Hospital, 2022[022].

papers.title: Mechanistic study of PHLDA1 in cognitive dysfunction of Alzheimer’s disease model mice via FoxO1‑mediated neuroinflammation
papers.authors: Liu X, Liu Z, Lv Z, Lei Y, Zhou Z, Xu Z, Duan J, Xing W, Xu P.
papers.abstract: Abstract Neuroinflammation is a core driver of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression. Pleckstrin homology-like domain family A member 1 (PHLDA1) is known to regulate Toll-like receptor-mediated immunity, but its role in AD-associated neuroinflammation remains unknown. Here we demonstrate that PHLDA1 suppresses FoxO1 phosphorylation and inactivation through a dual mechanism: it inhibits upstream AKT activation and competitively binds the 14-3-3 chaperone, thereby promoting FoxO1 nuclear retention and sustaining downstream TLR4-driven inflammatory transcription. In APP/PS1 mice, elevated PHLDA1 correlates with increased total FoxO1 but decreased phosphorylated FoxO1 (p-FoxO1), 14-3-3, and Akt, which collectively drive FoxO1 nuclear accumulation and persistent inflammatory signaling. Consequently, this triggers microglial overactivation, cascading release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β), an elevated Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, and aggravated plaque deposition, ultimately leading to neuronal apoptosis and cognitive deficits. Notably, hippocampal knockdown of PHLDA1 using AAV-shRNA reverses these molecular, pathological, and behavioral abnormalities. Collectively, the PHLDA1–FoxO1–TLR4 axis may significantly influence AD neuroinflammation, and targeting PHLDA1 provides a rationale for developing anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategies against AD.

papers.title: Calcium Regulation and Neural Control of Drosophila Flight Muscle: Linking Sarcomere Mechanics to Flight Behaviour
papers.authors: Hussain T.
papers.abstract: Flight in Drosophila melanogaster depends on a division of labour between asynchronous indirect flight muscles that supply power and synchronous steering muscles that modify wing motion. The indirect muscles operate through interactions between calcium-dependent activation, delayed stretch activation, sarcomere kinetics and thoracic mechanics. Their motor neurons do not command each wing stroke, but neural input can regulate the operating state of the flight motor. Understanding this system requires connecting measurements across scales: calcium signals, muscle force, wing kinematics, aerodynamic loading and behaviour. This narrative review examines the evidence for calcium-dependent power regulation and places it within the neural and mechanical organisation of flight. Published optogenetic studies illustrate how perturbing visual pathways, descending neurons or motor circuits can identify causal contributions to wing control, while also exposing the limits of interpreting a behavioural response as a direct measure of muscle function. Particular attention is given to tethered-flight arenas, open-loop and closed-loop visual stimulation, free-flight measurements and wingbeat recordings. Changes in wingbeat frequency, stroke amplitude or flight persistence can arise through several mechanisms and do not, on their own, establish changes in indirect-muscle force or power. A conceptual multiscale framework is proposed to organise these relationships and distinguish measured quantities from inferred states. An accompanying computational supplement illustrates energy-accounting and numerical checks in an imposed-strain simulated system; it is not a calibrated model of flight or evidence for calcium-dependent power generation. The central argument is that causal interpretation improves when perturbations and measurements span more than one level of the flight system.

papers.title: Interpretable Frequency-Aware Deep Learning for Multi-Class EEG Classification of Neurological Disorders
papers.authors: Bunterngchit C, Baniata LH, Baniata MH, Atwan JM, Alali M, Alsharaiah MA, Kang S.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) records cortical activity with high temporal resolution without radiation and at low cost, which makes it a practical signal for automated screening of neurological disorders. Deep learning classifies EEG with high accuracy, but most models distinguish only two conditions and give no account of their decisions, which limits their use in screening and decision support. This paper presents SpectraXAI, an interpretable frequency-aware deep learning model that assigns resting-state EEG to four diagnostic categories: Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, and healthy control. The model filters each EEG window into the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands and processes every band in a separate convolutional branch with squeeze-and-excitation recalibration. Softmax-weighted band attention and temporal attention then combine the spectral and temporal evidence, and the same attention weights are intrinsic explanations of each prediction. Under a subject-disjoint evaluation protocol that prevents window leakage, the model reached 94.43% accuracy, 96.74% balanced accuracy, and 93.82% macro-F1 on 20,760 windows from 173 unseen subjects while using only 0.10 million parameters. An ablation study confirmed that the attention modules account for most of the improvement over a plain convolutional baseline. Attention weights, feature-attention heatmaps, Grad-CAM, and t-SNE embeddings trace each decision to specific frequency bands, time segments, and learned features, therefore the frequency structure that drives the accuracy also makes the predictions inspectable.

papers.title: Long-Term Fluoxetine Treatment Alters Fecal Microbiota and Induces Systemic Disruption in Sprague-Dawley Rats
papers.authors: Rodríguez-Batista FA, Martín-Barrasa JL, Henríquez-Cabrera R, Martel-Benítez CJ, Alayón-Afonso R, Acero LA, Floren Zabala L, Llorente LI, Argüello Pérez I, Sierra E, Alonso-Almorox P, Espinosa de los Monteros y Zayas A, Nogueira Salgueiro P, Padilla Castillo D, Real F, Martel Quintana A, Almeida Peña C, Gómez-Pinchetti JL, Hernández Fleta JL.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder pathophysiology involves complex gut-brain axis interactions, yet the systemic non-neurochemical impacts of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors re-main poorly defined. This study evaluated the multidimensional effects of chronic fluoxe-tine administration in Sprague-Dawley rats. Male rats received fluoxetine (10 mg/kg/day) or water for 60 days, followed by behavioral phenotyping, fecal microbiological quantifi-cation, serum biochemistry, complete blood count analysis, and immunohistochemical assessment of the immediate-early gene product c-Fos (cellular proto-oncogene protein) in the striatum. Fluoxetine treatment significantly reduced immobility time in the forced swim test, whereas object recognition memory deteriorated without alterations in anxie-ty-like behavior. Pharmacological intervention markedly depleted fecal bacterial popula-tions and significantly decreased serum vitamin D concentrations. Hematologically, treated animals exhibited significant reductions in total leukocytes, red blood cells, and platelets, alongside elevated hematocrit and mean corpuscular volume. Concurrently, c-Fos-positive neuronal activation increased significantly within the striatal nucleus ac-cumbens. In conclusion, chronic fluoxetine exposure induces profound systemic disrup-tion, altering gut microbial homeostasis, depleting vitamin D, and modulating peripheral blood profiles while enhancing central striatal neuronal plasticity. These findings under-score the necessity of monitoring gut-brain axis integrity during prolonged antidepressant therapy.

papers.title: Targeting the Gut to Modify Parkinson's Disease: From Mechanisms to Potential Therapeutics.
papers.authors: Tai YC, Lin CH.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and its prevalence continues to rise with population aging. Its cardinal motor features arise from the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, accompanied by intraneuronal α-synuclein aggregates known as Lewy bodies. Neuropathological evidence suggests that, in a subset of patients, α-synuclein pathology first appears in the enteric nervous system and ascends to the brain via the gut-brain axis. Consistent with this "body-first" trajectory, a growing body of work has documented distinct alterations in gut microbial composition and microbiota-derived metabolites in people with PD relative to healthy individuals, with some changes detectable in the prodromal phase. Current management, whether dopaminergic pharmacotherapy or deep brain stimulation, alleviates motor symptoms but does not slow neurodegeneration, and long-term treatment is complicated by motor fluctuations and other adverse effects. Therapies directed at the underlying disease process are therefore urgently needed. Because early perturbations of the gut microenvironment appear to contribute to PD pathogenesis, interventions that restore gut homeostasis represent a rational disease-modifying strategy, particularly for patients whose pathology originates in the gut. This review synthesizes current understanding of how the gut microbiota shapes the gut-brain axis in PD, spanning immune, metabolic, neuroendocrine, and neural pathways, and critically appraises the emerging evidence for microbiota-directed interventions, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, and prebiotics, as candidate disease-modifying therapies.

papers.title: Candidate neurobiological pathways linking physical exercise to cognition in Parkinson's disease: a hypothesis-generating translational framework.
papers.authors: Byun K, Lee JY, Kim R.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a major nonmotor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet effective strategies for preserving cognitive function remain limited. Although physical exercise may confer cognitive benefits, the biological pathways linking exercise to cognition in PD remain incompletely established. This narrative review presents a hypothesis-generating translational framework for 4 candidate mechanistic domains that may contribute to exercise-related cognitive effects in PD. First, exercise-responsive neurotrophic signaling, particularly through brain-derived neurotrophic factor-tropomyosin receptor kinase B, insulin-like growth factor 1, and vascular endothelial growth factor pathways, may support synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and neurovascular function. Second, exercise may modulate dopaminergic, cholinergic, and noradrenergic systems and influence corticostriatal plasticity relevant to cognitive function. Third, muscle-derived factors and exercise-induced metabolites may affect neurotrophic signaling, neuronal metabolism, and autophagy-lysosomal clearance of α-synuclein. Fourth, exercise may regulate systemic and central inflammatory responses through cytokine signaling, glial activation, inflammasome pathways, and complement-mediated synaptic remodeling. The evidence supporting these pathways is derived from basic, preclinical, observational, and exercise-intervention studies, but the strength of evidence varies considerably across stages of translation. Direct evidence that exercise-induced biological changes mediate cognitive improvement in patients with PD is lacking. These pathways should therefore be regarded as candidate mechanisms for hypothesis-driven investigation of the cognitive effects of exercise in PD.

papers.title: Sparse neuronal C4 elevation induces network-wide transcriptomic and lipid-droplet remodeling in the cortical microenvironment.
papers.authors: Sánchez-Carbonell M, Bolshakova S, Ávila-Pagán JE, Sabir YA, Griffin-Derr C, Stich DG, Cieslewicz SV, Carmen Sifuentes SE, Phadke RA, Brack A, Hasche-Kluender A, Caley P, Dias C, Cruz-Martín A.
papers.abstract: The complement component C4 regulates synaptic refinement and plasticity in the brain and has been implicated in multiple neurological and psychiatric disorders, with especially strong genetic evidence linking elevated C4A expression to schizophrenia. However, it remains unclear whether localized C4 elevation in a small neuronal population is sufficient to reshape broader cortical gene-regulatory programs and cellular phenotypes. To address this question, we overexpressed mouse C4 in approximately 2% of prefrontal cortical neurons using in utero electroporation and performed bulk RNA sequencing on microdissected prefrontal cortex. Despite the sparse manipulation, C4-OE was associated with broad transcriptional remodeling across tissue composed predominantly of untransfected cells, including coordinated changes in cholesterol biosynthesis, axon- and synaptic-associated programs, vascular/ECM pathways, and immune- and stress-related responses. Comparison with a schizophrenia synaptic proteomic dataset identified limited global correspondence but selective gene- and pathway-level overlap in specific molecular programs. Reference-based projection of directional DEG signatures onto a cortical single-cell transcriptomic reference further identified cell-type-associated structure, including prominent astrocyte- and vascular-associated axes and distinct lipid/metabolic, vascular/endothelial-interferon-associated, and immune/stress correlation domains. Spatial validation with MFISH showed increased Hmgcr expression in neighboring GFP-negative cells, while PLIN2 imaging revealed increased DAPI-associated/perinuclear lipid-droplet burden within the local C4-OE field. Together, these findings support a model in which sparse neuronal C4 elevation is associated with broader remodeling of the local cortical environment, including a non-cell-autonomous component involving neighboring-cell lipid-associated responses. These results expand the interpretation of C4 risk biology beyond synapse elimination alone and suggest that focal immune-gene dysregulation can engage lipid-homeostatic, stress-related, and cell-type-associated transcriptional programs relevant to cortical circuit vulnerability.

papers.title: Predictors of Insufficient Awakening During Awake Surgery: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
papers.authors: Takada S, Hattori EY, Ikeda H, Sano N, Sawada M, Tanji M, Mineharu Y, Kikuchi T, Arakawa Y.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives Awake surgery (AS) is widely performed for the resection of brain tumors and for epilepsy surgery. However, a non-negligible proportion of patients experience insufficient intraoperative awakening, leading to inadequate neurological monitoring. This retrospective study investigated predictive factors associated with insufficient intraoperative awakening. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 78 consecutive AS procedures for brain tumors and epilepsy performed at our institution between 2021 and 2024. Previously reported predictive factors for AS failure and contraindications for AS were evaluated, along with the presence of basal ganglionic involvement (BGI), defined as a high-intensity area on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging involving the striatum and globus pallidus. Results Insufficient intraoperative awakening occurred in 13 cases (16.7%). Age (odds ratio [OR] per year, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.00-1.08), aphasia (OR, 4.18; 95% CI, 1.23-15.5), midline shift (OR, 7.85; 95% CI, 2.22-30.6), and BGI (OR, 118; 95% CI, 18.7-2352.2) were identified as factors associated with insufficient awakening using univariate logistic regression analysis. In multivariate logistic regression analysis, BGI remained independently associated with insufficient awakening (OR, 104.7; 95% CI, 16.4-2098.1). Preoperative corticosteroids were administered to 11 patients with glioblastoma to reduce peritumoral edema. Among 7 patients with glioblastoma and BGI at admission, BGI resolved preoperatively in 2 patients after corticosteroid therapy, and AS was successfully performed in both cases. Betamethasone was predominantly used, at a median dose of 4 mg/day and median preoperative treatment duration of 14 days. In both cases with resolved BGI, betamethasone was administered at 8 mg/day for more than 10 days. Conclusion BGI may be one of the independent predictors of insufficient intraoperative awakening across a broader AS population. Preoperative administration of an adequate course of betamethasone may facilitate sufficient intraoperative awakening in patients with glioblastoma and BGI. Further multicenter studies are warranted.

papers.title: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation for Fibromyalgia in Veterans: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Feasibility Study of Resting-State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Evaluate Pain and Treatment Response.
papers.authors: Woodbury A, Martini R, Ree A, Huang CYO, Denmon C, Vernon M, Lukemire J, Ramos J, Kim KSJ, Cui X, Stevens J, Krishnamurthy V, Guo Y, Napadow V, Rauch SAM.
papers.abstract: Background Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans. Methods In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function. Results Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred. Conclusions Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

papers.title: Microglial dynamics associate with the spatial pattern of tau deposition in early Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Öchsner M, Brendel M, Franzmeier N, Trappmann L, Zaganjori M, Ersoezlue E, Kurz C, Haeckert J, Utecht J, Schirge PM, Papazov B, Pogarell O, Janowitz D, Buerger K, Ewers M, Palleis C, Weidinger E, Biechele G, Schuster S, Finze A, Eckenweber F, Rupprecht R, Rominger A, Goldhardt O, Grimmer T, Keeser D, Stoecklein S, Dietrich O, Bartenstein P, Levin J, Höglinger G, Perneczky R, Rauchmann BS.
papers.abstract: Background Neuroinflammation is implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, yet how changes in TSPO PET signal are associated with tau deposition, and how brain network architecture shapes this relationship remain poorly understood. Methods We conducted a prospective, multimodal neuroimaging study in 56 participants: 35 amyloid-positive individuals across the AD spectrum (ADS) and 21 amyloid-negative healthy controls (HC). Amyloid status was classified primarily by CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 and, when eligible CSF was unavailable, by baseline amyloid PET. Participants underwent TSPO PET using [18 F]GE-180 and resting-state fMRI at baseline. A longitudinal subgroup additionally underwent follow-up tau PET using [18 F]PI-2620 (n = 24) and repeat TSPO PET (n = 18) approximately 18 months later. Results Baseline TSPO did not differ significantly between groups. Baseline TSPO was associated with regional tau in both groups; the reciprocal association between tau and TSPO change was numerically weaker in AD, but this group difference was not statistically significant. Connectivity to baseline-TSPO epicenters was associated with higher tau in both groups, whereas connectivity to TSPO-change epicenters was associated with lower tau in AD but not controls (group-by-connectivity interaction p < 0.001, participant-level slope difference p = 0.012), a dissociation replicated in independent participants. Conclusion These findings suggest that connectivity to established versus emerging TSPO epicenters carries distinct spatial information about tau in the AD spectrum, a pattern shaped by functional brain connectivity and absent in healthy controls. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06224920).

papers.title: An EEG-based framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis via single-channel multi-entropy fusion and ensemble learning.
papers.authors: Li J, Ling C, Peng Y, Yu Y, Feng G, Du W, Chen R.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers. Part H, Journal of engineering in medicine
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, and its early diagnosis is vital for timely intervention. However, most existing EEG-based diagnostic methods rely on multi-channel devices confined to hospital settings, limiting their accessibility for community screening. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a lightweight processing approach for portable, low-cost devices to support early AD diagnosis using single-channel EEG data, integrating signal purification with complementary entropy-based feature extraction and ensemble learning. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into five brain rhythms (δ, θ, α, β, γ) using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is then applied to extract Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) from the selected rhythm. Four entropy measures, including Differential Entropy (DE), Singular Spectral Entropy (SSE), Fuzzy Entropy (FE), and Sample Entropy (SE), are subsequently extracted from each IMF to construct the Multi-IMF Entropy Matrix (MIMFEM). After that, an ensemble learning framework combining five classifiers is designed to discriminate AD patients from healthy controls (HCs). The proposed method is evaluated on two public datasets using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). Using single-channel EEG data, our approach achieves classification accuracies of 97.92% on the Florida-based dataset and 81.54% on the AHEPA dataset, with corresponding F1-scores of 97.87% and 82.86%, respectively. These results, achieved with limited data sources, show that our approach provides an effective, practical solution for single-channel wearable AD screening and addresses the critical need for low-cost, accessible early diagnostic tools, advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare through a lightweight model.

papers.title: Altered Fronto-Cingulate Connectivity During Social Competition and Cooperation in Adolescents With Major Depressive Disorder: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study.
papers.authors: He Y, Wang Y, Jiang S, Liang F.
papers.abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescence is characterized by high prevalence (24.3% in China) and social dysfunction, particularly in competitive and cooperative behaviors. This study used fNIRS hyperscanning to explore cortical connectivity alterations during parent-adolescent interactions in adolescent MDD. Methods Thirty-three MDD adolescents (DD) and 29 healthy controls (HCs) completed competitive/cooperative maze tasks with parents under 52-channel fNIRS. Wavelet coherence analyzed functional connectivity (FC) in prefrontal/motor regions, which provides undirected connectivity estimates. Group × task effects were tested via GLMM and FDR correction. Results (1) Competition: DD exhibited hyperconnectivity in emotion regulation circuits between right opercular inferior frontal gyrus and left triangular inferior frontal gyrus (rIFGoperc and lIFGtriang, p = 0.047) but hypoconnectivity in executive networks between left dorsal superior frontal gyrus and left precentral gyrus (lSFGdor and lPreCG, p = 0.040). (2) Cooperation: DD showed enhanced motor-cognitive integration between right supplementary motor area and right middle frontal gyrus (rSMA and rMFG, p = 0.036) but impaired socioemotional processing between right triangular inferior frontal gyrus and left dorsal superior frontal gyrus (rIFGtriang and lSFGdor, p = 0.033). Task modulation: Within DD, cooperation preferentially engaged emotional resonance networks between right inferior orbital frontal gyrus and right medial superior frontal gyrus (rORBinf and rSFGmed, p = 0.031) while competition was associated with enhanced coupling in self-monitoring circuits between left dorsal superior frontal gyrus and right opercular inferior frontal gyrus (lSFGdor and rIFGoperc, p = 0.047). Conclusions Adolescent MDD involves context-dependent neural deficits in social cognition, suggesting targets for neuromodulatory interventions.

papers.title: Zero Echo Time Functional MRI in Humans: Technical Demonstration and Proof-of-Concept.
papers.authors: Ozen AC, Liu S, Ilbey S, Bock M, Emir U, Shih YI.
papers.abstract: Conventional EPI-based fMRI relies on the BOLD contrast to map activity changes, but is limited by high acoustic noise, susceptibility artifacts, and distortion near air-tissue interfaces. Ultra-short and zero-echo-time (ZTE) sequences have gained considerable attention in animal fMRI studies due to their robustness against susceptibility effects, low acoustic noise, and ability to capture signal sources distinct from those of conventional BOLD imaging. In this study, we present a feasibility-level proof-of-concept technical demonstration of ZTE-based fMRI in humans at 3T, while maintaining many of the advantages observed in preclinical studies. Phantom measurements demonstrate that the ZTE protocol is sensitive to oxygenation-related T1 changes at 3T, supporting its feasibility for detecting related functional signals. In five healthy volunteers, task-based visual stimulation and finger tapping experiments elicited activation in primary visual and motor cortices, respectively, using the ZTE sequence, demonstrating proof-of-concept feasibility in this small cohort. Resting-state components with spatial patterns consistent with canonical visual and sensorimotor networks were identified using independent component analysis in the same cohort. Compared to BOLD-EPI, ZTE showed significantly reduced acoustic noise and was largely insensitive to susceptibility-induced signal loss in this feasibility study. While this work represents our initial experience using ZTE for human fMRI at 3T, the presented results will motivate future studies to refine and extend this approach to explore complementary functional contrast mechanisms.

papers.title: AOR: adaptive orthogonal regression for depression feature selection with incomplete EEG channels.
papers.authors: Dong W, Gong Z, Xu X, Liu K, Wei F, Zhuo L.
papers.abstract: Objective Depression induces severe mental and physical impairments, highlighting the clinical need for rapid and reliable detection. Electroencephalography (EEG) directly reflects neural electrical activity and serves as a promising tool for depression investigation. However, the inherent non-stationarity, redundancy, and noise susceptibility of EEG signals, together with the common issue of incomplete channel data due to electrode loss or severe noise during acquisition, compromise the reliability of diagnostic models. Existing EEG feature selection methods lack adaptability to such incomplete data, leading to distorted feature evaluation and degraded performance. Approach To address this limitation, an adaptive orthogonal regression (AOR) method is proposed for EEG feature selection for depression detection under incomplete channel conditions. The method integrates three core innovations: embedding missing channel information into the orthogonal regression formulation to mitigate the impact of incomplete channels, incorporating adaptive channel-weighted learning to automatically quantify the relative importance of different channels, and applying global redundancy minimization to eliminate inter-feature redundancy while enhancing discriminability. The optimization problem is solved via Generalized Power Iteration and Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier methods. Main results AOR was validated on the MODMA and PRED-d003 datasets across 3-channel, 64-channel, and 128-channel configurations under single-modal and multi-modal scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that AOR consistently outperforms state-of-the art methods across various missing ratios and channel configurations. The average cross-subject depression recognition accuracy reaches 92.25 % and 95.12 % across different missing ratios on the two datasets. Additionally, feature weight analysis reveals that EEG kurtosis consistently exhibits high discriminative power across different configurations. Significance The proposed AOR method provides a robust and efficient solution for depression feature selection under incomplete EEG channel conditions, offering reliable diagnostic performance in real-world clinical scenarios.

papers.title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
papers.authors: Wei M, Luo X, Fu J, Li S, Ni H, Liu J, Dong GH.
papers.abstract: Background Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. Methods Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. Results The negative (r = 0.401, p <.001) and combined network (r = 0.480, p <.001) can significantly predict a reduction of addiction severity (baseline minus post-test). Specifically, the negative network was primarily centred on the motor, subcortical, and salience networks. The positive network primarily involved cerebellar-related connections. Incorporating these into a combined model significantly improved predictive accuracy, suggesting that cerebellar-related connectivity may contribute to the prediction of intervention-related clinical improvement. Finally, the treatment-sensitive network was validated in a separate data. Conclusions This study established a treatment-sensitive network based on the whole-brain connectome. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. Clinical trials registration The trial protocol was pre-registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (www.chictr.org.cn; ChiCTR2300077831(MM), ChiCTR2300075869(ApBm), ChiCTR2500095444(R-AC), ChiCTR2400090834(SAE)).

papers.title: When sex matters early: clues from pediatric onset multiple sclerosis.
papers.authors: Lorefice L, Zivadinov R.
papers.abstract: Introduction Pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis (POMS) provides a unique developmental model to investigate when sex differences first emerge in multiple sclerosis (MS). As disease onset occurs during immune, endocrine, and neural maturation, POMS offers an opportunity to understand how puberty may shape disease susceptibility and subsequent trajectories. Areas covered This review synthesizes evidence from epidemiological, clinical, neuroimaging, biomarker, and therapeutic studies across prepubertal, peripubertal, and post-pubertal stages. Articles published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through a PubMed/MEDLINE search using terms related to POMS, sex differences, and puberty. Available data indicate that the transition from childhood to adolescence coincides with the emergence of female predominance and sex-dependent patterns of tissue injury. MRI, retinal imaging, and fluid biomarkers suggest that differences in neuroaxonal vulnerability may be detectable early in the disease course. However, most studies remain sex-agnostic. Expert opinion Sexual dimorphism in MS may emerge earlier than previously recognized, with puberty representing a critical window in which sex-related biological changes begin to shape disease susceptibility and expression. Incorporating sex and pubertal stage into longitudinal POMS research may help elucidate the mechanisms driving these differences, refine early risk stratification, and ultimately support more individualized therapeutic strategies across the MS lifespan.

papers.title: Advances in monitoring the injured brain.
papers.authors: Rostami E, Hutchinson PJ, Depreitere B.
papers.abstract: Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.

papers.title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Zussy C, Mathias M, Vitalis M, Moujellil-Legagneur T, Malhaire F, Canet G, Desrumaux C, Claeysen S, Gómez-Santacana X, Goudet C, Llebaria A, Givalois L.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Carbon dot-based nanomaterials in neurodegeneration: addressing neurobiological barriers and targeting challenges.
papers.authors: Unnikrishnan B, Anand A, Fang CN, Wu SM, Wang CC, Huang CC, Chu HW, Chang HT.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, represent a major global health challenge due to their progressive nature and limited therapeutic options. One of the primary obstacles to treating these disorders is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts the delivery of most therapeutic agents into the central nervous system. In recent years, carbon-based nanomaterials, particularly carbon dot (CD) nanostructures, have emerged as promising platforms for neurological applications owing to their ultrasmall size, BBB-crossing ability, and anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties, in addition to tunable surface chemistry, strong photoluminescence, and favorable biocompatibility. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent research developments in the application of CD-based nanomaterials, including carbon nanodots, carbon quantum dots, graphene quantum dots, and carbon polymer dots, for the potential treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. The synthesis strategies and carbonization approaches used to produce these carbon nanomaterials are discussed, along with their physicochemical properties relevant to neurobiological applications, such as particle size, surface functionalization, heteroatom doping, optical properties, and stability in biological environments. Furthermore, the mechanisms by which CD-based nanomaterials can traverse the BBB are examined, including receptor-mediated and adsorptive-mediated transcytosis pathways. In addition, their applications are discussed, with particular focus on their roles in bioimaging, biosensing, inhibition of pathological protein aggregation, antioxidative activity, and targeted drug delivery. Finally, key challenges related to toxicity, biodistribution, large-scale synthesis, and clinical translation are discussed, along with future perspectives for the development of multifunctional theranostic platforms. Overall, use of CD-based nanomaterials represents a promising emerging strategy for overcoming neurobiological barriers and enabling the development of next-generation nanotherapeutics for the management of neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Striatal network dysfunction underlying speech impairment in early Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Rogers CP, Mournet S, Gallea C, Biondetti E, Mangone G, Sambin S, Chougar L, Villain N, Gaurav R, Arnulf I, Habert MO, Petrovska-Delacrétaz D, Corvol JC, Benali H, Vidailhet M, Lehéricy S, Jeancolas L.
papers.abstract: The pathophysiology underlying Parkinson's disease (PD) speech impairments and its potential sex differences remain unclear. We investigated sex-specific alterations in speech and striato-cortical networks in 104 patients with early PD (68M/36F), and 44 healthy controls (23M/21F), using quantitative speech markers and multimodal neuroimaging. Speech features related to prosody, phonation, articulation, fluency, and rhythm, were extracted from voice recordings; striatal dopaminergic loss was quantified using DaT-SPECT, and functional connectivity between striatal and cortical language networks was analyzed with resting-state fMRI. Results showed that PD-related speech impairments were more pronounced in males. Functional connectivity was globally reduced in PD, but female patients exhibited higher caudate-cortical connectivity. In males, speech deficits were associated with both dopaminergic loss and connectivity disruption, whereas in females, only connectivity changes were involved. These findings revealed sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms in early PD speech disorders, emphasizing the need for sex-stratified approaches in research and clinical practice.

papers.title: Childhood trauma and addiction: prevalence, comorbidity, and mediating mechanisms - a systematic review.
papers.authors: Murray N, Sánchez Belmar C, Sharma S, Subramanian N.
papers.abstract: Objectives To examine the association between childhood trauma and substance use and behavioural addictions in adults, including comorbid mental and physical illness, and to identify mediating and moderating mechanisms. Methods A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. Five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Cochrane) were searched for English-language studies published between 2006 and 2025, with an updated search in March 2026. Adults with a diagnosed substance use or behavioural addiction disorder, assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ or CTQ-SF), were included. Cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control designs were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results Sixty-seven studies encompassing 44,429 participants were included. Emotional neglect and emotional abuse were the most frequently reported trauma types. Alcohol was the most common addiction. Depression was the predominant mental health comorbidity, present in over half of reporting studies. Three themes emerged: psychological and psychosocial mediators (particularly impulsivity, emotional dysregulation, and negative self-concept); neurobiological correlates including structural, functional, and molecular brain alterations; and gender as a significant moderator, with women demonstrating more severe trauma profiles and stronger associations between trauma and relapse. Conclusions Childhood trauma is consistently associated with addiction across diverse populations and settings. The relationship is substantially mediated by modifiable psychological factors, supporting trauma-informed, gender-responsive approaches in addiction treatment. Routine trauma screening and integrated mental health care are indicated.

papers.title: miR-124 delivery to the hippocampus reduces excitability, enhances neurogenesis and affects microglia in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Polzer O, Salette L, van Wijhe M, Siva TL, Tsonkova A, Swildens A, Randoe RE, Ayyildiz D, Chameau P, Lucassen PJ, Salta E, Fitzsimons CP.
papers.journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
papers.abstract: MicroRNA-124 (miR-124) has been proposed as therapeutic candidate for Alzheimer's disease (AD), given its regulation of gene networks governing synaptic function, neurogenesis and inflammation. However, its functional role during early disease stages, and the cellular context-dependence of its effects, remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of targeted neuronal miR-124 delivery to the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) of AppNL-G-F mice. At an earlier 'presymptomatic' stage, miR-124 reduced intrinsic excitability of mature granule neurons and induced subtle changes in dendritic architecture. Integrative transcriptomic analyses revealed that predicted miR-124 targets were enriched among downregulated genes involved in synapse organization and cell junction assembly. At the same time, miR-124 increased the number of immature neurons and microglia, indicating structural and functional remodeling of the DG. At a later 'symptomatic' disease stage, where AD pathology is established, neuronal miR-124 supplementation reduced DG Aβ40 and Aβ42 levels and decreased local amyloid plaque burden, while also altering the plaque-associated microglial response. Together, these findings identify neuronal miR-124 as a context- and disease-stage-dependent regulator of the DG microenvironment and demonstrate effects extending from neuronal function to other cellular populations and local AD-associated pathology.

papers.title: Protective effects of Matricaria chamomilla L. extract against PTZ-induced epilepsy: Targeting neuroinflammations, glial reactivity and neurofilaments.
papers.authors: Hussein AM, Obydah W, Abouelnaga AF, Abass M, Ashmawy SA, Shaaban S, Soliman AF, Kamel B, Almetwaly RM, Saad S.
papers.abstract: Objectives The current study investigated the potential neuroprotective effect of Matricaria chamomilla L. extract (MCE) against PTZ-induced seizures in rats as well as its effects on the electrophysiological changes, neuroinflammatory cytokines, microglia and neurofilaments expression in hippocampus. Methods 36 male rats were randomly allocated into 3 equal groups, a) sham group, b) PTZ group (50 mg/kg i.p in 0.2 mL on alternate days for 2 weeks) and c) MCE group (200 mg/Kg MCE orally in 1.0 mL saline daily for 2 weeks with PTZ injection). Racine score and latency to the first sign of seizure were recorded with each PTZ injection. By the end of experiment, electrophysiological recording from CA1 region was done as well as biochemical assessment of oxidative stress markers (MDA, GSH and catalase), expression of IL6 and TNFalpha at level of mRNA and immunohistochemical assessment of Lc3, Nfl, NFH, IBA1 and GFAP were done. Results MCE considerably reduced the Racine score and lengthened the latency to the first seizure compared to PTZ group. Also, we observed a significant increase in delta and theta waves with a significant decrease in gamma waves in MCE group compared to other groups. When comparing the MCE group to the PTZ, we observed a substantial drop in MDA and an increase in GSH and catalase (p < 0.001), as well as a decrease in IL6 and TNFalpha expression at the mRNA level (p < 0.01). In addition, the MCE group showed a significant rise in NFL and Synaptophysin expression and decrease in IBA1, GFAP expression compared to the PTZ group (p < 0.001). Conclusions In rats, MCE demonstrated neuroprotective and antiseizure effects against seizures brought on by PTZ. These effects may be associated with normalization of hippocampal electrical activity, reduction of oxidative stress and inflammatory markers, attenuation of glial activation, and restoration of NFL expression.

papers.title: Abnormal resting-state EEG microstates correlate with objective sleep parameters in insomnia disorder.
papers.authors: Wu Q, Weng L, Lei X.
papers.abstract: Background Insomnia is a common sleep disorder, and Electroencephalogram (EEG) microstates, which mirror transient cerebral cortical functional activity, are linked to sleep disorder pathophysiology. The microstate characteristics in insomnia patients and correlations with objective sleep parameters remain to be further explored. Method This study enrolled 45 insomnia disorder (ID) patients and 48 healthy controls (HC), collecting awake resting-state EEG for microstate analysis; 27 ID and 13 H C participants additionally completed overnight polysomnography (PSG), and exploratory correlation analyses of microstate and PSG data performed for the ID group. Results Compared with HC, ID patients had markedly shorter duration of microstate A and B, higher occurrence and contribution of microstate C, and reduced duration, occurrence and contribution of microstate D (p < 0.05). ID patients also showed significantly lower transition probabilities of A→D, B→D, D→A and D→B (p < 0.01), and higher probabilities of A→C, B→C, C→A and C→B (p < 0.05). Correlation analyses revealed that in the ID, microstate D occurrence was negatively correlated with rapid eye movement sleep proportion (REM Sleep%, r = -0.427, p = 0.026) and positively correlated with non-rapid eye movement sleep stage 1 proportion (S1%, r = 0.385, p = 0.047). Conclusion ID patients present significant abnormalities in EEG microstates, and the occurrence of microstate D is correlated with objective sleep indicators of PSG. These findings suggest that EEG microstate parameters may reflect abnormalities in the sleep architecture of ID and may provide references for analyzing the cortical hyperarousal mechanism of chronic insomnia, constructing objective assessment schemes, and developing targeted neuroregulation interventions.

papers.title: The mechanism of the parkin-CMA-NLRP3-PANoptosis signaling axis in Parkinson's disease: From molecular basis to therapeutic strategies.
papers.authors: Tian X, Zhang B, Wang Y, Wei J.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder. Existing clinical interventions merely relieve symptoms and cannot reverse progressive neuronal injury. Neuroinflammation and dysregulated programmed cell death are central pathological drivers of PD. PANoptosis is an integrated pan-programmed cell death, can simultaneously trigger apoptosis, pyroptosis and necroptosis, with the NOD‑like receptor family pyrin domain‑containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome serving as a core molecular hub for PANoptosis initiation. Apart from its well‑characterized role in mitophagy, Parkin directly interacts with NLRP3 and mediates K63‑linked ubiquitination at the NLRP3‑K353 residue. This post‑translational modification targets NLRP3 for degradation through chaperone‑mediated autophagy (CMA), which suppresses excessive PANoptosis and preserves dopaminergic neuron survival. This review systematically delineates the molecular framework of the Parkin‑CMA‑NLRP3‑PANoptosis signaling axis. We further discuss its functional crosstalk with canonical PD‑associated pathological events, including α‑synuclein (α‑syn) aggregation and mitochondrial dysfunction, and summarize translational progress of small‑molecule compounds and gene therapies targeting individual components within this cascade. Critical bottlenecks are also addressed, such as unresolved molecular regulatory details, limitations of preclinical animal models, poor blood‑brain barrier permeability of candidate agents, and obstacles for early therapeutic intervention. This work intends to uncover promising targets for PD disease‑modifying treatments and support the advancement of precision therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Temporal interference stimulation for treating Wilson disease: A prospective clinical and functional MRI study.
papers.authors: Cheng N, Wang Y, Du H, Yu G, Han X, Huang Y, Xu C, Qiu B, Dong T.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: Wilson disease (WD) is an inherited disorder of copper metabolism caused by ATP7B mutations, and persistent neurological deficits, especially dystonia and motor disability, may remain despite standard anti-copper therapy. The putamen is a deep gray-matter nucleus frequently affected by copper deposition in WD and may therefore represent a plausible target for non-invasive neuromodulation. This prospective, single-arm, open-label study evaluated the clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of right putamen-targeted temporal interference stimulation (TIS) in patients with WD. Twenty-five patients received right putamen-targeted TIS once daily for 10 sessions. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Unified Wilson's Disease Rating Scale (UWDRS) total score and its neurological, hepatic, and psychiatric subscale scores. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) was used to evaluate regional homogeneity (ReHo) and seed-based functional connectivity (FC) of the right putamen. Paired tests compared pre- and post-treatment changes, and Spearman correlation analysis examined associations between imaging changes and clinical improvement. After treatment, the UWDRS total score decreased significantly from 59.40 ± 30.54 to 44.12 ± 24.96, with concurrent improvements in neurological, hepatic, and psychiatric subscale scores. The rsfMRI analysis showed increased ReHo in the right putamen and enhanced FC between the right putamen and right Rolandic operculum. After correction for multiple comparisons, greater increases in right putamen ReHo correlated significantly with larger reductions in UWDRS total and neurological scores. In this exploratory study, these preliminary findings suggest that right putamen-targeted TIS may improve clinical symptoms in WD, potentially through enhanced local functional synchronization within the putamen.

papers.title: Immunosenescence as a modifiable driver of neurodegenerative diseases: Pathways and multidimensional emerging strategies for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
papers.authors: Zhao J, Qu L, Guan H, Che H, Shi F, Yang Y.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: Immunosenescence represents a core upstream driver of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), exerting its pathological effects through four mechanistically interconnected cascades: chronic inflammatory imbalance mediated by the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), oxidative stress arising from immune-metabolic reprogramming, protein homeostasis dysfunction caused by autophagy-lysosomal failure, and disrupted neuro-immune crosstalk secondary to breakdown of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege. Current clinical practice remains largely constrained to neurotransmitter-based symptomatic management, which can neither arrest upstream pathological progression nor restore lost neuronal populations. Emerging intervention strategies targeting immunosenescence, including senolytic agents, antioxidant and metabolic modulators, autophagy restoration, and precision-targeted nanocarrier delivery, have demonstrated substantial capacity to delay disease progression in preclinical and early clinical investigations. These strategies act through selective clearance of senescent immune cells, remodeling of the neuroinflammatory microenvironment, and restoration of cellular quality-control mechanisms. The multidimensional treatment strategy approaches from the perspectives of artificial intelligence (AI) guided target discovery, nanocarrier engineering, and gut microbiota intervention to simultaneously address multiple nodes in the immunosenescence network, thereby overcoming the inherent limitations of single-target strategies. This review consolidates current mechanistic evidence and translational data to establish immunosenescence as an actionable therapeutic target and to provide a conceptual framework for precision disease-modifying therapy in AD and PD.

papers.title: Humanin attenuates neuronal cellular senescence and preserves neurotransmitter release in differentiated PC12 cells.
papers.authors: Tanahashi M, Kozuka A, Sasakawa N, Niikura T.
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence, characterized as a permanent arrest of cell proliferation, is triggered by various types of stress. Senescent cells are identified by markers, including senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and the secretion of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. These senescent phenotypes have been observed in neurons, suggesting that cellular senescence may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases. Humanin (HN), an endogenous short peptide, mitigates Alzheimer's disease-associated pathologies, including amyloid β-induced neuronal cell death. Overexpression of HN extends the lifespan of nematodes, suggesting a potential anti-aging role for this peptide. Here, we first investigated the effect of HN on cellular senescence in mouse primary cortical neurons. Chronic treatment with HNG, a highly potent HN derivative, attenuated prolonged culture-induced senescence. To further determine whether this anti-senescent effect is associated with preserved exocytotic function, we employed a glutamate-induced senescence model in neuronal-differentiated PC12 cells. In this system, HNG mitigated changes in senescence-associated markers, including increases in SA-β-gal activity, Ki67 expression, and SASP factor expression. In addition, acetylcholine-induced dopamine release was reduced in senescent PC12 cells, whereas chronic HN treatment sustained the expression levels of synapsin 1 and synaptophysin and attenuated the senescence-associated decrease in neurotransmitter release. These findings suggest that HN suppresses senescence and sustains exocytosis activity in neuronal cells, supporting an anti-aging function of HN at the cellular level.

papers.title: The histone variant H2A.Z regulates sex differences in Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology.
papers.authors: Hategan LA, Luo JQ, Creighton SD, Pirri F, McLean TAB, Hua S, Dahi TA, Jin Z, Winston SM, Reeves IL, Johnston K, Fahnestock M, Brimble MA, Walters BJ, Murphy PJ, Zovkic IB.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) disproportionately affects women, yet mechanisms underlying this sex difference remain unclear. Histone variants are overrepresented components of aging neuronal chromatin, but their contribution to AD is unknown. Here, we identify the histone variant H2A.Z as a sex-specific regulator of AD in the postmortem human hippocampus and in 5xFAD mice. H2A.Z occupancy decreased in female but increased in male AD patients. In females, reduced H2A.Z occupancy at the transcription start site (TSS) occurred despite increased total H2A.Z, indicating that H2A.Z is redistributed to sites of lower H2A.Z occupancy. Similar sex-dependent alterations were observed in 5xFAD mice over disease progression. Whereas H2A.Z.1 depletion improved memory and AD pathology in females at early and late disease stages, it impaired memory in male mice at early stages and improved memory in late stages. Together, these data identify H2A.Z as a regulator of sex- and stage-dependent AD outcomes, with implications for the sex-specific therapeutic targeting of chromatin factors.

papers.title: Walking and strength outcomes of targeted hip resistance training may be predicted by both MRI and clinical measures in multiple sclerosis.
papers.authors: Fritz NE, Eloyan A, Keller J, Zackowski KM.
papers.abstract: Background Compromised neural function contributes sensation, strength, and walking deficits in persons with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). Progressive resistance training (PRT) promotes neural adaptations, leading to favorable functional outcomes, while advances in MRI enable the evaluation of white matter tract pathology in vivo. The purpose of this work was to examine the utility of MRI with clinical measures to predict exercise responsiveness to PRT. Methods Twenty-eight PwMS (mean age: 49.3 and EDSS: 3.8) and 26 controls (mean age: 50) participated in 12-weeks of PRT. Primary outcomes were change in walk velocity and hip strength.
