Model predictors included baseline demographics, falls, walk velocity, strength, cognitive performance, quality of life, vibration sensation and 3T MRI measures of spinal cord area (SCA) and corticospinal tract (CST) fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and magnetization transfer ratio (MTR). A random forest procedure was used as an exploratory analysis for prediction of exercise responsiveness. The predictive accuracy was measured using the normalized mean squared error (MSE) within a leave-one-out cross-validation procedure, but was not externally validated. Results Strength change predictors included baseline strength, diagnosis, age, disease severity, falls, cognitive performance, quality of life, vibration, and CST (FA, MD, and MTR) (normalized MSE: 0.1792). Walk velocity change predictors included baseline walk velocity, age, disease severity, sex, cognitive performance, vibration, and CST (FA, MD, and MTR) (normalized MSE: 0.2147). Conclusion A combination of motor, cognitive, and MRI measures may predict responsiveness to a PRT program in PwMS. These data confirm that optimizing function relies on knowledge of pathology, disability level and intervention selection in pwMS, and that using imaging information in combination with functional performance may offer advantages to optimizing functional recovery for pwMS.

papers.title: Si-shen-san attenuates Alzheimer's disease pathology and cognitive deficits through multi-target regulation of astrocyte function and synaptic plasticity.
papers.authors: Li Y, Tang ZL, Liu FW, Chen M, Chang SQ, Ding FM, Bian QL, Pan JP, Qiu ZC, Kong MW, Li Y, Chen JX.
papers.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevance Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder pathologically characterized by cognitive decline, amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, tau hyperphosphorylation, synaptic dysfunction, and astrocyte dysregulation. The constituent herbs of the traditional Chinese medicine formula Si-Shen-San (SSS) have been used to ameliorate cognitive impairment. However, the comprehensive chemical profile, core bioactive constituents, and underlying mechanisms of action of SSS remain to be fully elucidated. Aim of the study This study aims to systematically investigate the therapeutic potential of SSS against AD and to clarify its multi-faceted mechanisms of action, with a focus on astrocyte-mediated neuroprotection, synaptic repair, and modulation of core AD pathologies. Materials and methods Ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole/time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q/TOF-MS) was used to characterize the chemical constituents of SSS extract and SSS-containing serum. In vivo, 3×Tg-AD mice were orally administered SSS. And cognitive function, AD-related pathology, synaptic integrity, and astrocyte-associated molecular changes were evaluated using behavioral, histological, biochemical, ultrastructural, and electrophysiological approaches. In vitro, an astrocyte-conditioned medium paradigm was used to examine whether SSS-induced changes in astrocytes were associated with protection of HT22 neurons against glutamate-induced injury. Results UHPLC-Q/TOF-MS tentatively annotated 525 and 318 compounds in the SSS extract and drug-containing serum. In 3×Tg-AD mice, SSS improved cognitive performance, reduced hippocampal 6E10-and ThS-positive Aβ-like immunoreactivity and tau phosphorylation at Thr231 and Ser404, and preserved synaptic structure and function. The reduction in tau phosphorylation was accompanied by changes in GSK-3β signaling. SSS treatment was also associated with reduced astrocyte reactivity, increased GLT-1 expression, and restoration of astrocyte-associated homeostatic markers. In vitro, conditioned medium derived from SSS-treated C8-D1A astrocytes alleviated glutamate-induced injury in HT22 neurons and was accompanied by activation of neuronal CREB-BDNF signaling. Conclusion SSS ameliorated cognitive deficits and multiple AD-related pathological alterations in 3×Tg-AD mice. These effects were associated with restoration of astrocyte-related homeostatic features, improved glutamate regulation, preservation of synaptic integrity, and activation of CREB-BDNF signaling. These findings provide an experimental foundation for SSS as a potential therapeutic strategy for AD and highlight astrocyte homeostasis as a promising target for future drug development.

papers.title: Attenuated attention engagement and sensorimotor resonance to social events in first-episode adolescent depression: Evidence from EEG oscillations.
papers.authors: Tang E, Zhang S, Qin W, Xu Y, Zheng J, Chen X, Wu R, Zhao H, Fu Y, Zhao C, Song W, Li J, Liu C, Liu Y, Yin J, Huang M, Chen H.
papers.abstract: Background Depressive symptoms may disrupt social brain development during adolescence, resulting in adverse long-term quality of life. Yet, little is known regarding the cognitive and neural changes during the processing of social interactions in adolescents with first-episode depression, particularly from an allocentric perspective. Methods We used electroencephalography (EEG) to assess two neural indicators during the observation of others' interactions, including sensorimotor mu suppression and occipital alpha-band activity, in 22 adolescents with first-episode major depressive disorder (MDD) and 23 healthy counterparts. Participants observed animated motions wherein actions were directed toward animate (human-like) or inanimate (rock) targets, comprising social (giving) and kinematically matched control events (disposing, taking and acquiring). Results Healthy controls (HCs) exhibited stronger central-parietal mu suppression in the lower sub-band during observation of socially interactive giving events than disposing events. In contrast, adolescents with MDD manifested no corresponding difference in mu suppression. Additionally, depressive adolescents demonstrated significantly higher occipital alpha power when viewing social (patient) than non-social (rock) targets, and this alpha power was significantly higher than that observed in HCs. Exploratory correlation analyses revealed that attenuated sensorimotor resonance of social interactions was significantly associated with increased severity of depressive symptoms in the MDD group. Conclusions Adolescents with first-episode depression showed difficulties in efficiently encoding social information and implicitly extracting the social-relational meaning of observed social interactions. These findings critically extend current understanding of neurocognitive mechanisms underlying social cognitive alterations in this population, and provide potential avenues for early screening and targeted interventions of social functioning impairment in adolescence.

papers.title: Therapeutic strategies in vascular cognitive impairment: Insights from the bilateral common carotid artery stenosis mouse model.
papers.authors: Hattori Y, Yamamoto Y, Mun J, Ihara M.
papers.abstract: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is a major consequence of cerebrovascular disease, but disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is increasingly recognized not simply as reduced cerebral blood flow, but as a sustained disturbance of oxygen delivery, capillary perfusion, neurovascular coupling, blood-brain barrier integrity, glial homeostasis, white matter maintenance, and synaptic network function. The bilateral common carotid artery stenosis (BCAS) mouse model is a central experimental platform for studying hypoperfusion-related VCI, as it exhibits reproducible cerebral blood flow reduction, white matter pathology, gliovascular injury, and cognitive impairment while permitting genetic manipulation, longitudinal imaging, retinal readouts, omics profiling, and therapeutic testing. This review synthesizes therapeutic studies in BCAS model mice across vascular/endothelial and hemodynamic mechanisms, oxidative and ferroptotic stress, ion-water transport, neuronal excitability and synaptic support, remote ischemic conditioning, regenerative and cell-based approaches, and biomarker-driven model refinement. Across these domains, successful interventions frequently converge on interconnected network nodes rather than isolated linear pathways, linking endothelial function, blood-brain barrier stability, redox-lipid balance, astrocytic ion-water regulation, microglial repair states, oligodendrocyte maturation, myelin integrity, and circuit plasticity. However, methodological heterogeneity concerning surgery, animal characteristics, behavioral testing, treatment timing, and outcome selection restricts translation. Future BCAS studies should prespecify treatment windows, particularly delayed-treatment paradigms initiated after objectively documented hypoperfusion, white matter injury, or cognitive impairment. Studies should also incorporate systemic dose-response assessments, biomarker-guided treatment stratification, clinically relevant comorbidities, and rational combination therapies. Such approaches may convert mechanistic insights from chronic hypoperfusion models into clinically credible therapeutic strategies for VCI.

papers.title: Constraint-induced movement therapy after ischemic stroke: From cortical reorganization to molecular plasticity.
papers.authors: Jung BH, Won MH, Yoo KY, Song SH.
papers.abstract: Stroke recovery is a dynamic, multilevel process involving structural, functional, and molecular reorganization of surviving neural circuits. Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) has emerged as one of the most effective rehabilitation strategies for improving upper-limb motor function after stroke by overcoming learned nonuse and promoting activity-dependent plasticity. This review integrates clinical and experimental evidence to provide a comprehensive mechanistic framework of CIMT-induced recovery. At the systems level, motor recovery is governed by peri-infarct plasticity, diaschisis reversal, and behavioral adaptation within a temporally defined plasticity window. Experimental studies using middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) models demonstrate that CIMT enhances synaptic remodeling, neurogenesis, angiogenesis, and neurovascular adaptation in peri-infarct regions. At the molecular level, CIMT engages coordinated signaling pathways, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-TrkB signaling, synaptic structural proteins (GAP-43, synaptophysin, PSD-95), modulation of axonal growth inhibition via the Nogo-A/ROCK pathway, and regenerative processes that support neural circuit reorganization. Comparative analysis indicates that CIMT primarily drives task-specific cortical plasticity, whereas treadmill exercise promotes global neuroplasticity through neurotrophic and neurovascular mechanisms. Combined rehabilitation strategies integrate these complementary effects, leading to synergistic recovery across multiple functional domains. From a translational perspective, optimal rehabilitation likely requires a multimodal framework integrating task-specific, aerobic, and neuromodulatory interventions. Future research should focus on identifying biomarkers of responsiveness and defining optimal timing, intensity, and sequencing of therapies to enable personalized rehabilitation strategies.

papers.title: Evaluation of anti-depressant, anxiolytic, and cognitive improvement effects of nanocurcumin using social isolation model in male mice: Behavioral and histopathological evaluation.
papers.authors: Irshad N, Ghafari H, Esmaeili S, Aminianfar H, Ghazi-Khansari M.
papers.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a heterogeneous mental illness that affects about 10% of people worldwide. Curcumin (Cur) is suggested as a treatment or adjunct treatment of MDD by multiple mechanisms of action. Its effectiveness is limited due to low solubility, poor bioavailability, and rapid metabolization. Different nano-formulations of Cur have been developed to boost its biological activity. The aim of this study was the evaluation of antidepressant/anxiolytic-like effects, and cognitive improvement of nanocurcumin (NCur) in male mice by post-weaning social isolation (PWSI) model to induce depressive/anxiety-like behaviors and cognitive deficits. Mice were housed either in a social group (SG) or an isolated group (IG) for four weeks. After two weeks, IG mice were treated intraperitoneally with NCur (5, 10, 20 mg/kg) and Cur (20 mg/kg) for two weeks. A battery of behavioral tests was used to evaluate depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment. NCur (20 mg/kg) showed antidepressant-like effect in forced swimming test (P < 0.001) and tail suspension test (P < 0.05), anxiolytic-like effect in elevated plus maze (P < 0.05) and open filed test (P < 0.01), and improved the memory and cognition in passive avoidance test (P < 0.05), but Cur (20 mg/kg) had no effect. Histopathology results showed that NCur (5 mg/kg) led to optimal neuronal survival in CA1, improved cellular organization in CA3, and the highest count of normal neurons in the dentate gyrus. NCur demonstrated potential to treat the depressive/anxiety-like behaviors and impaired cognition induced by the PWSI model in male mice. Histopathological data also showed improvements in hippocampal regions.

papers.title: Paraquat induced depression-related neurobehavioral abnormalities in zebrafish: Linkage between hepatic SAM biosynthesis and cerebral m⁶A methylation.
papers.authors: Yu Z, Li L, Jin C, Zhang Y, Zheng F, Hu H, Shao W, Yu G, Wu S, Li H.
papers.abstract: Accumulating epidemiological and toxicological evidence implicates the herbicide paraquat (PQ) as an environmental risk factor for depressive neuropsychiatric disorders. In this study, we demonstrated that PQ exposure induces depression-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in adult zebrafish. Subsequent examination revealed that chronic PQ exposure markedly suppressed hepatic biosynthesis of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), selectively downregulated methyltransferase METTL16 expression, and reduced global cerebral N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) abundance. Integrative analyses combining cerebral MeRIP-seq and transcriptome sequencing data further identified pervasive perturbations in the m⁶A epitranscriptomic landscape and transcriptional profiles of functional genes enriched in synaptic plasticity, neurotransmission and depression-associated signaling cascades. Notably, exogenous SAM supplementation effectively ameliorated impaired brain m⁶A methylation and PQ-evoked depression-related behavioral phenotypes. Collectively, our findings support inter‑organ crosstalk linking impaired hepatic SAM metabolism to reduced cerebral m⁶A abundance. The consequent epitranscriptomic disruption underpins PQ-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities, pointing to SAM as a promising candidate therapeutic agent against depressive disorders induced by environmental toxicants.

papers.title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus.
papers.authors: Boone PM, Harripaul R, Yadav R, Grzybowski M, Hanafy MK, Lee AC, Choi EY, Collins RL, Polesskaya O, Makhortova N, Larson MO, Kayir H, Wang Y, Avila RA, Frie JA, Eed A, Albeely AM, Vemuri S, Ayoub SM, Lemanski JM, Ben-Isvy D, Zhao X, Sanchis-Juan A, Handley M, Erdin S, de Esch C, Mohajeri K, Chen C, Tovar PG, Salani M, Moyses-Oliveira M, Tai DJC, Currall B, McGraw C, Slaugenhaupt S, Doan R, Gao D, Gusella JF, Sanchez-Roige S, Young JW, Khokhar JY, Geurts AM, Palmer AA, Talkowski ME.
papers.abstract: Recursive splice sites are rare motifs postulated to facilitate splicing across massive introns and shape isoform diversity. The necessity of recursive splicing (RS) and its role in human disease are unsubstantiated. Here, we use CRISPR to model intronic deletions eliminating an RS site (RS1) in CADM2 and conferring risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and other neurobehavioral traits. Ablating RS1 in human induced neurons alters the gradient of RNA abundance across CADM2's first intron, decreases CADM2 expression, and impacts transcript usage. Decreased CADM2 expression is reflected in reduced exon usage downstream of RS1 and global alteration to genes involved in neuronal processes. In vivo rodent models harboring Cadm2 RS1 deletions exhibit an attenuated effect on Cadm2 expression and modest changes in behavior and functional brain connectivity. This study demonstrates RS as a noncoding regulatory mechanism in a gene associated with a spectrum of neuropsychiatric and behavioral traits.

papers.title: Genomic structural equation modeling of impulsivity and risk-taking traits reveals three latent factors associated with brain structure and development.
papers.authors: Shishikura M, Liu L, Yu E, Zhu R, Vilar-Ribó L, Cupertino RB, Palmer AA, Sanchez-Roige S, Vainik U, Morys F, Gan-Or Z, Misic B, Dagher A.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Background Impulsivity is a multifaceted transdiagnostic trait that emerges in childhood. Research has identified genetic loci and brain systems associated with different facets of impulsivity and risk-taking. However, how these genetic underpinnings overlap across different facets, and how they are associated with brain development during childhood remain unknown. Methods Using genomic structural equation modeling on 17 impulsivity and risk-taking traits, we identified latent factors capturing underlying genetic architecture. We then calculated polygenic scores for these factors using Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data (N = 4,142) and examined their associations with brain structure, development, and behavior in children aged 9-14 years. Finally, we tested whether socioeconomic status modulated the associations between latent polygenic scores and brain structures. Results We identified three distinct genetic latent factors, which we label lack of self-control, reward drive, and sensation seeking. In children, polygenic scores for the three factors showed associations with partly differentiated brain patterns: lack of self-control associated with reduced prefrontal cortical thickness, reward drive with increased subcortical cellular density, and sensation seeking with increased cortical surface area and white matter integrity. Longitudinally, lack of self-control predicted variation in white matter development. We found little evidence that socioeconomic factors modulated associations between polygenic scores and brain structure. Conclusions Using genome-wide association study data of European genetic ancestry samples, we identified three genetically distinct dimensions of impulsivity and risk-taking. These genetic predispositions showed association with brain structure as early as ages 9-10, with limited evidence that these associations varied across socioeconomic context.

papers.title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia.
papers.authors: Simons NW, Patel V, Li H, Iyer S, Zhong Y, Cao D, Yu C, Obiajulu D, Keller K, Hynes G, Lee S, Nadukuru R, Cheng E, Chen EP, Hashemi A, Lund AN, Rogers HC, Jackson R, Preuss M, Thibeau H, Nadkarni GN, Liharska LE, Charney DS, Barbosa M, Marro SG, Kahn RS, Yang N, Dong Y, Charney AW.
papers.abstract: Background Few gene-disease associations identified by human genetic studies lead to new drugs that advance to first-in-human trials. Schizophrenia exemplifies this translational gap: thousands of gene-disease associations have been reported, but antipsychotics act via mechanisms introduced in the 1950s. To close the gap, clinical research strategies are needed that generalize across genes and diseases. Methods Candidate drug targets were defined as genes linked to schizophrenia by population-based studies. Clinical validation of candidate targets was performed through family-based studies. The molecular effects of clinically validated targets were confirmed by correcting mutations in the neurons from affected family members. For one validated target, a messenger RNA (mRNA) drug was developed, and pre-clinical studies of the drug were performed. Results Carriers of rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in schizophrenia risk genes were identified in 30,813 patients of a US healthcare system. These included two female relatives with a rare PTV in GRIA3, which encodes the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. Further investigation of the family found an X-linked pattern of inheritance between the PTV and severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in neurons of affected male family members restored GRIA3 expression. A GRIA3 mRNA drug was developed and in mice was well tolerated, resulted in broad brain expression of GluA3, and rescued behavioral abnormalities in a pharmacologically induced psychosis model (MK-801). Conclusions Further development toward clinical evaluation of a novel GRIA3 mRNA drug to treat schizophrenia is warranted.

papers.title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
papers.authors: Momi D, Wang Z, Oveisi MP, Kadak K, Bastiaens SP, Lissemore JI, Noda Y, Downar J, Rodriguez FV, Strafella R, Daskalakis ZJ, Zrenner C, Zomorrodi R, Rolle CE, Saggar M, Williams N, Keller CJ, Blumberger DM, Voineskos D, Griffiths JD.
papers.abstract: Background Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. Methods We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. Results We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. Conclusions These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

papers.title: Cytokine dysregulation and hippocampal neurogenesis: A shared mechanism underlying cognitive impairments across neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.
papers.authors: Tukiran N, Kolb T, Maggioni L, Rai S, Rafath Z, Borsini A.
papers.abstract: Neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders, such as major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease, all show a neuroimmune signature with dysregulated inflammatory cytokine profile and cognitive impairment. Although these deficits are clinically relevant, the immunological mechanisms that cause cognitive dysfunction across these conditions remain poorly defined. Recent studies demonstrate that inflammatory cytokines actively modulate adult hippocampal neurogenesis, a process critical for learning, memory, and affective regulation. Here, we synthesise clinical evidence to characterise the disorder-specific inflammatory profile of each of these five disorders, representing each profile with three frequently dysregulated cytokines rather than a single cytokine signature shared across conditions. We also integrate preclinical data where cytokines induce behavioural, cognitive, and hippocampal-related deficits in animal and cellular models. Hence, this review develops a mechanistic framework that links brain-immune communication directly to cognitive impairment through hippocampal neurogenesis, thereby suggesting neuroimmune targets for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Exercise-driven glucocorticoid signaling acts as a systemic circuit breaker to reprogram microglia and resolve post-stroke inflammation.
papers.authors: Liu Z, Zhang W, Si X, Zhao J, Xia Y, Qiao H, Wang J, Chai G, Hao J, Hou S.
papers.abstract: Following ischemic stroke, neuroinflammation drives severe secondary immunopathology, yet how systemic interventions coordinate peripheral and central immunity for neuroprotection remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that acute-phase exercise accelerates motor rehabilitation and neural repair by activating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis to function as a potent systemic circuit breaker. Systemically, exercise-driven glucocorticoids, validated via targeted receptor blockade, induce profound spleen atrophy to restrict the peripheral immune pool, effectively depriving the ischemic brain of infiltrating leukocytes. By leveraging high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics, we identify microglia as the primary, highly sensitive central sensors of this glucocorticoid-mediated immunosuppression. These endocrine-reprogrammed microglia transition from a highly pro-inflammatory state toward a regulated, homeostatic quiescence. Mechanistically, they decisively blunt interferon (IFN) signaling to abrogate CXCL9/10-CXCR3 chemotaxis, attenuate antigen presentation and co-stimulation, thereby arresting the recruitment and in situ activation of effector T and B cells. Furthermore, this early suppression of neuroinflammation limits neural tissue damage, preserving the broader neuroglial niche in a quiescent, physiological state. Accordingly, the reactive repair signals typically provided by microglia to astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are substantially attenuated, underscoring that early protection from neuroinflammation effectively obviates the need for intense compensatory repair. Collectively, our findings delineate a novel systemic-to-central neuroimmune axis. By demonstrating how exercise harnesses systemic endocrine signals to interrupt the pathological inflammatory cascade, we highlight microglial glucocorticoid signaling as a precise therapeutic target for post-stroke neuroimmune modulation.

papers.title: Blood-brain barrier disruption and microglia-associated synaptic pruning contribute to cognitive decline after electroconvulsive therapy.
papers.authors: Li Y, Xu S, Dai M, Wang T, Ji Y, Wu Y, Dai W, Tian Y.
papers.abstract: Background Modified electroconvulsive therapy (MECT) is a highly effective intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its broader clinical application is constrained by poorly understood cognitive side effects. We hypothesized that MECT disrupts hippocampal blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, permitting extravasation of peripheral factors that activate microglia, drive synaptic phagocytosis, and precipitate cognitive decline. Methods We employed a multi-modal translational approach integrating: (1) clinical neuroimaging (rs-fMRI and DCE-MRI) and cognitive assessments in 41 MDD patients undergoing MECT (including 9 with DCE-MRI); (2) a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model subjected to electroconvulsive shock (ECS), with behavioral, molecular, and transcriptomic analyses; and (3) causal validation via microglial depletion (PLX5622) and targeted BBB repair (Axitinib). In vitro, HT22 hippocampal neurons were stimulated with soluble inflammatory mediators released by primed microglia to assess direct synaptic injury. Results MECT significantly impaired immediate and delayed associative memory and reduced left hippocampal ALFF in MDD patients; memory decline correlated with ALFF reduction. In a paired subgroup of patients, DCE-MRI revealed increased hippocampal Ktrans after MECT, providing preliminary clinical imaging support for treatment-associated BBB hyperpermeability. In CRS mice, ECS downregulated tight junction proteins (Claudin-5, ZO-1, Occludin), induced Evans blue extravasation, and promoted hippocampal deposition of fibrinogen and complement C3. ECS also triggered microglial activation, enhanced PSD95 synaptic phagocytosis, elevated IL-6/IL-1β, and reduced synaptic proteins. Critically, both PLX5622-mediated microglial depletion and Axitinib-mediated BBB repair reversed these pathological changes and rescued cognitive function, establishing a dual causal validation system. Axitinib failed to suppress LPS-induced microglial activation, suggesting its protective effects were mediated via BBB restoration rather than direct immunomodulation. Conclusions In conclusion, this study identifies a hippocampus-centered neurovascular-immune mechanism underlying MECT/ECS-related cognitive impairment. Our findings demonstrate that BBB disruption is an early upstream event that permits peripheral factors to enter the brain, activate microglia, and drive synaptic injury and cognitive decline. These results establish a novel mechanistic framework for the cognitive side effects of MECT and highlight BBB protection and microglial modulation as potential strategies for cognitive protection.

papers.title: Individual susceptibility to disgust modulates neural and systemic immune responses to virtual infections.
papers.authors: Born M, Akselrod M, Trabanelli S, Girondini M, Papadopoulou G, Vanoni G, Cornu A, Bertoni T, Jandus C, Serino A.
papers.abstract: Disgust is a key psychological mechanism for avoiding pathogen exposure and constitutes a central component of the behavioral immune system. While disgust is thought to reduce infection risk through avoidance, it remains unclear how individual differences in disgust sensitivity shape downstream neuroimmune responses to perceived pathogen threats. Here, we show that lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger activation of type 1 innate lymphoid cells during exposure to infectious, compared with neutral, avatars in virtual reality. Disgust sensitivity further correlated with circulating signaling factors involved in immune regulation, including hormones related to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and eicosanoids. Linear models incorporating disgust sensitivity and threat exposure predicted these signaling factors, which in turn enabled accurate prediction of type 1 innate lymphoid cells responses using a pretrained neural network. Recreating this putative pathway, we were able to predict immune responses solely by disgust scores. Additionally, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed that exposure to infectious avatars altered hypothalamic connectivity with brain regions involved in visual processing, peripersonal space representation, and social cognition, and these effects were modulated by individual disgust sensitivity. Together, these findings suggest that disgust sensitivity modulates multiple levels of the neuroimmune response to perceived pathogen threats. Across two complementary experiments, our results are consistent with a model linking sensory threat detection, hypothalamic signaling, and systemic immune activation. Rather than uniformly amplifying immune responses, higher disgust sensitivity appears to bias pathogen defense toward neural processing, whereas lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger physiological immune activation.

papers.title: Toddler EEG power reflects behavioral social engagement state during naturalistic parent-child interaction.
papers.authors: Manning BL, Roberts MY, Wakschlag LS, Norton ES.
papers.abstract: Social engagement is a critical process for children's language and social development and is altered in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Although previous EEG studies have investigated correlates of children's social development in closely controlled experimental studies, few studies have examined how the brain reflects meaningful behavioral states, such as social engagement, within naturalistic parent-child interaction. This study collected EEG from typically developing toddlers of varying language ability and their parent (n = 49, 24-44 months) during the Social EEG paradigm; dyads completed contexts of dyadic interaction (book reading and puzzle play) and baseline (movie watching) during EEG recording. Videos of the interaction session were coded for social engagement using moment-by-moment behavioral coding and applied to the EEG data. As predicted, child EEG alpha power decreased (p < .001) and theta power increased (p = .01) during social engagement relative to baseline movie engagement. Further, the same pattern was replicated in an independent sample (n = 24, 25-47 months) including children diagnosed with autism, who showed the same pattern of power. These results demonstrate for the first time that EEG power is associated with naturally occurring moments of parent-child social engagement across a range of social/linguistic abilities and ages. This opens avenues for study of more naturalistic and meaningful developmental constructs.

papers.title: Exercise, DNA methylation, and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and future directions in intergenerational research.
papers.authors: Said G, Ramos da Silva AS, da Silva Rodrigues G.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia and remains without a cure; recently introduced disease-modifying therapies provide only modest slowing in selected patients. Physical exercise is associated with better cognitive and functional outcomes, but the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain incompletely understood. DNA methylation is a potential interface linking environmental stimuli to gene regulation and neural function. This narrative review examines evidence connecting exercise, DNA methylation, and AD, with emphasis on AD-related loci and on the possible intergenerational implications of parental exercise. We examine methylation findings involving amyloid precursor protein (APP) and presenilin-1 (PSEN1), which are relevant to amyloid-β production; microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT), which encodes tau; and apolipoprotein E (APOE), which influences lipid transport and amyloid-β clearance. These findings suggest potential epigenetic contributions to AD-related biology, although their direction and functional significance vary across studies. We also discuss exercise-responsive pathways involved in energy sensing, autophagy, and redox signaling. We also evaluate whether exercise-associated epigenetic remodeling could influence amyloid-β accumulation, Tau homeostasis, and neuronal function. Evidence that exercise modifies DNA methylation is growing, whereas studies that integrate exercise interventions, genome-wide methylation, and AD-related outcomes remain scarce. Evidence for an inherited reduction in AD susceptibility is even more limited and currently supports a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism. Future studies integrating behavioral, neuropathological, cell-type-resolved epigenomic, and other multi-omic outcomes are needed to determine whether exercise-induced DNA methylation changes mediate neuroprotection in AD or primarily reflect broader physiological adaptation.

papers.title: Ketamine's mechanisms of action in major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression: Is brain topological change a candidate convergent systems-level pathway?
papers.authors: Le GH, Wong S, Selby S, McIntyre RS.
papers.abstract: Ketamine is a rapid-acting antidepressant with demonstrated efficacy in major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression, yet the mechanisms by which its molecular actions translate into sustained clinical improvement remain incompletely understood. Prevailing models have emphasized N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonism and downstream glutamatergic signaling; however, convergent evidence indicates that ketamine engages a broader hierarchy of biological processes spanning synaptic plasticity, circuit dynamics, and large-scale brain network organization. This narrative review integrates molecular, cellular, circuit-level, neuroimaging, and electrophysiological findings to evaluate whether normalization of pathological brain topology represents a convergent systems-level pathway mediating ketamine's antidepressant effects. Across modalities, depressive disorders are characterized by disrupted network integration and segregation, stability of maladaptive configurations, and impaired flexibility of large-scale neural systems. Evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography indicates that ketamine rapidly modulates these abnormalities, increasing global connectivity, reducing rigid network organization, and enhancing neural signal diversity and network dynamics. These effects emerge within hours, are associated with clinical improvement, and show temporal and mechanistic distinctions from those observed with monoaminergic antidepressants, neuromodulation, psychotherapy, and serotonergic psychedelics. Integrating these findings, this review proposes that ketamine's molecular and circuit-level actions are necessary but not sufficient, with antidepressant efficacy shaped by how these processes are instantiated within large-scale network topology. Conceptualizing brain topology as an integrative systems-level framework may help reconcile diverse mechanistic observations, clarify sources of treatment resistance, and inform testable hypotheses for topology-based biomarkers and novel rapid-acting antidepressant strategies.

papers.title: From Contrasts to Representations: Rethinking fMRI Approaches for Cortico-Cerebellar Networks.
papers.authors: Irving CN, King M, LeBel A.
papers.abstract: The relationship between the cerebellum and cerebrum remains poorly understood in the neuroimaging literature, despite decades of functional magnetic resonance (fMRI) research. In this opinion article, we argue that this gap reflects fundamental methodological constraints rather than merely a lack of scientific interest. We first discuss challenges in acquiring fMRI data and analysis, with an emphasis on the cerebellum. We then critically evaluate the most common analysis approaches including functional connectivity, univariate contrasts, multivariate pattern analysis, and encoding models, examining the contributions and limitations of each to identify and quantify cortico-cerebellar networks. Through the lens of language processing, we briefly review how these approaches have been applied to characterize cortico-cerebellar networks underlying cognitive function. We conclude by proposing that encoding model frameworks, combined with ecologically valid naturalistic paradigms, offer advantages that can help resolve longstanding debates about cortico-cerebellar network function and organization.

papers.title: Normative Modeling of Amygdala Subfields and Disease-Specific Vulnerabilities Across Neurological Disorders.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Bai L, Shi D, Li W, Ai L, Ao F, Bai Y, Bai Y, Bao H, Cai Q, Cao J, Chai L, Chen F, Chen F, Chen K, Chen Y, Cheng D, Cole J, Cui Z, Dai H, Deng D, Du X, Du Y, Duan X, Fu Y, Gao Z, Gou L, Guo C, Guo M, Guo Y, Han X, He H, Hou Y, Hu B, Hu J, Hua T, Huang C, Huang P, Lei J, Li H, Li J, Li J, Li K, Li K, Li S, Li X, Li Y, Li Y, Li Y, Li Y, Liang P, Liao H, Liao L, Lin B, Lin CP, Liu J, Liu J, Liu W, Liu Y, Lu S, Luo J, Luo Y, Lui S, Ma H, Mao N, Meng L, Meng L, Qiu J, Shao J, Shen Q, Shi Y, Shu Z, Tian D, Tu Y, Wang F, Wang J, Wang J, Wang J, Wang W, Wang X, Wang Y, Wang Y, Wang Y, Wang Z, Weng J, Wu F, Wu Y, Wu Y, Wu H, Xia X, Xu C, Xu J, Xu J, Xu R, Yang R, Yin S, Yin X, Yin Y, Yu R, Yuan Z, Zhang F, Zhang H, Zhang J, Zhang N, Zhang R, Zhang T, Zhang Y, Zhang Z, Zhang Z, Zhao J, Zhao L, Zhao X, Zhao X, Zhao X, Zhe X, Zhou F, Zhu J, Zhu L, Zhuo Z, Fan G, Qian Y, Wang J, Duan Y, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: As an integrative center of the limbic system, the amygdala and its subfields participate in diverse neural functions and demonstrate heterogeneous structural changes in various neurological disorders. In this study, three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI data from 22,258 healthy participants were analyzed using normative modeling to establish normative references for the volumes of the amygdala and its subfields. These models elucidated the developmental and aging curves of the amygdala and identified distinct ages at peak volume across subfields, ranging from 24.6 to 43.7 years. Based on these references, individual centile scores were calculated for 4132 patients with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cerebral small vessel disease, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. These centile scores not only captured disease-specific deviation patterns of the amygdala subfields but also demonstrated utility in disease classification. Moreover, the centile scores correlated with clinical measures of cognitive function, emotional state, and motor performance across disorders. These findings suggest that normative references of the amygdala subfields provide insights into cross-disease alteration patterns and offer potential neuroimaging biomarkers to aid differential diagnosis and clinical assessment.

papers.title: Acute Ultra Low Dose THC Attenuates Anxiety-Like Behavior in a Mouse Model for Major-Depressive Disorder.
papers.authors: Grad M, Volkov H, Shomron N.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent psychiatric disorder, and is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Current treatments for MDD entail many side effects, and include a lag until the onset of therapeutic effects. The current hypotheses as for the etiology of MDD revolve around the monoamine hypothesis and the plasticity and neurodegeneration hypothesis. According to the latter, employing a neuroprotective treatment may help ameliorate depressive symptoms. Δ9 -Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the primary psychoactive component of the cannabis sativa plant. THC interacts with the endocannabinoid system, which was shown to be involved in the regulation of emotional states (e.g. anxiety) and stress through modulation of synaptic plasticity. Here, we show the potential of acute, ultra-low dose (0.002 mg/kg) THC in ameliorating anxious behavior in a chronic mild stress mouse model for MDD. We utilize next generation sequencing techniques to show the treatment's effect on neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity-related mRNAs, and specify Elmo domain containing 1 (Elmod1) as a molecular mediator of the observed anxiolytic effects. Moreover, we show the involvement of glucocorticoids-related mRNAs in the observed anxiolytic effect of acute, ultra-low dose THC.

papers.title: Reduced structural connectivity in age-related hearing loss aligns with the sensory deprivation theory.
papers.authors: Boons JHC, De Luca A, Dingemanse G, Vinke EJ, Kremer B, Vernooij MW, Goedegebure A.
papers.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) may contribute to cognitive decline through structural degeneration and brain reorganization, as posited by the sensory deprivation theory. These processes can be characterized by topological changes, such as strengthening and weakening of structural connections between brain regions. Stronger connections are more relevant to reorganization, as reorganization is thought to support speech processing by recruiting additional brain networks as a compensatory mechanism. We investigated connectivity changes associated with ARHL to improve the understanding of the sensory deprivation theory. Similar to the lateralization of speech processing, we hypothesized that structural reorganization associated with ARHL would be most evident in the left hemisphere. We assessed whole-brain structural connectivity using 1.5 Tesla diffusion-weighted MRI and structural T1 images in 2402 participants (median age = 66.1 years, females = 54.7%) from the population-based Rotterdam Study. Pure-tone audiometry was performed, and pure-tone averages (PTAs), for different frequency ranges including PTAlow (250-1000 Hz) and PTAall (250-8000 Hz), were determined for the better-hearing ear to reflect ARHL. ARHL was primarily associated with weaker connections involving frontal and subcortical gray matter regions. Contrary to our hypothesis, no lateralization in the connectivity alterations was observed. PTAlow and PTAall yielded the strongest associations, likely driven by low-frequency hearing thresholds. Adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors attenuated associations, especially for PTAlow . In conclusion, the findings contradict the hypothesized compensatory structural reorganization expected from the neural effects of sensory deprivation. While the observed weaker connectivity aligns with the sensory deprivation theory, the results also suggest cardiovascular health as a common risk factor.

papers.title: PPARγ Signaling in the Central Nervous System: A Review of the Implications in Synaptic Plasticity, Neuroinflammatory and Neoplastic Processes.
papers.authors: de Oliveira Maciel VCB, de Moura Arruda J, Silva RC, da Rosa MM.
papers.abstract: Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is a ligand activated nuclear receptor traditionally associated with lipid and glucose metabolism. Emerging evidence, however, identifies PPARγ as a central immunometabolic regulator in the central nervous system (CNS), coordinating mitochondrial function, neuroinflammation, synaptic plasticity, and neurovascular integrity. Beyond its classical metabolic actions, PPARγ regulates microglial activation, astrocytic inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby influencing neuronal resilience and circuit stability. This narrative review synthesizes knowledge of PPARγ structure, activation, CNS distribution, endogenous ligands, and synthetic agonists, including thiazolidinediones and selective modulators. We highlight how PPARγ controls transcriptional programs related to energy homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, including NF κB dependent pathways, and blood brain barrier function. Attention is devoted to synaptic remodeling and plasticity, positioning PPARγ as a molecular bridge between metabolic state and neuronal adaptability. We propose that PPARγ signaling dysregulation represents a convergent mechanism in neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and adrenoleukodystrophy; psychiatric conditions, such as depression and anxiety; and neurooncological processes. Integrating evidence across these conditions supports PPARγ as a master regulator of neuroimmune metabolic coupling in the brain. Finally, we discuss translational challenges and opportunities, including brain penetrant, functionally selective ligands, clarification of cell type specific signaling, and expansion of rigorous clinical trials. Integrating mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical trial evidence, this review critically examines the therapeutic potential of PPARγ across neurodegenerative, psychiatric, and neurooncological CNS conditions, while identifying priorities for future therapeutic development in diverse brain disorders.

papers.title: From Computational Models to Clinical Decision-Making in Epilepsy: Bridging the Gap Between Theory and Practice.
papers.authors: Dlima N, Carrere M, Sorrentino P, Jirsa V, Bedoui MH, Depannemaecker D.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most heterogeneous and unpredictable neurological disorders, characterized by complex brain dynamics, significant interindividual variability, and a therapeutic response that is often difficult to predict. Despite major advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and antiepileptic treatments, clinical decision-making still faces major challenges, including precisely localizing the epileptogenic zone, predicting seizures, identifying drug-resistant patients, and optimizing personalized therapeutic strategies. Over the past two decades, computational models have gradually emerged as promising tools for addressing these challenges. Early approaches relied primarily on mechanistic biophysical models aimed at reproducing the neural dynamics and mechanisms of hyperexcitability involved in epileptogenesis. More recently, the rise of artificial intelligence and deep learning has facilitated the development of predictive models capable of leveraging large-scale multimodal data. Finally, the emergence of digital brain twins and adaptive closed-loop systems now paves the way for personalized computational medicine integrating simulation, prediction, and real-time therapeutic intervention. This review provides a critical analysis of the major international initiatives developed between 2004 and 2026, including the EPICLUSTER/EBRAINS, EPINOSTICS, ENIGMA-Epilepsy, NeuroPace RNS, SeizeIT, EpiBioS4Rx, and NeuroVista projects, as well as several translational platforms based on artificial intelligence and biophysical modeling. We evaluate the actual contribution of these models to clinical decision-making in epilepsy, their translational contributions, their methodological limitations, and the challenges associated with their integration into hospital settings. We argue that the future of computational epileptology does not rest on the opposition between artificial intelligence and mechanistic models, but on their convergence within explainable, personalized, and clinically interpretable hybrid architectures.

papers.title: Fixed-Sequence OFF-to-ON Differences in Low-Beta State Dynamics in Parkinson's Disease: A Paired Source-Space Resting-State EEG Study.
papers.authors: Wang H, Cheng Y, Wu G, Du X, Fan H, Yan J, Du G.
papers.abstract: Resting-state EEG studies in Parkinson's disease (PD) have largely emphasized static power or connectivity, whereas fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session differences may also involve the temporal organization of network states. Paired source-space evidence under such fixed acquisition protocols remains limited. We analyzed 64-channel eyes-closed resting-state EEG in 39 patients with PD contributing paired OFF/ON recordings for the prespecified 90 s primary analysis; 24 also contributed paired 178 s recordings for duration robustness. After individual MRI-based source reconstruction, low-beta (13-20 Hz) dynamic amplitude-envelope connectivity was computed with 2 s windows. Primary endpoints were switching rate (SR) and normalized Shannon entropy (H); fractional occupancy (FO_path) and mean dwell time (MDT_path) of an internally defined OFF-dominant state were prespecified secondary conditional endpoints and are interpreted only as conditional summaries. PD-only linear mixed-effects models quantified the fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session contrast; medication state and session order were necessarily collinear. In the 90 s analysis, the later ON session showed higher SR (β = 3.3224, Holm p = 0.00406) and H (β = 0.06781, Holm p = 0.000749) than the earlier OFF session. FO_path (β = -0.09167, Holm p = 1.08 × 10⁻⁵) and MDT_path (β = -1.05171, Holm p = 0.00524) were lower in the later ON session. The 178 s reanalysis preserved the same directions, although SR and especially MDT_path were more parameter-sensitive across sensitivity analyses. The fixed OFF-then-ON protocol was associated with reproducible within-subject differences in low-beta state dynamics, with the strongest evidence arising from SR and H. Because medication state was perfectly collinear with session order, these findings cannot distinguish medication-specific effects from order-, time-, vigilance-, fatigue-, or adaptation-related influences. FO_path and MDT_path remain conditional summaries tied to an internally defined OFF-dominant state, and MDT was less stable in the 178 s and OFF-only sensitivity analyses.

papers.title: The cGAS-STING signaling axis in Type 2 diabetes-associated cognitive decline: from mitochondrial DNA sensing to neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Nirala N, Kuwar OK, Rana D, Padhy DS, Choudhary RK.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to cognitive decline, substantially elevating the risk of dementia through mechanisms that extend beyond chronic hyperglycemia. Among the interconnected pathological processes underlying diabetic neurodegeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a pivotal upstream event that promotes oxidative stress, impairs mitophagy, and leads to the cytosolic release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Recent evidence identifies the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway as a critical innate immune sensor that detects aberrant cytosolic mtDNA and orchestrates sustained neuroinflammatory responses. Activation of the cGAS-STING axis initiates TBK1/IRF3- and NF-κB-dependent signaling, driving the production of type I interferons and pro-inflammatory cytokines that amplify glial activation, compromise blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, disrupt synaptic homeostasis, and suppress adult hippocampal neurogenesis, ultimately contributing to progressive cognitive impairment. Although the cGAS-STING pathway has been extensively investigated in infection, cancer, and autoimmune disorders, its mechanistic contribution to diabetes-associated cognitive decline remains insufficiently synthesized. This review proposes cGAS-STING as a central molecular hub that integrates mitochondrial damage with innate immune activation, thereby linking metabolic dysfunction to neurodegeneration. We critically evaluate current experimental and emerging clinical evidence and examine the interplay among cGAS-STING, mitochondrial quality control, neurovascular dysfunction, and key signaling networks, including AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1α, the NLRP3 inflammasome, PI3K/Akt-mTOR, and autophagy. Finally, we discuss the therapeutic potential of targeting the cGAS-STING axis and identify major knowledge gaps that must be addressed to facilitate biomarker development and the development of disease-modifying interventions for T2DM-associated cognitive decline.

papers.title: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.
papers.authors: Sahu S, Jain P, Dharme KK, Yadav K.
papers.journal: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
papers.abstract: Background Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Purpose CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity. Methods Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. Results The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy. Conclusions This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

papers.title: Preoperative Functional Imaging Predicts Deep Brain Stimulation Outcome in Craniocervical Dystonia.
papers.authors: Fan H, Boutet A, Elias GJB, Hua T, Wang R, Yin Z, Xu Y, Zhao Z, Su YH, Loh A, Pijar J, Bogojevic I, Au HCT, Wang Y, Hu T, Yuen J, Iskin S, Chavira-Hernandez G, Yang A, Lozano AM, Bai Y, Germann J, Zhang J.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Background Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established treatment for craniocervical dystonia (CCD), yet postoperative benefit varies widely and cannot be estimated before surgery. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has shown prognostic value across DBS indications. The objective of this study was to develop and externally validate preoperative rs-fMRI models estimating DBS response in CCD. Methods Forty-two patients from two independent centers underwent preoperative 3 T rs-fMRI (discovery, n = 26; validation, n = 16). Using 12 literature-informed, symptom-relevant regions of interest, we quantified the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation as a measure of intrinsic regional neural activity. We applied regularized modeling to classify super-responders, distinguish responders from non-responders, and estimate improvement in Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Rating Scale motor subscore. Results When applied to the validation cohort, the imaging models achieved a three-category classification accuracy of 75.0% (50.5%-89.8%) using a sequential two-step procedure (Pperm = 0.002). Predicted continuous improvement was also correlated with empirical improvement (Rext = 0.65, Q2 = 0.34, Pperm = 0.004). Within the discovery cohort, nested leave-one-out-cross-validation, in which feature selection and decision-threshold derivation were repeated independently within each training fold, yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.73 (0.50-0.96) and 0.77 (0.51-1.00). Across models, baseline primary motor cortex activity was consistently associated with diminished postoperative benefit. Conclusions Preoperative rs-fMRI captures clinically relevant variation in baseline brain state in CCD, with predictive performance supported in an external validation. These findings provide preliminary support for rs-fMRI as a potential source of information to aid patient counseling and clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Self- and other-directed harmful behavior following deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus for drug-resistant epilepsy.
papers.authors: Roth RW, Sloan J, Yun W, Karpychev V, Villarreal H, Teagarden D, Carns D, Hacker C, Laxpati N, Gleichgerrcht E.
papers.abstract: Objective The current study examined the occurrence, clinical predictors, and neuroanatomical correlates of self- or other-directed harmful ideation or behavior (HIB) following deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT-DBS) for drug-resistant epilepsy. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 90 ANT-DBS patients followed longitudinally, tracking stimulation parameters, seizure outcomes, and psychiatric status. HIB was defined as documented suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, homicidal ideation, threats, or physical aggression requiring clinical intervention. Preoperative predictors were identified using Firth penalized logistic regression. Lead reconstructions, volumes of tissue activated, sweet spot analysis, and normative structural and functional connectivity mapping were performed in Lead-DBS to compare patients with and without HIB. Stimulation parameters associated with symptom emergence and resolution were examined within patients longitudinally. Results Eleven of the 90 patients (12.2%) developed new or worsening HIB following ANT-DBS. Preoperative HIB predicted postoperative HIB (odds ratio = 8.07, p = .003). Neither the volume of tissue activated by stimulation nor the structural or functional connectivity of the stimulated tissue differed between patients who developed HIB and those who did not. Within patient analyses (n = 11), eight patients' symptoms were resolved by changing from high- to low-frequency stimulation, and three were resolved via contact and amplitude changes. Significance HIB following ANT-DBS occurs in a clinically meaningful minority of patients and is strongly associated with preoperative psychiatric vulnerability rather than differences in lead location or network engagement. Most cases were resolved through stimulation parameter adjustments, particularly frequency reduction, suggesting these complications are often reversible through routine DBS reprogramming. Careful preoperative psychiatric evaluation and close postoperative monitoring are recommended for patients undergoing ANT-DBS.

papers.title: Transcriptomic analysis reveals distinct expression patterns in focal cortical dysplasia.
papers.authors: Sonawane S, Hendrych M, Ručková M, Jugas R, Vrbský J, Pail M, Straka B, Strnadová M, Krsková L, Vácha A, Koblížek M, Splítková B, Koželková K, Hloušková E, Vaňková T, Zámečník J, Aulická Š, Hermanová M, Kršek P, Slabý O, Brázdil M.
papers.abstract: Objective Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is a common cause of drug-resistant epilepsy in children and adults and exhibits substantial clinical and histopathological heterogeneity. However, morphological classification alone does not fully explain variability in epileptogenicity, disease severity, or treatment response. Methods We aimed to define molecular mechanisms underlying FCD heterogeneity using integrated transcriptomic and regulatory analyses. RNA and small RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) were conducted on cortical tissue resected during epilepsy surgery from 66 patients with histopathologically confirmed FCD subtypes IA (n = 17), IIA (n = 25), and IIB (n = 24), along with 15 postmortem cortical control samples. Differential expression and weighted gene coexpression network analysis were used to identify coordinated transcriptional programs, and microRNA (miRNA) profiling was integrated to assess posttranscriptional regulatory mechanisms. Integrative multivariate analyses (DIABLO and sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis) were used to evaluate subtype discrimination, and findings were validated using an independent RNA-seq dataset. Results FCD subtypes showed distinct but partially overlapping molecular profiles. FCD IA showed a comparatively subtle transcriptional profile, dominated by reduced expression of genes involved in cortical development, neuronal signaling, ion regulation, and metabolic stress. FCD IIA displayed a modest yet coherent molecular signature involving developmental and neuronal disruption, together with metabolic stress and autophagy. FCD IIB exhibited the most extensive transcriptional remodeling, including activation of antigen presentation pathways, complement activation, cytoskeleton reorganization, synaptic alterations, and extracellular matrix organization. Differential miRNA profiling identified shared miRNAs, including miR-320 family, miR-27a-5p, miR-142-5p, and miR-21-5p, alongside subtype-specific regulatory patterns. Integration of messenger RNA and miRNA data revealed concordant alterations, indicating that miRNA dysregulation may contribute to stabilization of subtype-specific transcriptional states. Significance These findings demonstrate that FCD is characterized by coordinated transcriptional and posttranscriptional network alterations that extend beyond morphological classification and may contribute to variability in epileptogenicity across subtypes.

papers.title: Comprehensive transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of mTOR-related epilepsy.
papers.authors: Ji K, Miyashita S, Iijima K, Yagita K, Owa T, Shimaoka K, Tabe NKN, Mizuno M, Hosaka A, Nishitani K, Murayama K, Komatsu K, Sone M, Sano T, Taya S, Nishioka T, Kaibuchi K, Takao M, Iwasaki M, Hoshino M.
papers.abstract: Objective Malformations of cortical development (MCDs) are a major cause of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in children. A subset of MCDs, including focal cortical dysplasia type II, tuberous sclerosis complex, and hemimegalencephaly, shares characteristic histopathological features and somatic mutations in genes within the Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-AKT-mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling cascade, and is collectively termed mTORopathies. However, mechanisms driving epileptogenesis and drug-resistant seizures remain poorly understood. Methods We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses of 56 surgical brain specimens from 41 patients with MCDs and 15 with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. Targeted genomic sequencing identified 19 somatic mutations in PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway genes, including novel variants in AKT3 (L51H) and MTOR (A512T). Results RNA sequencing with independent cohort comparison identified 160 consistently differentially expressed genes. Downregulated genes were enriched in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and mitochondrial metabolic pathways, whereas upregulated genes were associated with developmental process. Proteomic analysis revealed directionally concordant reductions in several mitochondrial proteins, and pathway-level alterations in some biological cellular processes. Significance This study provides a patient-matched, multi-omics dataset of human mTOR-related epilepsies from a single-institution cohort. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses suggested impaired OXPHOS as a molecular hallmark, potentially contributing to focal hypometabolism in mTOR-related epilepsy. These findings offer mechanistic insights into epileptogenesis and provide a resource for understanding molecular pathologies and developing mechanism-based therapies for mTOR-related epilepsy.

papers.title: Baihe Zhimu Decoction ameliorates anxious depression via PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway-mediated neuroprotection and inhibition of hippocampal neuronal apoptosis.
papers.authors: Han Y, He K, Yang H, Dai J, Chen R, Liu Y, Wang Y, Tang L, Zhao H.
papers.abstract: Background Anxious depression involves severe emotional dysregulation with a high risk of relapse and suicide. Although the classical Traditional Chinese Medicine formula Baihe Zhimu Decoction (BZD) is widely used for affective disorders, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Methods In this study, the chemical constituents of BZD were first identified using UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, followed by a maximum-dose safety evaluation. The therapeutic effects of BZD were then investigated in an anxious-depression mouse model induced by chronic restraint stress (CRS) combined with corticosterone (CORT) administration. Behavioral assessments, including the open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), sucrose preference test (SPT), and forced swim test (FST), were performed, together with histopathological examination of hippocampal tissues. Network pharmacology was employed to analyze the relationships between active compounds and potential targets and to predict related signaling pathways. Subsequently, western blot analysis, immunofluorescence staining, Hoechst staining, and flow cytometry, combined with pathway-specific inhibitors, were used to examine the involvement of the signaling pathway in hippocampal tissues and primary hippocampal neurons. Results Forty-one constituents were identified in BZD. In vivo results showed that BZD significantly alleviated hippocampal pathological injury and improved anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in stressed mice. Network pharmacology analysis identified 19 active compounds and 622 potential targets, highlighting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. Mechanistically, BZD activated this pathway and protected against neuronal injury, while these effects were attenuated by the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. Conclusions BZD exerts potent neuroprotective and therapeutic effects against anxious depression, primarily driven by activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and preserving hippocampal neuronal integrity.

papers.title: Hemispheric Complementarity is Associated with Distinct Functional and Structural Brain Profiles
papers.authors: Labache L, Beyh A, Cooper R, Parkes L, Holmes AJ.
papers.abstract: Hemispheric specialization is thought to follow a principle of complementarity, with homotopic functions such as language and attention lateralizing to opposite hemispheres, yet its consistency across individuals and relevance for cognition remain unclear. Using multimodal neuroimaging and twin-family data from 987 Human Connectome Project participants, we identified three sustained attentional lateralization phenotypes (right, left, bilateral) that were independent of handedness, differed by sex, and tracked broad shifts in brain organization, with bilateral individuals showing stronger intrahemispheric and homotopic connectivity. Examining attention and language revealed three multidomain profiles (crowded, mixed, split) reflecting whether functions colocalize within or are distributed across hemispheres. Mixed organization was linked to higher planum polare myelination, whereas crowded organization showed higher fiber density connectivity across dorsal attention–default network. Both phenotypes were heritable, yet neither predicted cognitive performance. These findings reveal a brain organization in which specialization emerges from flexible, heritable patterns linking function, structural connectivity, and myeloarchitecture.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal AI modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain
papers.authors: Hao Y, Park CY, Theesfeld CT, Troyanskaya OG.
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable AI transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 brain regions, 30 cell types, and seven developmental stages. Seal predictions enable characterization of both germline and somatic brain variants, and provide mechanistic interpretation by linking sequence variants to transcriptional regulators in spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify cell types and developmental windows relevant to neuropsychiatric disease risk, revealing shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing a cell-type and developmentally specific regulatory burden. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

papers.title: rpSTS Stimulation Disrupts Shared Neural Responses to Social Content during Naturalistic Viewing
papers.authors: Thompson JC, Marsh C, Kakalec P, Rawlings K, Roy R.
papers.abstract: Shared understanding of common experiences can foster feelings of social closeness and friendship, and help us understand those experiences. Recent work has suggested that patterns of neural activity shared across individuals, especially throughout the default mode network, may underlie shared representations. Here we used repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging during movie watching to show that shared neural patterns to common experiences rely on the encoding of social information from the environment by the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (rpSTS). An encoding model of movie features showed that rTMS selectively degraded social feature encoding in rpSTS, leaving low-level visual encoding in early visual cortex intact. Using natural language processing (NLP)-based analysis, we found that rpSTS stimulation was associated with reduced memory and intersubject pattern similarity across DMN and limbic networks during scenes central to the movie narrative. Projecting scene embeddings onto NLP-based concept axes revealed reductions in memory and neural pattern similarity for scenes conveying helplessness and empathy following rTMS. These findings provide causal evidence that the rpSTS is a key region that encodes shared social information into common neural representations, and suggest that disrupting its input leads DMN representations to become idiosyncratic.

papers.title: An astrocytic AMPAR-dependent parity signal preserves synaptic strength
papers.authors: Elazar N, Ravenel JR, Kim J, Vaidyanathan T, Shields BC, Wirfel-Farenchak O, Uryu K, Lim SS, Roach JM, Zhang W, Cao X, van Praag ME, Yan H, Yu G, Tadross MR, Eroglu C.
papers.abstract: Astrocytic processes closely associate with excitatory synapses and express AMPARs, positioning them to sense the same glutamate signals as neurons. Whether a mismatch between neuronal and astrocytic glutamate sensing affects synaptic physiology is unknown. Using AstroHTP, an extension of Drug Acutely Restricted by Tethering (DART) for cell-type-specific pharmacology, we found that acute astrocytic AMPAR inhibition spared neuronal AMPARs and basal transmission yet converted ongoing glutamatergic activity into a remarkably potent form of long-term depression (LTD) in mouse striatal projection neurons (SPNs). Unlike canonical presynaptic LTD, this form of LTD manifests postsynaptically, requires non-ionotropic NMDA receptor signaling, and arises when glutamate transmission occurs without a matching astrocytic signal. Astrocytic glutamate sensing through AMPARs, therefore, acts as a parity signal that verifies transmission and stabilizes active synapses.

papers.title: Attention warps visual-semantic representations across the human cerebellum
papers.authors: LeBel A, Visconti di Oleggio Castello M, Gallant JL, Ivry RB.
papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly shift their attention between objects and events in the environment. These attentional shifts modulate the representation of information in many regions of the cerebral cortex, including those that represent visual-semantic information. Based on recent evidence that the cerebellum also represents semantic information, we hypothesized that attention would also shift semantic representations in the cerebellum. To test this hypothesis, we used fMRI to measure brain activity while participants watched naturalistic movie clips and were instructed to attend to either people or vehicles. We used a voxelwise encoding model framework to recover visual-semantic representations in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum under the two conditions, and quantified the direction and magnitude of visual-semantic tuning shifts between conditions. Attention to different semantic categories had a large effect on visual-semantic tuning in the cerebellum. Representations in some regions shifted toward the attended category, and representations in other regions shifted away from the attended category. Within cerebellar regions that best represent visual-semantic information, the tuning shifts were most pronounced in Crus I and II and in lobule VI. Further, the magnitude of attentional tuning shifts was greater in the cerebellum than in the cerebral cortex, particularly for tuning shifts towards the attended category. These differences suggest that attentional modulation in the cerebellum is different than in the cerebral cortex and may not solely be driven by cerebral inputs.

papers.title: Static and dynamic noise abolish altruistic biases in Parkinson’s disease independent of deep brain stimulation
papers.authors: Hubschmid F, Sellitto M, Bahners BH, Pirenne T, Kalenscher T, Schnitzler A, Van Wingerden M, Florin E.
papers.abstract: There are known alterations in decision-making attributed to Parkinson’s disease. Yet little is known about how those alterations affect decisions in social contexts. We aimed to assess social decision-making in healthy human volunteers as well as people with Parkinson’s disease treated with deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus. Twenty healthy controls and twenty-two people with Parkinson’s in both the stimulation ON and OFF conditions took part in a social discounting task that measured the degree of generosity toward others as a function of social-emotional distance. Using a computational approach, we modelled mechanisms of social discounting across three different models that differed in how they mapped choice valuation onto observed decisions. People with Parkinson’s less often made generous choices than controls. Across all analyses, we found converging evidence that this effect was attributable to increased static and dynamic decision noise, i.e. inhibitory and attentional processes, but not changes in prosocial valuation. While stimulation sped up decisions, there was no effect of deep brain stimulation on social decision-making. Present results indicate that people with Parkinson’s are more prone to random processes such as increased impulsivity and attentional lapses during choices in social situations. Such changes attributed to the disease appear to evade clinical care with dopaminergic compensation and deep brain stimulation.

papers.title: Mapping polygenic risk scores to brain cells: insights for neurodegenerative diseases
papers.authors: Simmonds E, McKeever A, Yaman Ü, Leonenko G, Kimatova K, Taylor P, Chandran S, Ryten M, Khakh B, O’Brien JT, Spires-Jones T, Salih DA, Escott-Price V.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are driven by multiple related yet distinct pathological processes that evolve over decades, resulting in substantial clinical and neuropathological heterogeneity. Postmortem examinations of older individuals frequently reveal multiple coexisting neuropathologies, however, the underlying pathological processes cannot be easily assessed directly in living individuals.
