To quantify pathology-specific genetic signatures, we analysed a spectrum of NDDs using polygenic risk scores (PRSs) in the UK Biobank, restricting analyses to genes reported to be expressed in major brain cell-types, including microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons. We found substantial overlap among purportedly cell-type specific gene sets (21-29%), with APOE or neighbouring genes from the APOE locus represented in all gene sets, indicating that current cell-type specific annotations capture considerable shared genetic variation across cell-types. Jointly, cell-type specific PRSs explained a large proportion (60-93%) of the genetic liability for NDDs in which dementia is a major clinical manifestation. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) showed associations across all cell-types, with oligodendrocyte- and astrocyte-based PRSs demonstrating strong effects independent of APOE . AD PRS and APOE status independently differentiated Parkinson’s disease (PD) with dementia from PD without dementia. PD without dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibited distinct genetic profiles, with limited overlap with other NDDs. Collectively, these findings reveal both shared and disease-specific genetic contributions across neurodegenerative disorders and demonstrate that currently available cell-type specific gene sets capture substantial overlapping genetic risk. The imperfect alignment between clinical phenotypes and underlying pathology, coupled with the extensive overlap of gene expression across these cell types, underscores the persistent challenges in resolving the genetic architecture of neurodegenerative diseases and elucidating their underlying biological mechanisms.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.authors: Rohani F, Mostafavi S, Ebrahimifakhar P, Zomorrodi R, Mueller A.
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: Retinal arteriolar tortuosity as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature: distributed sharing with blood pressure at CSK and PAWR and a roadmap for larger hearing GWAS
papers.authors: Yang L, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Background The inner ear is supplied by the labyrinthine artery, which is functionally close to an end artery with limited collateral reserve. Microvascular abnormalities have been implicated in sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) and age-related hearing loss, yet inner-ear microvasculature cannot be assessed in vivo and current hearing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are underpowered. We evaluated the shared genetic architecture of retinal arteriolar tortuosity (retina_AT) with blood pressure, cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) and hearing phenotypes, and examined whether retinal microvasculature could serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature. Methods We used linkage-disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) to estimate SNP heritability for 19 phenotypes and genome-wide genetic correlations (rg) for 11 prespecified pairs. We ran approximate Bayes-factor colocalization (coloc.abf) between 19 independent retinal loci and systolic blood pressure (SBP), together with 95% credible-set fine-mapping, UCSC gene annotation, colocalization with GTEx aortic and tibial-artery expression QTL (eQTL) data and with white-matter hyperintensities (WMH), hearing-GWAS power calculations, and univariable and multivariable Mendelian randomization (MR) of blood pressure and heart rate on hearing. Results Only retina_AT with SBP was significant genome-wide (rg = 0.10, P = 4.2×10⁻⁵, FDR q = 0.00042). The strongest retinal locus, 13q34, did not colocalize (PP.H3 = 0.996; peaks about 267 kb apart; allelic heterogeneity), whereas two secondary loci colocalized strongly—CSK at 15q24 (PP.H4 = 0.98; 3/3 credible variants within CSK) and PAWR at 12q21 (PP.H4 = 0.99; 3/5 within PAWR)— supported by tissue-matched, moderate eQTL evidence (PP.H4 = 0.71–0.75). At 13q34, retina_AT with WMH was an adequately powered null (PP.H4 = 0.019; only this region and phenotype were tested). On the hearing side, sharing of the blood-pressure magnitude (rg ≈ 0.10) was a near-powered null (about 1.5-fold larger sample needed for 80% power under that assumption, versus about 15-fold for weak rg ≈ 0.03 sharing), and rg ≥ 0.12 was excluded; MR found no robust causal effect. Conclusions Retinal arteriolar tortuosity shows limited, distributed genetic sharing with blood pressure at the vascular-tone genes CSK and PAWR; no sharing with WMH was observed at 13q34 (only this region was tested). Retinal microvasculature may serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature, but this analogy awaits direct testing by larger, vessel-oriented hearing GWAS and inner-ear tissue functional studies.

papers.title: Latent Brain-Symptom Dimensions Characterize Heterogeneity in Clinical High Risk for Psychosis
papers.authors: Feng J, Genon S, Eickhoff SB, Li F, Jiang L, Wang Y, Dong D.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical high risk (CHR) for psychosis is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in symptoms, functioning, and outcomes. Although distributed resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) abnormalities have been reported, it remains unclear whether this heterogeneity can be organized into consistent multivariate brain-symptom dimensions and clinically meaningful subgroups. METHODS: We analyzed RSFC and 34 clinical variables from 701 CHR participants in the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Schizophrenia Program (AMP SCZ). Partial least squares analysis identified latent brain-symptom dimensions, which were further examined using transcriptomic annotation, independent psychosocial and cognitive measures, hierarchical clustering, and Month 2 follow-up data. RESULTS: Two significant brain-symptom dimensions emerged. The first reflected general psychopathology and was associated with somatomotor-salience and higher-order connectivity, with enrichment for genes related to neuronal development. The second, capturing symptom differentiation, spanned negative/internalizing features with psychobehavioral overactivation and involved cerebellar-thalamic-somatomotor circuitry, with enrichment for genes related to synaptic signaling. These dimensions showed dissociable associations with broader psychosocial and cognitive measures, and their loading patterns were substantially reproducible at Month 2. Clustering based on these dimensions identified two biotypes with distinct clinical and connectivity profiles that remained broadly similar at Month 2 despite divergent short-term RSFC changes. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support complementary dimensional and categorical representations of CHR heterogeneity that link clinical variation with distributed brain connectivity and molecular signatures, while demonstrating short-term reproducibility of the identified dimensions and divergent RSFC changes across biotypes. This multilevel framework may help characterize biologically meaningful variation in psychosis risk.

papers.title: DAP12-deficient microglia adopt a TREM2-independent antigen-presenting state with a glial-to-neuronal cascade in Nasu-Hakola disease
papers.authors: Leon J, Yoshinaga S, Koya I, Palafox G, Ando Y, Kubo K, Moody J, Takao M, Carninci P, Shin J, Condello C, Okano H, Hon CC, Morimoto S.
papers.abstract: Nasu-Hakola disease (NHD), a dementia with about 200 cases worldwide, is caused by loss-of-function mutation of TYROBP , encoding DAP12, or its receptor TREM2 . TREM2-DAP12 is the switch that converts microglia from a surveillant to a reactive state; what DAP12-deficient microglia become and to what extent they reshape their microenvironment is unknown. We profiled prefrontal cortex and hippocampus from an NHD donor and control by single-nucleus RNA sequencing and mapped the glial changes in situ by spatial transcriptomics. NHD microglia adopted a CIITA-driven, MHC class II-high antigen-presenting state with complement, iron and glycolytic programs and Fc receptors but not the TREM2-dependent lipid program. Astrocytes became pan-reactive and lost metallothionein expression, oligodendrocytes lost mature cells and cholesterol synthesis, and excitatory neurons lost presynaptic and activity programs, consistently between regions and across a published cohort. DAP12 deficiency left microglia in an antigen-presenting state short of the TREM2-dependent arm, accompanied by a glial-to-neuronal cascade.

papers.title: A representation of the visual environment in the human basolateral amygdala supports learning and choice
papers.authors: Jang G, Riels K, Aberman E, Tao G, Kragel PA.
papers.abstract: Animals continuously transform sensory inputs into representations that guide behavior. Although the amygdala is a brain structure critical for learning and choice, how natural sensory experience is represented within this circuit remains unknown. Here, we identify a representation of the visual environment in the human basolateral amygdala (BLA) that contains information relevant for learning and choice. Using image-computable encoding models trained on responses to naturalistic videos, we recover a continuous, low-dimensional representation of visual experience in the BLA. The representation generalizes across individuals and independent datasets and prospectively predicts BLA responses to novel visual stimuli generated through closed-loop image synthesis. Signals derived from the representation also informed reinforcement-learning models of human choice. Together, these findings show that the human BLA organizes complex visual experience into a structured representation that can support learning and flexible behavioral responses.

papers.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
papers.authors: Deb S, Bhunia D, Singh VAV, Muralidharan V, Roy D.
papers.abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF ± 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

papers.title: Impacts of different SETD1A mutations and genetic backgrounds on human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived hippocampal neurons
papers.authors: Hong Y, Zhao T, Yang Q, Zhang H, Ma X, Su X, Liu J, Zhang S, Mendez-Maldonado K, Zhou Y, Zou J, Kreimer A, Sawa A, Christian KM, Pang ZP, Duan J, Song H, Ming G.
papers.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a translational platform to interrogate the impact of genetic risk factors for various disorders on human biology. It has been a common practice to engineer premature stop codons to model predicted loss-of-function mutations using isogenic hiPSCs, yet effects of mutation position for the same gene and genetic background have been rarely tested systematically and at multiple levels for comparison to those of patient-specific mutations. Ultra-rare, heterozygous, and predicted loss-of-function mutations in the SETD1A gene, which encodes a H3K4 methyltransferase, are highly penetrant genetic risk factors for schizophrenia. Here, we generated a large panel of isogenic heterozygous SETD1A mutant hiPSC lines, including premature stop-codon mutations in one early exon and one late exon in five genetic backgrounds and two patient-specific mutations, to gain insight into molecular, cellular, and functional changes in a disease-relevant and highly pure population of human hippocampal dentate granule cell-like neurons. Our multi-level analyses showed that different SETD1A mutations lead to divergent molecular and cellular phenotypes related to synapses, but convergent neuronal network deficits, while the genetic background influences gene expression with no substantial effects at cellular and network levels. Mechanistic analysis confirmed the early exon patient mutation as loss-of-function, but revealed that the predicted loss-of-function patient mutation in the late exon is likely gain-of-function. Consequently, while all mutations decreased global H3K4me3 levels, deficits were only partially rescued by inhibiting H3K4 demethylase LSD1 for early exon mutations, but not for late exon mutations. Together, these results suggest that highly penetrant mutations can lead to similar cellular and functional phenotypes across different genetic backgrounds, whereas different premature stop-codon mutations could have contrasting impacts due to distinct mechanisms. Our findings have practical implications for applying genome-editing in hiPSCs to model disorders, highlight the value of modeling patient-specific mutations and testing multiple mutations, and suggest the need for tailored mutation-dependent therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Mapping reward processing circuits: the orbitofrontal-nucleus accumbens white matter pathways and their associations to psychopathological traits
papers.authors: Mezzano S, Saini F, Orbecchi V, Fernández-Borkel T, Raghavan M, Irfanoglu M, Beyh A, Dell’Acqua F.
papers.abstract: Dysfunctions in reward circuits, including projections from the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) to the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), have been implicated in psychopathology. The OFC is functionally divided into the medial OFC (mOFC), which processes rewards, and the lateral OFC (lOFC), which responds to non-reward or punishment stimuli. We investigated the structural connectivity of the lOFC-NAcc and mOFC-NAcc pathways and their associations with psychopathological traits using tractography-defined ROI analysis. Diffusion-weighted imaging data from 165 participants (aged 22 - 35, 53% male) in the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were analysed using spherical deconvolution tractography. MegaTrack, a novel tool, enabled tract segmentation via a single manual dissection mapped back to native space. Virtual dissection identified four bilateral pathways connecting the lOFC and mOFC to the NAcc, from which fractional anisotropy (FA) was extracted, and an lOFC/mOFC ratio was computed. Psychopathological traits were measured using HCP Achenbach Adult Self-Report scores. The lOFC-NAcc pathway showed positive associations with psychopathology and the mOFC-NAcc pathway negative associations. The lOFC/mOFC ratio emerged as a stronger predictor than individual pathways, with significant associations for depression, somatic problems, anti-social personality traits, and inattention. Effects were lateralized to the left hemisphere. These findings show that the lOFC-NAcc and mOFC-NAcc pathways can be structurally separated with tractography and display opposing correlations with psychopathological traits in a healthy population. Their ratio may index reward-processing dysfunction, and future research should test whether it is sensitive to dysfunction in clinical populations.

papers.title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
papers.authors: Coopmans CW, Martin AE.
papers.abstract: Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic marking modulates the neural processing of syntax, with phrase closures being encoded more strongly when accompanied by strong prosodic boundaries. Conversely, syntactic structure shapes prosodic encoding, such that boundary strength is neurally encoded primarily at points of syntactic phrase closure. These findings demonstrate that syntax and prosody are encoded not independently, but in a context-dependent and mutually constraining manner, highlighting their joint role in guiding structure building during naturalistic spoken language comprehension. Significance statement How the brain transforms continuous sensory stimulation into structured representations is a central question in cognitive neuroscience. Spoken language comprehension provides a particularly compelling case: as the acoustic signal alone underdetermines linguistic meaning, the brain must integrate bottom-up sensory information with top-down linguistic knowledge, such as syntax. Here, we recorded brain activity during audiobook listening to examine how syntax and prosody jointly shape neural responses to narrative speech. We find evidence for a bidirectional neural interaction: prosody modulates the neural encoding of syntax, and syntactic context shapes the neural encoding of prosody. These findings suggest that the brain flexibly integrates bottom-up and top-down information depending on how informative each cue is for extracting structured meaning from naturalistic speech.

papers.title: Transcriptomic reconstruction of an interregional molecular connectome in schizophrenia
papers.authors: Kwon O, Kim U, Webster MJ, Kim S, Lee D.
papers.abstract: Background Schizophrenia is increasingly viewed as a disorder of multi-regional brain networks, but molecular and pathophysiological hypotheses are often studied at the level of single brain regions or neurotransmitter systems. A multi-regional, multi-neurotransmitter analysis is needed to clarify how molecular abnormalities relate to circuit-level hypotheses of the disorder. Methods Transcriptomic data from 2,209 post-mortem brain samples spanning five brain regions in 1,037 individuals were integrated. Directed connectivity strengths between regions were estimated using co-expression between presynaptic and postsynaptic neurotransmission-related genes. These estimates constitute an “interregional molecular connectome”. Macaque transcriptomic data were used to benchmark the estimation pipeline against reference macaque connectomes. Connectivity differences between healthy controls and patients with schizophrenia were calculated, and a directional consistency filter was applied to identify candidate dysregulations. An LLM-augmented literature screening framework was used to assess the level of literature support for our candidates. Results Our estimation pipeline showed concordance with reference connectomes, outperformed whole-transcriptome and random-gene co-expression measures, and remained stable when applied to macaque data. A total of 10 connections were marked as candidate dysregulations in schizophrenia at a nominal permutation threshold. Three of the candidates align with established anatomical connectivity, and another three with anatomical connections through relay regions. These candidates were characterized by bidirectional abnormalities in the cortico-striatal circuitry. The remaining four candidates had no well-established monosynaptic connection between two regions. These candidates were interpreted as co-regulated co-expression coordination changes. Literature screening quantified the number of articles discussing each candidate and how many of the articles directly support or refute each candidate. Our candidates collectively highlight the role of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Conclusions Interregional co-expression of neurotransmission-related genes carries more anatomical information than whole-transcriptome co-expression. Applied to schizophrenia, our analysis recapitulates known hypotheses and also proposes hypothesis-generating data-driven findings for experimental follow-up. This approach complements conventional region-wise analyses. Our approach could support a unified, multi-regional, and multi-neurotransmitter perspective of schizophrenia and point to candidate molecular mechanisms for further studies.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.authors: Radwan M, Lind PG, Yazidi A.
papers.abstract: A bstract Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7–82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2–5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9–60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm .

papers.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
papers.authors: Gulati D, Rao MB, Mundlamuri RC, Arimappamagan A, Sadashiva N, Sinha S, Kenchaiah R, Asranna A, Viswanathan LG, Ray S.
papers.abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl’s gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

papers.title: Subtype-Selective Neuronal Vulnerability and Compensatory Neuroglial Remodeling in Human Cortical Dementia
papers.authors: Roy B, Roy PK.
papers.abstract: Whether the nodal vulnerability in dementia is solely represented by changes in cellular abundance or attrition of cellular transcriptomic landscape attribute to that transition in aging brain is yet to uncover with minutiae. To understand this complication, we have analyzed two snRNA-seq data specific to (I) dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC): A comprehensive study of cellular profiling among cognitively normal and pathological ageing and dementia (AD) brain, (II) occipital cortex (OC) in the context of Nasu Hakola disease along with a tissue level bulk RNA-seq data corresponds to temporal cortex. We pinpoint cellular subpopulations their proportional changes within the nodal points and their transcriptomic profiling. In DLPFC we observed alteration of mitochondrial and synaptic maintenance program in the pathological manifestation of disease. In OC we noticed depleted upper layer CUX2 neuron, PVALB and SST neurons on the contrary an enrichment of RORB and LAMP5 neurons with compromised metabolic states in the disease context. Glial populations are marked by representation of fibrous astrocyte, neuronal-supporting subpopulations associated with extracellular matrix remodeling programs. Proportional increment of intermediate myelinating oligodendrocyte and a decrease in mature myelinating subpopulation highlighted a compromised myelin repair attempt. In temporal cortex at tissue level we observed transcriptomic landscape adopted a neuroglial phenotypes in dementia brain. Cell-Chat analysis demonstrated a shift in cellular coordination towards glial population from neuron in NHD brain. A single cell-based drug reprofiling approach identified efatutazone and balaglitazone as broad-spectrum candidates for major cell types in occipital cortex, whereas major actionable biological targets belong to CDK subtypes and proteasome subunits. Overall, our findings imply cellular persistence do not necessarily substantiate molecular preservation, also the coexistence of cellular vulnerability alongside selective remodeling features, present a cellular framework on how to cope up with degenerative changes.

papers.title: Probable neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease in an Asian woman without detectable NOTCH2NLC repeat expansion on routine testing
papers.authors: Xie S, Wen J, Liu Y, Lin X.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID) is a clinically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. GGC repeat expansion in NOTCH2NLC is strongly associated with adult-onset NIID in East Asian populations. Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), associated with an FMR1 CGG premutation, can overlap with NIID clinically, radiologically, and pathologically. Negative targeted repeat-expansion results therefore require interpretation alongside clinicopathological findings. Case presentation: A 67-year-old Asian woman with no known family history of neurological disease developed progressive cognitive decline in 2021, followed by limb ataxia and bilateral lower-limb weakness. In 2025, her ADL and mRS scores were 51/56 and 3; MoCA and MMSE scores were 8/30 and 19/30. Electrophysiological findings suggested predominantly motor demyelinating polyneuropathy. Brain MRI showed bilateral corticomedullary-junction hyperintensities on DWI and confluent periventricular and deep white-matter abnormalities on FLAIR and T2WI. A skin biopsy obtained above the lateral malleolus showed eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in sweat gland epithelial cells and fibroblasts, with positive SQSTM1/p62 and SUMO1 immunostaining. RP-PCR did not detect a NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansion. Both FMR1 alleles were reported to contain 29 CGG repeats, below the premutation range. During 14 months of follow-up, no impaired consciousness, seizures, or encephalopathy-like episodes occurred, and the mRS Scale score remained 3. Cognitive scores changed in opposite directions, precluding conclusions about cognitive change or treatment response. The clinical, radiological, and previously reported pathological findings supported probable NIID, apparently sporadic, without molecular confirmation. Conclusions: Characteristic MRI and skin biopsy findings remain diagnostically informative when routine NOTCH2NLC screening detects no expansion. FMR1 analysis aids differentiation from FXTAS. A negative targeted result alone should neither exclude NIID nor imply a novel causative gene; confirmation using an independent repeat-expansion assay or long-read sequencing should be considered when available.

papers.title: An EEG-informed fNIRS framework uncovers stage-associated cortical dynamics during unassisted upper-limb movement after stroke
papers.authors: Wang M, Chen X, Li Z, Gong Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Upper-limb impairment after stroke is primarily characterized by the emergence and resolution of spastic synergies. Brunnstrom staging captures these recovery phases and provides a clinically grounded framework for studying cortical reorganization. Applying functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during ecological gross-motor tasks introduces task-related systemic hemodynamic artifacts that obscure focal cortical signals. This study aims to determine whether an EEG-informed multimodal framework can effectively mitigate these artifacts and extract stage-sensitive patterns of cortical reorganization. Methods After multimodal quality control, 32 participants with stroke (Brunnstrom stages III–VI) and 15 healthy controls were enrolled. EEG and fNIRS were recorded simultaneously during an auditory-cued unilateral arm-raising task with concomitant fist clenching, comprising movement initiation, sustained elevation, and rest. Our framework combined Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) with an EEG-informed General Linear Model (GLM). FBCSP extracted focal sensorimotor features, while EEG-derived motor-intention regressors improved GLM modeling of task-related hemodynamic responses. Model performance was evaluated using R ² and ΔAIC, and feature discriminability using AUC from a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier. Results The proposed FBCSP-GLM framework demonstrated improved model fit and spatial discriminability compared with conventional analytical approaches. Participant-level FBCSP estimates revealed a distinct non-linear, stage-associated trajectory of cortical reorganization. Specifically, the FBCSP-derived EW-LI significantly decreased from 0.46 at Stage III to − 0.55 at Stage IV, and rebounded to 0.13 at Stage V. The target-M1 response t -score similarly dropped from − 0.06 to − 1.05 before increasing to 0.85 at Stage V (all FDR-corrected q < 0.01). The standard GLM did not capture these stage-associated patterns, as its corresponding comparisons did not survive FDR correction. Conclusions By improving hemodynamic model fit during ecological gross-motor execution, the EEG-informed multimodal framework reveals cortical reorganization patterns associated with post-stroke synergistic recovery stages. Its artifact-resilient EW-LI and target-M1 response t -score provide a robust computational assessment of neural state transitions.

papers.title: Mechanical Digitorum Sensory Stimulation Enhances Hemiplegic Upper Limb Motor Function in Stroke Patients by Increasing Cortical Excitability and Functional Connectivity
papers.authors: Huang W, Zhang H, Yu J, Ma Y, Li Q, Wu R, Yao Y, Zhang S, Hong Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Relieving flexor spasticity, enhancing extensor strength, and improving hand function in patients with stroke remain significant clinical challenges. Mechanical Digitorum Sensory Stimulation (MDSS), a novel therapy that applies precise mechanical pressure to the affected fingers, may address these issues; however, its effects and mechanisms have not been thoroughly studied. Methods Sixty convalescent patients with post-stroke hemiplegia were randomly assigned to a Control group (conventional rehabilitation + sham MDSS) or an MDSS group (conventional rehabilitation + MDSS) for 3–4 weeks. Muscle spasticity, strength, upper-limb motor function, and activities of daily living were assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), Manual Muscle Testing (MMT), Fugl-Meyer Assessment–Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI), respectively. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to measure oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentrations in regions of interest (ROIs) during the resting state (RS) and task state (TS; i.e., MDSS) to evaluate cortical excitability and functional connectivity (FC) by calculating correlations of HbO concentration changes between specific ROIs. Results After the intervention, the MDSS group showed significantly lower MAS scores for all finger flexors ( P < 0.001) and significantly higher MMT scores for all finger extensors, as well as higher FMA-UE and MBI scores ( P < 0.01) compared with the Control group. Regarding cortical excitability, increases in HbO concentration were higher in most ROIs in the MDSS group than in the Control group, including 10 ROIs (83.33%) during RS and 11 ROIs (91.67%) during TS. Moreover, increases in FC across all ROI-to-ROI pairs were greater in the MDSS group than in the Control group during both RS and TS. Conclusions MDSS effectively alleviates flexor spasticity, enhances extensor strength, and improves upper-limb motor function in patients with stroke. These effects are associated with enhanced cortical excitability and strengthened functional connectivity, supporting MDSS as a promising rehabilitation strategy for hemiparetic hand recovery. Trial registration The study protocol was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Website https//www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=176575 Registration Number ChiCTR2200063792)

papers.title: Depressive and PTSD symptoms are associated with regional differences in light-evoked brain responses in chronic ocular pain
papers.authors: Moulton E, Karakoleva E, Valdes-Arias D, Pattany P, Faria V, Helix E, Galor A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background/Objectives: Chronic ocular pain (COP) often co-occurs with depression or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), but whether these comorbidities confer a distinct biological signature is unknown. Thus, we compared light-evoked blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) responses in individuals with COP, stratified by the presence or absence of clinically relevant depressive and/or PTSD symptoms. Subjects/Methods: 43 individuals with COP (pain intensity ≥ 1/10 for ≥ 3 months) underwent event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging using bright-light. Thirty participants were classified as COP with mental health comorbidity (COP + MHC+) based on a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score ≥ 5 and/or a PTSD Checklist-Military Version (PCL-M) ≥ 33; 13 were classified as COP without MHC (COP + MHC-). BOLD responses exceeding an exploratory voxelwise threshold of Z > 2.3 were compared within predefined bilateral regions of interest (ROIs) comprising the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC), anterior insula, and amygdala. Regional parameter estimates were correlated with clinical symptoms. Result Demographics were similar between groups. Participants with COP + MHC+ reported greater dry-eye symptom burden and non-ocular pain, whereas measured ocular surface signs and in-scanner eye-pain and unpleasantness ratings did not differ significantly between groups. In exploratory ROI analyses, COP + MHC+ participants demonstrated greater light-evoked BOLD responses in the right ACC and caudal right aMCC, whereas COP + MHC- participants demonstrated greater responses in the rostral right aMCC and right anterior insula. Conclusions These findings suggest that depressive and PTSD symptoms may contribute to heterogeneity in central pain processing among individuals with COP. If confirmed, such differences could help refine COP phenotyping and inform more targeted, mechanism-based treatment strategies.

papers.title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome during enfortumab vedotin therapy: a case report
papers.authors: Ishii M, Hirata I, Kiyota K, Funakoshi R.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) are widely used to treat solid malignancies. Enfortumab vedotin (EV) is an effective therapeutic option for advanced urothelial carcinoma. Although EV-associated neurotoxicity is most commonly reported as peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system complications, particularly posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), are rare. We report a case of PRES associated with EV therapy. Case presentation: A man in his 50s underwent right nephroureterectomy for urothelial carcinoma, followed by adjuvant nivolumab therapy. Subsequently, multiple liver metastases developed, and treatment with EV was initiated. One day after EV administration during the second cycle, the patient developed acute visual impairment and altered consciousness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences revealed hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, predominantly involving both occipital lobes, consistent with PRES. EV was discontinued, and conservative management was initiated. The patient's neurological symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the lesions. Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

papers.title: Common Data Elements for Preclinical High-Frequency Oscillations in Epilepsy.
papers.authors: Wang Z, Guo J, Lisgaras CP.
papers.abstract: Normal brain function relies on coordinated oscillations within and across neural circuits. In epilepsy, disruption of these oscillations may reflect pathological excitability associated with seizure generation and/or the emergence of comorbidities. Among these oscillatory activities, high-frequency oscillations (HFOs, typically within 80-500 Hz) are increasingly considered promising electrophysiological biomarkers of epileptogenicity. Preclinical models provide a powerful platform for elucidating the mechanisms underlying HFO generation and for evaluating candidate therapeutic strategies. However, substantial heterogeneity persists across preclinical HFO studies in recording techniques, signal definitions, and reporting practices. This variability limits reproducibility and hampers comparisons between preclinical findings and human data, highlighting the need for greater harmonization. To that end, we propose a set of common data elements (CDEs) organized across 4 domains: (1) HFO recording, (2) HFO definition and detection, (3) HFO reporting and quantification, and (4) biological and disease context CDEs to capture subject- and model-specific parameters that may affect HFO interpretation and comparisons across studies. CDEs are classified as either core, representing the essential information recommended for all HFO studies; or optional, representing additional information recommended when relevant to the experimental design or research question. For practical implementation, CDEs are operationalized through structured case report forms that can be integrated into Research Electronic Data Capture systems for scalable implementation. By promoting harmonized practices, HFO CDEs aim to facilitate a common reporting language in preclinical and translational HFO research in epilepsy, enhance methodological rigor and transparency, and facilitate comparisons across laboratories and experimental models.

papers.title: Arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acid supplementation affects white matter microstructure in preterm infants.
papers.authors: Gunnarsdottir G, Maximov II, Geier OM, Nordvik T, Ramm-Pettersen A, Stiris T, Moltu SJ, Pfeiffer HCV.
papers.abstract: Arachidonic acid and docosahexaenoic acid are long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that serve as key structural components of neuronal cell membranes and exhibit anti-inflammatory properties. They accumulate most rapidly during the third trimester of pregnancy, leaving very preterm infants deprived at birth. We conducted a double-blind randomized controlled trial comparing arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acid supplementation to medium chain triglycerides oil and assessed effects on white matter maturation using advanced diffusion imaging techniques. We used tract-based spatial statistics to localize significant changes across major tracts. Diffusion kurtosis imaging and Bayesian rotation invariant approach were applied to describe white matter microstructure within the intra- and extra-axonal water compartments enabling a more detailed characterization of tissue changes. These advanced diffusion MRI data were acquired at term-equivalent age for 64 infants born before 29 weeks of gestation, including 33 in the supplemented group and 31 in the control group. We identified significantly higher fractional anisotropy and lower radial diffusivity in several white matter regions in the supplemented group, mostly pronounced in areas that myelinate early. There were no significant differences in diffusion kurtosis imaging metrics between the two groups, but the Bayesian rotational invariant approach revealed several significant differences. This might illustrate a different developmental trajectory in the supplemented group compared to the control group. Applying advanced diffusion models can potentially provide a deeper understanding of early brain development and facilitate opportunities for early detection and intervention for preterm children.

papers.title: Vagal sensing of altered gut microbiota links to externalizing behaviors.
papers.authors: Lee MJ, Kim IS, Ahn SH, Chung W, Kang YE, Jeon SM, An JH, Pyo CH, Jeong J, Kim YE, Yoon J, Choi KY, Lee SE, Kim HS, Lee S, O'Keeffe S, Park JO, Lee JY, Bae JW, Kim DE, Lee H, Kim SH, Yeo WH, Yeo MK, Oh E, Jo EK, Heo JY.
papers.abstract: Interoceptive brain responses triggered by intestinal microbiota influence mood-related behaviors such as anxiety and depression. Although genetic mutations can alter the gut microbiome, how alterations in the gut microbiome associated with host genetic variations relate to behavioral outcomes is not fully understood. We investigated how Sirtuin 3 (Sirt3 ) deficiency is linked to altered gut-brain interactions and mood-related behaviors. Gut microbiota composition and behavior were compared between Sirt3 -knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice. Cohousing and heterozygous littermate controls were used to assess microbiome-related contributions to behavioral differences. Transcriptomic profiling assessed region-specific gene expression in the limbic system. Metabolites in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), potentially related to gut-brain vagal signaling, were analyzed. The role of the vagus nerve was further tested using subdiaphragmatic vagotomy in the Sirt3 -KO mouse model, along with measurements of plasma choline levels in mice. Sirt3 -KO mice displayed mood-related neurobehavioral changes and alterations in synaptic plasticity-related genes in the amygdala and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), accompanied by alterations in gut microbiome composition. Elevated plasma choline levels in Sirt3 -KO mice, together with reduced neurotransmitter-related metabolites (e.g., γ -aminobutyric acid [GABA] in the NTS), suggest that externalizing behaviors in Sirt3 -KO mice involve vagus nerve-dependent gut-brain axis signaling. Consistent with the involvement of vagal signaling, vagotomized Sirt3 -KO mice were similar to WT mice in these measures, including GABA levels in the NTS and synaptic plasticity-related changes in the amygdala and BNST. Our findings support a model in which host genetic variation-associated microbiome alterations are sensed through sustained gut-vagal signaling under non-stressed conditions, correlating with NTS neurotransmitter alterations and externalizing behavioral phenotypes.

papers.title: Association of mitochondrial copy number and heteroplasmy with cognitive function in the ACCORD trial.
papers.authors: Odden MC, Li Y, Jotwani V, Eswarappa MS, Scherzer R, Shlipak MG, Arking DE, Shi W, Ix JH, Jones R, Sharma A, McGeever L, Desprez PY, Tranah GJ.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in cognitive decline and dementia, but the relationship between mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy and copy number with cognitive function remains poorly understood. We aimed to study these associations among individuals with diabetes who face elevated risk for mitochondrial dysfunction and cognitive impairment. We analyzed data from 954 participants (mean age 62.8 years, 52.1% female) in the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Blood Pressure trial. Mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden was quantified using the modified mitochondrial local constraint score sum (mMSS) from whole mitochondrial genome sequencing. Mitochondrial copy number was measured using quantitative PCR. Cognitive function was assessed using the Digit Symbol Substitution Test for processing speed and the Mini-Mental State Examination for global cognition at baseline, 20 months, and 40 months. Our primary regression models adjusted for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and mitochondrial haplogroup. Participants with mMSS > 0.5 had significantly worse processing speed at baseline compared to those with mMSS= 0 (β=-4.94 points, 95% CI: -9.44, -0.43) after adjustment. Higher mitochondrial copy number was associated with better processing speed at baseline among men (β=1.67 per SD, 95% CI: 0.31, 3.03). Neither heteroplasmy nor copy number was significantly associated with global cognition or with longitudinal cognitive decline. Higher mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden and lower copy number (in men) were associated with worse processing speed but not global cognition or cognitive decline. Mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to domain-specific cognitive impairment in diabetes, with potential sex differences. Further research is needed to elucidate mechanisms and evaluate mitochondrial measures in brain tissue.

papers.title: Postnatal corpus callosum microstructural deviations are linked to neurobehavioral outcomes in preterm infants.
papers.authors: Wang W, Yang L, Wu K, Li S, Peng S, Gong G.
papers.abstract: The neonatal period surrounding term represents a critical window for corpus callosum (CC) maturation, when axonal growth, pre-myelination, and fiber organization rapidly advance to support emerging motor and cognitive functions, yet preterm birth disrupts this process with unclear mechanisms and long-term consequences. To address this gap, we employed a normative modeling framework, based on a large term-born cohort, to characterize segment-specific CC developmental trajectories and then quantify individual deviations in preterm infants at term-equivalent age (TEA). Preterm infants exhibited selective CC microstructural abnormalities-most pronounced in the genu, anterior body, and splenium-while midsagittal area remained within normative limits. Using partial least squares correlation, we examined associations with neurobehavioral outcomes during toddler period and identified a multivariate brain-behavior coupling unique to the preterm cohort. Specifically, higher gross motor and cognitive scores but lower fine motor score were linked to a coordinated CC profile of increased anisotropy, higher splenial neurite density, reduced diffusivity, and lower genu orientation dispersion. This relationship was absent in term-born controls. These findings suggest that microstructure-informed deviation mapping at TEA may be sensitive to subtle CC alterations that are not apparent on macrostructural measures and are associated with later functional outcomes. This sensitivity to subtle and outcome-related variation highlights the value of this approach as a complement to conventional imaging, and lays the groundwork for future efforts to characterize early white matter development and identify preterm infants at elevated neurodevelopmental risk.

papers.title: Alterations in the populations of peripheral immune cells in the blood of a mouse model of progressive myoclonus epilepsy of Lafora type.
papers.authors: Baños-Carrión L, Campos-Rodriguez A, Garcia-Gimeno MA, Sanz P.
papers.abstract: Lafora disease (LD, OMIM#254780) is a rare, devastating form of progressive myoclonus epilepsy characterized by the accumulation of aberrant insoluble forms of glycogen (polyglucosans) in the brain and peripheral tissues. Recently, we reported that neuroinflammation could be considered a second hallmark of LD in mouse models, since brains from LD mice present high levels of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, produced by reactive astrocytes and microglia. We also reported that the TNF and IL6/Jak2 signaling pathways were the main contributors to this neuroinflammation, and that there was an infiltration of peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocytes in their brain parenchyma, contributing to neuroinflammation. In this work, we explored whether there was any correlation between the reported inflammation in the brain of LD animals and changes in the populations of peripheral immune cells. By flow cytometry, we observed an upregulation of myeloid cells (CD11b + ) along with a decrease in neutrophils (CD11b + Ly6G + high) and in B cells (B220 + ). We hypothesize that these alterations may be due to compromised hematopoiesis, disrupted cell survival, or aberrant peripheral cell trafficking, possibly driven by the inflammatory condition and polyglucosan-induced metabolic stress in LD mice.

papers.title: Sigma-1 Receptor Mitigates Poly-GR-Associated Redox Dysregulation by Restoring NRF2/HO1 Signaling in C9orf72-Associated ALS.
papers.authors: Tsai CY, Wu HC, Su TP, Weng EF, Wang SM.
papers.abstract: Hexanucleotide GGGGCC repeat expansions in C9orf72 produce arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins, including poly-GR and poly-PR, that contribute to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia. Although poly-GR has been linked to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, the mechanisms that determine whether antioxidant defenses are preserved or suppressed in poly-GR-expressing motor neurons remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether Sigma-1 receptor (Sigma-1R) modulates poly-GR-associated redox dysregulation in cellular and mouse models. In NSC34 cells, both EGFP-PR42 and EGFP-GR50 expression reduced NRF2 protein levels. EGFP-GR50 expression was also associated with reduced NRF1 and HO1 levels and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. Sigma-1R overexpression or pharmacological activation with fluvoxamine or PRE084 restored NRF2 and HO1 expression and attenuated both cellular and mitochondrial oxidative stress in EGFP-GR50 -expressing cells. Co-treatment with the Sigma-1R antagonist NE100 attenuated the agonist-induced restoration of NRF2 and HO1. Furthermore, the NRF2 inhibitor ML385 attenuated agonist-mediated HO1 restoration, supporting the involvement of NRF2 activity in this downstream response. In an AAV-mediated EGFP-GR50 mouse model, Sigma-1R deficiency was associated with shortened survival, reduced NeuN-positive neuronal counts, and decreased NRF2 immunoreactivity in the brain. Together, these findings identify Sigma-1R as a modulator of poly-GR-associated redox dysregulation and neuronal vulnerability and support further investigation of Sigma-1R modulation as a potential therapeutic strategy for C9orf72-associated ALS.

papers.title: Data-Driven Prediction of Speech-in-Noise Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Machine Learning Models.
papers.authors: Athukorala P, Nair A, Mishra SK.
papers.abstract: Purpose Difficulty understanding speech in noise (SIN) is a major determinant of communication ability and quality of life, affecting individuals with hearing loss as well as some with normal hearing. Data-driven prediction methods offer a promising approach for modeling complex, multidimensional factors underlying speech perception. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated computational approaches for predicting SIN-related outcomes, compared predictive performance across model classes where quantitative synthesis was feasible, and identified methodological factors relevant to model selection, generalizability, and clinical translation. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies using machine learning (ML), neural networks, automatic speech recognition (ASR), or auditory model-based approaches to predict, simulate, or evaluate SIN-related outcomes. Quantitative synthesis was performed using random-effects models for studies reporting support vector machine (SVM) or random forest (RF) performance, and between-study heterogeneity was assessed. Results Eligible studies included traditional ML, neural network, ASR-based, and mechanistic auditory modeling approaches. SVM accuracy pooled at 0.71 and SVM area under the curve at 0.84, while RF accuracy pooled at 0.86 and RF recall at 0.81. Bootstrap estimates were broadly consistent with the primary random-effects estimates, although between-study heterogeneity ranged from moderate to very high across analyses. Conclusion Data-driven prediction approaches show promise for predicting SIN-related outcomes, but high heterogeneity precludes identifying a single optimal model. Model selection should reflect the prediction target, data type, sample size, interpretability, and intended use. Current evidence supports proof-of-concept performance more strongly than clinical utility, highlighting the need for larger, standardized, externally validated studies.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic complexity and cognitive decline: Insights from approximate entropy across aging and dementia.
papers.authors: Cacciotti A, Fabbrocino A, Pappalettera C, Ginatempo F, Loi N, Sottana D, Deriu F, Rossini PM, Vecchio F.
papers.abstract: Introduction Physiological aging involves gradual modifications of brain activity patterns sometimes leading to pathological outcomes. Understanding changes in brain signal complexity from healthy aging to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) may provide insights into cognitive decline and support early diagnosis. Methods Electroencephalography (EEG) data were collected from 269 participants divided into three groups: healthy elderly (HE, n = 109), MCI (n = 75), and AD (n = 85). Approximate entropy (ApEn) was computed for the total EEG spectrum and frequency bands. A random forest classifier with a one-versus-one strategy and recursive feature elimination (RFE) was used for group discrimination. Additionally, group comparisons and correlations with neuropsychological scores were performed to further investigate the functional relevance of these entropy changes by assessing their association with cognitive and functional performance. Results Significant group differences in total ApEn were found, particularly in central brain regions, with progressive decreases from HE to MCI and AD. Frequency-specific patterns emerged: (1) delta ApEn was increased in those with AD across the scalp; (2) alpha 1 ApEn showed frontal decreases and occipital increases in the AD group, with an intermediate pattern in MCI; (3) gamma ApEn was markedly reduced in those with AD compared to both HE and MCI groups, with central and frontal localization, and extended occipital differences in those with MCI versus AD. The classifier achieved 66.55% accuracy, with sensitivities of 78.90% (HE), 49.33% (MCI), and 65.88% (AD). Positive correlations were found between ApEn and cognitive scores in both the total EEG spectrum and gamma band; conversely, delta and alpha 1 ApEn showed negative correlations with cognitive and functional scores. Discussion The distinct entropy patterns observed across frequency bands and scalp/brain regions may help characterize electrophysiological changes associated with cognitive decline and AD.

papers.title: Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Impairment: Pathophysiology and Emerging Therapies.
papers.authors: Corbali O, Menon P, Corbali HI, Jagannathan R, Levey AI.
papers.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
papers.abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive impairment (DACI) is a common yet underrecognized condition, manifesting along a spectrum from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. DACI encompasses patients who develop vascular dementia (VaD) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) with diabetes as a risk factor; however, in certain patients, particularly those lacking clear VaD or AD features, diabetes may act as a primary driver of neurodegeneration. Mechanistically, DACI can be conceptualized as a neurovascular-metabolic disorder characterized by disruption of the neurovascular unit, impaired cerebral glucose metabolism, brain insulin resistance, and chronic neuroinflammation, contributing to small vessel disease, regional brain atrophy, and accelerated brain aging. In this narrative review, we synthesize current evidence on the clinical and imaging features of DACI, outline key mechanistic pathways linking diabetes to neurodegeneration, and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies, including GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors, with potential neuroprotective effects. Greater recognition of DACI as a neurovascular-metabolic entity may facilitate earlier identification, inform biomarker development, and guide future trials aimed at preserving cognitive function in individuals with diabetes.

papers.title: Dose dependent impact of global Cc2d1a reduction on cognitive, social, and metabolic phenotypes
papers.authors: Heller AT, Bhattacharya A, Routray P, Rauf S, Uppalapati V, Suzuki E, Weiss S, Manzini MC.
papers.abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Intellectual disability (ID) share an increased male prevalence, but the biological mechanisms underlying this male bias remain poorly understood. Mice deficient for CC2D1A, a protein scaffold mutated in ASD/ID, have shown multiple male-specific deficits both in ASD-like behaviors and in the regulation of neuronal intracellular signaling pathways. However, previous research relied on conditional knockout (cKO) models due to early postnatal lethality of global Cc2d1a KO strains. Thus, the ability to define the developmental impacts of CC2D1A LOF in mice has been limited. While generating a Cc2d1a knock-in strain with V5-HA epitope tags, we found that homozygous animals ( Cc2d1a VH/VH ) resulted in a hypomorph line that can be used to study developmental loss of CC2D1A. Methods We assessed gross morphology, behavior, and intracellular signaling in male and female Cc2d1a VH/VH animals, where only ∼20% of CC2D1A is present. We then crossed this line with a null allele to obtain a more severe hypomorph ( Cc2d1a -/VH ) and explore phenotypic penetrance thresholds. In addition to the previous phenotypic characterization, we also assessed body composition, feeding, and molecular hallmarks of metabolic function in both sexes. Results We found that ∼80% CC2D1A reduction in Cc2d1a VH/VH mice did not recapitulate any of the behavioral or molecular disruptions seen in cKO models. In contrast, ∼90% CC2D1A reduction in Cc2d1a -/VH mice resulted in ASD/ID-like behavioral phenotypes in males, similar to those reported in cKO lines, with distinct intracellular signaling disruptions. Male and female Cc2d1a -/VH mice also showed subtle but significant adult weight deficits associated with distinct metabolic changes. Limitations These models still do not fully recapitulate the complete CC2D1A LOF found in patients. Due to the analysis of two independent strains over multiple metrics, these studies are not powered to compare statistical differences between sexes and data were analyzed in males and females independently. Conclusions We identified a strikingly narrow CC2D1A expression threshold for the emergence of ASD/ID-like behavioral deficits in males. In addition, we revealed a novel role for CC2D1A in adult weight gain. These mouse strains will be useful to better understand CC2D1A LOF phenotypes.

papers.title: Using the aperiodic slope across learning to predict sleep-based memory consolidation
papers.authors: Anesbury A, Caldwell HB, Lushington K, Al Safadi M, Chatburn A.
papers.abstract: Homeostatic mechanisms adjust synaptic strengths to regulate neuronal activity across wake-sleep cycles. Although sleep supports memory consolidation, limited research has explored how sleep-induced homeostatic changes influence memory outcomes in humans. The EEG-derived aperiodic slope (1/f) could be a candidate measure of homeostatic memory processes through its reflection of neural excitation-inhibition balance. In this study, 27 participants learned object-word pairs, and completed an immediate recognition test before either a nap or equivalent wakeful period. Resting-state EEG was recorded, both before and after learning and the interval, to derive changes in aperiodic slope values. A delayed recognition test then assessed whether changes in the aperiodic slope (i.e., homeostatic activity) across learning and the interval predicted memory accuracy and N400 amplitude, an index of stimulus expectancy and recognition. Our study found evidence to suggest homeostatic renormalisation, for the nap condition only, indicated by a shift towards inhibition across sleep which was inversely related to the slope change across learning. Although the aperiodic slope change across the nap and wake intervals did not predict delayed memory accuracy, a shift towards inhibition during learning was beneficial for memory accuracy, only in the nap condition. Similarly, a shift towards inhibition across learning, followed by a shift towards excitation in the nap condition, predicted reduced N400 amplitudes. This suggests that homeostatic renormalisation across the nap influenced model updating and stimulus expectancy. This study provides evidence for a link between synaptic homeostatic processes and memory consolidation, emphasising the importance of encoding-related aperiodic activity in this relationship.

papers.title: A Bayesian approach to volumetric analysis in rare neurodegenerative disorders
papers.authors: Shan Ho SY, Schmidt T, Ghosh B, Rowe JB, Rittman T.
papers.abstract: Identifying regional brain atrophy is critical for understanding neurodegenerative disorders. Traditionally, group comparisons rely on frequentist statistics, utilising p -values and point estimates that offer limited characterization of uncertainty. Bayesian methods provide an alternative by estimating effect sizes and credible intervals while incorporating prior knowledge and uncertainty. This study evaluated the feasibility of Bayesian hierarchical modelling to assess regional brain atrophy in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) and Corticobasal Syndrome (CBS) compared to healthy controls. Participants meeting diagnostic criteria for CBS or PSP, together with healthy controls, were recruited from the Cambridge Centre for Parkinson-plus. Grey matter volume, cortical thickness, and subcortical volumes were derived using FreeSurfer for 210 cortical and 36 subcortical regions defined by the Human Brainnetome Atlas. Participants with PSP were classified into Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS), corticobasal syndrome variant (PSP-CBS), frontal variant (PSP-F), and other presentations (PSP-Other). Bayesian hierarchical ANOVA models with appropriate priors were used to estimate group differences. Regions of practical equivalence (ROPE) were calculated to assess evidence of meaningful group effects. A total of 428 people were included (113 PSP-RS, 30 PSP-CBS, 23 PSP-Other, 19 PSP-F, 81 CBS, and 162 healthy controls). For grey matter volume, there was evidence of whole brain volume loss compared to controls for all disease groups except PSP-Other, which showed evidence of no difference. For cortical thickness, there was evidence of global cortical thinning in CBS compared to controls, but for no other group. For subcortical volume all groups showed evidence of volume loss compared to controls. Patterns of regional atrophy were identified in keeping with previous literature, with the largest effect observed in the left pre-motor thalamus (30% reduction in CBS). There was greater loss of subcortical volume in PSP-RS compared to other PSP subgroups. Bayesian hierarchical modelling provides a feasible framework for quantifying regional brain atrophy, with interpretable effect size estimates and uncertainty measures. This approach complements conventional statistical methods, particularly in the assessment of rare neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders.

papers.title: ASC specks and α-synuclein amplify microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation and co-localize with Lewy body pathology
papers.authors: Thakur K, Péladeau C, Hewitt M, Baumann K, Cai D, Woulfe JM, Tomlinson JJ, Schlossmacher MG, Sandhu JK.
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of several chronic neurodegenerative disorders, including Parkinson’s disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies, and is closely associated with microglial activation. The inflammasome adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase activation and recruitment domain (ASC) undergoes oligomerization upon inflammasome activation, resulting in the formation of ASC specks. These structures are recognized by microglia as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby promoting inflammatory signaling. Recent studies have demonstrated that extracellular ASC specks associate with amyloid-β (Aβ), and that uptake of ASC-Aβ composites by microglia amplifies pro-inflammatory responses. Although ASC specks have also been shown to potentiate α-synuclein (αSyn) preformed fibril-induced pathology, their interaction with monomeric αSyn and their effects on inflammasome activation remain poorly understood. Here, we co-stimulated murine SIM-A9 microglia with ASC-αSyn assemblies and evaluated their effects on NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Electron microscopy revealed a close association between ASC fibrils and αSyn monomers. Exposure of microglia to ASC-αSyn enhanced NLRP3 inflammasome activation, as evidenced by increased ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activation, and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18, when compared to ASC or αSyn alone. In addition, immunohistochemical analyses of post mortem brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies demonstrated ASC expression in regions exhibiting αSyn pathology and showed ASC co-localization with αSyn within Lewy bodies. Collectively, these findings identify ASC-αSyn assemblies as potent amplifiers of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and suggest a mechanism through which they may contribute to sustained neuroinflammation in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Connectome and Depression: Towards Precision Psychiatry Based on Brain Networks
papers.authors: Majul Conte Grand MV, Dines M, Bulacia AV.
papers.abstract: In recent decades, the study of the human connectome —the comprehensive map of the brain's neural connections— has redefined our understanding of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) as a spectrum of functional and structural alterations in specific brain networks. This review explores evidence on functional connectivity patterns in MDD, highlighting the involvement of networks such as the default mode network (DMN), frontoparietal network (FPN), salience network (SN), and reward circuits. We analyze patterns detected using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and their potential as biomarkers to predict treatment response to interventions currently included in clinical guidelines and widely used in practice, such as psychotherapy, first-line antidepressants (SSRIs), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine. For this purpose, we conducted an integrative narrative review of the scientific literature, selecting articles based on clinical relevance and methodological quality (GRADE), including meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and randomized controlled trials. These findings may contribute to a paradigm shift toward precision psychiatry, increasingly centered on the individual. Although methodological challenges persist that limit their clinical application, understanding the connectome and its relationship with MDD pathogenesis is a fundamental step toward truly personalized mental healthcare.

papers.title: Maturational constraints on tracking of temporal attention in infant language acquisition.
papers.authors: Snijders TM, Menn K.
papers.abstract: Children are active learners: they selectively attend to important information. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech is central to active language learning. This chapter evaluates recent research showing that neural oscillations in the infant brain synchronise with the rhythm of speech, tracking it at different frequencies. This process predicts word segmentation and later language abilities. We argue that rhythmic neural speech tracking reflects infants’ attention to specific parts of the speech signal (e.g., stressed syllables), and simultaneously acts as a core mechanism for maximising temporal attention onto those parts. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech puts a constraint on neural processing, which maximises the uptake of relevant information from the noisy multimodal environment. We hypothesise this to be influenced by neural maturation. We end by evaluating the implications of this proposal for language acquisition research, and discuss how differences in neural maturation relate to variance in language development in autism.

papers.title: Ketogenic Diet and Neurological Health: A Narrative Review with Natural Language Processing-Assisted Thematic Mapping Using BERTopic.
papers.authors: Jin B, Chen Z, Xie R, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Background The ketogenic diet (KD) is an established therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy and is increasingly investigated across other neurological disorders. Objective To provide an updated narrative synthesis of recent mechanistic and clinical evidence on KD across neurological disorders, including its therapeutic applications, potential mechanisms, and current evidence gaps, and to use BERTopic as a supplementary natural language processing tool to characterize major research themes and temporal changes in research emphasis. Methods Literature published from 2021 to early 2026 was retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. After deduplication and eligibility screening, 1017 records were included in BERTopic analysis. PubMedBERT, UMAP, HDBSCAN, and c-TF-IDF were used for thematic mapping; interpretation and evidence synthesis remained expert-guided. Temporal analyses were restricted to 2021-2025. Results Seven thematic clusters were retained, with increased representation of gut-brain-axis-related publications after 2023. Narrative synthesis highlighted energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter regulation, and the gut-brain axis as major mechanistic domains. Clinical evidence was strongest for drug-resistant epilepsy, while findings for Alzheimer's disease and migraine were less mature and those for Parkinson's disease remained preliminary. Conclusion KD is an established therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy and shows potential across other neurological disorders, particularly Alzheimer's disease and migraine. Its effects may involve energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter regulation, and the gut-brain axis. BERTopic-assisted mapping complemented the narrative synthesis by summarizing major research themes and temporal trends.

papers.title: Cerebral cavernous malformations: epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, diagnosis and therapy.
papers.authors: Yu S, Zheng W, Pan Y, Chen L, Ma J, Gao M, Zou W, Lu Y, Zhao Y.
papers.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are cerebrovascular diseases characterized by vascular lesions of the central nervous system (CNS) that can result in epileptic seizures, headaches, focal neurologic deficits (FNDs), and hemorrhagic stroke. Germline and somatic loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in one of the three established CCM-associated genes, namely CCM1 (or krev interaction trapped protein 1, KRIT1), CCM2, and CCM3 (or programmed cell death 10, PDCD10), which have been validated as core drivers of CCM pathogenesis and progression. Over the past few decades, a substantially improved understanding of the hallmarks and molecular basis of CCMs has been achieved. Key pathological hallmarks include but are not limited to excessive angiogenesis, vascular leakage, endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), defective autophagy, inflammation and immune response, oxidative stress, influenced gut microbiome and altered brain vascular microenvironment. These hallmarks are orchestrated by dysregulated signaling cascades, notably MEKK3-KLF2/4, PI3K-mTOR, and RhoA-ROCK, which integrate genetic, inflammatory, and hemodynamic cues. Concurrently, sophisticated neuroimaging (MRI with SWI/QSM) and genetic testing now enable precise diagnosis and risk stratification. Although surgical resection remains the mainstay for accessible symptomatic lesions, a wave of mechanism‑based pharmacological candidates has shown promising efficacy in preclinical models, and several have advanced to early‑phase clinical trials. This review summarizes the current understanding of CCM epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, diagnosis and therapy, highlighting how the evolving multi‑hit concept and the dissection of downstream signaling are paving the way towards personalized management of this complicated vascular disease.

papers.title: Prevalence and impact of cerebral small vessel lesions in mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease patients in memory clinic: Preparation for anti-amyloid therapy in Thailand.
