papers.authors: Smitasiri T, Pongpitakmetha T, Thanprasertsuk S, Likitjaroen Y.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) raises global concern with its impact on daily living. Anti-amyloid therapy (AAT) are specific treatments used in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia stage of AD (mild AD). Severe cerebral small vessel disease (SVD) lesions such as microbleeds, superficial siderosis, lacunes, white matter hyperintensities are listed as exclusions criteria for AAT. In Thailand, there is no prevalence study of SVD lesions specifically in these patient groups.ObjectiveThe purpose of this study is to report the prevalence of SVD burdens which are excluded in AAT, in MCI and mild AD patients in Thailand.MethodsThe study was carried out at Memory Clinic in King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital. Patients with amnestic MCI and mild AD were diagnosed using clinical criteria, cognitive tests and brain MRI. Visual rating scales were used to evaluate SVD burden based on STRIVE-2 criteria. Baseline characteristics and cognitive tests were retrieved from electronic medical records.ResultsThe study involving 102 patients, 73.5% had MCI, and 26.5% had mild AD. Twenty-one individuals (20.6%) had either more than 4 microbleeds, more than 2 lacunes, or Fazekas score of 3. There was no evidence of superficial siderosis. Individuals without microbleeds had a higher TMSE score (25.4 versus 23.5; p = 0.009).ConclusionsAmong patients with MCI and mild AD, 20.6% met the exclusion criteria for AAT, in part of SVD lesions. These findings provide important information for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of AAT, which become a treatment option for Thai AD patients.

papers.title: Retinal Microvascular Abnormalities, White Matter Injury, and Cognitive Impairment in Carotid Stenosis or Occlusion.
papers.authors: Cao L, Chen Y, Wang H, Kwapong WR, Zhou S, Lan T, Liu R, Pan R, Yan Y, Tao W, Liu G, Zhao Y, Wu B.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
papers.abstract: Background Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlusion (CASO) is associated with white matter injury and cognitive impairment, but markers of accompanying microvascular dysfunction remain incompletely characterized. We investigated the relationships among retinal microvascular abnormalities on optical coherence tomography angiography, white matter hyperintensities (WMH), and cognitive impairment in severe unilateral CASO. Methods In this multicenter cross-sectional study, 860 participants were included: 566 patients with severe unilateral CASO without acute cerebral infarction and 294 control participants with similar age and sex distributions. All participants underwent multimodal imaging, including automated WMH segmentation on brain magnetic resonance imaging and macular optical coherence tomography angiography. Cognitive function was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Results Compared with controls, patients with CASO showed lower vessel length density across retinal layers and greater WMH burden. Within the group with CASO, the retina ipsilateral to the stenosis showed lower vessel length density and greater vessel dilation, paralleling the greater burden of deep WMH in the ipsilateral hemisphere (all adjusted P <0.05). Retinal microvascular abnormalities and greater WMH burden were both associated with worse concurrent cognitive performance. Adding optical coherence tomography angiography metrics to clinical and WMH-based models provided modest additional discrimination for identifying concurrent cognitive impairment in internal cross-validation, increasing the area under the curve from 0.652 to 0.695 (Δarea under the curve, 0.043 [95% CI, 0.021-0.064]). Conclusions In severe unilateral CASO, retinal microvascular abnormalities were associated with ipsilateral white matter injury and lower cognitive performance. Optical coherence tomography angiographymetrics provided modest complementary discriminatory information beyond conventional clinical variables and WMH for identifying concurrent cognitive impairment, although external validation is required. Registration URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/. Unique identifier: ChiCTR2300074640.

papers.title: USP11 Drives Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury Via Promoting Ferroptosis by Deubiquitinating and Stabilizing ASK1.
papers.authors: Hu S, Wang K, He M, Zhang Y, Wang H, Yang M, Zhang P, Li Z, Lu Z.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
papers.abstract: Background Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) represents a pivotal pathological mechanism underlying ischemic cerebrovascular disorders including cerebral stroke. Currently, there are lack of effective preventive or therapeutic methods. Ubiquitin-specific protease 11 (USP11) is a member of the most prevalent ubiquitination-specific protease (USP) family. It has been shown that USP11 plays diverse and significant roles in a variety of diseases, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate cancer, and intervertebral disc degeneration. However, its precise function and molecular mechanisms involvement in CIRI remain unknown. Methods USP11 knockout (USP11-KO) and adeno-associated virus 9-mediated USP11 over-expression (USP11-OE) mice were established as a mouse model of CIRI, and USP11 knockdown and overexpression adenovirus were used to establish a cell model, to investigate the effect of USP11 on CIRI in vivo and in vitro. Molecular biological studies were used to clarify the mechanism of USP11 mediated ferroptosis during CIRI. Results The expression of USP11 is increased during CIRI. Functionally, USP11 deficiency attenuated neurological deficits, cerebral infarction, neuroinflammation, and ferroptosis during CIRI, whereas specific overexpression of USP11 exacerbated these pathological processes. Furthermore, USP11 knockdown inhibited neuronal injury, inflammatory response and ferroptosis, while USP11 overexpression promoted these processes. Mechanistically, USP11 bind to ASK1 and inhibit its K48-linked ubiquitination, thereby enhancing the activity of the ASK1-JNK/p38 signaling pathway. More importantly, the regulation of USP11 on neuronal ferroptosis and CIRI relied on its regulation of the ASK1-JNK/p38 signaling axis. Conclusions Our study clarified the new functions and mechanisms of USP11 during CIRI. Targeting USP11-ASK1-JNK/p38-ferroptosis may be a new promising strategy for the prevention and treatment of CIRI.

papers.title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms.
papers.authors: Berger L, Rojczyk P, Seitz-Holland J, Zhang F, Pankatz L, Sollmann N, Kaufmann E, Carrington H, Puri T, Coleman MJ, Pasternak O, Bouix S, Rathi Y, Cetin-Karayumak S, O'Donnell LJ, Falkai P, George MS, McAllister TW, Zafonte R, Stein MB, Shenton ME, Koerte IK.
papers.abstract: Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI). Diffusion parameters (mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, MD, AD, RD; fractional anisotropy, FA) in major WM tracts were extracted from diffusion MRI. CM was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Multiple regression models examined associations between CM severity and WM diffusion. Moderation analyses assessed the effect of PTSD and/or mTBI on these associations. Mediation analyses examined how WM diffusion affects the associations between CM and both PTSD and post-concussive symptom severity. Greater CM severity was associated with lower MD and AD, independent of PTSD and/or mTBI. WM diffusion, particularly in the corpus callosum and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, mediated the associations between CM severity and both PTSD (MD bab = 0.022, AD bab = 0.019-0.034) and post-concussive symptoms (MD bab = 0.028-0.040, AD bab = 0.032-0.047). Findings suggest that WM alterations are more strongly associated with CM itself than with either PTSD and/or mTBI. Mediating effects in regions critical for sensory integration highlight the role of WM microstructure as a neurobiological pathway through which CM might predispose to post-traumatic symptoms.

papers.title: Sex differences in responses to neurosteroid therapy after preterm birth.
papers.authors: Hirst JJ, Palliser HK, Glover R, Pavy CL, Shaw JC, Moloney RA.
papers.abstract: Progesterone production by the placenta leads to elevated levels of neurosteroids in both the maternal and fetal circulations during late gestation. Allopregnanolone levels are crucial because they provide both neuroprotective and trophic support in the fetal brain. These include protecting against excessive excitation and supporting oligodendrocyte development and myelination. Pregnancy compromises and particularly premature birth reduce or totally deprive the newborn brain of this neurosteroid mediated protection and support. The premature fall in allopregnanolone levels may increase susceptibility to damage from hypoxic episodes and excitotoxicity. Reduced neurosteroid support is also associated with alterations in oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination, which may contribute to subsequent neurodevelopmental and behavioural abnormalities. This in turn contributes to the onset of behavioural disorders including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Importantly male offspring have been shown to do more poorly after preterm birth as well as after other compromises. Increasing allopregnanolone action using the synthetic analogue, zuranolone, markedly improved myelination after premature delivery in an animal model. Treatment with the mitochondrial translocator protein (TSPO) ligand etifoxine, which promotes endogenous allopregnanolone production, provided protective effects in primary cell cultures following oxygen-glucose deprivation in vitro. Prematurely delivered male offspring showed markedly increased hyperactive behaviour which was also reversed by zuranolone therapy. Female offspring exhibited reduced myelination following preterm birth, without evidence of oligodendrocyte maturational arrest, and this hypomyelination was restored by zuranolone therapy. In contrast, males showed oligodendrocyte maturational arrest and a hyperactive behavioural phenotype. Together, these findings suggest that the effects of preterm birth on white matter development may differ between males and females. These findings support further investigation of allopregnanolone replacement therapy after preterm birth, including pharmacokinetic, safety, toxicology and efficacy studies in neonatal populations.

papers.title: Sex differences in functional connectivity in individuals with internet gaming disorder: a resting-state fMRI Study.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Xu X, Cui S, Dong GH.
papers.abstract: Objective Sex differences may help explain the heterogeneity of internet gaming disorder (IGD), but their neural basis remains unclear. This study examined sex-related alterations in functional connectivity (FC) in IGD. Methods 373 participants (85 males with IGD, 62 females with IGD, 141 male recreational game users [RGUs], and 85 female RGUs) underwent resting-state fMRI. The study used a 2 (group: IGD/RGU) × 2 (sex: male/female) between-subjects design. ReHo and FC were analyzed under this design with age as a covariate. ReHo interaction clusters served as seed ROIs for whole-brain FC analyses, followed by simple effect analyses for significant FC interactions. Results ReHo showed significant sex-by-group interactions in the bilateral postcentral gyrus, right middle cingulate cortex, and right fusiform gyrus. Seed-based FC showed significant interactions involving these regions. Simple effects indicated that, relative to same-sex RGUs, males with IGD predominantly showed lower FC, whereas females with IGD more often showed higher FC in connections involving perceptual processing, sensorimotor integration, behavioral regulation, self-related processing, and executive control. Conclusions IGD-related brain functional abnormalities may exhibit sex differences across multiple inter-regional FC patterns, providing new evidence for the sex-related heterogeneity in IGD. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings reflect associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Altered stimulus-intensity encoding occurs in the primary somatosensory cortex of a central post-stroke pain rat model.
papers.authors: Nagasaka K, Takashima I, Ogawa Y, Nagao A, Suzuki T, Bando D, Otsuru N, Onishi H, Higo N.
papers.abstract: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP) is a chronic form of pain that develops after ventral posterolateral thalamus (VPL) lesions and may involve maladaptive plasticity within central somatosensory pathways. Although abnormalities in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are observed in patients and animal models, the mechanism by which thalamic lesions alter cortical processing of sensory stimuli remains unclear. Here, we investigated stimulus intensity encoding and dendritic remodeling in S1 using a VPL-lesion CPSP rat model. Behavioral assessments were conducted, and mechanical allodynia was observed 3 weeks after lesion induction. Accordingly, the animals were examined during the early (1 week) and late (4-5 weeks) phases after VPL lesions. A distorted stimulus-response relationship was observed in S1 during the late phase, as indicated from voltage-sensitive dye imaging. The responses to low-intensity stimuli were enhanced, and response scaling at higher stimulus intensities was reduced. Increased cortical sensitivity to weak stimuli was associated with the severity of mechanical allodynia. Additionally, morphological analyses were conducted on layer II/III pyramidal neurons. Distinct patterns of dendritic remodeling were observed. Apical dendritic length and branching diminished during the early phase, while basal dendritic arborization increased during the late phase. These findings suggest that time-dependent structural and functional reorganization occurs in S1 following thalamic injury. This reorganization may contribute to abnormal sensory processing in patients with CPSP and offer new insights into the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms.

papers.title: Beyond the brain-centric view: A systems physiology framework for exercise-induced neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Wan C, Wang F, Fan Y, Yang Y, Wei J.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is regarded as a multifactorial disease that combines central pathological changes and peripheral organ dysfunction. Its core features include Aβ protein deposition, tau protein pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Exercise has been proven to be one of the most effective non-pharmacological intervention measures. However, its mechanism of action in AD has not been fully elucidated from the traditional brain-centered research perspective. Moreover, most existing studies focus on isolated organ systems or a single signaling pathway, failing to fully reflect the overall peripheral-cerebral physiological interaction mechanism required for neuroprotective effects of exercise. This article provides a structured narrative synthesis of current evidence regarding how exercise may influence AD-related pathological processes through multiple peripheral organ systems. It clarifies the communication mechanisms between these systems and the central nervous system through endocrine, immune, metabolic, neural, and vascular pathways. The study shows that exercise functions by coordinating the regulation of peripheral physiological functions, rather than relying on a single target mechanism. Exercise can regulate multiple signaling pathways such as muscle-brain, gut-brain, liver-brain, adipose-brain, bone-brain, and immune-brain, improving overall metabolic flexibility, inflammation regulation, vascular function, and neuroimmune homeostasis; these peripheral adaptive changes further act on the central nervous system, regulating blood-brain barrier(BBB) integrity, microglial cell activity, neuronal energy metabolism, neurovascular coupling, and synaptic plasticity. In summary, the neuroprotective effect induced by exercise stems from the integration of multiple systems' physiology, rather than isolated molecular signal transduction. This review synthesizes current evidence on exercise-induced peripheral-central interactions in AD from a systems physiology perspective, highlighting the significance of integrating peripheral biomarkers, multi-organ interactions, and central outcomes. It provides a theoretical framework for future personalized and mechanism-oriented exercise intervention studies.

papers.title: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Xu A, Wei Y, Liu E, Tong W, Lu A, Zhang F, Flatt P, Gault V, Irwin N, Hölscher C, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) class of drugs is on the market to treat diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 drugs have also shown neuroprotective effects in animal models and clinical trials in PD patients. Apelin (APJ) is an adipokine peptide hormone with neuroprotective actions in preclinical studies. Here, we test the effects of a rationally designed bifunctional peptide, namely ELA (exendin-4-linker-apelin), in the MPTP mouse model of PD. The single GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide was used as a comparator. Motor activity was improved by both drugs (open field, pole test, Rotarod), and the inflammation response was reduced (activation of microglia and astrocytes, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels). In addition, synapse numbers were improved in the striatum (Golgi strain, TEM), expression of synapse-associated proteins was enhanced, alongside reduced expression of genes that increase mitochondrial fission. Mitochondrial fusion gene expressions (Opa1, Mfn2, Drp1) and mitochondrial morphology were also normalized (TEM). ELA was superior to liraglutide in some, but not all, parameters measured. The results suggest that the rational design of bifunctional peptides targeting both GLP-1 and APJ pathways-with optimized pharmacokinetics and enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability-merits further investigation as a strategy for developing more effective treatments for PD.

papers.title: Targeting tau acetylation in Alzheimer's disease: Molecular mechanisms, pathological consequences, and therapeutic opportunities of dietary phytochemicals.
papers.authors: Basavaraju KC, Priyadarshini P.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by cognitive decline, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal loss. Emerging evidence identifies tau acetylation as a crucial post-translational modification that contribute significantly to tauopathies associated pathology in AD. Aberrant tau acetylation results in autophagy dysregulation, DNA damage, altered lipid metabolism, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and neuroinflammation ultimately leading to cognitive decline and neuronal death. Dysregulation of acetyltransferases such as p300/CBP and reduced deacetylase activity, including sirtuins, further promote pathological tau accumulation and propagation. Dietary phytochemicals have emerged as promising multi-targeted neuroprotective agents due to their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and epigenetic regulatory properties. Notably, studies investigating dietary phytochemicals that directly regulate tau acetylation remain very limited, making this an important and promising area for future research. Nevertheless, several dietary phytochemicals have been reported to modulate the activities of SIRT1 and EP300 across a range of experimental models and various disease conditions. Future investigations should focus on incorporating these dietary phytochemicals into experimental models of AD to elucidate their potential to modulate tau acetylation and associated pathogenic mechanisms. Such studies will provide critical insights into their therapeutic potential and may facilitate the development of novel phytochemical-based interventions for tau acetylation in AD. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms by which tau acetylation contributes to AD pathology and highlights therapeutic opportunities of dietary phytochemicals.

papers.title: The Gut-Brain Axis and Neurodegenerative Diseases: From Mechanistic Pathways to Therapeutic Interventions.
papers.authors: Lin W, Shu Z, Liu G, Fang J, Ding S.
papers.abstract: As the global population ages, the incidence of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) has increased. Neurodegenerative diseases have complex pathogenesis and currently lack fundamental treatment methods. The gut-brain axis (GBA) participates in the pathogenesis of NDDs through bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the central nervous system (CNS). This review systematically introduces the pathogenic characteristics of representative NDDs such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and multiple sclerosis (MS), as well as the association mechanisms between these diseases and GBA. The pathogenic characteristics of NDDs are closely related to changes in the composition of the gut microbiota and differences in gut microbiota metabolites (such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), neurotransmitters, tryptophan metabolites, etc.). These changes influence the CNS through multiple pathways, including neuroendocrine, vagus nerve, and immune regulation, ultimately contributing to the onset and progression of the diseases. Furthermore, we have collected and summarized preclinical and clinical evidence from recent years regarding therapeutic interventions based on the GBA mechanism, including probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Nevertheless, major knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding causality between gut microbiota changes and NDDs, the underlying molecular mechanisms, and the clinical efficacy of GBA-targeted therapies. This article aims to review the mechanisms of the interaction between the gut microbiota and the brain in neurodegenerative diseases, and based on the existing experimental evidence, provide theoretical basis and future development directions for future prevention and treatment strategies targeting GBA.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic and Interactome Analyses Prioritize Candidate Genes for Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.authors: Maglio GM, de Melo NC, de Carvalho LM.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by complex molecular alterations and diverse cognitive, behavioral, and neuropsychiatric manifestations. Although transcriptomic studies have identified several pathways associated with AD, the integration of molecular signatures with disease-related phenotype annotations and pathological aging remains incompletely understood. Therefore, this study aimed to integrate transcriptomic profiling, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, pathological aging assessment, and curated clinical phenotype annotations to prioritize candidate molecular signatures associated with AD. Differential expression analyses and network-based approaches were applied to publicly available transcriptomic datasets derived from distinct brain regions. Candidate genes and pathways were prioritized through interactome reconstruction, functional enrichment analyses, cluster-based analyses, and independent validation in an external dataset. In addition, transcriptomic signatures were integrated with curated clinical phenotype annotations using a knowledge-based gene overlap strategy. The analysis identified molecular signatures associated with neuroinflammatory signaling, synaptic dysfunction, endocytosis, and pathological aging. Pathways related to MAPK, PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, and TGF-β1 signaling emerged as candidate dysregulated pathways in AD. Comparative analyses of physiological aging and the AD aging comparison enabled the prioritization of candidate genes potentially more closely associated with the AD condition than with aging alone, including FOS and TAB2. Independent validation reinforced the reproducibility of several prioritized genes, including GFAP, CXCR4, CCL2, HSPA1A, FCGR2A, TLR2, CD44, TLR4, FOS, TAB2, CDC42, and SH3GL2. Integration with curated clinical phenotype annotations suggested partially overlapping molecular signatures across neuropsychiatric and cognitive phenotype annotations in AD. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of integrative bioinformatics approaches for prioritizing candidate genes, pathways, and molecular signatures associated with AD. This systems-level framework may contribute to future mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the molecular heterogeneity of AD and its associated phenotypic complexity.

papers.title: The Gut Microbiota-Epilepsy Axis: Bibliometric Trends, Mechanistic Insights, and Microbiota-Targeted Next-Generation Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.authors: Khan A, Ullah Z, Siraj M, Younas S, Wahab S, Waris A, Hong ST.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a complex neurological disorder with diverse underlying causes. Growing evidence suggests that gut dysbiosis may promote epileptogenesis by disrupting short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan-kynurenine metabolism, immune signaling, and neuronal excitability. In this review, we combine findings from human and animal studies to explain how gut dysbiosis may influence seizures through the gut-brain axis. We highlight emerging and less-discussed mechanisms, including vagus nerve signaling, microbial amyloids, bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs), the queuosine salvage pathway, and multi-kingdom microbiota interactions. We also summarize microbiota profiling studies and describe dysbiosis patterns linked to seizure. To support translation, we propose a peri-ictal multi-omics strategy for biomarker discovery. This includes standardized sampling and integration of metagenomics, metabolomics, and host transcriptomics. In addition, our bibliometric analysis further shows rapidly growing global interest in this topic. Recent studies increasingly focus on the gut-brain axis, ketogenic diet, and inflammation-driven mechanisms. Finally, we outline both established approaches and emerging next-generation microbiome-based therapeutic strategies, including SCFA-restoring synbiotics, engineered psychobiotics, bacteriophage therapy, and AI-guided personalization. These advances highlight the microbiota as modifiable target for adjunctive epilepsy management and provide a translational roadmap for future mechanistically informed research and clinical interventions.

papers.title: Characterizing hippocampal activation during pattern separation with multi-echo fMRI in cognitively normal older adults.
papers.authors: Solar KG, Kashyap S, Deom N, Uludağ K, Zotovic L, Lanctôt K, Black SE, McAndrews MP.
papers.abstract: Hippocampal hyperactivity, detected with mnemonic similarity task (MST) fMRI, is both a promising marker of risk and a probable driver of degeneration in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, implementation of such fMRI in interventional research is limited by long scan times and the absence of a framework for identifying prospective participants with hyperactivity who could be targeted with therapeutic approaches aimed at reducing this activity. We used multi-echo fMRI during the MST, an episodic memory task previously shown to engage hippocampal subfields CA3 and dentate gyrus (DG), to characterize activity profiles in 33 cognitively normal older adults. We compared MST-related CA3 and DG activation and behavioural performance across subsets of eight task runs. Behavioural and activation effects were equivalent for the first set of four runs (Runs-A) and the second set (Runs-B), suggesting that robust data can be obtained with four runs. Left and right CA3 + DG activation did not differ. We provide an exemplar framework for the derivation of a threshold for single-participant classification of elevated hippocampal activation as an indicator of AD risk in cognitively normal older individuals. Scalable (~22 min) multi-echo MST fMRI robustly captures hippocampal activation and provides a framework for individual-level characterization of hippocampal function in cognitively normal older adults. This enables individualized detection of elevated hippocampal activation as a modifiable risk factor and may guide enrolment into prevention trials targeting preclinical AD.

papers.title: Olive leaf-derived exosome-like vesicles attenuate neurotoxicity in an in vitro rotenone model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Sahsahi A, Degirmenci NS, Aydın M, Şahin F, Işık S.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease primarily characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Despite extensive research, current therapeutic options remain limited to symptomatic management, underscoring the need for neuroprotective strategies targeting disease pathology. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective potential of exosome-like vesicles derived from olive (Olea europaea) leaves (Ole-ELVs) in an in vitro PD model induced by rotenone in SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells. To evaluate the protective impact of olive leaf-derived ELVs, oxidative stress, cell viability, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation were assessed by measuring reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential staining, and Thioflavin S staining for α-synuclein aggregation. Our findings indicate that treatment with Ole-ELVs significantly attenuated rotenone-induced ROS production, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced protein aggregation. Collectively, these results suggest that Ole-ELVs exert neuroprotective effects through antioxidative, protection against cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial-stabilizing mechanisms, offering a promising natural nanoscale therapeutic candidate for PD.

papers.title: EEG Microstates are Not Associated with Psychotic Symptoms, Neurocognitive Domains or Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults with Clinical High Risk for Psychosis.
papers.authors: Liebrand M, Wedekind C, Katsarakis A, Diezig S, Michel C, Schultze-Lutter F, Kaess M, Hubl D, Koenig T, Kindler J.
papers.abstract: EEG microstates are brief and discrete topographic patterns of electrical brain activity. Microstates last for 60-120 milliseconds, are thought to represent transient, quasi-stable neural networks, and traditionally four distinct classes (A-D) are distinguished. One of the core concepts of present neuroscience is that neuroimaging is able to capture meaningful networks of brain activity, which can be translated into specific cognitive functions. Following this idea, each microstate might correspond to specific core brain functions. Importantly, these cognitive functions are impaired in mental disorders. Clinical high-risk (CHR) refers to a state associated with an increased risk of developing psychosis. Previous research has demonstrated consistent microstate alterations in CHR individuals (especially in class D), as well as in psychosis. However, the neurobiological and functional meaning of microstate alterations in CHR populations is still elusive. Since the CHR state is associated with reduced neurocognition (e.g., processing speed, verbal memory, executive functions) in combination with specific clinical symptoms and impairments in psychosocial functioning, relationships between resting-state microstates and these domains were examined in a large cross-sectional cohort of CHR individuals (n = 100). Contrary to our expectations, no significant correlations were found for these clinical measures. The finding suggests that while microstate parameters may differ between CHR individuals and controls, these alterations do not seem to directly reflect the neurobiology of clinical symptoms or neurocognitive and psychosocial functions. EEG microstate deviations as candidate trait biomarker therefore require further investigation and validation in longitudinal studies to establish their stability and predictive value.

papers.title: Cerebellar Network Organization in Parkinson's Disease: Functional Connectivity across Motor and Cognitive Circuits.
papers.authors: Lin CR, Magalhães TNC, Yonce SS, Rampalli I, Mahabir R, Bernard JA, and the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Background The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to cognitive reserve and network organization in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, the relationship of cerebello-cortical and cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity with cognitive status and nigrostriatal integrity remains incompletely understood. Methods Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 172 participants with PD in the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative were analyzed. Cerebello-basal ganglia and cerebello-cortical connectivity were investigated using region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel approaches. Cerebellar connectivity was examined in relation to cognitive status, age, disease duration, motor severity, dopaminergic medication exposure, and contralateral putaminal striatal binding ratio (SBR). Results PD participants demonstrated robust positive cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity, particularly between lobule VI/vermis VI and the pallidum. Greater age was associated with widespread reductions in cerebello-basal ganglia coupling. Longer disease duration was associated with stronger connectivity within cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits, and among cognitively unimpaired participants, stronger lobule V connectivity with temporal regions. After adjustment for contralateral putaminal SBR, cognitively unimpaired participants generally demonstrated greater connectivity between left cerebellar regions and frontal networks, whereas cognitively impaired participants showed greater connectivity from posterior cerebellar and vermal regions, including regions implicated in cognitive processing, to temporal, parahippocampal, occipital, parietal, and somatosensory regions. Conclusions Cerebellar functional connectivity in PD shows region-specific differences across cognitive status rather than uniform network loss with cognitive impairment. These findings support further investigation of cerebellar functional connectivity as a candidate biomarker of cognitive resilience and network adaptation in PD. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

papers.title: Cerebral Hemodynamic Changes in Older Adults With Cognitive Complaints According to the Presence of Peripheral Artery Disease.
papers.authors: Noh S, Shin HE, Shim Y.
papers.abstract: Objective As a systemic expression of atherosclerosis, peripheral artery disease (PAD) has the potential to alter cerebral hemodynamics in elderly individuals presenting with cognitive concerns. However, how PAD status shapes the longitudinal trajectory of cerebral hemodynamics has not been well characterized. Methods We conducted a single-center longitudinal observational study enrolling 132 participants (21 controls, 39 mild cognitive impairment, 72 mild Alzheimer's disease). All participants underwent transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasonography, ankle-brachial index (ABI) measurement, brain MRI, and cognitive assessments at baseline and follow-up (~13.45 months). PAD was defined as ABI < 0.90. Bilateral mean flow velocity (MFV), pulsatility index (PI), and resistance index (RI) of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) were tracked longitudinally across both time points. Results PAD was identified in 13 participants (9.8%). Baseline TCD parameters, vascular risk factors, white matter lesions on brain MRI, and cognitive measures were comparable between groups. At follow-up, the PAD group showed significantly higher MCA MFV after age adjustment (left p < 0.001; right p = 0.005). MFV increased in the PAD group (left +16.45 cm/s) but decreased in the non-PAD group (left -3.37 cm/s), with a significant between-group difference. PI and RI did not change in either group. Cognitive and functional outcomes were similar across groups throughout the study. Conclusion These findings identify PAD as a condition associated with progressive MCA MFV elevation in the context of preserved cognition, implying that subclinical cerebrovascular changes are detectable by TCD before overt clinical worsening. Future research involving larger cohorts and extended follow-up is required to determine whether such hemodynamic changes forecast eventual cognitive deterioration.

papers.title: Microstructural heterogeneity of white-matter aging and its age-dependent coupling to cognition
papers.authors: Chin R, Hu X, Ranieri J, Kim J, Oh H.
papers.abstract: Brain white matter (WM) microstructure undergoes extensive changes with age, yet the regional and cellular heterogeneity of age-related WM alterations and their impact on cognition remain unclear. Leveraging Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging (NODDI), an advanced microstructural modelling to capture specific WM cellular properties, we investigated age-dependent relationships between advanced microstructural markers and cognitive performance, indexed by six cognitive domains derived from principal component analysis. Using a suite of standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and NODDI techniques in eighty-six cognitively normal adults (Young: n=33, Older: n=53), we show that age group differences are widespread across whole brain white matter, with converging region-based and voxel-level evidence implicating commissural, association, and limbic pathways. Older adults exhibited significant and widespread reductions in global fractional anisotropy (FA) and neurite density index (NDI), concomitant with increases in mean diffusivity (MD), orientation density index (ODI), and free water fraction (FWF). Critically, age moderated WM-cognition associations in a domain- and tract-specific manner: younger adults exhibited stronger coupling between commissural and association tract microstructure and language and visual memory, whereas older adults showed greater dependence on projection and limbic tracts for executive and language function. The observed age-dependent coupling between specific microstructural metrics and cognition underscores the value of advanced diffusion models for capturing heterogeneity in brain aging, reveals age-specific biomarkers of cognitive health. These patterns align with phylogenetic and ontogenetic patterns of white matter vulnerability in callosal, long-range association, and limbic pathways, and suggest cellular specificity in white matter changes associated with cognitive decline. Significance Statement Aging affects brain white matter in complex and regionally specific ways, yet the biological bases of these changes and their relevance to cognition remain challenging to disentangle. Using multi-parameter diffusion MRI modeling, we found that age-related decline follows organized spatial patterns, with the greatest vulnerability in long-range association, callosal, and limbic pathways. These regional effects arise from distinct microstructural processes, including widespread extracellular alterations and more localized changes in neurite density and fiber organization. The strength and direction of white matter–cognition relationships differ between younger and older adults, revealing age-dependent shifts in how brain structural connections support behavior. Together, these findings identify biologically meaningful dimensions of white-matter vulnerability that may explain individual differences in cognitive aging.

papers.title: A Blood-Based Synaptic Biomarker in Neuronally-Enriched Extracellular Vesicles Predicts Disability Progression in Progressive Multiple Sclerosis
papers.authors: Jank L, Kumar MK, Joshi D, Minney V, Eskinder R, Thapa R, Heller JG, Filippatou AG, Siavoshi F, Smith MD, Harp C, Abioye I, Sotirchos ES, Dewey BE, Saidha S, Fitzgerald KC, Calabresi PA, Mowry EM, Bhargava P.
papers.abstract: Progressive multiple sclerosis (PMS) lacks blood-based biomarkers of the neurodegenerative processes driving disability. We measured synaptopodin, a postsynaptic protein, in neuronal-enriched extracellular vesicles (NEVs) across two independent cohorts: the SPRINT-MS trial (n=184) and a real-world validation cohort (n=268). A one SD increase in baseline synaptopodin was associated with ∼32% lower risk of confirmed disability progression in PMS (p=0.011), with the strongest effect in secondary PMS (SPMS) (∼57% lower odds, p=0.019). This SPMS association was replicated in the validation cohort (∼60% lower odds, p=0.009). Higher baseline synaptopodin was associated with future slower whole-brain atrophy and preserved microstructural integrity across MRI metrics (p=0.007-0.013). Longitudinal changes in NEV synaptopodin were associated with disability worsening (p=0.007) and paralleled MRI microstructural changes. NEV synaptopodin, but not NfL, was associated with confirmed disability progression in PMS participants with both biomarkers measured (HR 0.71 vs 1.12, p=0.007 vs 0.22 for NEV synaptopodin and NfL, respectively) and SPMS (HR 0.58 vs 1.10, p=0.003 vs 0.50). Adding synaptopodin, but not NfL, to a base model improved discrimination for disability progression in SPMS in both cohorts (e.g. validation AUC 0.755 to 0.838, p=0.005). These findings identify NEV synaptopodin as a prognostic and longitudinal, blood biomarker of synaptic integrity in PMS, particularly SPMS, complementing NfL.

papers.title: A deep learning-generated hASIC1a miniprotein inhibitor confers neuroprotection in stroke
papers.authors: Sörmann J, Epitropaki K, Vicino MF, Fjorbak CL, Pugh CF, Lang B, Beyer EK, Comaposada-Baró R, Hink F, Friis S, Usher S, Cai C, Autzen HE, Rogers JM, Pless SA.
papers.abstract: Ion channels remain notoriously recalcitrant drug targets despite their extensive pathophysiological significance. Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that cause neuronal death when excessively activated, such as during ischaemic stroke. This acidosis-driven injury pathway remains unchallenged by existing therapeutics. Here we generate two de novo designed hASIC1a-specific miniproteins by developing a platform that integrates computational miniprotein design, high-throughput automated patch clamp screening, biophysical and structural characterisation, and in vivo validation. We identify a subtype-selective hASIC1a inhibitor, Denasin1, which achieves near-complete inhibition with nanomolar potency. Denasin1 is disordered in solution but adopts the computationally predicted helix-turn-helix fold when bound to the extracellular acidic pocket of hASIC1a. Crucially, Denasin1 reduces infarct volume by > 50% in a murine model of ischaemic stroke. We thereby establish our de novo design platform as a route to develop potent and selective ion channel modulators.

papers.title: Multi-Dimensional Feature Adaptive Gating Network for Multi-View and Whole-Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification.
papers.authors: Zhou Y, Zhu L, Liu Z, Zhang Q, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder associated with structural brain alterations detectable by structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI). Accurate classification of normal control (NC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD remains challenging because disease-related changes are subtle, spatially distributed across multiple brain regions, and difficult to interpret in a biologically meaningful manner. Existing deep learning methods often rely on either whole-brain volumetric features or two-dimensional slice-level representations, which may limit the integration of complementary structural information and reduce model interpretability. This study presents a reproducible and explainable deep learning framework, termed the multidimensional feature adaptive gating network (MDFAG-Net), for sMRI-based AD classification and neuroimaging analysis. The framework integrates multidimensional structural MRI representations by combining 2D slice-level features extracted from sagittal, coronal, and axial views using a Vision Transformer backbone with global whole-brain features extracted using a three-dimensional convolutional neural network. An Enhanced Sparse Multiple Instance Learning module is employed to identify informative slices and suppress redundant information in long slice sequences, while an adaptive gating module dynamically fuses multiview and whole-brain features according to sample-specific feature contributions. The framework was evaluated on 842 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset for NC/MCI/AD classification. MDFAG-Net demonstrated competitive classification performance and outperformed representative two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and multibranch comparison models under the same experimental setting. The model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.798. Furthermore, Grad-CAM and DeepSHAP analyses revealed anatomically relevant regions associated with AD progression, including the hippocampus, amygdala, posterior cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and ventricular system.

papers.title: How auditory rhythm perception shapes speech production: The influence of neural synchronization and rhythmic patterns.
papers.authors: Tan C, Yan Q, Zhang Q.
papers.abstract: Auditory rhythm perception facilitates language processing, yet it remains unclear how neural synchronization to external rhythms contributes to speech production. The present study examined whether individual differences in neural synchronization modulate rhythmic priming effects during speech production and whether such effects depend on the rhythmic structure of the target utterance. Eighty-six native Mandarin speakers performed a speech production task involving two four-syllable rhythmic patterns as targets: the dominant [2+2] pattern (boundary after the second syllable) and the less common [1+3] pattern (boundary after the first syllable). Each target was preceded by a rhythmically congruent or incongruent pure-tone prime. Neural synchronization to the primes was quantified using cerebral-acoustic coherence (CACoh) between EEG activity and the temporal envelope of the auditory rhythms, and rhythmic priming was assessed using response latencies. K-means clustering of CACoh measures identified two participant groups characterized by relatively high and low levels of neural synchronization. Behavioral analyses revealed a significant Group × Target Type interaction. For the less common [1+3] pattern, low synchronizers exhibited reliable rhythmic priming, whereas high synchronizers showed little or no priming benefit. In contrast, priming effects for the dominant [2+2] pattern were modest and comparable across groups. Furthermore, higher theta-band CACoh was associated with smaller priming effects for [1+3] targets, indicating that stronger neural synchronization predicted reduced behavioral facilitation. These findings suggest that the influence of auditory rhythm on speech production depends jointly on individual neural synchronization capacity and the rhythmic structure of the planned utterance. The results provide new evidence that auditory-motor interactions in speech production are shaped by both listener-specific and utterance-specific factors.

papers.title: Brain network changes in patients with glioma-related epilepsy after frontal resection.
papers.authors: Fang S, Wang J, Zhang Z, Li Y, Sun Z, Zhou C, Wang Y, Fan X, Jiang T.
papers.abstract: Objective Clinical factors such as IDH status, preoperative seizures, and frontal tumor location influence the prognosis of postoperative glioma-related epilepsy (GRE), but the underlying network-level mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to identify network-based predictors of postoperative GRE. Methods The authors retrospectively analyzed 109 patients with frontal glioma (76 left sided). All patients underwent preoperative and 1-week postoperative resting-state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging. Changes in network characteristics, including structural-functional coupling and functional connectivity (FC), were evaluated. Using the left-sided cohort as the training set, Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was applied to identify network-based risk factors for postoperative GRE and construct a predictive model. The right-sided cohort served as a validation set. Results Patients with postoperative GRE showed reduced structural-functional coupling between the dorsal attention network (DAN) and the frontoparietal network (FPN), along with decreased FC within and between these networks. Increased DAN-FPN coupling and higher FC between the lesional-hemisphere prefrontal thalamus and the whole brain were protective against postoperative GRE. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.785 in the training cohort and 0.922 in the validation cohort (both p < 0.0001). Conclusions Altered structural-functional coupling and FC between attention-related networks are associated with postoperative GRE in frontal glioma. Enhanced DAN-FPN coupling and thalamocortical connectivity may serve as protective network markers.

papers.title: MBB-AVR: a mind-brain-body dataset with dynamic affective states in immersive virtual reality
papers.authors: Fourcade A, Ciston AB, Roellecke L, de Mooij J, Leos H, Villringer A, Carletto S, Malandrone F, Gaebler M.
papers.abstract: We present MindBrainBody-AffectiveVR (MBB-AVR), a multimodal dataset capturing continuous affective experience and both central and peripheral physiological responses during naturalistic emotional stimulation in immersive virtual reality. Forty-seven healthy adults (24 female, 22 male, 1 non-binary; age = 27.1 ± 5.4) viewed a 23-minute stereoscopic 360° video sequence, composed of computer-generated, language-free content designed to elicit high affective variability over time, presented via a head-mounted display (HTC Vive Pro Eye). While immersed, participants continuously rated their momentary valence and arousal using a previously validated rating tool with real-time visual feedback. Synchronized recordings include 64-channel EEG, ECG, respiration, photoplethysmography, galvanic skin response, and head and eye tracking with pupillometry. Participants additionally completed questionnaires including interoceptive sensibility and alexithymia. The dataset is organized following the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) and includes extracted low-level audio and video features of the stimulus. It may support research on the temporal dynamics of affect, multimodal physiological correlates of emotion, and affective computing. The dataset is available at https://gin.g-node.org/fourcade_a/mbb-avr.

papers.title: Mapping the Representational Basis of Object-Based Guidance: How Colour Availability Shapes Contributions Across the Hierarchy
papers.authors: Massironi A, Bricolo E, Petilli MA.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that colour is one of the most robust attributes guiding attention during visual search and can dominate guidance, with its removal prompting substantial reweighting toward alternative features. However, naturalistic object search differs in several respects from the simplified displays and controlled designs typically used to investigate the role of colour: observers often do not know exactly how the target will appear, and even when its colour is preserved, many candidate objects may share that colour, reducing its diagnostic value and increasing the relevance of information that generalises across variations in appearance. Does colour retain the same importance under these more naturalistic conditions, and how does the relative contribution of other guiding information change when colour is unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational approach to characterising the representational basis of object-based guidance in natural scenes across multiple representational levels and examine how this profile depends on colour availability. Using eye-movement data from the Potsdam Eye-Movement Corpus, we related fixation-by-fixation object selection to cue-object similarity across multiple computational representational spaces, including layer-specific image representations from a deep convolutional neural network, category-level visual prototypes derived within the Vision Spaces framework, and distributional semantic representations derived from linguistic and scene-based spatial statistics. Image-based, category-level visual, and semantic information made complementary contributions to object selection in both colour and grayscale scenes, while cue-object colour similarity explained only part of this broader representational profile. Critically, removing colour altered the strength of some image-based associations but left the broader pattern of multilevel representational contributions largely preserved. These findings suggest that, in more naturalistic search scenarios, object-based guidance draws on target-relevant evidence across multiple representational formats and levels, with colour accounting for only a limited part of the information supporting guidance. At the methodological level, the computational framework introduced here allows us to characterise the representational basis of object-based guidance across perceptual and semantic levels and to track how the contributions of these representations vary across experimental conditions.

papers.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
papers.authors: Mwilambwe-Tshilobo L, Tsoi L, Speer S, Zada Z, Burns SM, Falk EB, Tamir D.
papers.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.

papers.title: Increasing cerebellar beta rhythms shifts cerebral oscillatory signatures of context-driven language processing
papers.authors: Ambichler S, Portier T, Piai V, Klaus J.
papers.abstract: While there is growing consensus that the cerebellum is part of the cerebrally centred network underlying language processing, the direct nature of its contribution to comprehension and production remains unknown. In particular, while both processes require lexical access, production additionally involves motor processes linked to articulatory planning, which has fuelled the view that the cerebellum is primarily involved in motor control in language production. Cortically, both lexical access and articulatory planning are known to be driven by alpha-beta power decreases. To disentangle cerebellar involvement in language, this study investigated the modulatory effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the right cerebellum on context-driven language comprehension and production. In a cross-over, double-blind, sham-controlled within-participants design, 32 healthy volunteers received 20 minutes of 20-Hz tACS (2 mA peak-to-peak) targeting the right posterior cerebellum. Immediately afterwards, they performed a context-driven language task while EEG was recorded from 32 channels. In the task, visually presented lead-in sentences creating a constraining or unconstraining context were followed by a picture depicting the final word of the sentence. Participants were instructed to name the picture (production) or judge its animacy (comprehension). Responses became slower overall following active compared to sham tACS, and this increase was more pronounced in the comprehension task. In line with previous work, reliable context-related oscillatory power decreases were observed in response to the context manipulation, but exhibited a different pattern across tasks and stimulation conditions. For production, beta-centred power decreases following sham shifted to temporally and spatially extended alpha power decreases following active tACS. By contrast, alpha-centred power decreases following sham tACS in the comprehension task increased following active tACS. Increasing beta activity in the right posterior cerebellum thus affected early stages of context-driven language processing linked to lexical access in both language domains. The stimulation-induced spectral, spatial and temporal shifts suggest recruitment of alternative cortical resources as a consequence of cerebellar network modulation. This interpretation is consistent with the cerebellum functioning as a network node coordinating temporal dynamics across distributed language regions.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Beat Processing in Infancy and Their Association With Later Grammar Development: Evidence for the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis
papers.authors: Ladanyi E, Nayak S, Bush CT, Wang Y, Woynaroski TG, Lense MD, Leonard MK, Gordon RL.
papers.abstract: Infants show evidence of beat processing from birth, but its neural correlates in infancy remain poorly understood. Moreover, although rhythm and grammar abilities are closely linked in older (school-aged) children, it is not known whether individual differences in infant beat processing lay the foundations for those associations. This longitudinal EEG study examined neural correlates of beat processing in 6–12-month-old infants (N=37) and their relation to sentence comprehension skills in the same children at 4 years. We analyzed infants’ evoked time–frequency responses to rhythmic tone–tone–rest sequences presented in physically accented conditions and in inferred-beat conditions, in which accents were removed after an initial exposure phase.. Analyses revealed a significant increase in power to physically accented beats (9–24 Hz, p < .001). Individual differences in this response were positively associated with receptive grammar performance at age 4, assessed with the TROG-2 (r = .48, p = .005), and remained significant after controlling for infant age, parent education, and home music environment (β = .45, p = .011). The inferred beat effect was not related to later sentence comprehension performance. These findings indicate that infant neural activity tracks beat structure, with neural correlates broadly similar to those reported in adults, and that early neural sensitivity to beat is associated with later grammar development, supporting the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis.

papers.title: Tetrachloro-1,4-benzoquinone Exerts Neurotoxicity through Neuroinflammation and the TLR4 Signaling Pathway, which is a Risk Factor for Alzheimer's Disease: An Integrated Network and Mendelian Randomization Analysis.
papers.authors: Li M, Lv S, Cui L, Fang S.
papers.abstract: Introduction Research has found that the disinfection byproduct Tetrachloro-1,4- Benzoquinone (TCBQ) in drinking water increases the risk of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). However, the mechanism by which TCBQ increases the risk of AD remains unclear. Methods This study employs a comprehensive approach that includes network toxicology (PPI network, hub genes, KEGG analysis), Mendelian randomization, computational simulations (molecular docking and dynamics), and cellular experiments to systematically elucidate the neurotoxic mechanisms of TCBQ. Results Key findings indicate that TCBQ induces neurotoxicity by activating the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway, AD, and the apoptosis pathway. All ligand-receptor docking energies are recorded at ≤ -1.8 kcal/mol, suggesting that TCBQ demonstrates a stable interaction with the targets. Molecular simulations confirm that TCBQ tightly binds to targets such as Caspase3 and TLR4. Mendelian randomization found that XDH, FABP3, IMPDH1, ACBD7, and CASP3 are common targets and play a potential role in AD. Immunofluorescence experiments revealed that APP expression increased after TCBQ treatment. Cellular experiments verified that TCBQ significantly upregulates the expression of inflammation- and apoptosis-related proteins, including IL-1B, MyD88, NFκB, TLR4, Cleaved-Caspase3, and Cyt C, leading to neuronal cell death. Notably, the TLR4 inhibitor effectively reversed the expression of these proteins and alleviated cell death. Discussion The discussion indicates that TCBQ induces neurotoxicity by activating the TLR4 pathway and apoptotic signals, and Caspase3 is a potential co-target. TLR4 inhibitors can reverse protein alterations and cell death, suggesting that intervention in this pathway may alleviate TCBQrelated nerve damage. Conclusion Our research provides a theoretical basis for the clinical assessment of potential neurotoxicity risks in populations exposed to TCBQ.

papers.title: Advances in the Antidepressant Effects of Electroacupuncture Through Regulation of Microglia-Mediated BDNF Signaling and Hippocampal Neurogenesis.
papers.authors: Liu H, Wang J, Yang Q, Zhang Z, Peng Z, Lei X, Zhao Y, Zhao D, Gu J.
papers.abstract: Objective To summarize the regulatory network linking microglia, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signaling, and hippocampal neurogenesis, and to clarify the potential antidepressant mechanisms of electroacupuncture. Methods We systematically reviewed and integrated recent findings from preclinical and clinical studies regarding microglial activation, BDNF/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling, hippocampal neurogenesis, and electroacupuncture intervention in depressive disorders, retrieved from PubMed, Web of Science, and CNKI databases up to June 2026. Results Depression is closely associated with neuroinflammation, impaired neuroplasticity, and disrupted hippocampal neurogenesis. Aberrant microglial activation may inhibit hippocampal neurogenesis by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines, excessively engulfing synapses, and disturbing the neural microenvironment. These pathological changes interact with dysregulated BDNF/TrkB signaling and jointly contribute to depressive phenotypes. Electroacupuncture may exert antidepressant effects by modulating microglial phenotypic transformation, suppressing pro-inflammatory mediator release, and upregulating BDNF/TrkB signaling and its downstream pathways. Conclusion Electroacupuncture may improve depression through coordinated regulation of microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and BDNF-related neuroplasticity. This mechanism provides a scientific basis for further mechanistic research and clinical application of acupuncture in depression.

papers.title: MTHFR*677C>T produces distinct prodromal disease signatures in a mouse model of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease
papers.authors: Kotredes KP, Pandey RS, Reagan AM, Sarica Z, O'Rourke R, Herrick S, Davis A, Garceau D, Sasner M, Carter GW, Howell GR.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD) comprises more than 95% of all AD cases. Transgenic, overexpression animal models have off-target side effects, do not effectively produce the heterogeneity observed clinically in LOAD patients, and are therefore not best suited for preclinical therapeutic development. The Model Organism Development and Evaluation for Late-onset Alzheimer’s Disease (MODEL-AD) Consortium was established to develop novel mouse strains to model human-relevant genetic and environmental risk factors for LOAD. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) is an enzyme in the folate/methionine pathway. Variants in the MTHFR gene, notably 677C > T , are associated with ADRD, and we have previously shown the Mthfr 677C>T mouse model phenocopies humans carrying the variant and develops cerebrovascular deficits. Methods To examine the contributions of Mthfr 677C>T in the context of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD), MODEL-AD created a novel mouse strain on the C57BL/6J (B6) background that was homozygous for Mthfr 677C>T , in combination with humanized Aβ , APOEe4 , and Trem2*R47H ( referred to as LOAD2.Mthfr 677C>T ) . Mice were assessed over multiple ages for disease-relevant phenotypes. Regular behavior measurements and biometric samples were collected longitudinally to 24 months of age. Blood and brain tissue were collected for transcriptomics, proteomics, human disease correlation, and neuropathology. Results Despite lacking hallmark pathologies such as amyloid deposition and significant neuroinflammation, compared to LOAD2 controls, LOAD2.Mthfr 677C>T mice showed transcriptional and proteomic signatures in the brain that relate to the cerebrovasculature, myelination, and synaptic biology, similar to those seen in human LOAD patients. Conclusions These data further support the use of the LOAD2.Mthfr 677C>T mouse model to study aspects of ADRD such as cerebrovascular compromise.

papers.title: α-Synuclein pathology induces conserved lipid acyl-chain remodeling across mouse brain and human dopaminergic neurons
papers.authors: Dinter E, Szegö ÉM, Luksch H, Höfs L, Falkenburger BH.
papers.abstract: Abstract Membrane lipid composition regulates diverse cellular functions and directly affects alpha-synuclein binding and aggregation, a major hallmark of Parkinson’s disease. Here we used shotgun lipidomics to investigate changes in mouse midbrain and in human dopaminergic neurons after induction of alpha-synuclein (aSyn) pathology, a major hallmark of Parkinson’s disease. In mouse midbrain, aSyn pathology was induced by stereotactic injection of recombinant adeno-associated vectors. Human dopaminergic neurons were generated from LUHMES cells; lipidomic analysis were conducted during differentiation and 7 days after lentiviral transduction with aSyn. Samples were analyzed by shotgun lipidomics. In mouse midbrain, aSyn pathology altered multiple lipid classes, including increased triacylglycerol, ceramide and sphingomyelin and decreased phospholipids. More strikingly, aSyn pathology induced coordinated remodeling of acyl-chain composition, characterized by shorter and more saturated acyl chains across multiple lipid classes, whereas phosphatidylinositol showed a distinct response. This acyl-chain remodeling was partially conserved in human dopaminergic neurons expressing aSyn. In mouse midbrain, aSyn-associated lipid changes were largely reversed by intermittent fasting, an intervention previously shown to reduce aSyn pathology in this model, whereas constitutive STING activation did not reproduce the acyl-chain phenotype. Together, these findings identify coordinated lipid acyl-chain remodeling as a conserved and reversible response associated with α-syn pathology and implicate altered lipid synthesis and remodeling as potential underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Ginsenoside Rg1 attenuates hippocampal damage and improves ASD-like behaviors in a VPA-induced rat model by modulating SIRT1 expression
papers.authors: Chen M, Lv x, Du M, Guo L, Zhou X, Cheng S, Liu H, Duan C, Song F.
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective: To evaluate the effects of different doses of ginsenoside Rg1 on the structural development of hippocampal neurons in rats and explore its potential underlying mechanisms. Methods: Rats exhibiting ASD-like behaviors were induced by a single intraperitoneal injection of valproic acid (VPA, 600 mg/kg, 250 g/L) on day 12.5 of gestation in pregnant Wistar rats. The following experimental groups were utilized: saline group (NS group, n=3), autism spectrum disorder group (ASDgroup, n=3), high-dose ginsenoside Rg1 group (Rg1-H group, n=3), and low-dose ginsenoside Rg1 group (Rg1-L group, n=3). The rats in the Rg1-H and Rg1-L groups received daily intraperitoneal injections of ginsenoside Rg1 from Postnatal Day 21 (PND 21) to PND 35 (Rg1-H: 40 mg/kg; Rg1-L: 20 mg/kg). The rats in the NS and VPA groups received the same volume of saline (1 mL/kg) during the same period. Behavioral tests were conducted on day 35 to assess ASD-like behaviors, and hippocampal tissues were extracted for the detection of neuronal apoptosis, autophagy, and inflammatory biomarkers. Results: Ginsenoside Rg1 normalized the levels of inflammatory response, apoptosis, and autophagy biomarkers in the hippocampus by downregulating SIRT1 expression, thereby improving social communication deficits and repetitive stereotyped behaviors. Conclusions: This study demonstrated that ginsenoside Rg1 can ameliorate atypical behaviors in rats exhibiting ASD-like behaviors by ameliorating pathological morphology of the hippocampal, thereby suggesting its potential as a promising therapeutic agent for ASD.

papers.title: A temporal transcriptomic framework resolves age-specific polygenic vulnerability and prioritizes therapeutic targets for brain disorders
papers.authors: Xue C, Yu X, Ye L, Luo Y, Zhang L, Tang B, Gui H, Jiang L, Li M.
papers.abstract: Abstract Translating thousands of genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits into actionable clinical targets remains a major bottleneck in precision medicine. This difficulty partly stems from using static functional annotations that ignore the dynamic, age-dependent nature of human brain development. To address this, we developed a temporal-specific statistical framework (tDESE) that maps large-scale psychiatric polygenic signals onto continuous lifespan transcriptomic trajectories from the human prefrontal cortex. Applying this framework across five major brain disorders revealed a precise chronological alignment: polygenic risk loci consistently reach peak cortical expression exactly when typical clinical onset occurs. The underlying genetic architecture dictates a distinct spatial migration in synaptic vulnerability, shifting from pan-synaptic networks in childhood to strict postsynaptic dominance in adult-onset psychiatric conditions. We also identified sex-divergent molecular lags that closely mirror known epidemiological differences in onset rates. Importantly, anchoring post-GWAS functional annotation to these developmental timeframes substantially improves the predictive accuracy for recovering clinically established therapeutic targets. Expanding this approach to pharmacogenomics, we screened age-resolved gene profiles against in vitro drug perturbation signatures. The results isolated a concentrated 20-to-40-year therapeutic window where targets of standard psychiatric interventions are most actively expressed. This dynamic is powerfully exemplified by PDE4D , a schizophrenia risk gene showing adult-specific expression and profound downregulation by targeted interventions. Ultimately, this time-aware genomic framework provides a powerful, data-driven engine for unraveling disease etiology and optimizing post-GWAS target discovery pipelines.

papers.title: Autism: From Behavioral Syndrome to Systemic Biological Disorder—Communication I: Beyond Kanner’s Behavioral Diagnosis Toward a Biological Framework for Autism
papers.authors: Alibek K, Kravitz S.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is usually diagnosed by looking at behavioral and developmental traits. This approach helps identify the autistic profile, describe strengths and challenges, set clinical baselines, and monitor changes. Still, focusing only on behavior does not explain the biological reasons for how autistic features appear, change, or improve. Studies in genetics, neuroscience, immunology, microbiology, mitochondrial biology, and metabolomics show that autism involves many complex and interacting processes. These include immune and inflammatory regulation, gut health and the microbiome, mitochondrial and metabolic function, oxidative balance, neural signaling, and more. There is no single cause or set of abnormalities that applies to all autistic people. Similar behaviors can come from different biological factors, which may change as a person grows. Autism should be seen as a dynamic biological process, a behavioral syndrome, or a set of fixed biological factors that interact with changing physiological states, health, environment, and treatment. Diagnosis should combine behavioral and developmental information with ongoing, broad biological assessment, while avoiding the early use of unproven biomarkers in clinical care. This approach can help separate stable risk factors from those that can be changed, identify key patterns, and clarify how different biological systems relate to clinical symptoms. Future treatments should look beyond behavior and focus on proven, mechanism-based strategies tailored to each person’s biology as it changes over time. Considering biological mechanisms alongside observed traits may improve long-term assessment, biomarker validation, treatment, and precision medicine in autism.

papers.title: Estradiol-dependent memory and hippocampal spine remodeling require proteasomal protein degradation.
papers.authors: Beamish SB, Gross KS, Kuehn RK, Frank K, Valentine EP, Jarome TJ, Frick KM.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Although 17β-estradiol (E2 ) is a critical neuromodulator of hippocampus-dependent memory and synaptic plasticity, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Previous studies showed that E2 enhances dorsal hippocampus-dependent memory consolidation by activating signaling pathways that promote protein synthesis and dendritic spine formation. However, these studies largely overlooked the contribution of protein degradation mediated by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), despite extensive evidence implicating UPS activity in long-term memory and synaptic plasticity. Here, we combined temporally specific dorsal hippocampal infusions of the proteasome inhibitor β-lactone with three-dimensional spine morphometry to examine the role of UPS-mediated protein degradation in E2 -induced memory consolidation and CA1 spinogenesis. Immediate post-training bilateral infusion of β-lactone into the dorsal hippocampus of ovariectomized female mice blocked E2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and attenuated E2 -associated improvements in spatial memory. Arbor-wide Golgi-based analyses revealed robust E2 -induced increases in spine number across the apical dendritic tree and smaller parallel effects within the basal arbor. Segment-level analyses showed that E2 produced the greatest structural changes on tertiary apical dendritic segments, increasing total, mushroom, and thin spine density and enhancing multiple morphometric features, including mushroom spine surface area and head-to-neck ratio. Secondary basal dendritic segments exhibited smaller, more variable changes. Many E2 -associated structural effects were attenuated or abolished by β-lactone. Together, these findings provide the first evidence that proteasomal protein degradation contributes to estrogenic enhancement of hippocampus-dependent memory and CA1 dendritic spine remodeling, identifying UPS-mediated protein degradation as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating estrogenic memory consolidation and structural plasticity.Significance Statement 17β-estradiol (E2 ) rapidly enhances hippocampal memory consolidation and promotes CA1 dendritic spinogenesis, yet the molecular mechanisms that support these effects remain unclear. Here, we combine temporally specific dorsal hippocampal proteasome inhibition with three-dimensional Golgi-based spine analyses to show that proteasomal protein degradation is required for E2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and contributes to E2 -associated improvements in spatial memory in ovariectomized female mice. We further demonstrate that proteasome activity contributes to E2 -induced increases in apical CA1 spine density and morphology. These findings reveal new insights into estrogenic modulation of cognition that may provide novel protein targets whose levels could be regulated to reduce memory dysfunction related to menopause, depression, and other conditions for which women are at greater risk.

papers.title: Mitochondria Beyond Bioenergetics: Canonical and Non-Canonical Functions in Ischemic Stroke and Aging.
papers.authors: Berezka P, Piekarczyk N, Kaczor JJ.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, yet effective neuroprotective therapies beyond reperfusion strategies are still lacking. Emerging evidence highlights mitochondria as central regulators of neuronal fate, expanding their traditional role in cellular energy homeostasis through ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Together with calcium buffering and redox regulation, these represent canonical mitochondrial functions. Mitochondria also regulate cellular adaptation to stress through mitochondrial quality control (MQC), mitochondrial ferritin-dependent iron buffering, signaling mediated by mitochondrial metabolites and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and intercellular organelle transfer. These non-canonical functions link mitochondrial state to ferroptotic cell death, innate immune activation, and epigenetic regulation of nuclear responses. During cerebral ischemia, mitochondrial dysfunction involves impaired OXPHOS, the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), opening of the permeability transition pore, disruption of organelle dynamics, and dysregulation of non-canonical functions, collectively promoting neuronal injury, inflammation, and impaired recovery.
