A complementary, report-independent endpoint, the intermodulation response to two-frequency stimulation, is proposed. State-dependence is tested as the drug-by-rhythmicity interaction in a 2 × 3 factorial design (placebo or psilocybin × rhythmic SLS, arrhythmic control, or no stimulation), with the sign of any interaction evaluated on a pre-declared scale. An adequately precise negative interaction would count against the central state-dependence prediction for the tested conditions. The framework organizes five axes around this prediction: titration of experiential intensity at fixed dose, content shaping through frequency specificity, modulation of difficult-experience phenomenology, testing whether resting-state signatures depend on sensory context, and individual-difference profiling of SLS responsiveness. The framework makes no claim of therapeutic enhancement. Its aim is mechanistic and methodological.

papers.title: Temporal association between adjunctive repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and seizure reduction in a pediatric patient with DNM1L-associated EMPF1: a case report.
papers.authors: Chen X, Sun P, Ren X, Liu G, Bai X, Guo F, Guo R, Wu S, Wang H.
papers.abstract: Background Encephalopathy, lethal, due to defective mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission 1 (EMPF1) is a rare, severe mitochondrial disorder characterized by acute-onset refractory seizures that rapidly progress to status epilepticus and are associated with a poor prognosis. Conventional therapies, including antiepileptic drugs and the ketogenic diet, exhibit limited efficacy. Although repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has shown promise in other forms of drug-resistant epilepsy, its potential role in managing EMPF1 remains unexplored. Case presentation A 7-year-old boy, previously healthy with normal development, presented with right-hand clonic movements and impaired consciousness, which progressed to status epilepticus. Brain MRI revealed diffuse cytotoxic edema involving the bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, basal ganglia, and thalami. EEG recording showed generalized periodic spike-wave discharges with background slowing. Genetic testing identified a novel de novo DNM1L mutation (c.1949T > C, p.Leu650Pro), which was classified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG/AMP guidelines and provided strong support for the diagnosis of EMPF1. In addition to a regimen of antiepileptic drugs and a metabolic "cocktail," 1-Hz rTMS (90% of the resting motor threshold, 40 trains daily) was applied over the left primary motor cortex on Day 16. Following initiation of this combined therapy, seizure frequency was temporally associated with a marked reduction, decreasing from ∼20 to 5-6 episodes/day after one day, 2-3 by Day 27 (12 days after rTMS initiation), and 0-1 by Day 36 (21 days after rTMS initiation). Despite this reduction in clinical seizure burden, the patient developed progressive pneumonia leading to sepsis and acute heart failure, and died on Day 65 (hospital day 65). Conclusions In this case, adjunctive rTMS applied alongside standard antiepileptic and metabolic "cocktail" therapy was temporally associated with a pronounced reduction in seizure frequency in a patient with DNM1L-associated EMPF1. This temporal association is hypothesis-generating and does not permit attribution of the observed seizure reduction to rTMS; further investigation in larger cohorts is warranted.

papers.title: Nutritional intervention targeting muscle-brain axis in dementia continuum: from mechanisms to practice.
papers.authors: Topcuoglu MA, Guler A, Gulhan Halil M, Hanagasi H, Midi I, Saka B, Saka Topcuoglu E.
papers.abstract: Rapid aging of global population has led to an attention increasingly focusing on age-related changes in muscle and cognitive functions, specifically the interplay between sarcopenia, frailty and cognitive impairment as the interconnected geriatric syndromes with major health consequences. Despite being the central pathophysiological substrate across these geriatric syndromes, skeletal muscle loss is still insufficiently prioritized as a treatment objective. Incorporating the "malnutrition-sarcopenia-frailty" triad into dementia care is essential for continuity of management, as muscle preservation is fundamental to sustaining cognitive function within an active aging paradigm. This perspective reframes longevity by shifting emphasis from anticipating frailty to living with strength, valuing added years through resilience rather than decline. This narrative review, prepared by experts in neurology and geriatrics, explores the muscle-brain crosstalk and highlights skeletal muscle loss as a modifiable target for nutritional intervention in cognitive impairment and dementia. In conclusion, given the bidirectional links between malnutrition, sarcopenia, frailty, and cognitive decline through shared aging mechanisms, a high protein oral nutritional supplement [enriched with beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB)] and vitamin D emerges as a practical, compliant strategy to support muscle health and potentially contribute to preservation of cognitive health in older adults with or at risk of dementia, although direct evidence for cognitive benefit remains limited.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction and PANoptosis-related signaling in acute central nervous system injuries: mechanistic convergence and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.authors: Zhang H, Tu R, Zhang D, Tian H, Yin H.
papers.abstract: Acute central nervous system (CNS) injuries comprise a heterogeneous group of disorders caused by vascular or traumatic factors, including ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), traumatic brain injury (TBI), and spinal cord injury (SCI). These injuries initiate secondary cascades that combine metabolic failure, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Mitochondrial dysfunction is positioned near the center of these processes because impaired bioenergetics, excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), abnormal fission and fusion, defective mitophagy, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release can simultaneously disturb cellular homeostasis and activate inflammatory signaling. PANoptosis is an inflammatory form of regulated cell death that integrates pyroptotic, apoptotic, and necroptotic machinery through PANoptosome complexes. Emerging evidence suggests that mitochondrial stress can create conditions that favor PANoptotic convergence by increasing mtROS and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), activating DNA-sensing and inflammasome pathways, and sustaining receptor-interacting protein kinase and caspase signaling. This review examines the potential mechanistic links between mitochondrial dysfunction and PANoptosis-related signaling across ischemic stroke, ICH, SCI, and TBI. We summarize changes in mitochondrial bioenergetics, oxidative stress, dynamics, mitophagy, mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs), and mitochondrial transfer, and evaluate how these changes intersect with PANoptosis-related signaling. Importantly, we distinguish direct evidence of PANoptosis from studies that only demonstrate coordinated changes in individual death pathways. We also assess therapeutic strategies that target mitochondrial oxidative stress, dynamics, mitophagy, biogenesis, mitochondrial DAMP signaling, and mitochondrial transplantation and transfer. Current findings support mitochondria as a promising upstream intervention point, but complete causal evidence linking mitochondrial damage to defined PANoptosome assembly remains limited in acute CNS injury. Clarifying cell-specific and time-dependent mechanisms will be essential for translating this framework into effective neuroprotective strategies.

papers.title: Case Report: Right frontal periventricular heterotopia underlying secondary network epilepsy with a Lennox-Gastaut phenotype: multimodal SEEG, CCEP, and rs-fMRI evidence.
papers.authors: Wang C, Hong J, Ji J, Zhang C, Chen W, Xu J.
papers.abstract: Objective Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is generally regarded as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy involving distributed brain networks, although a focal structural abnormality may occasionally recruit bilateral cortical and thalamic circuits and produce an LGS phenotype. We characterized the spatiotemporal organization of such a network and its changes after focal SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC). Methods A 50-year-old woman with drug-resistant epilepsy, multiple seizure types, diffuse slow spike-and-wave discharges, generalized paroxysmal fast activity, intellectual impairment, and right frontal periventricular heterotopia (PVH) underwent stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG). Cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) were acquired before and after SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC). Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), obtained before and 3 months after RF-TC, was analyzed using three seeds: the entire right frontal PVH and the right and left centromedian thalamic nuclei (CM). Results SEEG identified the earliest sustained ictal activity within the sampled right frontal PVH-related medial contacts, accompanied by high-frequency activity. This was followed by ipsilateral lateral frontal recruitment, contralateral frontal synchronization, and subsequent bilateral CM involvement. Two-stage RF-TC of the onset and early-recruited networks was followed by seizure freedom through 9 months. After RF-TC, right-sided stimulation produced markedly attenuated lesion-related CCEP responses, whereas left-sided responses and responses between thalamic contacts showed little appreciable change. Descriptive rs-fMRI difference maps demonstrated decreased local frontal connectivity around the treated territory and increased long-range connectivity for the PVH seed; both CM seeds showed predominantly increased connectivity with distributed cortical and cerebellar regions. Conclusion In this patient, a focal PVH-related epileptogenic network was associated with secondary bilateral cortical and thalamic recruitment underlying an LGS phenotype. CCEP and rs-fMRI captured complementary aspects of postoperative network change: attenuation of stimulation-evoked propagation and postoperative changes in intrinsic functional connectivity, respectively.

papers.title: Complementary white matter networks support flexible concept learning.
papers.authors: Gumus M, Alizadeh Saghati N, Mack ML.
papers.abstract: Introduction Concept learning is not an isolated act of cognition; it recruits a host of core mechanisms, including working memory, decision making, and attention. A wide range of brain networks spanning cortical and subcortical areas support these operations, which have been identified via activation patterns related to concept learning. A critical open question, however, is whether the white matter architecture connecting these regions serves as the structural scaffold that makes such flexible learning possible. Methods We employed a rule-plus-exception learning paradigm wherein participants categorized visually complex stimuli. While some items closely followed the rules, exceptions violated them, acting as a behavioural index of flexible learning. We quantified the integrity of white matter tracts across the whole human brain using diffusion-weighted imaging and leveraged correlational tractography to uncover their behavioural relevance. Results Correlational tractography revealed two distinct white matter networks associated with individual variability in either rule or exception learning. The network supporting exception learning was predominantly subcortical-limbic, comprising the fornix, thalamic radiations, and forceps minor alongside the left frontal-parietal cingulum, a pattern consistent with hippocampal-prefrontal communication and cognitive control over atypical exemplars. Conversely, the network for rule-based items was distinguished by long-range cortico-cortical and cortico-cerebellar pathways, including the right frontal-parietal cingulum, the middle longitudinal fasciculus, and the middle cerebellar peduncle, reflecting the integration of visual features with abstract rule representations and their gradual automatization. Discussion These findings provide novel evidence that complementary white matter networks support flexible concept formation and offer a neuroanatomical basis for characterizing individual differences in flexible concept learning.

papers.title: A consistent vigor network in Parkinson's disease: a potential target for brain stimulation effects.
papers.authors: Kavian Z, Hajipour Sardouie S, Arasteh E, Mirian MS, Sreenivasan V, Yazdani M, McKeown MJ.
papers.abstract: Introduction In motor tasks with repetitive trials, motor vigor varies substantially from trial to trial in people with Parkinson's disease (PD). A key question is whether neural variability reflects behavioral variability or whether additional variability emerges as the neural signal is translated into movement. We aimed to identify a vigor-related neural network that could provide a candidate target for brain stimulation. Methods We analyzed individual-trial fMRI data from 18 participants with PD who performed an overlearned ballistic hand-squeeze task in OFF- and ON-medication sessions while receiving subthreshold galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) with different stimulus waveforms. Single-trial fMRI responses were estimated using GLMsingle and entered into a constrained optimisation framework designed to identify a network that was task-active, encoded behavior, showed low trial-to-trial variability, and was spatially coherent. Results The analysis identified a distributed vigor network whose activity remained related to behavioral vigor while showing lower variability than behavior itself. The network included motor, striatal, cerebellar, thalamic, parietal, temporal-limbic, and orbitofrontal regions and showed limited overlap with the standard task-activation map. GVS waveforms associated with faster responses were accompanied by corresponding changes in vigor-network activity, but not in the broader task-activation network. Dopaminergic medication was also associated with stronger local functional connectivity within the vigor network. Discussion These findings suggest that movement variability in PD may arise partly when a relatively stable central vigor-related command is translated downstream into movement. The identified network may therefore provide a potential target for neuromodulation approaches aimed at increasing motor vigor in people with PD. Independent validation and future causal testing are needed.

papers.title: Differential mechanisms of continuous theta burst stimulation and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for chronic tinnitus: preliminary efficacy dissociation by local focalization vs. network dispersion.
papers.authors: Zhang M, Qin L, Jin E, Shi C, Ni J, Wang J, Gao S, Ma Y, Li X, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to preliminarily compare clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting the auditory cortex in chronic subjective tinnitus. Differential effects on tinnitus loudness and distress, as well as the moderating role of disease duration, were explored. Methods Twenty-nine patients were randomly assigned to cTBS (n = 16) or rTMS (n = 13) groups. Neuronavigation-guided stimulation was applied to the individualized auditory cortex peak activation site. Outcome measures included the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at baseline, post-treatment, 1-month, and 3-month follow-ups. Resting-state fMRI was used to analyze amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo). Functional connectivity (FC) analysis was performed to explore the network-level changes. Results Clinically, cTBS was associated with a rapid reduction in VAS-rated tinnitus loudness (p = 0.004), while low-frequency rTMS demonstrated sustained improvements in THI scores up to the 3-month follow-up (p = 0.007). Mixed-model ANCOVA yielded significant time-by-group interactions for THI and VAS, verifying different therapeutic profiles between cTBS and rTMS. Resting-state fMRI uncovered separable brain plasticity: cTBS induced focal changes in left auditory cortex, whereas rTMS remodeled extensive limbic-cognitive networks. Two-way ANCOVA confirmed shared left prefrontal interaction signals, supporting stronger prefrontal suppression by cTBS. Baseline tinnitus duration was negatively correlated with 3-month THI improvement rates. Collectively, clinical and dual resting-state imaging results identified separable therapeutic and neuromodulatory signatures of cTBS and low-frequency rTMS. Conclusion Our exploratory results suggest that cTBS may facilitate a rapid reduction in tinnitus loudness possibly through focal auditory modulation, while low-frequency rTMS eases persistent tinnitus distress through large-scale network remodeling. Our findings provide preliminary evidence for the divergent prefrontal inhibitory profiles of the two inhibitory protocols. Shorter tinnitus duration predicts better therapeutic outcomes, highlighting the value of early intervention. These exploratory results provide evidence for personalized TMS-based neuromodulation in chronic tinnitus.

papers.title: Increased visual reliance for postural control in multiple sclerosis: preliminary evidence from task-related cortical desynchronization.
papers.authors: Braunsmann L, Stolz I, Rosiny F, Pöhlau D, Abeln V, Schneider S, Abel T, Knaepen K.
papers.abstract: Background Balance impairment is one of the most disabling symptoms in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the underlying cortical mechanisms remain poorly understood. This exploratory study investigated how postural demands modulate brain activity in MS. Methods Seven individuals with MS (mean age: 51.1 ± 9.7 years; 5 women; median Expanded Disability Status Scale: 5.5, IQR: 4.5-6.0) and seven age- and sex-matched healthy controls (mean age: 51.0 ± 9.6 years) performed three static balance tasks on a force plate: quiet stance with eyes open, quiet stance with eyes closed, and narrow stance with eyes open. Electroencephalography (EEG) and center of pressure (COP) were simultaneously recorded. Group differences were assessed using Linear Mixed Models. Significant effects are reported with false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected q -values, and otherwise with uncorrected p -values. Results MS patients demonstrated greater postural sway than healthy controls, with FDR-corrected group × condition interactions across COP parameters (semi-partial R 2 = 0.225-0.441; all q < 0.05), most pronounced during eyes closed (semi-partial R 2 = 0.124-0.282; all p < 0.05). Resting-state EEG revealed no consistent group differences except for an uncorrected elevation of occipital theta power in MS patients (p = 0.017; r = -0.76). During stance, uncorrected group × condition interactions indicated that MS patients exhibited a greater task-induced decrease of theta, alpha, and beta power relative to their matched resting baseline compared to healthy controls (semi-partial R 2 = 0.193-0.318; all p < 0.05). These effects were specific to the eyes-closed condition. Conclusion These preliminary findings are consistent with an increased reliance on visual information for postural control in MS, accompanied by a task-related cortical desynchronization specifically upon visual deprivation. The observed effect sizes, while likely subject to inflation given the small sample size, suggest that oscillatory EEG parameters warrant investigation in larger confirmatory studies.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of diffusion models for detecting gray matter microstructural alterations in post-stroke depression patients.
papers.authors: Zhang F, Zhang J, Zhang L, Jin H, Li D, Zhao W.
papers.abstract: Background Post-stroke depression (PSD) is often underdiagnosed because its gray matter microstructural abnormalities can be subtle. This study compared four diffusion models (DTI, DKI, MAP, and NODDI) to identify objective imaging biomarkers for the early detection of PSD. Methods Sixty-four participants were enrolled, including 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), 26 patients with acute cerebral infarction without PSD (non-PSD; HAMD-21 < 7), and 15 patients with PSD (HAMD-21 ≥ 7). Clinical assessments (HAMD-21, ADL, MoCA, and MMSE) and diffusion spectrum imaging were performed. Intergroup differences in gray matter microstructure, diagnostic performance based on the area under the curve (AUC), and partial correlations adjusted for age, sex, and years of education were analyzed. Infarct location was not included as a covariate. Results Significant differences among the three groups were observed in age, years of education, and all clinical scale scores (p < 0.05). Altered gray matter microstructure was primarily identified in the middle frontal gyrus, posterior cingulate gyrus, paracingulate gyrus and amygdala. For group discrimination, the left anterior cingulate DKI MD_p10 demonstrated the best performance for distinguishing HC from non-PSD (AUC = 0.916). The left putamen NODDI ODI_p10 showed the highest AUC (0.916) for distinguishing HC from PSD, whereas the left putamen NODDI ODI_p50 yielded the highest AUC (0.856) for distinguishing non-PSD from PSD. After FDR correction, multiple diffusion metrics were significantly correlated with MMSE and MoCA scores, whereas no imaging parameter showed a significant correlation with HAMD-21. Conclusion Multimodal diffusion MRI detects microstructural abnormalities within emotion- and cognition-related circuits, particularly the amygdala and cingulate cortex, across the three groups. Temporolimbic NODDI parameters showed relatively higher AUC values in distinguishing PSD from HC, whereas anterior cingulate DKI metrics showed relatively higher AUC values in differentiating non-PSD stroke patients from HC. Combining multiple diffusion models may aid in the identification of PSD; however, these findings require further validation because infarct location was not adjusted for in the analyses.

papers.title: An innovative framework based on GMV-ALFF multi-modal MRI and Gaussian data augmentation for psychiatric disorder classification.
papers.authors: Zhu W, Jiang X.
papers.abstract: Objective Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) exhibit significant overlap in clinical symptoms, posing substantial challenges to accurate diagnosis. This study proposes an innovative multi-modal fusion framework based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), integrating structural and functional MRI biomarkers-gray matter volume (GMV) and amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF). Methods Total 31 patients with schizophrenia, 48 patients with bipolar disorder, and 38 healthy controls (HC) were enrolled and underwent resting-state fMRI scans. The framework comprises three core components: Gaussian data augmentation to mitigate the limitation of small sample sizes; a dedicated CNN architecture for processing GMV and ALFF features to generate class probability outputs for SZ, BD, and HC; and DempsterShafer (D-S) evidence theory for robust multi-modal decision fusion. Results Extensive 5-fold cross-validation confirms the framework's efficacy: it achieves superior performance metrics (Accuracy: 0.9656 ± 0.0324, Precision: 0.9698 ± 0.0319, Recall: 0.9656 ± 0.0324, F1-Score: 0.9661 ± 0.0324) and outperforms traditional machine learning methods (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, KNN). Conclusion The findings demonstrate that the proposed multi-modal fusion approach enhances the ability to differentiate among SZ, BD, and HC compared to unimodal classification methods, providing a reliable technical support for the auxiliary diagnosis of psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture inhibits pyroptosis to improve motor function in an MPTP-induced mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Ying YC, Dong YY, Chen GY, Wang X, Fan Q, Wu XC, Chen YL.
papers.abstract: Objectives To investigate whether electroacupuncture (EA) ameliorates motor dysfunction and protects nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD) mice by inhibiting NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis. Methods Male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned before model induction to seven groups: saline-treated control, MPTP model, MPTP plus EA, MPTP plus Nigericin, MPTP plus EA and Nigericin, MPTP plus MCC950, and MPTP plus EA and MCC950 groups. Mice in the control group received equal-volume saline, whereas mice in the other six groups were administered 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP; 30 mg/kg, intraperitoneally) once daily for five consecutive days. Following model induction, EA was applied at Baihui (GV20) and Dazhui (GV14) at 100 Hz for 20 min per session over 14 days. Nigericin and MCC950 were used as an NLRP3 inflammasome activator and inhibitor, respectively. Motor function was assessed using the open-field and pole tests. Dopaminergic neuronal integrity, neuronal injury, microglial activation, and the cellular localization of NLRP3 were evaluated using immunohistochemistry, hematoxylin-eosin staining, and immunofluorescence. The expression levels of tyrosine hydroxylase, NLRP3, ASC, Caspase-1, and the N-terminal fragment of gasdermin D (GSDMD-N) were determined using immunofluorescence and western blotting. Results EA alleviated abnormal open-field hyperlocomotion and prolonged pole-descent latency in MPTP-treated mice, preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, restored striatal tyrosine hydroxylase expression, and reduced neuronal injury and microglial activation. NLRP3 was predominantly colocalized with tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons, whereas limited colocalization was observed with IBA-1-positive microglia. Electroacupuncture significantly suppressed the MPTP-induced upregulation of NLRP3, ASC, Caspase-1, and GSDMD-N. Nigericin exacerbated motor abnormalities, nigrostriatal injury, and pyroptosis-related signaling and largely abolished the protective effects of EA. Conversely, MCC950 produced protective effects comparable to those of EA, whereas their combined administration provided no significant additional benefit. Conclusion EA improves motor dysfunction and protects the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system in MPTP-induced PD mice, at least partly by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in dopaminergic neurons. These findings identify the NLRP3 inflammasome as an important mechanistic target underlying the neuroprotective effects of electroacupuncture in experimental PD.

papers.title: Resting-state cortical alpha frequency in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy: associations with diagnosis, age, and symptom burden.
papers.authors: Chen D, Tang H, Pan Y, Sang H, Gu S, Wang X, Li K, Li F, Sun Y, Chen J, Sun W, Zhang J, Wang Z, Wei L.
papers.abstract: Background Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are clinically overlapping neurodegenerative disorders that present with a complex, heterogeneous burden of motor and non-motor symptoms. Resting-state EEG reveals that cortical alpha slowing is a hallmark of pathological aging, yet its specific presence and clinical significance in these distinct synucleinopathies remain incompletely understood. Therefore, precisely quantifying the individual alpha frequency serves as a critical, non-invasive approach to characterize cortical network dysfunction across synucleinopathies and evaluate how aging moderates its association with clinical symptom burden. Methods We analyzed source-reconstructed resting-state EEG data from 104 participants, comprising patients with PD, patients with the parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar subtypes (MSA-C) of MSA, and healthy controls. To accurately capture oscillatory dynamics, a data-driven masking empirical mode decomposition approach was applied to extract the individual alpha frequency across canonical cortical networks. General linear models tested diagnostic group differences, age-related effects, and age-dependent associations between individual alpha frequency and clinical symptom scores. Results Relative to healthy controls, both PD and MSA-C exhibited significant lower cortical IAF, whereas MSA-P showed no significant global IAF difference. At the network level, significant reduction of IAF was detected in the visual and dorsal attention networks in both PD and MSA-C. Advancing age independently contributed to alpha slowing across all participants without accelerating the disease-related trajectories. Notably, chronological age significantly moderated the relationship between alpha slowing and non-motor symptoms. In older patients, reduced individual alpha frequency was strongly associated with a higher burden of overall non-motor, autonomic, and psychiatric/cognitive symptoms, a relationship not observed in younger patients or with motor symptom severity. Conclusion Cortical alpha slowing was detected in PD and MSA-C, but not in MSA-P. Age independently contributes to alpha slowing and strengthens its association with non-motor symptom burden, supporting age-aware interpretation of resting-state electroencephalography biomarkers in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Selective autophagy inhibition alleviates oxidative stress-associated neurodegeneration in an AD+CCH model.
papers.authors: Huang X, Chen J, Lu Z, Wang J, Luo X, Qin Q, Yang Q, Jian C, Li X, Shang J.
papers.abstract: Dysregulated autophagy is increasingly implicated in the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), particularly when chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (CCH) coexists and exacerbates neurodegeneration. However, the relationship between autophagy dysregulation and oxidative stress responses under combined AD+CCH conditions remains incompletely understood. Here, APP/PS1 transgenic mice subjected to CCH were used to evaluate the effects of autophagy modulation with 3-methyladenine (3MA) and rapamycin (RAPA). CCH worsened cognitive impairment and neuronal injury in APP/PS1 mice and was accompanied by altered LC3-II and p62 expression, consistent with disturbed autophagy-related processing. These changes occurred together with increased expression of proteins associated with oxidative stress responses, including Keap1, Nrf2, HO-1, HIF-1α, and NOX-1. Notably, 3MA improved behavioral performance, reduced Aβ40 burden, and was associated with partial normalization of p62, Keap1, Nrf2, and downstream oxidative stress-related proteins. In contrast, RAPA did not confer detectable protection in this model. Age-stratified analyses further showed that abnormalities in autophagy- and oxidative stress-related markers were more severe at 12 months than at 9 months. Collectively, these findings support an association between altered autophagy-related processing and oxidative stress signaling in AD with chronic hypoperfusion and nominate the p62-Keap1-Nrf2 pathway as a candidate mechanism for further causal investigation.

papers.title: A peri-tumoral TREM2-high myeloid state, myeloid continuum polarization, and white matter disconnection in long-term cognitive survivorship after diffuse glioma: a neuroimmune-connectomic cohort study.
papers.authors: Zhang Z, Qi Y.
papers.abstract: Background Whether a TREM2-high myeloid state and myeloid continuum polarization are associated with long-term cognitive survivorship in diffuse glioma has not been integrated with white matter connectomics and systemic neuroinflammation in a longitudinal framework. Methods In a single-center retrospective cohort of 214 adults with WHO grade 2-4 diffuse glioma (168 IDH-mutant and 46 IDH-wildtype; median follow-up, 5.2 years), a 6-plex tyramide-amplified multiplex immunofluorescence panel was applied to 186 tumors. FlowSOM meta-clustering of 2.41 × 106 myeloid cells across the tumor core, peri-tumoral white matter, and infiltrative margin generated a patient-level Glioma-Associated Myeloid Polarization Continuum Index (GAM-PCI). Connectome-based lesion-symptom mapping, longitudinal serum biomarker profiling, and observational mediation models were integrated. The tissue-connectomic mediation model included 162 complete cases, and the serum-path model included 45 patients with complete paired serum and tissue data. Results FlowSOM resolved six marker-defined meta-clusters (bootstrap Jaccard, 0.78-0.88). C4 was TREM2-high with all other panel markers intermediate (17.1% of myeloid cells), was enriched in peri-tumoral white matter relative to tumor core (21.0% vs. 13.8%, P < 0.001), and remained associated with arcuate fasciculus (AF) disconnection after adjustment for GAM-PCI (β = 0.21 per 10-percentage-point increase, P = 0.002). CD163+CD206+ cells showed greater spatial colocalization with myelin basic protein fragments in peri-tumoral white matter (Morisita-Horn index, 0.71 [0.58-0.82]) than at the infiltrative margin (0.42 [0.31-0.55]; P < 0.001), and their mean distance to the white matter boundary was 38 ± 14 µm versus a null median of 87 µm (P < 0.001). In 45 paired serum-tissue cases, T2 serum sTREM2 was associated with the peri-tumoral C4 proportion (Spearman ρ = 0.42, P = 0.004). Long-term cognitive decline occurred in 88 of 214 patients (41.1%), and AF disconnection independently predicted impairment (adjusted odds ratio, 1.52 per 10% increase; 95% CI, 1.25-1.88). In 162 complete tissue-connectomic cases, the model-based serial indirect association through MBP loss and AF disconnection was β = -0.19 (95% CI, -0.29 to -0.10; P < 0.001). In a separate 45-patient serum-path model, the estimated indirect association through T2 sTREM2/IL-6 was β = -0.06 (95% CI, -0.11 to -0.02; P = 0.004). The AF × IDH interaction was significant (P = 0.032), whereas a difference in C4 proportion by IDH status was not detected and equivalence was not established (TOST P = 0.078). Conclusion In this observational cohort, marker-defined peri-tumoral myeloid states, white matter disconnection, and systemic neuroimmune abnormalities were associated with long-term cognitive outcome. The mediation analysis provide model-dependent structural decompositions under stated assumptions and do not establish causal direction, cellular origin, or treatment effects.

papers.title: Parsing structured semantic knowledge from arbitrary text with GenAI
papers.authors: Lopes Rego A, Snell J, Meeter M.
papers.abstract: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). However, applying Frame Semantics to arbitrary text has historically required either laborious manual annotation or complex, task-specific classification pipelines that presuppose known targets and/or frames. Here we present an open-source method that leverages Generative AI (GenAI) to automatically parse semantic frames and their FEs from any input text, without requiring pre-specification of frames or target spans, or task-specific model training. The tool combines a retrieval step, in which candidate frames are identified via embedding-based semantic similarity, with a selection step, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) is prompted, using zero- or few-shot examples, to determine which frames are evoked, which spans trigger them, and which spans fill their FEs, returning a structured, machine-readable output. We detail installation, execution, and output interpretation, and provide a built-in evaluation module supporting exact, semantic, and graph-based matching against FrameNet's human-annotated data. This freely available tool lowers the barrier to frame-semantic analysis for researchers across linguistics, who wish to explore structured semantic content in naturalistic text, including in relation to behavioral and neural measures of language comprehension.

papers.title: From Exposure to Experience: Measuring Gaze-Based Visual Experience with Faces During Naturalistic Viewing
papers.authors: Guy N, Malka G, Yovel G.
papers.abstract: Research across face recognition, social cognition, and clinical psychology treats visual experience as a primary mechanism for learning and successful categorization. As the field has shifted toward naturalistic, dynamic stimuli, there is a need to dissociate between exposure, which is the amount of time a target is presented, and experience, which is the amount of time an observer is looking at a certain target. Here, we present a pipeline that dissociates exposure from experience with faces during naturalistic viewing of a movie with multiple characters. This is achieved by combining screen-based eye tracking with deep neural network-based face detection and recognition to measure each participant's gaze-based visual experience with faces during naturalistic viewing, on a frame-by-frame basis. With a sample stimulus, we benchmarked our pipeline as an identity exposure extractor and achieved high face detection (~98%) and face recognition (85-88%) accuracies. In a proof-of-concept experiment, participants watched two episodes of a television series while their gaze was recorded. Our pipeline revealed participants looked at individual characters for less than 27% of their appearance time on average indicating that character appearance time overestimated participants' actual visual experience. Moreover, participants showed reliable individual differences in face-directed gaze, both in overall face-viewing tendencies and in character-specific preferences, with stable idiosyncratic preferences emerging when two characters competed for visual attention. Together, these findings demonstrate a meaningful gap between exposure and idiosyncratic gaze-based visual experience, highlighting the importance of dissociating experience from exposure when studying the role of visual experience in naturalistic viewing.

papers.title: PSYCHIATRY The Case for Starting Over
papers.authors: Peled A.
papers.abstract: AbstractPsychiatry is the only branch of medicine that still diagnoses without reference to the organ it treats. Psychiatry: The Case for Starting Over argues that this is a structural failure rather than a temporary gap. The descriptive nosology inherited from Kraepelin and formalized in the DSM achieved diagnostic reliability at the cost of validity. Its categories were assembled by committee consensus rather than grounded in mechanism, and so it cannot guide the circuit-targeted therapies now reshaping the field.The book traces this problem historically and then builds an alternative from three converging lines of work. The first is computational neural-network modeling of psychopathology, from Hopfield and Hinton through Hoffman's simulations of schizophrenia and the author's own work. The second is systems neuroscience, including large-scale networks, global workspace and integrated information theories, attractor dynamics, and small-world connectivity. The third is Friston's Free Energy Principle and predictive processing.From this synthesis the book introduces Neuroanalysis and its clinical instrument, Clinical Brain Profiling (CBP). CBP treats mental disorders as disturbances of dynamic brain-network organization and organizes them across four timescales of plasticity:•Cognizance plasticity (milliseconds) is centered on the central executive network and linked to psychosis and negative signs.•Reactive plasticity (minutes to hours) is centered on the salience network and linked to anxiety.•Adaptive plasticity (days to weeks) sits at the salience–default mode interface and is linked to depression and mania.•Developmental plasticity (lifetime) is centered on the default mode network and linked to personality disorder patterns.The book reviews the neuromodulation toolkit: ECT, DBS, TMS, tDCS/tACS, psychedelic-assisted therapy, and focused ultrasound. It then proposes an entity-matched "grammar of plasticity" for selecting, combining, and sequencing these interventions. Guiding principles include strengthening prefrontal regulation before driving motivation, opening plasticity windows before directing them, and continuous biomarker monitoring.Throughout, the author separates established science from theoretical proposal and untested hypothesis. He outlines what validation would require: prospective outcome trials, clinically feasible network measures, and a cultural shift from single-label diagnosis to multidimensional profiling. The result is a case for rebuilding psychiatry as a measurement-based, mechanism-guided clinical neuroscience.

papers.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of relationships and actions in dynamic social scenes
papers.authors: Garcia K, Isik L.
papers.abstract: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts typically rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations remains largely unknown. We collected 53,223 odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 232 participants on 250 naturalistic dyadic-interaction videos and trained a sparse-positive embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. We show the learned dimensions explain twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, capture interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships with actions), and fractionate broad semantic content (e.g., parent-child interactions separate into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions predict fMRI responses in the visual cortex, including lateral visual pathway and superior temporal sulcus, better than pre-labeled annotations. Together, these results suggest that human representations of social scenes combine social relationships and actions in ways that pre-defined taxonomies miss, offering a behaviorally grounded target for future studies of social vision.

papers.title: Electroencephalography in Subjective Cognitive Decline and Mild Cognitive Impairment: Systematic Review of Biomarkers, Classification, and Prognostic Evidence.
papers.authors: Lu S, Hu S, Huang J, Shi Y, Yu D, Cao W, Yin M, Petersen JD, Huang B.
papers.abstract: Background Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) are heterogeneous clinical states that may represent early or at-risk stages of Alzheimer disease (AD) and other dementias in some individuals. Improved characterization and risk stratification in these populations may facilitate timely evaluation and intervention. Electroencephalography (EEG), a noninvasive, cost-effective neurophysiological technique with high temporal resolution, holds significant potential for elucidating neural mechanisms and providing candidate neurophysiological markers associated with SCD and MCI. Objective The study aims to systematically synthesize evidence on group-level EEG biomarkers, EEG-based classification models, the evaluation of EEG in screening or diagnostic pathways, and EEG-based prediction of progression in SCD and MCI. Methods A search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (via Ovid), Scopus, Wanfang Data, CQVIP, Yiigle, and CNKI databases to include reports published in English or Chinese, which reported group-level EEG differences, EEG-based classification, screening or diagnostic evaluations, or prognostic outcomes in SCD and MCI. A total of 2 independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts. Prediction-model reports were assessed using PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool and Applicability Assessment for AI), prognostic-factor reports using QUIPS (Quality in Prognosis Studies), and other observational reports using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system. Results A total of 20 reports were included, representing a maximum of 3853 confirmed-deduplicated participants after correction of a nested subsample and removal of confirmed duplicate participants across reports, of whom 2927 diagnosed with SCD/MCI/AD or other dementias. Of these, 10 reports were assessed as prediction or AI model reports, 9 as nondiagnostic observational reports, and 1 as a prognostic-factor study. Although potentially informative between-group EEG differences and preliminary model performance were reported, no conventional diagnostic test-accuracy study was identified. The certainty of evidence was very low across all 4 evidence bodies. Conclusions The available evidence suggests that EEG is a promising noninvasive modality for characterizing neurophysiological alterations associated with SCD and MCI. EEG-based classification and prognostic models have also shown encouraging preliminary performance. However, the current evidence is more supportive of biomarker discovery and model development than of established clinical screening or diagnosis. Translation into routine practice will require prospective reports with standardized EEG procedures, representative clinical populations, prespecified thresholds, participant-level data separation, and independent external validation. These findings provide a basis for evaluating EEG as a potential adjunctive or triage tool in future clinical pathways.

papers.title: Beyond Fuel: Metabolic Intermediates as Signaling Molecules in Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Wang S, Wang S, Sun Y, Zhang S, Wu J, Xie D.
papers.abstract: Historically, research has viewed substantial brain metabolic activity through the lens of energy production, primarily treating metabolites as substrates and products in bioenergetic pathways. However, this paradigm is now evolving. Key metabolic intermediates are recognized not only as components of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, but also as potent signaling molecules that establish intricate communication networks. This "metabolic signaling language" profoundly influences inflammation, epigenetics, and cell fate by translating cellular metabolic conditions into certain functional outcomes. In this review, three prototypical metabolites, namely succinate, itaconate, and α-Ketoglutarate (α-KG), were discussed. We investigated succinate accumulation during ischemia and mitochondrial stress, which serves as an early alarm that drives inflammation through both intracellular and extracellular receptor-mediated mechanisms. Conversely, itaconate, an inducible metabolite produced by myeloid cells, exerts inhibitory effects and actively alleviates inflammation by covalently modifying proteins. Finally, we highlighted α-KG, a central metabolic hub that links metabolic status to cellular identity and aging by epigenetically regulating DNA and histone demethylase activity. By summarizing the functions of these metabolites across neurological disorders, including ischemic stroke, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis, we delineate a fundamental layer of biological regulation. Deciphering and therapeutic modulation of this metabolic language represent a frontier in neuroscience, offering novel targets for intractable neurological diseases.

papers.title: N1-methylnicotinamide Mediates Multi-Target Cognitive Deficit Relief via AMPK-Lysosome Axis Regulation.
papers.authors: Qiu X, Zhang Q, Meng Y, He Y, Tang Z, Chu L, Tan Y.
papers.abstract: Introduction/objective Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progresses via interconnected Aβ aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and lysosomal failure, while current single-target drugs only relieve cognitive symptoms without halting pathogenesis. Gut microbiota-derived N1-methylnicotinamide (MNAM) is associated with lower AD risk, yet its comprehensive multilevel regulatory mechanism remains unclear. This study systematically elucidated MNAM's neuroprotective network using in vitro neuronal/microglial injury models and two AD-relevant mouse models. Methods In silico prediction and LC-MS verified MNAM's BBB permeability. TMT proteomics, siRNA knockdown and pharmacological rescue validated the CAB39L-AMPK-lysosomal axis. Immunofluorescence, enzyme assays and molecular docking assessed MNAM's CTSB inhibitory capacity. 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomics characterized gut microbiota and NAD+ metabolic remodeling. Results In vitro, MNAM crossed the blood-brain barrier, improved neuronal viability, reduced ROS and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α). In AD-like mice, it alleviated cognitive deficits, tau hyperphosphorylation, Aβ deposition, microglial activation, and restored SOD activity. MNAM upregulated CAB39L to activate AMPK, stabilized lysosomes, and restrained CTSB leakage. It reshaped protective intestinal flora, suppressed hepatic NNMT, and restored NAD+ balance. In LPS-challenged mice, MNAM selectively alleviated microglial activation and IL-1β accumulation. Discussion MNAM targets multiple AD pathological nodes (Aβ deposition, tau phosphorylation, neuroinflammation, lysosomal dysfunction, gut microbiota-metabolite interactions) via the CAB39L-AMPK-lysosomal axis and gut microbiota/NAD+ metabolism regulation, which is distinct from single-target drugs. Its ability to cross the BBB and regulate host-microbiota metabolic crosstalk provides a novel mechanistic basis for AD therapy, supporting a shift from single-target to multi-target intervention strategies. Conclusion MNAM targets the CAB39L-AMPK-lysosomal axis, inhibits CTSB, and remodels gut microbiota-NAD+ metabolism to concurrently suppress core AD pathologies. This metabolite serves as a promising multi-target disease-modifying candidate for AD, warranting further validation in transgenic AD models and human neurons.

papers.title: Simulating the Effects of Gamma Oscillation Treatment on Selective Neurotransmitters Using The Virtual Brain and Complex Pathway Simulator
papers.authors: Nago B, Qu C.
papers.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer's Disease (AD), the most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, is caused by a variety of factors that lead to neuronal injury and an alteration in neurotransmitter production and release. This study aimed to identify changes in acetylcholine and glutamate following gamma oscillation treatment in the context of AD. Current AD treatments are limited, often relying on infusions of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies or the ingestion of less accessible chemical compounds like glutamate and cholinesterase inhibitors. Gamma oscillations represent a relatively new experimental treatment showing positive benefits in early studies. Using The Virtual Brain (TVB) and data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), a brain model with Late Mild Cognitive Impairment (LMCI) was simulated under gamma oscillation therapy. Utilizing COPASI and associated analysis, changes in neurotransmitter proxies were quantified. Results indicate an increase in both acetylcholine and glutamate. This finding is significant because acetylcholine levels are typically decreased, and glutamate is elevated in patients with AD, creating a unique biochemical scenario within this experimental context. These observations further support the potential of gamma oscillation modulation as a promising therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: The ballon model revisited
papers.authors: Gore J, Lee T, Jiaao Y, Knutsson AL, boschen w, Li M, Schilling KG, Anderson AW, Ding Z, Gao Y.
papers.abstract: Abstract Functional MRI based on the blood oxygenation level–dependent (BOLD) effect infers neural activity from hemodynamic changes through a hemodynamic response function (HRF). We revisit the balloon model of the BOLD effect and show that Grubb’s empirical flow–volume power law can be used to determine how vascular transit time varies with flow and is governed by a single index of venous distensibility. Linearizing the resulting equations yields an explicit closed-form HRF, expressed in physiologically recognizable parameters, that reproduces the canonical response. The initial dip, time to peak and poststimulus undershoot are each traced to identifiable terms, and the relations assumed in calibrated BOLD signals emerge as outputs. When oxygen consumption is specified independently of flow, as in earlier generalizations, the analytic solution quantifies the specific relationships between the latency and depth of an initial dip and a neurovascular delay. The new model will prove useful for explaining variations in HRF in white matter, across the brain, and between different populations.

papers.title: How Robust Are Machine-Learning Biomarkers of Depression? A Leakage-Controlled Benchmark
papers.authors: Faridi A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Machine-learning models are increasingly used to identify predictive markers of depression, yet reported performance may be sensitive to data leakage, non-independent observations, site effects, and validation procedures that do not adequately approximate deployment in independent clinical populations. Moreover, increasingly complex algorithms may provide limited incremental value over simpler statistical models once leakage is controlled. This study examined how validation design and leakage-prone predictors influence estimates of depression-classification performance and whether complex machine-learning models outperform logistic regression under more rigorous evaluation conditions. Methods A controlled synthetic multisite psychiatric dataset comprising 13,159 observations from 8,000 unique synthetic participants across 10 simulated sites was used to benchmark five classification approaches: logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), support vector machine, and a neural network. The dataset incorporated repeated observations, demographic characteristics, depression- and anxiety-related symptom measures, sleep and activity indicators, physiological measures, cognitive performance, treatment variables, site and device effects, and realistic missingness. Depression case status was defined using a synthetic PHQ-9-like total score threshold of ≥ 10, yielding a prevalence of 35.4%. To prevent direct target leakage, the PHQ-9-like total score was excluded from predictive models. Two deliberately post-outcome, leakage-prone variables were additionally manipulated to quantify performance inflation. Leakage-controlled models were evaluated using conventional random row splitting, participant-independent splitting, and site-independent validation. Discrimination and probabilistic performance were assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and Brier score. Results Allowing leakage-prone post-outcome predictors produced markedly optimistic performance, with random-split AUROCs of approximately 0.988–0.989 and AUPRCs of 0.981–0.983. For logistic regression, removal of leakage-prone predictors reduced AUROC from 0.9891 to 0.9548 and AUPRC from 0.9827 to 0.9253, while the Brier score increased from 0.0367 to 0.0788. In leakage-controlled analyses, discrimination nevertheless remained high across validation strategies. AUROCs ranged from 0.9488 to 0.9548 under random row splitting, 0.9516 to 0.9585 under participant-independent validation, and 0.9502 to 0.9555 under site-independent validation. Corresponding AUPRCs ranged from 0.9116 to 0.9254, 0.9246 to 0.9383, and 0.9183 to 0.9356, respectively. Logistic regression achieved an AUROC of 0.9585 and AUPRC of 0.9383 under participant-independent validation and performed comparably to random forest, XGBoost, support vector machine, and neural-network classifiers. Increasing algorithmic complexity therefore yielded little improvement in discrimination after leakage control. Conclusions Apparent performance in psychiatric machine-learning benchmarks can be substantially influenced by leakage-prone predictors, even when underlying predictors contain strong signal. In this controlled synthetic benchmark, removing post-outcome information materially reduced apparent discrimination, whereas participant- and site-independent validation did not produce a further collapse in performance. Complex machine-learning algorithms provided little predictive advantage over logistic regression. These findings illustrate why leakage auditing, explicit separation of outcome-derived variables, clinically realistic validation, calibration assessment, and comparison against simple baselines should be routine components of psychiatric machine-learning research. Because the present findings derive from synthetic data, they demonstrate methodological mechanisms rather than establishing the magnitude of performance inflation in real clinical populations; replication using independent empirical psychiatric datasets is required.

papers.title: Thalamic volume links milder symptoms but faster dopaminergic decline in prodromal Parkinson disease
papers.authors: Wang Z, Xie L, Wu J, Wang C, Ni R, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Biological changes such as α-synuclein deposits and brain structural changes related to Parkinson’s disease (PD) may precede both clinical diagnosis and dopaminergic dysfunction. However,whether magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived structural features are associated with clinical burden and can predict subsequent dopaminergic changes remains unclear. Purpose: To determine whether multilevel baseline MRI phenotypes are associated with concurrent clinical status (including motor severity, overall disease stage, and global cognitive performance) and longitudinal changes in the dopamine transporter (DAT) ratio, to localize the anatomical regions involved. Materials and Methods: In this longitudinal cohort study, we analysed T1-weighted MRI from 340 participants from the PPMI who were cerebrospinal fluid α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA)-positive, DAT-negative and without a clinical diagnosis of PD at baseline. Longitudinal mixed-effects models sequentially evaluated four broad MRI summary measures, seven prespecified regional measures and 25 thalamic nuclei. We assessed the link between MRI measures with motor severity, disease stage and cognition in the PPMI chohrt, and independently assessed in the Quebec Parkinson Network Neuroimaging Cohort. Results: None of the four broad MRI summary measures were associated with longitudinal changes in the DAT. Baseline thalamic volume was associated with an additional decrease in the annual DAT ratio of 0.018 (β = -0.018, 95% CI, [-0.031, -0.005]; F DR = 0.046). Nucleus-level analysis revealed five FDR-significant nuclei in the basal ganglia–thalamocortical loops. In the primary cohort, the five-nucleus composite was associated with lower Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale Part III (UPDRS-III) scores (β = -0.790, F DR = 0.022). In the independent Quebec PD cohort, greater thalamic volume was associated with lower UPDRS-III scores (β = -4.382, F DR = 0.040), lower Hoehn–Yahr stages (OR = 0.320, F DR < 0.001) and higher Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores (β = 1.709, F DR = 0.002). Conclusion: Thalamic structure was selectively associated with subsequent decreases in the DAT among patients with broad baseline MRI phenotypes. Despite its association with faster subsequent DAT decline, the concurrent association of greater thalamic structure with milder clinical involvement indicates that the brain structure, current clinical state and subsequent dopaminergic dysfunction may not evolve synchronously during early PD.

papers.title: Neuronal ABHD6 Exacerbates Ischemic Brain Injury Through 2-AG Depletion and DDIT3/BNIP3-Dependent Autophagy Dysregulation
papers.authors: Liu D, Cao Z, Zhao L, Yue K, Tian Z, Qi K, Zhang Z, Wang Y, Xue H, Luo P, Gao X, Li X.
papers.abstract: Abstract The endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) confers critical neuroprotection against ischemic stroke (IS) by restricting neuronal apoptosis. While monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) mediates 85% of central nervous system 2-AG hydrolysis, its chronic inhibition induces severe cannabinoid receptor desensitization. In contrast, postsynaptic alpha/beta hydrolase domain 6 (ABHD6) governs a highly localized 4% pool of 2-AG degradation, uniquely positioning it as a precise, on-demand therapeutic target devoid of off-target effects. However, its exact pathological contribution to ischemic neuronal death remains elusive. This study investigates the molecular mechanisms by which ABHD6 regulates apoptosis and autophagic crosstalk following IS. Utilizing a middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion mouse model and an in vitro oxygen-glucose deprivation followed by 24-hour reoxygenation (OGD/R) model in primary neurons, assays demonstrated that ABHD6 expression and enzymatic activity were significantly upregulated post-ischemia. This elevation accelerated postsynaptic 2-AG hydrolysis, restricted neuroprotective endocannabinoid activation, and aggravated apoptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of ABHD6 with WWL70 and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genetic ablation effectively suppressed enzymatic activity, preserved endogenous 2-AG levels, and attenuated OGD/R-induced programmed cell death. Mechanistically, ABHD6 impaired neuroprotective autophagy by modulating the DDIT3/BNIP3 pathway; the consequent suppression of autophagic flux directly exacerbated neuronal apoptosis and subcellular structural disintegration. In conclusion, ABHD6 exerts a dual detrimental role in IS by depleting neuroprotective 2-AG and suppressing DDIT3/BNIP3-dependent autophagy. Targeting postsynaptic ABHD6 to restore endocannabinoid homeostasis and autophagic flux represents a highly specific molecular strategy for attenuating ischemia-induced neuronal apoptosis.

papers.title: Diagnosing Susac Syndrome Despite Incomplete Clinical Triad: A Case Report of Convergent Atypical Neuroimaging and Inflammatory Cerebrospinal Fluid Findings: Case Report
papers.authors: Lei J, Salim M, Garcia E, Feigin S, Montgomery C, Landman A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Susac syndrome (SuS) is a rare autoimmune endotheliopathy involving the brain, retina, and inner ear. Because patients frequently present without the complete clinical triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions (BRAO), and sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), diagnosis can be challenging. The European Susac Consortium (EuSaC) criteria classify SuS according to objective involvement of the brain, retinal, and vestibulocochlear domains; however, many patients do not fulfill criteria for probable or definite disease at initial presentation. Furthermore, neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings may overlap with inflammatory demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS). We report a case where EuSaC criteria was not met, however there was strong clinical and radiographic evidence to support the diagnosis of SuS. This case brings to question whether strict fulfillment of EuSaC criteria is needed to initiate early inpatient treatment to prevent irreversible neurological deficits. Case presentation We report the case of a woman in her early forties with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, recurrent ischemic strokes, and an unspecified hypercoagulable disorder who presented with progressive gait instability, dizziness, and bilateral lower extremity weakness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated characteristic central corpus callosum “snowball” lesions and cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement. CSF analysis revealed elevated immunoglobulin G (IgG) index, elevated IgG synthesis rate, and markedly elevated myelin basic protein (MBP) in the absence of oligoclonal bands (OCB). At the time of presentation, only the brain domain of the EuSaC criteria was objectively fulfilled, and the patient therefore did not meet criteria for probable or definite SuS. Nevertheless, the characteristic neuroimaging phenotype, inflammatory CSF profile without oligoclonal bands, and absence of typical MS features strongly favored SuS and prompted treatment with high dose steroids and further diagnostic evaluation. Conclusions This case demonstrates that strict fulfillment of EuSaC criteria may not be required to recognize SuS when characteristic neuroradiographic findings and supportive clinical features are present. Recognition of central corpus callosum “snowball” lesions and cerebellar leptomeningeal enhancement may facilitate earlier diagnosis and treatment, potentially reducing irreversible neurologic, retinal, and auditory morbidity.

papers.title: The Half of Everything: Glucose Imbalance Hazards and Brain Vulnerability at the Extremes of Life
papers.authors: Canepa M, Panfoli I, Mangini S, Calandrino A, Vinci F, Malova M, Striano P, Gagliardi L, Ramenghi L.
papers.abstract: Glucose is more than an energetic substrate: its homeostasis emerges from continuous interactions between peripheral glucose-regulatory organs and the brain, where glucose availability, sensing, and utilization must be dynamically matched to metabolic demands. This narrative review examines how disruption of this balance may intersect with oxidative stress, inflammation, and brain vulnerability at the extremes of life. In preterm neonates, the definition of pathological glycaemic states remains heterogeneous, while hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, and particularly glycaemic variability may represent different manifestations of dysglycaemia within an immature homeostatic system. Experimental and clinical evidence links these disturbances, with different degrees of certainty, to oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, adverse neurological outcomes, and white matter vulnerability. The developing brain is particularly susceptible to redox imbalance because of maturation-dependent antioxidant defenses and the vulnerability of developing white matter. At the opposite extreme of life, aging is accompanied by alterations in cerebral glucose and energy metabolism, while neurodegenerative disorders show disturbances in glucose transport and utilization together with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and neuronal and white matter abnormalities. We propose the Biochemical and Physiological Mirror as a conceptual interpretation of these apparently distant conditions: developmental immaturity and age-related decline represent distinct biological trajectories that may converge on partially shared glucose–redox–inflammatory intersections. Within the Crossword Effect, glucose therefore acquires biological meaning not as an isolated concentration but through its context-dependent relationships with metabolic, redox, inflammatory, cellular, and developmental information. Viewing dysglycaemia as a systems-level disturbance rather than solely as deviation from a numerical threshold may provide a more integrated framework for understanding brain vulnerability across the lifespan.

papers.title: Glial Transcriptomic Convergence in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Disease with Independent Retinal and Aqueous-Humor Evidence
papers.authors: Tawfik M.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are usually studied as distinct neurodegenerative disorders, yet both involve molecular changes that extend beyond vulnerable neuronal populations. We asked whether the two diseases share reproducible transcriptional organization across homologous human glial cell classes and whether components of that shared signal are independently represented in retinal and ocular proteomic datasets. We reanalyzed five human single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets using donor-level pseudobulk models for astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), and oligodendrocytes. Disease effects were estimated and replicated within AD and PD before cross-disease comparison. Across matched genes, AD and PD showed modest but permutation-supported positive effect-vector concordance in all four cell classes. Concordance was strongest in oligodendrocytes (Spearman ρ = 0.253; 60.7% directional agreement), whereas no individual gene survived a conservative AD–PD conjunction FDR criterion. Reactome analysis identified 29 pathways with formal same-direction AD–PD FDR convergence in one glial class and a broader set of 665 pathways with recurrent same-direction enrichment across at least three classes. The recurrent pathway structure exceeded a profile-preserving permutation null (95% interval, 411–476; empirical P = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴), supporting a global excess of recurrent pathway organization without implying significance for every individual recurrent pathway. We then integrated healthy retinal expression, AD retinal proteomics, and PD aqueous-humor proteomics with the brain-concordance results. Of 17,745 genes in the integrated candidate universe, 14,469 were detected in at least two healthy retinal donors. The AD retinal reanalysis tested 4,995 genes and identified 227 nominal and two FDR-significant effects; the PD aqueous-humor reanalysis tested 5,691 proteins and identified 2,713 nominal and 1,803 FDR-significant differences. No candidate reached Class A, which required AD–PD brain concordance, healthy-retinal expression, and FDR-level support in both ocular disease datasets. The highest-ranked multimodal candidates included SCAMP5, XYLB, RABEPK, ITGAM, CD38, CTCF, UBTD2, and NAPEPLD. Together, these results support a distributed, cell-class-dependent molecular architecture shared between AD and PD. Independent retinal and ocular measurements provide an additional layer for prioritizing components of this shared biology, but they do not establish clinically validated retinal or ocular biomarkers.

papers.title: LRRK2 G2019S Parkinson’s Disease Mutation and Astrocyte-Neuron Crosstalk: How Diseased Astrocytes Program the Susceptibility to Inflammation and Oxidative Stress Predisposing to Nigrostriatal Degeneration
papers.authors: Marchetti B, Serapide MF.
papers.abstract: A complex interplay between genes and environmental factors is recognized to contribute to the death of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain (mDAn) in Parkinson’s disease (PD). Within the known genes associated with PD, there is Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase (LRRK2), recognized as one most frequent causes of PD, of either familial or sporadic nature. On the other hand, the mechanisms involved in LRRK2 dysfunction that contribute to PD pathogenesis are not defined. Within the environmental factors that are involved in PD pathogenesis, there is the ageing process and inflammatory reactions, as crucial actors participating to the vulnerability to both PD and also LRRK2-PD. Both processes, i.e., ageing and inflammation, can result in increased activation of glial cells, i.e. astrocytes and microglia. Remarkably, earlier and more recent evidence corroborate “a developmental hypothesis” for PD pathogenesis, whereby genes, crucial transcription factors and developmental pathways linked to mDAn vulnerability, interacting with early life events and key hormonal and inflammatory/anti-inflammatory signalling systems, are suspected to play important roles via their expression and/or intimate dialogue with astrocytes, as developed in this work, putting forward the hypothesis that early developmental astrocyte-neuron crosstalk dysregulation may predispose individuals to increased neuronal vulnerability later in life. Of importance, as herein reviewed, the interactions between astrocytes and neurons play a vital role during development as well as in the adult brain. In our laboratory we have been studying for at least thirty years the role, mechanisms and consequences of a physiological or pathological dialogue between mDAns and astrocytes during the development of mDAns, as well as during an inflammatory/oxidative stress response and brain ageing. Here, we aimed at reviewing the evidence in support of a decisive role of LRRK2-diseased astrocytes as predisposing elements for PD susceptibility, asking a. whether and how a malfunction of astrocyte-neuron crosstalk during development might in turn affect dopaminergic neuron vulnerability in adult life; b. what underlying mechanisms of LRRK2-astrocytes are involved ; c. the extent to which astrocyte-microglia maladaptive interactions form part of such dysfunctional interplay; d. what are the consequences for programming the susceptibility of mDAns in adult life and ageing, with their implications for the ongoing understanding of PD pathology and therapeutic developments targeting the dynamics of astrocyte-neuron dialogue.

papers.title: Association between craniofacial trauma and traumatic brain injury in patients admitted to a tertiary care hospital: a prospective cross-sectional study.
papers.authors: Aziz PA, Wajid A, Ahmed E, Mehmood A, Qureshi BA, Khan H, Bhatti ZN.
papers.abstract: Purpose Craniofacial trauma and traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) frequently coexist due to their close anatomical proximity, making it essential to understand their correlation for optimal patient management. This study examines the association between specific types of craniofacial fractures and corresponding brain injuries in patients admitted to a tertiary care hospital. Methods A prospective cross-sectional study was carried out in the Department of Neurosurgery, Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences, from October 2024 to February 2025. Fifty-six patients with both craniofacial and brain injuries were included. Data collection involved systematic clinical evaluation, imaging studies, and statistical analyses using Pearson correlation coefficients, Spearman correlation coefficients, and ordinal logistic regression. Results The most common mechanism of injury was road traffic accidents (87.5%), and the most frequent craniofacial injuries were midface fractures (82.1%), with zygomaticomaxillary complex and naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures showing a significant association with pneumocephalus (P<0.05). Le Fort type I fractures were associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Patients with more than two midface fractures were 4.16 times more likely to sustain brain injuries (B=1.069; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.301-1.837; P=0.006). Frontal air sinus fractures, especially with bilateral and both-table involvement, were strongly correlated with contusions and pneumocephalus (B=1.627; 95% CI, 0.569-2.684; P=0.003). Palatal fractures demonstrated a significant association with diffuse axonal injury (P=0.032). Conclusions The study highlights a significant correlation between craniofacial fractures and TBI severity, highlighting the importance of early detection and multidisciplinary management. Further large-scale studies are warranted to refine predictive models and improve clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Differential Cortical and Thalamic Engagement of Cholinergic Interneurons in the Nucleus Accumbens Core.
papers.authors: Jang EV, Dao N, Cole L, Carter AG.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) play a key role in regulating motivated behaviors. Here we examine the connectivity and functional impact of cortical and thalamic inputs onto CINs in the NAc core of mice of either sex. We first use cell type-specific retrograde anatomy to identify the prefrontal cortex and thalamus as putative afferents. We then combine ex vivo slice physiology and optogenetics to characterize the properties of synapses onto CINs. We demonstrate that thalamic inputs strongly facilitate, whereas cortical inputs exhibit marked depression. We also show that a combination of AMPA and NMDA receptors contribute to both cortical and thalamic responses. Lastly, we establish how these inputs and receptors evoke action potentials and influence spontaneous firing. Our findings show how CINs in the NAc core process long-range inputs, highlighting differences from equivalent circuits in other parts of striatum.

papers.title: Temporal Progression of Auditory Brainstem Dysfunction and Behavioral Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Tauopathy.
papers.authors: Nguyen AM, Lo H, Fields J, Cramer KS, Zeng FG, Dong W, Xu X.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) frequently cooccurs with motor and sensory processing impairments. While auditory abnormalities were reported in beta-amyloid-based models before cognitive decline, the effects of tau pathology on auditory circuit function remain poorly understood. The PS19 mouse model expressing the P301S tau mutation exhibits tau pathology associated with frontotemporal dementia. When combined with the humanized ApoE ɛ4 allele, these mice show accelerated tau accumulation and neurodegeneration. We investigated the temporal progression of auditory and behavioral deficits in PS19 and ApoE4/PS19 mice of either sex at 3 and 7 months. Auditory processing was assessed using auditory brainstem response (ABR) recordings, while anxiety-like and motor behaviors were evaluated using the elevated plus maze and rotarod assays. PS19 mice exhibited auditory pathway dysfunction at 3 months, characterized by reduced and delayed neural responses to acoustic stimuli. These auditory deficits occurred without detectable behavioral changes in anxiety- or motor-related measures. By 7 months, cochlear nucleus-derived ABR activity shifted from an initial reduction to elevation relative to controls, suggesting compensatory hyperexcitability. In contrast, ApoE4/PS19 mice showed reduced ABR amplitudes and shortened response latencies that persisted with age, accompanied by altered anxiety-like behavior and motor performance. Together, these results demonstrate that auditory pathway dysfunction may represent an early marker of tau pathology preceding behavioral impairment. The divergent temporal patterns of ABR alterations across genotypes suggest that genetic context, particularly ApoE4, modulates the progression of tau-driven circuit dysfunction, highlighting ABR as a potential noninvasive biomarker for early tau-related neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Microglia-derived extracellular vesicle content as a biomarker for early detection of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Woudstra AL, Holtman L, van Vliet EA.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid-beta aggregation, tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal loss. While current biomarker frameworks such as the A/T/N classification have advanced diagnosis, they predominantly reflect relatively late stages of disease, limiting opportunities for early intervention. This underscores the urgent need for biomarkers that are not only accessible and sensitive but also specific to the earliest pathogenic mechanisms of AD. Recent work has underscored the pivotal role of disease-associated microglia (DAM) in the onset and progression of AD. DAM exhibit dual roles: they promote protection by phagocytosing amyloid and debris, metabolizing lipids, and remodelling synapses, yet can also drive pathology through excessive cytokine release, chronic inflammatory signalling, and impaired aggregate clearance.
